case_title: ICICI Bank Limited vs Palogix Infrastructure Private Limited
bench: Principal Bench, New Delhi (arising from NCLT Kolkata Bench, C.P. No. 37 of 2017)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: ICICI Bank Limited is the Financial Creditor; Palogix Infrastructure Private Limited is the Corporate Debtor. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: ICICI Bank filed a Section 7 application alleging default by Palogix under credit facilities extended to it (specific facility terms not detailed in the judgment, which focused on a procedural maintainability issue). 3. DEFAULT METRICS: exact default amount and date are not specified in this judgment; the dispute centered on procedural maintainability rather than quantum of default. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: original Section 7 application filed before NCLT Kolkata Bench (C.P. No. 37 of 2017); Division Bench passed split verdict on maintainability via Power of Attorney holder; matter referred to NCLT President under Section 419(5) Companies Act 2013 for a larger bench; by majority, order dated 12 April 2017 directed rectification of defects (specific authorization) within 7 days; subsequent order dated 16 May 2017 admitted the application after removal of defects, declared moratorium and appointed an Interim Resolution Professional. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: ICICI Bank relied on Board Resolutions dated 3 May 2002 and 30 October 2009 authorising bank officers to execute Power of Attorney and handle legal proceedings; Corporate Debtor argued that a general, pre-Code Power of Attorney without specific IBC authorization was insufficient. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: three connected appeals were filed and heard together - Corporate Debtor's appeal against the 12 April 2017 order (CA 30/2017), Financial Creditor's cross-appeal against the same order (CA 37/2017), and Corporate Debtor's appeal against the 16 May 2017 admission order (CA 54/2017); all were decided together by NCLAT on 20 September 2017.
legal_issues: Whether a Power of Attorney Holder, without specific authorization referencing the IBC, is competent to file and maintain an application under Section 7 of the IBC on behalf of a Financial Creditor.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A general Power of Attorney Holder is not competent to file an application under Section 7, 9 or 10 of the IBC on behalf of a Financial Creditor, Operational Creditor or Corporate Applicant; only a duly 'Authorised Representative' can do so. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Form-1 under the Adjudicating Authority Rules requires disclosure of the authorised person's name, address, enclosed authorisation, and position in relation to the Financial Creditor; general authorisation by Board Resolution empowering officers to act in legal proceedings satisfies this requirement even if loosely termed a 'Power of Attorney', since substance prevails over label. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Where a defect in authorization exists, the applicant must be granted seven days (excluding holidays) to rectify by producing the underlying Board Resolution, rather than having the application rejected outright. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Since ICICI Bank held valid subsisting Board Resolutions authorising its officers and had rectified the defect within the permitted time, the admission of the Section 7 application was valid and the appeals challenging it failed.
operative_order: All three connected appeals dismissed; the order of admission of the application under Section 7 is affirmed; no order as to costs.
summary: ICICI Bank filed a Section 7 IBC application against Palogix Infrastructure through a Power of Attorney holder. NCLT Kolkata initially split on whether specific IBC authorization was needed, then directed rectification of defects, and later admitted the application after compliance. Both parties appealed to NCLAT on the authorization issue. NCLAT held that a general Power of Attorney Holder cannot file IBC applications, but a person authorised via Board Resolution (even loosely called 'Power of Attorney') qualifies as an Authorised Representative if disclosed properly. Finding ICICI Bank's authorization valid and timely rectified, NCLAT dismissed all appeals and affirmed admission of the insolvency application.

case_title: M/s. Unigreen Global Private Limited vs Punjab National Bank & Ors.
bench: Principal Bench, New Delhi (arising from NCLT Principal Bench, New Delhi, C.P. No. (IB)-39(PB)/2017)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: M/s. Unigreen Global Private Limited is the Corporate Debtor/Corporate Applicant (Appellant); Punjab National Bank (lead consortium banker), Corporation Bank, Vijaya Bank and Oriental Bank of Commerce are the consortium Financial Creditors (Respondents). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: consortium credit facilities extended by the PNB-led bank consortium to Unigreen Global, secured by mortgages over properties at Khari Baoli, Defence Enclave and Dayanand Block, Delhi, with personal guarantees from Directors Anurag Garg and Ritu Garg; the account was restructured via a Joint Lender Forum letter dated 31 March 2015 before turning NPA. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: precise default amount and date are not specified in the judgment, which centered on procedural rejection of the Section 10 application rather than quantum of default. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: SARFAESI Section 13(2) demand notice issued by the bank on/around 10 May 2016, followed by allegedly collusive civil suits; NCLT Principal Bench rejected the Corporate Debtor's Section 10 application and imposed a Rs. 10 lakh penalty under Section 65 by order dated 8 May 2017. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Corporate Debtor filed its Section 10 application (Form 6) with list of creditors, security details, company master data and balance sheets; the Bank alleged suppression of pending civil suits (Mayank Maheshwari v. Anurag Garg; Jagat Nath Mehto v. Vedika Overseas Tradex Ltd.; Anurag Garg v. Punjab National Bank SARFAESI proceedings) concerning the mortgaged properties, alleging these were collusively engineered to shield assets from the banks. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Principal Bench, New Delhi rejected the Section 10 application on 8 May 2017 for alleged suppression of facts/non-disclosure of pending litigation and imposed a Rs. 10 lakh penalty under Section 65 without prior notice to the applicant; the Corporate Debtor appealed to NCLAT.
legal_issues: (i) Whether non-disclosure of facts beyond the statutory requirements of Section 10 and Form 6 can be a ground to dismiss a Section 10 application; (ii) whether the Section 65 penalty imposed by the Adjudicating Authority was legally valid.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Once debt and default are established and the Corporate Applicant is not ineligible under Section 11 of the IBC, the Adjudicating Authority has no discretion but to admit a Section 10 application; it cannot reject the application on grounds extraneous to Section 10 and Form 6. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: 'Suppression of facts' sufficient to deny admission is confined to matters Form 6 and Section 11 actually require disclosure of (e.g., disqualifications under Section 11); pendency of unrelated third-party civil suits concerning mortgaged properties, to which the Corporate Debtor is not a party, is not a mandated disclosure. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: A penalty under Section 65 requires the Adjudicating Authority to record a prima facie finding that the application was filed 'fraudulently' or with 'malicious intent', after giving the party a reasonable opportunity of hearing; an unreasoned penalty imposed without notice violates natural justice and cannot stand. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLT erred both in rejecting the Section 10 application for suppression of unrelated litigation facts and in imposing an unreasoned, unnoticed penalty; both parts of the order were set aside and the matter remitted for admission.
operative_order: Impugned order dated 8 May 2017 set aside; the case is remitted to the Adjudicating Authority for admission of the Section 10 application if otherwise complete, or to grant time to cure defects if incomplete; no order as to costs.
summary: Unigreen Global, a Corporate Debtor, filed a Section 10 application for its own insolvency resolution. Punjab National Bank-led consortium opposed it, alleging suppression of pending civil suits linked to mortgaged properties and colluded litigation to shield assets, leading NCLT to reject the application and impose a Rs. 10 lakh penalty under Section 65. NCLAT held that undisclosed third-party litigation unrelated to Form 6's requirements cannot justify rejection, and that penalties under Section 65 require a reasoned prima facie finding of fraud plus a hearing. Finding neither satisfied, NCLAT set aside the rejection and penalty and remitted the matter for admission.

case_title: M/s. Innoventive Industries Ltd vs ICICI Bank & Anr.
bench: New Delhi (arising from NCLT Mumbai Bench, C.P. No. 1/I&BP/NCLT/MB/MAH/2016)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: ICICI Bank Ltd. (Respondent No. 1) is the Financial Creditor and lead consortium banker; M/s. Innoventive Industries Ltd. is the Corporate Debtor/Appellant; Respondent No. 2 is another consortium lender. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: consortium credit facilities were extended to Innoventive Industries under a Joint Lender Forum (JLF) arrangement, restructured via a Master Restructuring Agreement (MRA) dated 8 September 2014 between the lenders and the Corporate Debtor. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: exact default amount and date are not specified in the judgment; default was ascertained by NCLT Mumbai from records of a credit information company (CIBIL) rather than a formal Information Utility record. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: NCLT Mumbai passed an admission order on 17 January 2017 (declaring moratorium, appointing Interim Resolution Professional) without prior notice to the Corporate Debtor, followed by a clarificatory order on 23 January 2017 addressing a pending interim application (IA No. 6/2017). 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Corporate Debtor contended the MRA discharged prior debts and produced an auditor's certificate alleging that ICICI Bank itself had failed to perform its MRA obligations; Corporate Debtor also argued the Financial Creditor lacked Joint Lender Forum consent to independently initiate insolvency proceedings, and invoked the Maharashtra Relief Undertaking (Special Provisions) Act, 1958 for protection. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: ICICI Bank filed a Section 7 application before NCLT Mumbai Bench; NCLT admitted the application on 17 January 2017 without prior notice, followed by a clarificatory order on 23 January 2017; the Corporate Debtor filed two connected appeals before NCLAT challenging lack of notice/natural justice, applicability of the state Relief Undertaking Act, and adequacy of default ascertainment.
legal_issues: (i) Whether notice to the Corporate Debtor is required before admission of a Section 7 application; (ii) whether the Maharashtra Relief Undertaking (Special Provisions) Act, 1958 prevails over the IBC, 2016; (iii) whether prior Joint Lender Forum consent is required before a consortium member files a Section 7 application.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Under Section 424 of the Companies Act, 2013 (applicable to IBC proceedings via Section 60), the Adjudicating Authority is generally bound to issue a limited notice to the Corporate Debtor before admitting a Section 7/9 application, to allow it to contest the existence of default, though this does not create an absolute right to a full hearing in every case. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The IBC's non-obstante clause (Section 238) overrides inconsistent state legislation such as the Maharashtra Relief Undertaking Act, since the two statutes operate in different legislative fields and the IBC, being a later and more specific Parliamentary enactment, prevails; the Relief Undertaking Act's protection is confined strictly to enactments listed in its own Schedule. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The 'useless formality' doctrine applies - where the Corporate Debtor's objections were in substance heard and considered by the Adjudicating Authority (even absent a formal prior notice) and the outcome on remand would be no different, the absence of notice does not vitiate the order; no requirement of Joint Lender Forum consent is read into Section 7. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Since the Appellant had already intervened and its objections were considered before admission, the lack of formal prior notice was not fatal; the Relief Undertaking Act does not shield the Corporate Debtor from IBC proceedings; no JLF consent was legally required; the admission order was upheld.
operative_order: Both connected appeals dismissed; NCLT Mumbai's admission orders dated 17 and 23 January 2017 upheld; no order as to costs.
summary: ICICI Bank sought initiation of insolvency proceedings against Innoventive Industries under Section 7 for default on consortium credit facilities. NCLT Mumbai admitted the application without prior notice to the debtor, prompting an appeal on natural-justice grounds, reliance on the Maharashtra Relief Undertaking Act, and lack of Joint Lender Forum consent. NCLAT held that while limited notice is generally required, its absence was not fatal here since the debtor's objections were already considered; the state Relief Act cannot override the IBC's non-obstante clause; and no JLF consent was needed. The appeals were dismissed and admission upheld.

case_title: Parag Gupta & Associates vs B.K. Educational Services Pvt. Ltd. (with M/s. Speculum Plast Pvt. Ltd. vs PTC Techno Pvt. Ltd. and Ashlay Infrastructure Pvt. Ltd. vs LDS Engineers Pvt. Ltd.)
bench: New Delhi (arising from NCLT New Delhi Bench, C.P. Nos. (IB)-41(ND)/2017, (IB)-27(PB)/2017 and (IB)-77(ND)/2017)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: three connected appeals were heard together - (i) M/s. Speculum Plast Pvt. Ltd. (Operational Creditor/Appellant) vs PTC Techno Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor); (ii) Parag Gupta & Associates (Financial Creditor/Appellant) vs B.K. Educational Services Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor); (iii) Ashlay Infrastructure Pvt. Ltd. (Operational Creditor/Appellant) vs LDS Engineers Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: in Speculum Plast's case, invoices were raised against PTC Techno for the period 1 April 2013 to 19 September 2013 for goods/services supplied; in Parag Gupta's case, amounts were paid/loaned to B.K. Educational Services between 1 October 2012 and 5 February 2013, reflected as short-term borrowings exceeding Rs. 8 crores in the Corporate Debtor's Income Tax Returns for AY 2014-15 and 2015-16; details of the LDS Engineers transaction are not separately elaborated beyond the dispute being time-barred. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: exact claimed default amounts are not separately quantified in the judgment (focus is on the limitation question); default in Speculum Plast's case is stated to have occurred after September 2013; in Parag Gupta's case, dues arose from payments made between October 2012 and February 2013. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: NCLT New Delhi passed impugned orders dismissing all three applications as time-barred - dated 11 April 2017 (Speculum Plast, CP No. (IB)-41(ND)/2017), 25 April 2017 (Parag Gupta, CP No. (IB)-27(PB)/2017), and 4 May 2017 (Ashlay Infrastructure, CP No. (IB)-77(ND)/2017) - each holding that claims filed beyond three years from accrual were barred by the Limitation Act, 1963. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: in Parag Gupta's case, Income Tax Returns of the Corporate Debtor for AY 2014-15 and 2015-16 reflecting short-term borrowings of over Rs. 8 crores (including the disputed loans) were placed on record but were held by NCLT not to extend limitation; in Speculum Plast's case, invoices dated between April and September 2013 were on record. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: each Corporate Applicant/Creditor filed applications under Sections 7, 9 or 10 before NCLT New Delhi, which rejected all three on the ground that the underlying debts were time-barred under the Limitation Act, 1963 (applied via Section 433 of the Companies Act, 2013); the Appellants preferred these three connected appeals, all raising the common question of whether the Limitation Act applies to trigger CIRP under the IBC, and were heard together with Sr. Advocate A.S. Chandhiok assisting as Amicus Curiae.
legal_issues: Whether the Limitation Act, 1963 is applicable for triggering 'Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process' under the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The Limitation Act, 1963 (including Section 433 of the Companies Act, 2013 which imports it) does not apply to applications filed under Sections 7, 9 or 10 of the IBC for initiating Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process, since the IBC is a self-contained code with its own distinct scheme of time periods, and Section 433 of the Companies Act was not amended or incorporated into the IBC's Eleventh Schedule (unlike Section 424). 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The retention of a specific, narrower limitation-exclusion provision (Section 60(6), excluding moratorium periods from limitation computation) without a general applicability clause (unlike the repealed Presidency-Towns Insolvency Act, 1909 and Provincial Insolvency Act, 1920, which expressly imported limitation provisions) signals a deliberate legislative intent to exclude the general operation of the Limitation Act from CIRP initiation; separately, Sections 24 (DRT Act) and 36 (SARFAESI Act), which import limitation into other recovery regimes, were also not carried over into the IBC framework despite amendments to those Acts. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Even if the Limitation Act were held applicable, the right to apply under Sections 7, 9 or 10 accrues only from 1 December 2016 (the date the IBC came into force), under residuary Article 137 (three years from accrual of the right to apply) of the Limitation Act - so no application filed after that date could yet be time-barred on this basis; separately, though the general 'law of limitation' as codified does not apply, the equitable Doctrine of Limitation and Prescription (guarding against stale claims and laches) remains relevant, and the Adjudicating Authority may call on an Applicant to explain long delay in Section 7/9 filings (though this laches-based scrutiny does not apply to Section 10 applications by a Corporate Applicant against itself). 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Limitation Act, 1963 does not bar initiation of CIRP under the IBC; all three NCLT orders rejecting the applications as time-barred were therefore erroneous and were set aside, with the matters remitted for fresh consideration on completeness and admission without regard to limitation.
operative_order: All three impugned orders (dated 11 April 2017, 25 April 2017, and 4 May 2017) are set aside; all three matters are remitted to the Adjudicating Authority, New Delhi, to determine after notice and hearing whether each application is complete, and to admit the applications without going into the question of limitation; if any application is incomplete, the Appellant concerned is to be granted seven days to remove defects under the proviso to Section 9(5); if any application is not maintainable on other grounds, the Adjudicating Authority is to record such reasons; all appeals allowed with no order as to costs.
summary: Three connected NCLAT appeals raised a common question: does the Limitation Act, 1963 apply to bar initiation of Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process under the IBC when the underlying debt is more than three years old? NCLT New Delhi had rejected all three applications (under Sections 7, 9 and 10) as time-barred. NCLAT, assisted by an Amicus Curiae, held that the IBC is a self-contained code that impliedly excludes the general Limitation Act, since only a narrow limitation-exclusion provision (Section 60(6)) was retained and Section 433 of the Companies Act, 2013 was not incorporated into the Code. All three impugned orders were set aside and the matters remitted for admission without regard to limitation, though the Tribunal noted an equitable laches-based scrutiny may still apply to stale Section 7/9 claims.

case_title: Indian Overseas Bank vs Mr. Dinkar T. Venkatsubramaniam (Resolution Professional for Amtek Auto Ltd.)
bench: New Delhi (arising from NCLT Chandigarh Bench, CA No. 142/2017 in CP (IB) No. 42/Chd/Hry/2017)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Indian Overseas Bank (Hosur Branch), a minority Financial Creditor holding 4.08% of total financial debt, is the Appellant; Mr. Dinkar T. Venkatsubramaniam, the Interim Resolution Professional for Corporate Debtor M/s. Amtek Auto Ltd., is the Respondent; Corporation Bank was the original Financial Creditor whose Section 7 application triggered the CIRP. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Amtek Auto Ltd. maintained a current account with Indian Overseas Bank's Hosur Branch holding Rs. 6,65,13,958/-; separately, the Corporate Debtor had borrowed funds from Indian Overseas Bank, which sought to appropriate the current account balance towards those borrowings rather than release it to the IRP. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: this appeal did not concern default/quantum of debt, but rather the IRP's demand for release of Rs. 6,65,13,958/- lying in the Corporate Debtor's current account post-admission of CIRP. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Corporation Bank's Section 7 application was admitted on 24th July 2017; moratorium declared and Interim Resolution Professional appointed on 27th July 2017; IRP issued a letter dated 1st September 2017 (enclosing cheque No. 870093 dated 1st September 2017) directing Indian Overseas Bank to transfer the account balance via RTGS to Amtek Auto's account with Corporation Bank; despite reminders, the Bank did not comply, leading to an application before the Adjudicating Authority; NCLT Chandigarh's order directing transfer was passed on 13th October 2017; NCLAT's order was passed on 15th November 2017, directing transfer by 30th November 2017. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: the Bank's written correspondence and refusal to transfer funds despite the IRP's letter and reminder; the Bank argued the account balance was neither a 'security interest' nor an 'asset' available for transfer but rather appropriable against the Corporate Debtor's borrowings from it. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: the IRP applied before NCLT Chandigarh Bench (CA No. 142/2017 in CP (IB) No. 42/Chd/Hry/2017) seeking a direction to Indian Overseas Bank to transfer the account funds; NCLT rejected the Bank's objection and directed transfer by order dated 13th October 2017; Indian Overseas Bank appealed this order to NCLAT.
legal_issues: Whether, after admission of a Section 7 application and declaration of moratorium under Section 14 of the IBC, a bank holding the Corporate Debtor's current account funds can refuse to transfer those funds to the Corporate Debtor's account (as directed by the Interim Resolution Professional) on the ground that it wishes to appropriate the funds towards the Corporate Debtor's outstanding borrowings from that bank.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Once moratorium is declared under Section 14 of the IBC following admission of a Section 7 application, no person - including a Financial Creditor holding the Corporate Debtor's deposit account - may recover any amount from or appropriate any amount lying in the Corporate Debtor's account towards its own dues. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Under Section 17(1)(d) of the IBC, financial institutions maintaining accounts of the Corporate Debtor must act on the instructions of the Interim Resolution Professional and furnish all relevant account information and funds as directed; funds in a Corporate Debtor's current account, once CIRP is admitted, are treated as assets of the Corporate Debtor subject to the IRP's control, not as sums a creditor bank may unilaterally set off. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The characterisation of the account balance as 'not a security interest or asset' was rejected as a basis for refusal to transfer; instead, if the bank has a bona fide claim as a Financial Creditor for amounts borrowed by the Corporate Debtor, its remedy lies in filing a claim before the IRP under the IBC's claims process, not unilateral appropriation. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The bank's refusal to transfer funds and attempted appropriation during moratorium was impermissible; the bank was directed to comply with the transfer direction while being given liberty to pursue its claim as a Financial Creditor (including potential membership of the Committee of Creditors) through the proper IBC claims mechanism before the IRP.
operative_order: Appeal dismissed with the observation that Indian Overseas Bank is at liberty to raise its claim as a Financial Creditor before the Interim Resolution Professional and seek inclusion in the Committee of Creditors, to be considered in accordance with law; the Bank is directed to comply with the Adjudicating Authority's order and transfer the amount of Rs. 6,65,13,958/- to the Corporate Debtor's account with Corporation Bank not later than 30th November 2017; no order as to costs.
summary: After Corporation Bank's Section 7 application against Amtek Auto Ltd. was admitted and moratorium declared, the Interim Resolution Professional directed Indian Overseas Bank to transfer over Rs. 6.65 crore lying in the Corporate Debtor's current account. The Bank refused, claiming a right to appropriate the funds against the Corporate Debtor's separate borrowings from it. NCLT Chandigarh rejected this and ordered transfer; the Bank appealed. NCLAT held that moratorium under Section 14 bars any creditor from recovering or appropriating funds from the Corporate Debtor's accounts, and that the Bank's remedy was to file its claim as a Financial Creditor before the IRP. The appeal was dismissed, with the Bank directed to transfer the funds by 30th November 2017 and given liberty to pursue its creditor claim through proper channels.

case_title: Uttam Galva Steels Limited vs DF Deutsche Forfait AG & Anr.
bench: New Delhi (arising from NCLT Mumbai Bench, C.P. No. 5/Mah/2017)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Uttam Galva Steels Limited is the Corporate Debtor/Appellant; DF Deutsche Forfait AG and a second entity (Respondent No. 2) are joint Operational Creditors/Respondents claiming rights under assigned Bills of Exchange. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: AIC Handles GmbH (supplier) entered into a sales contract with Uttam Galva Steels for supply of steel billets valued at US$ 10,787,040, secured by collateral Bills of Exchange of US$ 5,387,040 and US$ 5,400,000; the debt/receivables under these Bills of Exchange were subsequently assigned by the supplier to the two Respondents via a forfeiting agreement; Appellant contended the actual end-user/consignee, 'Aartee Commodities (UK) Limited', was liable to pay and had not done so. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: exact default amount is tied to the Bills of Exchange values (US$ 5,387,040 and US$ 5,400,000) but was itself disputed as to quantum and as to who (Appellant or the UK end-user) was liable; no undisputed default date is recorded. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Respondents issued a winding-up notice to the Appellant on 8 December 2016 (prior to any Section 8 notice); Appellant replied disputing the claim in detail on 3 January 2017; a purported Section 8 demand notice dated 28 February 2017 was issued jointly by the two Respondents through their advocate (not by the Operational Creditors themselves or an authorised officer); the Section 9 joint application was filed thereafter; NCLT Mumbai admitted the application by order dated 10 April 2017. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: a disputed document dated 27 December 2013 (unsigned by Appellant) was relied upon by Respondents to fix liability; an email dated 10 April 2014 was cited by Appellant as evidence of a pre-existing bona fide dispute; a bank certificate dated 6 March 2017 was furnished by Respondents from 'Misr Bank' (a foreign bank not notified as a 'financial institution' under Section 3(14) IBC) rather than a recognised financial institution; the Form-5 affidavit accompanying the Section 9 application was incomplete; a suit filed by the Appellant was pending before the Bombay High Court, where Appellant did not dispute the underlying sale transaction but contested liability on the ground that the end-user had not paid. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: the two Respondents filed a joint Section 9 application before NCLT Mumbai Bench (C.P. No. 5/Mah/2017); NCLT admitted the application by order dated 10 April 2017, rejecting the Appellant's objections and referring the matter to IBBI for appointment of an Interim Resolution Professional; the Appellant appealed the admission order to NCLAT.
legal_issues: (i) Whether a joint application by two or more Operational Creditors under Section 9 of the IBC is maintainable; (ii) whether filing a certificate from a recognised financial institution is mandatory under Section 9(3)(c); (iii) whether a Section 8 demand notice can be validly issued by a lawyer on behalf of an Operational Creditor; (iv) whether a pre-existing dispute existed between the parties barring admission of the Section 9 application.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Unlike Section 7 (which expressly permits joint applications by Financial Creditors), Section 8 requires an Operational Creditor to individually deliver a demand notice and Section 9 requires an individual Operational Creditor to file the application; a joint Section 9 application by multiple Operational Creditors is not maintainable, and Rule 23A of the NCLT Rules (permitting joint petitions) has not been adopted for Section 9 proceedings. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The requirement under Section 9(3)(c) to furnish a certificate from a 'financial institution' (as defined in Section 3(14)) confirming non-payment is mandatory, not directory, following the earlier ruling in Smart Timing Steel Ltd. vs. National Steel and Agro Industries Ltd.; a certificate from a foreign bank not notified as a financial institution in India does not satisfy this requirement. Similarly, Forms 3/4 under Rule 5 require the demand notice to be signed by the Operational Creditor personally or by a person holding an authorised 'position with or in relation to' the Operational Creditor - an advocate/lawyer's notice issued without such demonstrated authority or stated position is not a valid Section 8 notice, being merely a 'lawyer's notice' distinct from what the Code requires. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Following Kirusa Software Pvt. Ltd. vs. Mobilox Innovations Pvt. Ltd., 'existence of a dispute' under Section 8(2) is to be given a wide, non-exhaustive meaning covering any genuine pre-existing dispute relatable to the existence/amount of debt, quality of goods/services, or breach of warranty - not confined only to a pending suit or arbitration - and a spurious or illusory dispute raised only in reply to the demand notice does not qualify, but a dispute raised and evidenced well before the demand notice (such as via a prior winding-up notice reply) does. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Section 9 application was invalid on three independent grounds - impermissible joinder of Operational Creditors, absence of a valid financial institution certificate, and an invalid Section 8 notice issued by an unauthorised lawyer - and separately, a genuine pre-existing dispute (evidenced by the Appellant's detailed reply dated 3 January 2017 to the December 2016 winding-up notice, predating the purported Section 8 notice) rendered the application not maintainable; the admission order was accordingly illegal and set aside.
operative_order: Impugned order dated 10th April 2017 admitting the Section 9 application set aside; all consequential orders and actions of the Adjudicating Authority and the Interim Resolution Professional (including moratorium, account freezing, and public advertisement calling for claims) declared illegal and set aside; the joint Section 9 application is dismissed; the Adjudicating Authority is directed to close the proceeding; the Appellant company is released from all consequences and permitted to function independently through its Board of Directors with immediate effect; the Adjudicating Authority will fix the Interim Resolution Professional's fee, to be paid by the Respondents for the period he functioned; appeal allowed; no order as to costs.
summary: DF Deutsche Forfait AG and a second entity, both claiming to be Operational Creditors under assigned Bills of Exchange from a steel supply contract, jointly filed a Section 9 application against Uttam Galva Steels, which NCLT Mumbai admitted. On appeal, NCLAT held the joint application impermissible since Section 9 (unlike Section 7) contemplates only individual Operational Creditor applications; found the accompanying financial institution certificate invalid as it was issued by an unrecognised foreign bank; held the Section 8 demand notice invalid as it was issued by a lawyer without demonstrated authority or stated position; and found a genuine pre-existing dispute existed, evidenced by the Appellant's detailed reply to an earlier winding-up notice predating the Section 8 notice. NCLAT set aside the admission order and all consequential actions, dismissed the Section 9 application, and released the company back to its Board of Directors.

case_title: Nikhil Mehta and Sons vs AMR Infrastructure Ltd.
bench: New Delhi (arising from NCLT Principal Bench, New Delhi, C.P. No. (ISB)-03(PB)/2017)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Nikhil Mehta and Sons (along with other joint appellants) are investors/purchasers claiming to be Financial Creditors; AMR Infrastructure Ltd. is the Corporate Debtor, a real estate developer. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Appellants entered into Memoranda of Understanding with the Corporate Debtor to purchase three units (a residential flat, a shop, and office space) in projects named Kessel-I Valley, One Mall and One Home under a 'Committed Return Plan', whereby appellants paid a substantial portion of the sale consideration upfront and the Corporate Debtor undertook to pay a fixed monthly 'Committed Return/Assured Return' until physical possession was handed over; a specific MOU dated 12 April 2008 involved Shop No. E-47 (1453.432 sq. ft.) for total consideration of Rs. 46,67,402, with payment of Rs. 27,00,000 and Rs. 9,00,000 via cheques dated 19 March 2008, leaving Rs. 10,17,402 payable at possession, and a monthly committed return of Rs. 99,600 (less TDS) from January 2009 until possession. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: the Respondent stopped paying committed returns unilaterally and without reason from January 2014 for most appellants and from April 2014 for Appellants No. 3 and 4; exact aggregate default amount is not separately quantified in the judgment beyond individual MOU terms. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Appellants jointly filed a Section 7 application before the Adjudicating Authority on 16 January 2017; the application was dismissed by NCLT Principal Bench, New Delhi by order dated 23 January 2017; a 7-day delay in filing the appeal under Section 61(2) was condoned by NCLAT on the ground that the number of petitions was wrongly mentioned in the original impugned judgment. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Appellants relied on the Respondent's audited annual return dated 31 March 2014 showing the amount owed to investors listed as 'Commitment Charges' of Rs. 15,30,91,296 (and Rs. 32,32,97,199 in the comparative year) under the head 'Financial Costs' alongside 'Interest on Loans'; Form 16A and Form 26AS showing TDS deducted under Section 194A of the Income Tax Act (applicable to 'Interest other than Interest on Securities') on payments made to appellant Nikhil Mehta; a SEBI order dated 19 December 2014 in the matter of M/s MVL Limited holding that similar assured-return real estate schemes constitute a Collective Investment Scheme under Section 11AA of the SEBI Act rather than pure real estate transactions; the Respondent did not file any reply or affidavit denying the appellants' averments despite being given the opportunity. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Principal Bench, New Delhi, by order dated 23 January 2017, held the appellants were not 'Financial Creditors' under Section 5(7) and that the Section 7 application was not maintainable in light of pending winding-up petitions against the Corporate Debtor before the Delhi High Court (where a Financial Liquidator had been appointed); the appellants appealed to NCLAT.
legal_issues: (i) Whether purchasers/investors under a 'Committed Return Plan' real estate agreement qualify as 'Financial Creditors' under Section 5(7) read with Section 5(8) of the IBC; (ii) whether a Section 7 application is maintainable where winding-up petitions are already pending against the Corporate Debtor before the High Court.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A 'financial debt' under Section 5(8) requires two essential elements - (i) a debt owed to the claimant (including by assignment/transfer), and (ii) that the debt, along with interest, is disbursed against the consideration for the time value of money, falling within one or more of the modes enumerated in clauses (a) to (i); a real estate purchase agreement structured as a 'Committed Return/Assured Return' plan, where the developer commits to periodic payments in exchange for upfront receipt of substantially the entire sale consideration, satisfies this test and constitutes a financial debt under Section 5(8)(f) (amount raised under a transaction having the commercial effect of a borrowing), making the investor a Financial Creditor. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The presence of an 'assured return' clause tied merely to delivery of possession does not, by itself, disqualify a transaction from being a financial debt; what matters is whether the disbursement was made against consideration for the time value of money and whether the developer treated the funds as borrowed capital rather than as an ordinary sale advance. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Corroborating documentary evidence - crediting the amounts as 'Commitment Charges' under 'Financial Costs' alongside 'Interest on Loans' in the Corporate Debtor's own audited annual returns, and deduction of TDS under Section 194A (applicable to interest payments) - is determinative evidence that the Corporate Debtor itself treated the transaction as a borrowing bearing interest, thereby satisfying the 'time value of money' requirement, irrespective of the Adjudicating Authority's characterisation of the transaction as a 'pure and simple agreement of sale/purchase of property'. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Adjudicating Authority correctly stated the legal test for 'Financial Creditor' but erred in applying it to the facts by treating the transaction as ordinary real estate sale rather than examining the Corporate Debtor's own accounting and TDS treatment of the payments; on correct application, the appellants qualified as Financial Creditors and their Section 7 application ought to have been admitted, subject to completeness.
operative_order: Impugned judgment dated 23rd January 2017 passed in C.P. No. (ISB)-03(PB)/2017 set aside; matter remitted to the Adjudicating Authority to admit the Section 7 application if otherwise complete, and to pass appropriate orders; if incomplete, appellants to be given seven days to complete the application per the proviso to Section 7; appeal allowed; no order as to costs.
summary: Investors under a real estate 'Committed Return Plan' with AMR Infrastructure filed a joint Section 7 application after the developer stopped paying assured monthly returns. NCLT rejected the application, holding the investors were not Financial Creditors since the transaction was a simple sale-purchase agreement lacking the 'time value of money' element, and also cited pending High Court winding-up petitions against the developer. NCLAT held that the developer's own annual returns (listing the payments as 'Commitment Charges' under 'Financial Costs' alongside interest on loans) and TDS deductions under Section 194A of the Income Tax Act (applicable to interest payments) proved the transaction was in substance a borrowing with a commercial effect, satisfying Section 5(8)(f)'s definition of financial debt. NCLAT set aside the rejection and remitted the matter for admission of the Section 7 application, subject to completeness.

case_title: Macquarie Bank Limited vs Uttam Galva Metallics Limited
bench: New Delhi (arising from NCLT Chandigarh Bench, Chandigarh)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Macquarie Bank Limited, a company incorporated under the laws of Singapore with its office at Marina Bay Financial Centre, Singapore, claiming to be an Operational Creditor, is the Appellant; Uttam Galva Metallics Limited, alleged to be the Corporate Debtor, is the Respondent. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: the nature of the underlying commercial debt/transaction giving rise to the claimed operational debt is not detailed in the judgment, which focuses entirely on procedural maintainability issues; the appellant maintained its banking relationship with 'Macquarie Bank', Australia, not any India-recognised financial institution. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: exact default amount and date are not specified in this judgment, as the appeal turned entirely on procedural defects in the Section 9 application rather than the merits of default. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: a purported Section 8 demand notice was issued to the Corporate Debtor by an Advocate based in Singapore (date not specified); NCLT Chandigarh Bench passed the impugned order dated 1st June 2017 rejecting the Section 9 application as not maintainable. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: the appellant did not enclose any certificate from a 'Financial Institution' (as defined under Section 3(14) of the IBC) maintaining its accounts confirming non-payment of the unpaid operational debt, relying instead on its banking relationship with Macquarie Bank, Australia (not a scheduled bank, RBI-recognised financial institution, or Companies Act 'public financial institution' in India, and not centrally notified); the appellant also failed to enclose any 'record of default with the information utility' as an alternative; the Form-5 application was otherwise found deficient. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Macquarie Bank filed a Section 9 application before NCLT Chandigarh Bench seeking to trigger CIRP against Uttam Galva Metallics Limited; NCLT rejected the application by order dated 1st June 2017 on the grounds that the Section 8 demand notice was issued through a Singapore-based advocate and no valid financial institution certificate was furnished; the appellant appealed to NCLAT.
legal_issues: (i) Whether a foreign entity whose bank is not a 'financial institution' as defined under Section 3(14) of the IBC can satisfy the mandatory certificate requirement under Section 9(3)(c) using a certificate from that foreign bank; (ii) whether a Section 8 demand notice issued by a foreign advocate/lawyer without demonstrated authority or stated position in relation to the Operational Creditor is a valid notice under the IBC.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The requirement under Section 9(3)(c) of the IBC to furnish a certificate from a 'Financial Institution' (as defined in Section 3(14) - a scheduled bank, an RBI Section 45-I financial institution, a Companies Act Section 2(72) public financial institution, or a centrally notified institution) confirming non-payment of the unpaid operational debt is mandatory, not directory, and cannot be satisfied by a certificate from a foreign bank that does not meet this definition, nor can the requirement be circumvented by relying on Form-5's mention of an 'information utility' record instead. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Form-5 (the prescribed application form) cannot override the substantive statutory mandate of Section 9(3)(c); its listing of alternative evidentiary categories (such as information utility records) does not substitute for the specific financial institution certificate requirement, especially where the applicant furnished neither. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Per Forms 3 and 4 read with Rule 5 of the Adjudicating Authority Rules, a Section 8 demand notice must be signed either by the Operational Creditor itself or by a person holding a stated 'position with or in relation to' the Operational Creditor and demonstrably authorised to act on its behalf; a notice issued by an advocate/lawyer without such demonstrated authority or stated position is merely a 'lawyer's notice', distinct from and insufficient to satisfy Section 8, regardless of the seriousness of its content. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Since Macquarie Bank's certifying bank (Macquarie Bank, Australia) did not qualify as a 'financial institution' under Section 3(14), and since the Section 8 notice was issued by an unauthorised Singapore-based advocate without demonstrated authority or stated position, the Section 9 application was invalid on both independent grounds and correctly rejected as not maintainable.
operative_order: Appeal dismissed; no order as to costs.
summary: Macquarie Bank Limited, a Singapore-incorporated entity claiming to be an Operational Creditor, filed a Section 9 application against Uttam Galva Metallics Limited, which NCLT Chandigarh rejected as not maintainable because the Section 8 demand notice was issued by a Singapore-based advocate and no certificate from a recognised 'financial institution' was furnished. On appeal, NCLAT held that Macquarie Bank's certifying bank (Macquarie Bank, Australia) did not meet the IBC's definition of 'financial institution' under Section 3(14), so its certificate could not satisfy the mandatory requirement under Section 9(3)(c). NCLAT also held that the Section 8 notice, issued by an advocate without demonstrated authority or stated position in relation to the Operational Creditor, was merely a lawyer's notice and not a valid statutory notice. On both grounds, the Section 9 application was not maintainable, and the appeal was dismissed.

case_title: Smart Timing Steel Ltd. vs National Steel and Agro Industries Ltd.
bench: New Delhi (arising from NCLT Mumbai Bench, C.P. No. 06/I&BP/NCLT/MAH/2017)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Smart Timing Steel Ltd., a foreign company incorporated in Hong Kong with no office or bank account in India, claiming to be an Operational Creditor, is the Appellant; National Steel and Agro Industries Ltd. is the Corporate Debtor/Respondent. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: the underlying commercial transaction giving rise to the operational debt is not detailed beyond the fact that a Final Arbitral Award was rendered in the appellant's favour by a Sole Arbitrator in the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region, People's Republic of China, dated 18th August 2014, purportedly finding the Corporate Debtor liable to pay a determined sum. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: exact default amount is not specified in this judgment; the appellant relied on the arbitral award as evidence of an unpaid amount, but no independent proof of non-payment (via a financial institution certificate) was furnished. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: NCLT Mumbai Bench had granted the appellant additional time to furnish the mandatory financial institution certificate under Section 9(3)(c), which the appellant failed to do, leading to rejection of the application by order dated 31st January 2017; the appellant likewise failed to cure the defect within the seven-day period before NCLAT despite the opportunity being available. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: the appellant enclosed a copy of the Hong Kong arbitral award dated 18th August 2014 as evidence of the Corporate Debtor's liability, but did not enclose any certificate from a 'Financial Institution' (as defined under Section 3(14) of the IBC) maintaining its accounts confirming non-payment, since its bank was situated outside India and did not qualify as a scheduled bank, RBI Section 45-I financial institution, Companies Act 'public financial institution', or centrally notified institution. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: the appellant filed a Section 9 application before NCLT Mumbai Bench without enclosing the mandatory financial institution certificate; despite being granted time to furnish it, the appellant's counsel argued compliance should be exempted since its bank was located outside India; NCLT rejected the application by order dated 31st January 2017 for non-compliance with Section 9(3)(c); the appellant appealed to NCLAT.
legal_issues: Whether filing a copy of the certificate from a 'Financial Institution' (as defined under Section 3(14) of the IBC) maintaining accounts of the Operational Creditor, confirming non-payment of the unpaid operational debt, as prescribed under Section 9(3)(c), is a mandatory or merely directory requirement for a Section 9 application.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The requirement under Section 9(3)(c) of the IBC to furnish a certificate from a 'Financial Institution' (as defined in Section 3(14)) confirming non-payment of the unpaid operational debt is mandatory, not directory or an empty statutory formality; the word 'shall' in Section 9(3) is to be given its plain, mandatory meaning. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Unlike procedural timelines (such as the 90-day period considered directory in Kailash vs. Nanhku), Section 9(3)(c) is a substantive evidentiary requirement whose absence prevents the Adjudicating Authority from independently verifying non-payment; reliance on an arbitral award alone (even a foreign award establishing liability) does not substitute for this requirement, since the Authority cannot assume non-payment of the awarded sum absent the prescribed certificate. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Applying the mandatory/directory test from State of Mysore vs. V.K. Kangan (considering the provision's subject matter, its relation to the statute's general object, and legislative intent), and following the Tribunal's own earlier ruling in J.K. Jute Mills Company Ltd. vs. Surendra Trading Company (holding the proviso allowing seven days to cure defects is itself mandatory), an Operational Creditor who fails to furnish the required certificate even after being given the opportunity to cure the defect within seven days cannot have its application admitted. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Since the appellant's bank was located outside India and did not meet the statutory definition of 'financial institution', and since the appellant failed to cure this defect despite being granted time to do so, the application was rightly rejected; the argument that foreign creditors without Indian bank accounts would be prejudiced was rejected, as such creditors retain alternative remedies (e.g., a civil suit) outside the IBC framework.
operative_order: Appeal dismissed; no order as to costs.
summary: A Hong Kong-based company, Smart Timing Steel Ltd., filed a Section 9 application against National Steel and Agro Industries Ltd. relying on a Hong Kong arbitral award as proof of debt, but did not furnish the mandatory certificate from a 'Financial Institution' confirming non-payment, since its bank was located outside India and did not meet the IBC's definition of 'financial institution'. NCLT Mumbai rejected the application after the appellant failed to cure this defect despite being given time to do so. NCLAT held that Section 9(3)(c)'s certificate requirement is mandatory, not directory, and cannot be dispensed with merely because the creditor's bank is foreign and ineligible; since the appellant failed to cure the defect within the permitted time, the rejection was upheld and the appeal was dismissed, with NCLAT noting that foreign creditors retain other legal remedies such as a civil suit.

case_title: Kirusa Software Private Ltd. vs Mobilox Innovations Private Ltd.
bench: New Delhi (arising from NCLT Mumbai Bench, C.P. No. 02/I&BP/NCLT/MAH/2017)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Kirusa Software Private Ltd. is the Operational Creditor/Appellant, which had provided services (a campaign under purchase orders) to Mobilox Innovations Private Ltd., the Corporate Debtor/Respondent. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Kirusa provided certain services to Mobilox pursuant to purchase orders (POs) and corresponding invoices for a campaign, claiming an aggregate unpaid debt of Rs. 20,08,202.55; the parties had also entered into a Non-Disclosure Agreement (NDA), which Mobilox alleged Kirusa had breached by disclosing confidential client information. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: the claimed default amount was Rs. 20,08,202.55, arising from invoices raised on the Corporate Debtor for services rendered under the POs. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Kirusa issued a Form-3 demand notice under Section 8 of the IBC (Adjudicating Authority Rules, 2016) on 23rd December 2016; Mobilox, through its advocates M/s Desai & Diwanji, replied on 27th December 2016 disputing the claim, alleging it was not contractually due, calling the notices misconceived, mala fide, and a pressure tactic, and separately alleging Kirusa's breach of the NDA by disclosing confidential information; NCLT Mumbai rejected the Section 9 application by impugned order dated 27th January 2017. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Kirusa's Section 9 application included invoices aggregating Rs. 20,08,202.55, transaction details, and the demand notice; upon NCLT's direction, Kirusa additionally filed the notice of dispute dated 27th December 2016 issued by Mobilox's advocates, which NCLT treated as conclusive proof of a 'dispute' under Section 8(2), leading to rejection of the application under Section 9(5)(ii)(d). 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Kirusa filed a Section 9 application before NCLT Mumbai Bench; NCLT initially directed Kirusa to furnish the notice of dispute it had received, and upon filing, treated the mere existence of a reply disputing the claim as sufficient to reject the petition under Section 9(5)(ii)(d) without independently examining whether the dispute met the statutory threshold; Kirusa appealed to NCLAT.
legal_issues: What constitutes a 'dispute' and 'existence of a dispute' for the purposes of Section 8(2) read with Section 5(6) of the IBC, and whether an Adjudicating Authority may reject a Section 9 application merely because the Corporate Debtor sent a reply disputing the claim, without assessing whether that reply raises a dispute falling within the statutory definition.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The definition of 'dispute' in Section 5(6) of the IBC is inclusive, not exhaustive, and is not confined to disputes pending in a suit or arbitration proceeding; 'existence of a dispute, if any' under Section 8(2)(a) is disjunctive from 'record of the pendency of the suit or arbitration proceedings', so a dispute can be shown either by demonstrating a pending suit/arbitration relatable to clauses (a)-(c) of Section 5(6), or by otherwise establishing the existence of a genuine dispute as to the debt, quality of goods/services, or breach of warranty/representation, even absent a pending proceeding, provided it was raised before any competent court, tribunal, or authority (or is proposed to be raised) and is not a mala fide or got-up defense to stall insolvency proceedings. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: 'Dispute' for Section 8/9 purposes must be read together with 'operational debt' under Section 5(21), and the reference to a dispute 'pending' in a suit or arbitration proceeding is illustrative rather than an exhaustive limitation; a dispute discernible from any document, correspondence, or proceeding before a court, tribunal, labour court, mediation, conciliation forum, or in reply to statutory notices (e.g., under Section 80 CPC, Section 433 of the Companies Act 1956, or Section 59 of the Sale of Goods Act) can satisfy the 'existence of dispute' test, so long as it genuinely relates to the existence/amount of debt, quality of goods/services, or breach of representation/warranty. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Adjudicating Authority must independently examine whether the Corporate Debtor's reply, on its substance, raises a genuine dispute meeting the three categories in Section 5(6)(a)-(c) - mere assertion of disagreement, denial, or allegation (without concrete substantiation relatable to debt, quality, or warranty) is insufficient and cannot defeat an otherwise valid Section 9 application; a vague, unsubstantiated, or 'got up' dispute raised solely to evade payment does not qualify, and the Authority errs by mechanically treating the mere receipt of any reply disputing the claim as conclusive without this substantive scrutiny. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: NCLT acted mechanically in rejecting Kirusa's application solely because Mobilox had sent a reply denying liability, without examining whether that reply's allegations (breach of NDA, vague denial of contractual dues) actually constituted a dispute falling within Section 5(6); since the reply's dispute appeared vague, unsubstantiated, and possibly motivated to evade payment rather than a genuine dispute as to debt, quality, or warranty, the rejection was set aside and the matter remitted for reconsideration on the correct legal standard.
operative_order: Impugned order dated 27th January 2017 passed by the Adjudicating Authority in C.P. No. 02/I&BP/NCLT/MAH/2017 set aside; matter remitted to the Adjudicating Authority for consideration of admission of the application if it is otherwise complete; appeal allowed with the aforesaid observations; no order as to costs.
summary: Kirusa Software, an Operational Creditor owed Rs. 20,08,202.55 for services rendered under purchase orders, filed a Section 9 application against Mobilox Innovations after Mobilox's advocates sent a reply disputing the claim and alleging NDA breach. NCLT Mumbai rejected the application solely because a dispute-raising reply existed, without examining its substance. NCLAT held that 'existence of a dispute' under Section 8(2) is to be given a wide, non-exhaustive meaning covering any genuine dispute relatable to debt, quality of goods/services, or breach of warranty - not limited to pending suits/arbitration - but that a vague or unsubstantiated denial raised merely to evade payment does not qualify. Since NCLT had mechanically accepted the mere existence of a reply as sufficient without this scrutiny, NCLAT set aside the rejection and remitted the matter for fresh consideration on the correct legal standard for what constitutes a genuine 'dispute' under the IBC.

case_title: Dr. B.V.S. Lakshmi vs Geometrix Laser Solutions Private Limited
bench: New Delhi (arising from NCLT Hyderabad Bench, CP (IB)/19/7/HBD/2017)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Dr. B.V.S. Lakshmi, a shareholder and (per disputed Articles of Association) alleged first Director of the Corporate Debtor, claiming to be a Financial Creditor, is the Appellant; Geometrix Laser Solutions Private Limited is the Corporate Debtor/Respondent. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: the Appellant advanced funds totalling Rs. 91,47,864 to the Respondent across fifty-two transactions between 26th April 2013 and 9th March 2015, purportedly to (a) service the Respondent's bank loan interest/instalments to prevent default/NPA classification, and (b) ensure payment of salaries and vendor dues to keep the business running; the terms of the loan were not reduced to writing, though the Appellant relied on an email from the Managing Director directing interest be added for shareholder loans, and an auditor's report dated 31 August 2016 noting interest credited on loans. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: the Appellant claimed a financial debt of Rs. 91,47,864 sought to be recovered; the Respondent's books of account showed varying acknowledged amounts across years - Rs. 98,37,596 (2012-13), Rs. 38,74,767 (2013-14), Rs. 89,85,792 (2014-15), and Rs. 85,20,548 (2015-16) - though the Respondent contended the amount had since been repaid/adjusted and that as of 3 September 2016 the Appellant ceased to be a creditor. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: the Appellant issued a repayment demand notice dated 7th September 2016; the Respondent replied on 26th September 2016 asserting the balance as of 31 March 2015 had been repaid/adjusted and that the Appellant was no longer a creditor as of 3 September 2016; NCLT Hyderabad Bench rejected the Section 7 application by order dated 13th March 2017. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Form-32 and annual ledger statements from the Respondent (2013-14 to 2015-16) showed amounts against the Appellant's name under Schedule-D 'Unsecured Loan' in the Balance Sheet; the Respondent's Auditor's report and qualification stated that in the absence of documentation approving any loan, interest erroneously credited on the alleged loan should not be provided for or accounted; the Respondent alleged the Appellant submitted a fabricated Memorandum and Articles of Association (misstating the first Directors' names) and alleged fund siphoning by the Appellant, supported by a criminal complaint/FIR lodged in August 2016. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: the Appellant filed a Section 7 application before NCLT Hyderabad Bench (CP (IB)/19/7/HBD/2017); NCLT held the Appellant did not qualify as a 'Financial Creditor' and rejected the application by order dated 13th March 2017; the Appellant appealed to NCLAT.
legal_issues: Whether amounts advanced by a shareholder to a company, recorded as 'unsecured loans' in the company's books and allegedly carrying interest, but without documented terms establishing disbursement against consideration for the time value of money, qualify as a 'Financial Debt' under Section 5(8) of the IBC, making the shareholder a 'Financial Creditor' under Section 5(7) entitled to trigger a Section 7 application.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: To qualify as a 'Financial Creditor' under Section 5(7), a claimant must establish (i) a debt (with interest, if any) is owed to them, and (ii) that debt was disbursed against consideration for the time value of money, falling within one or more of the modes enumerated in Section 5(8)(a)-(i); merely being recorded as an 'unsecured loan' creditor in a company's books, without more, does not establish the 'time value of money' element required for a financial debt. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The 'time value of money' element is the key defining feature of a financial debt; a claimant seeking to invoke Section 5(8)(f) (transactions having the commercial effect of a borrowing) must produce concrete evidence that the recipient company actually raised/borrowed the amount as such, and expectation of indirect future benefit (such as anticipated share value appreciation or future dividends as a shareholder) does not, without documented loan terms or disbursement evidence, satisfy the statutory requirement. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Disbursement against consideration for time value of money must be affirmatively evidenced - through documented loan terms, interest agreements, or other concrete proof that a borrowing transaction occurred - and cannot be inferred solely from ledger entries labelling amounts as 'unsecured loan' where the auditor has separately qualified that no documentation exists for loan approval and interest credited should not be accounted for. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Appellant failed to produce evidence that the amounts advanced were disbursed against consideration for the time value of money or that the Respondent had raised the funds through a borrowing-type transaction; accordingly, she did not qualify as a Financial Creditor under Section 5(7), and the NCLT's rejection of her Section 7 application was correctly upheld.
operative_order: Appeal dismissed; the impugned order dated 13th March 2017 rejecting the Section 7 application is upheld; no order as to costs.
summary: Dr. B.V.S. Lakshmi, a shareholder of Geometrix Laser Solutions, advanced over Rs. 91 lakh to the company across multiple transactions to help it service bank loans and pay vendors/salaries, and later sought to trigger insolvency proceedings as a Financial Creditor when the company disputed owing her further amounts. NCLT Hyderabad held she was not a Financial Creditor and rejected her Section 7 application. NCLAT upheld this, holding that while the amounts were recorded as 'unsecured loans' in the company's books, the Appellant failed to produce evidence that the disbursement was made against consideration for the time value of money (such as documented interest terms or proof the company treated the funds as a formal borrowing) - a shareholder's expectation of indirect benefit through future share appreciation or dividends does not satisfy this requirement. The appeal was dismissed and the rejection of her Financial Creditor status was affirmed.

case_title: Cyrus Investments Pvt. Ltd. & Anr. vs Tata Sons Ltd. & Ors.
bench: New Delhi (arising from NCLT Mumbai Bench, C.P. No. 82/241,242,244/NCLT/MAH/2016)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Cyrus Investments Pvt. Ltd. and Sterling Investment Corp Pvt. Ltd., both minority shareholders of Tata Sons Limited (holding 9.19% equity each, an aggregate 18.37% equity but only about 2.17% of total issued share capital including preference shares), are the Appellants; Tata Sons Ltd. (Respondent No. 1) and various individual respondents (including Respondent No. 2, Respondent No. 3, and others) are Respondents; Cyrus Pallonji Mistry (Respondent No. 11), removed as Executive Chairman and later as Director of Tata Sons, supported the Appellants' case. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Tata Sons Limited is the apex holding company of the Tata Group, with a complex capital structure comprising Trusts (Sir Dorabji Tata Trust, Sir Ratan Tata Trust, etc. holding ~65.89% of equity), Tata group companies, the Mistry family entities (Appellants), and various individuals, with the Appellants' equity valued at over Rs. 1 lakh crore against an overall company valuation of about Rs. 6 lakh crore; under Articles 121 and 121-A of the Articles of Association, Tata Sons' Board (with Tata Trust-nominated directors having decisive voting power) controls key decisions across major Tata group companies including Tata Steel, Tata Motors, Tata Teleservices, Tata Power, and Air Asia (India). 3. DEFAULT METRICS: not applicable - this is a company law oppression and mismanagement dispute, not a debt/default matter. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: NCLT Mumbai passed a consent order on 22 December 2016; Tata Sons issued notice on 5 January 2017 for an EGM on 6 February 2017 to remove Cyrus Pallonji Mistry as Director; appellants filed a contempt petition and an application for waiver under the proviso to Section 244 (I.A. No. 26 of 2017); NCLAT rejected an interim relief application by order dated 3 February 2017; the EGM was held on 6 February 2017 removing Mistry from the Board, prompting an amendment to the petition on 10 February 2017; NCLT decided maintainability first by order dated 6 March 2017 (finding the Company Petition not maintainable) and then decided the waiver application by a second impugned order dated 17 April 2017 (dismissing the waiver application and thereby the Company Petition); both orders were appealed to NCLAT, which decided the appeals on 21 September 2017. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: a detailed shareholding table as of 21 December 2016 was placed on record showing 51 shareholders of Tata Sons, with only Ratan Naval Tata (31.43% of total capital) and Narotam S. Sekhsaria (17.01%) individually meeting the 1/10th issued share capital threshold, and the Appellants collectively holding only 2.17% of total issued share capital (equity plus preference); allegations in the underlying petition included claims relating to a Colaba flat sale, the Corus acquisition, the Tata Nano project, dealings with Mr. C. Sivasankaran/Siva Group (Rs. 694 crore dispute), Air Asia India dealings, and the manner of Mistry's removal as Executive Chairman and Director; Respondents contended these allegations were stale, time-barred, directorial complaints, or related to third-party companies, and alleged suppression of facts and unclean hands by the Appellants. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appellants filed Company Petition No. 82/241,242,244/NCLT/MAH/2016 before NCLT Mumbai Bench alleging oppression and mismanagement under Sections 241, 242 and 244 of the Companies Act, 2013; NCLT held by order dated 6 March 2017 that the petition was not maintainable since Appellants held less than 1/10th of the issued share capital, then considered and dismissed the waiver application by order dated 17 April 2017 (thereby dismissing the petition); Appellants preferred Company Appeal (AT) No. 133 of 2017 against the maintainability order and Company Appeal (AT) No. 139 of 2017 against the waiver-rejection order, both disposed of by this common NCLAT judgment.
legal_issues: (i) Whether the expression 'issued share capital' in Section 244(1) of the Companies Act, 2013 refers to the aggregate of equity and preference share capital, or only the 'relevant' class of share capital held by the petitioning member(s), for determining eligibility to file a petition under Section 241; (ii) if the Appellants do not meet the eligibility threshold, whether they have made out a case for waiver of the requirements under the proviso to Section 244(1), and what factors the Tribunal may consider (or must exclude, as being merit-based) when deciding a waiver application.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The expression 'issued share capital' in Section 244(1) of the Companies Act, 2013 (pari materia with Section 399(1) of the 1956 Act) refers to the aggregate of both equity and preference share capital of the company, not merely the 'relevant' class of share capital held by the petitioning member(s); eligibility under Section 244(1)(a) must be computed against this total issued share capital. Separately, an application for waiver under the proviso to Section 244(1) is a distinct, threshold gatekeeping stage that precedes any merits determination under Section 241/242, and the Tribunal cannot decide the merits of the (proposed) Section 241 application - or any merits-dependent sub-issues (limitation, prima facie case, whether allegations pertain to a third company, arbitrability, whether allegations are directorial complaints, or waiver/acquiescence/estoppel of the applicant) - while deciding whether to grant waiver. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The word 'class of members' added in Section 241(1)(b) (absent from the corresponding 1956 provision) only expands the subject matter of grievances that may be raised under Section 241; it does not alter or import a class-based reading into the separate eligibility/locus provision in Section 244(1), which remains identical in substance to erstwhile Section 399(1) and has been consistently interpreted (including by the Bombay High Court in Northern Projects, affirmed by the Supreme Court) to mean the aggregate of equity and preference share capital. Where the legislature intended a class-specific reference (e.g., 'issued equity share capital' in Section 236, or 'issued shares of that class' in Section 48), it did so expressly, which by implication confirms Section 244(1) uses the unqualified term deliberately. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: In assessing waiver, the Tribunal is confined to non-merits factors: whether the applicants are members of the company; whether the proposed Section 241 application, on its face, pertains to oppression/mismanagement of the company (not frivolous); whether a similar allegation has already been conclusively decided; and whether exceptional circumstances exist warranting waiver (e.g., an inequitable structural bar preventing genuinely aggrieved minority shareholders from ever meeting the numerical/shareholding threshold, or where the company's control extends materially over other group companies implicated in the allegations). Merits-based inquiries (prima facie case strength, limitation, directorial-complaint characterization, acquiescence) must be left for the Section 241 hearing itself. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: On maintainability, since the Appellants held only 2.17% of Tata Sons' total issued share capital (equity plus preference combined), well below the 1/10th threshold, the Company Petition as filed was not maintainable, and NCLT's finding on this point was affirmed. On waiver, however, NCLT erred by effectively deciding merits-based factors while assessing the waiver application; properly confined to non-merits considerations - including the practical impossibility for minority shareholders (other than two dominant individual shareholders) to ever independently meet the 1/10th threshold, the Appellants' substantial economic interest (over Rs. 1 lakh crore) in a company valued at roughly Rs. 6 lakh crore, and Tata Sons' structural control (via Articles 121/121-A) over the affairs of major group companies implicated in the allegations - the Appellants made out an exceptional case warranting waiver.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) No. 133 of 2017 dismissed, affirming NCLT's finding that the original Company Petition was not maintainable under Section 244(1) as filed. Company Appeal (AT) No. 139 of 2017 allowed: the impugned order dated 17th April 2017 rejecting the waiver application is set aside, and waiver is granted to the Appellants to enable them to file an application under Section 241; the matter is remitted to NCLT to register the proposed Section 241 application, admit it, and after notice to the parties, decide it on merits uninfluenced by the impugned orders, preferably within three months. Parties to bear their own costs.
summary: Minority shareholders of Tata Sons Ltd. (holding under 2.2% of total issued share capital when preference shares are included) filed an oppression and mismanagement petition after Cyrus Mistry was removed as Executive Chairman and Director. NCLT held the petition not maintainable under Section 244(1) since the petitioners fell far short of the 1/10th issued-share-capital threshold, and separately rejected their application for waiver of that threshold. On appeal, NCLAT upheld that 'issued share capital' under Section 244(1) means the combined total of equity and preference shares (following settled precedent under the analogous 1956 Act provision), so the maintainability appeal was dismissed. However, NCLAT held that NCLT had wrongly imported merits-based considerations into its waiver analysis; confining itself to proper non-merits factors - including the practical impossibility for genuinely aggrieved minority shareholders to reach the statutory threshold, their substantial economic stake, and Tata Sons' structural control over major group companies implicated in the allegations - NCLAT found an exceptional case for waiver, set aside the rejection, granted waiver, and remitted the underlying oppression petition to NCLT for a merits decision.

case_title: Mr. Jitendra Virmani vs MRO-TEK Realty Ltd. & Ors.
appeal_number: IA No. 221 of 2017 in Company Appeal (AT) No. 138 of 2017
bench: New Delhi (arising from NCLT Bengaluru Bench, T.P. No. 88/2016 in C.P. No. 22/2016)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Mr. Jitendra Virmani is the Appellant/Applicant seeking review and recall of an earlier NCLAT dismissal order; MRO-TEK Realty Ltd. & Ors. are the Respondents. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: not applicable - this is a procedural review application concerning limitation for filing an appeal against an interim order in a company law proceeding (T.P. No. 88/2016 in C.P. No. 22/2016), not a substantive commercial dispute on its own facts. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: not applicable. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: NCLT Bengaluru Bench passed an order on 5th January 2017 rejecting interim relief in T.P. No. 88/2016; certified copy was served on the applicant on 7th January 2017; the statutory 45-day period for filing an appeal expired on 21st February 2017, and the further 45-day condonable period expired on 7th April 2017; the applicant filed a defective appeal on 31st March 2017 (54 days after service); defects were pointed out the same day, and under Rule 26(2) of NCLAT Rules the applicant had 7 days (until 7th April 2017) to cure them, but instead re-filed only on 1st May 2017; NCLAT's original order dismissing the appeal for want of jurisdiction to condone delay beyond 45 days was passed on 3rd May 2017; the present review/recall application (IA No. 221 of 2017) was disposed of on 15th May 2017. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: the applicant did not explain the initial delay in filing (from 7th January to 31st March 2017), nor the further 31-day delay in curing defects (from 31st March to the eventual re-filing on 1st May 2017); no application was filed to seek condonation of the minor defects or to explain the delay before the re-filing. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: the applicant's original appeal (challenging NCLT Bengaluru's interim order dated 5th January 2017) was dismissed by NCLAT on 3rd May 2017 on the ground that the Appellate Tribunal lacked jurisdiction to condone delay exceeding 45 days beyond the initial 45-day limitation period; the applicant then filed IA No. 221 of 2017 under Rule 11 of the NCLAT Rules seeking review and recall of that dismissal order, which is the subject of this order.
legal_issues: Whether NCLAT has inherent power under Rule 11 of the NCLAT Rules, 2016 to review and recall its own order dismissing an appeal for delay, where the delay in filing and curing defects exceeded the statutory limitation period prescribed under Section 421(3) of the Companies Act, 2013 (45 days plus a further condonable 45 days).
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Where a statute prescribes a specific limitation period for filing an appeal along with an express, capped extension for condonation of delay (here, 45 days plus a further 45 days under the proviso to Section 421(3)), the Appellate Tribunal has no jurisdiction - inherent or otherwise - to entertain an appeal or condone delay beyond that statutorily capped period; procedural 'review' power under Rule 11 (to correct a palpably erroneous order passed under misapprehension) is distinct from a substantive review on merits, and cannot be used to circumvent an express statutory limitation bar. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Under Rule 26 of the NCLAT Rules, an appeal found defective on scrutiny must be cured within 7 days of notice, failing which it is placed before the Registrar for appropriate orders (including possible refusal to register); however, if defects are not cured within 7 days and are cured later, the re-filed appeal is treated as a fresh filing - and if such fresh filing falls outside the maximum statutory window (45 days plus 45 days condonable), the Appellate Tribunal has no jurisdiction to entertain it regardless of any registry lapse in enforcing Rule 26(4). 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Following Union of India vs. Popular Construction Company, where a statute uses language such as 'but not thereafter' or otherwise expressly caps an extension period, this constitutes an express exclusion of general condonation principles (including inherent equitable power), and courts/tribunals cannot entertain applications beyond that capped period; an applicant seeking to invoke inherent review power must at minimum explain the delay and laches on their part - unexplained delay at every stage (initial filing, defect-curing, and re-filing) defeats any claim to equitable/inherent relief. 4.
