DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Since the applicant's original appeal, initial defect-curing delay, and eventual re-filing (1st May 2017) all fell beyond the outer statutory limit of 7th April 2017 (90 days from service of the NCLT order), and since the applicant offered no explanation for any of the delays at any stage, the original dismissal for want of jurisdiction to condone delay was correct, and no basis existed to exercise inherent review/recall power to reopen it.
operative_order: The Interlocutory Application (IA No. 221 of 2017) is dismissed with costs of Rs. 50,000 payable by the applicant to the Library of the Appellate Tribunal, via demand draft in the name of Pay and Accounts Officer, Ministry of Corporate Affairs, New Delhi, to be deposited with the Registrar within 30 days.
summary: After NCLAT dismissed Jitendra Virmani's appeal against an NCLT Bengaluru interim order for being filed beyond the statutory limitation period (45 days plus a further condonable 45 days under Section 421 of the Companies Act, 2013), Virmani sought review and recall of that dismissal, arguing NCLAT possessed inherent power to correct the order since the Registrar had not acted on the defective filing within the prescribed time. NCLAT held that while procedural review power to correct palpably erroneous orders does inhere in tribunals, it cannot override an express statutory limitation cap; since the applicant's appeal, defect-curing, and eventual re-filing all occurred beyond the outer 90-day statutory window, and the delay at every stage remained unexplained, the Tribunal had correctly held it lacked jurisdiction to condone the delay. The review application was dismissed with costs of Rs. 50,000 payable to the Appellate Tribunal's library.

case_title: M/s. Starlog Enterprises Limited vs ICICI Bank Limited
bench: New Delhi (arising from NCLT Mumbai Bench, C.P. No. 12/I&BP/NCLT/MAH/2017)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: the Appellant (a crane/logistics services company referred to as Corporate Debtor, part of a group with subsidiaries including Starport Logistics Ltd, ABG Turnkey Pvt Ltd, Kanla Container Terminal Pvt Ltd and ABG Projects & Services Ltd, UK) challenged admission of a Section 7 petition; ICICI Bank Limited is the Financial Creditor/Respondent, a member of the Joint Lenders' Forum (JLF) constituted for the Appellant per RBI guidelines, with L&T Infrastructure Finance Company as Lead Lender. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: consortium/JLF credit facilities were extended to the Appellant; the JLF, formed on 14th June 2014, had periodically met and unanimously adopted 'rectification' as the Corrective Action Plan (CAP) for the Appellant, including at a meeting held on 2nd February 2017, the minutes of which were later disputed by ICICI Bank. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: ICICI Bank's demand notice dated 6th February 2017 (received by Appellant on 8th February 2017) claimed an overdue amount of Rs. 10,02,28,271.60; however, the Section 7 application filed on 8th February 2017 claimed a default amount of Rs. 29,81,02,395.62, including 'Principal Unmatured' amounts not yet due and payable, resulting in a mismatch between the demanded and claimed default figures; the impugned order recorded satisfaction of default of Rs. 27.77 crores. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: JLF meeting held 2nd February 2017 (minutes later disputed by ICICI Bank on 16th February 2017); demand notice dated 6th February 2017 received by Appellant on 8th February 2017; Section 7 application filed by ICICI Bank on 8th February 2017 (the same day, before the Appellant could respond, and before correct minutes of the 2nd February JLF meeting were circulated); NCLT Mumbai passed an ex-parte admission order on 17th February 2017 without notice to the Appellant; IRP issued a public notice in the Economic Times on 1st(?) March 2017 calling for creditor claims. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: the letter accompanying service of the Section 7 application did not specify whether the application had been filed, its filing number, or any hearing date; the JLF's disputed minutes and RBI's 24.9.2015 JLF guidelines (providing dissenting lenders an exit option rather than unilateral individual action) were relied upon to show ICICI Bank acted outside the JLF structure; post-admission, the IRP's mismanagement allegedly caused termination of a major client contract (with GE, resulting in an alleged loss of Rs. 2.7 crore) and resignation of several long-serving employees, and the IRP allegedly attempted to change authorized signatories on bank accounts of the Appellant's subsidiaries despite Section 18's Explanation excluding subsidiary assets from the corporate debtor's estate. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: ICICI Bank filed a Section 7 application before NCLT Mumbai Bench on 8th February 2017; NCLT admitted the application by ex-parte order dated 17th February 2017 without issuing notice to the Appellant/Corporate Debtor, appointing an Interim Resolution Professional and declaring moratorium; the Appellant appealed to NCLAT under Section 61 of the IBC.
legal_issues: (i) Whether an Adjudicating Authority's failure to issue notice to the Corporate Debtor before admitting a Section 7 application violates principles of natural justice, warranting the admission order be set aside; (ii) whether a Financial Creditor's demand notice and Section 7 application containing a materially inflated/mismatched default amount (including unmatured principal) can sustain an admission order; (iii) whether a JLF member's unilateral filing of a Section 7 application, contrary to a Joint Lenders' Forum's collectively adopted corrective action plan, affects the validity of the application.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Following Innoventive Industries Ltd. vs. ICICI Bank & Anr. and the Calcutta High Court's ruling in Sree Metaliks Ltd., the Adjudicating Authority is bound to issue a limited notice to the Corporate Debtor before admitting a Section 7 application, to ascertain existence of default based on material the Corporate Debtor may submit and to verify completeness of the application; while this does not mandate a full hearing in every case, an ex-parte admission without any notice, absent recorded reasons for dispensing with natural justice, is impermissible. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Sub-rule (3) of Rule 4 of the Adjudicating Authority Rules requires the financial creditor to 'dispatch forthwith' a copy of the application 'filed with the Adjudicating Authority' - i.e., a post-filing notice, not a pre-filing communication - and such notice must meaningfully inform the debtor whether the application has been filed, its filing number, and hearing date; a notice/covering letter omitting these essentials does not satisfy the Rule's purpose of providing adequate and informed notice. Under Section 3(12), 'default' requires the debt to be actually due and payable; unmatured principal not yet due cannot be included in the default amount claimed. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: A material, unexplained mismatch between the amount specified in the Section 8-type demand notice (Rs. 10.02 crore) and the amount claimed as default in the Section 7 application (Rs. 29.81 crore, including unmatured principal) reflects non-application of mind by the Adjudicating Authority in ascertaining default under Section 7(4)-(5), and an admission order recording satisfaction of a default figure (Rs. 27.77 crore) inconsistent with the financial creditor's own demand notice is perverse and unsustainable; the IBC contains no mechanism allowing a financial creditor to modify its claimed default amount post-admission to cure such a discrepancy. Separately, following Innoventive, the Adjudicating Authority is not required to examine whether JLF consent was obtained before a Section 7 application is filed, and a financial creditor's independent filing despite a JLF's collective corrective action plan does not, by itself, invalidate an otherwise valid application - though evidence of misrepresentation or mala fide conduct before the Tribunal remains independently relevant to natural justice and good faith. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Since the ex-parte admission order was passed without any notice to the Corporate Debtor and was based on an inflated, internally inconsistent default figure not corroborated by the financial creditor's own demand notice, the order was vitiated both for breach of natural justice and non-application of mind, warranting it be set aside along with all consequential actions.
operative_order: Ex-parte impugned order dated 17th February 2017 passed by the Adjudicating Authority, Mumbai Bench, in C.P. No. 12/I&BP/NCLT/MAH/2017 set aside; appeal allowed. The appointment of the Interim Resolution Professional, the moratorium order, account freezing, and all other orders and actions taken pursuant to the impugned order (including the newspaper advertisement calling for claims) are declared illegal; the Adjudicating Authority is directed to close the proceeding; the Appellant company is released from the rigour of law and permitted to function independently through its Board of Directors with immediate effect. Cost of Rs. 50,000 imposed on the Respondent-Financial Creditor (ICICI Bank), payable to the Registrar, NCLAT, by demand draft within one month towards development of its library.
summary: ICICI Bank, a member of a Joint Lenders' Forum for Starlog Enterprises, filed a Section 7 application on the same day it served a demand notice, claiming a default of Rs. 29.81 crore (including unmatured principal) though its demand notice had claimed only Rs. 10.02 crore. NCLT Mumbai admitted the application ex-parte, without notice to the Corporate Debtor, and recorded a default finding of Rs. 27.77 crore. On appeal, NCLAT held that admission without any notice violated natural justice per its own Innoventive Industries precedent and the Calcutta High Court's Sree Metaliks ruling, and separately found the admission vitiated by non-application of mind given the stark mismatch between the demanded and claimed default amounts, with unmatured principal wrongly included as 'default' under Section 3(12). NCLAT also noted (without disturbing Innoventive's holding that JLF consent isn't legally required) that ICICI Bank's unilateral filing despite the JLF's collectively adopted rectification plan, and its subsequent mismanagement through the IRP (causing loss of a major client and staff resignations), reflected adversely on the fairness of the process. The ex-parte admission order and all consequential actions were set aside, the company was released back to its Board, and costs of Rs. 50,000 were imposed on ICICI Bank.

case_title: APC Credit Rating Pvt. Ltd. vs ROC, NCT of Delhi & Haryana
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) No. 206 of 2017 and Company Appeal (AT) No. 221 of 2017
bench: New Delhi (arising from NCLT orders dated 26th September 2016 and 28th April 2017)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: APC Credit Rating Pvt. Ltd. is the Appellant, having violated various provisions of the Companies Act, 1956; the Registrar of Companies (ROC), NCT of Delhi & Haryana, is the Respondent. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: not applicable in the conventional sense - this concerns compounding of statutory/regulatory offences committed by the Appellant company under the Companies Act, 1956, rather than a commercial debt transaction. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: not applicable - the dispute concerns compounding fees imposed for regulatory defaults/violations of the Companies Act, 1956, characterized by NCLT as involving a 'long period of defaults', rather than a financial debt default. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: the Appellant filed two separate compounding petitions under Section 441 of the Companies Act, 2013; NCLT dismissed both by two separate orders dated 26th September 2016; the Appellant then filed two rectification/review applications under Rule 154 of the NCLT Rules, 2016, which NCLT dismissed by two further orders dated 28th April 2017; the Appellant then appealed to NCLAT against both the rectification-dismissal orders and the original September 2016 orders; by the time of the NCLAT appeal, more than 9.5 months had passed since the original orders, exceeding the maximum permissible 90-day window (45 days plus a further condonable 45 days) under Section 421(3) for appealing the original orders. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: the Appellant argued that NCLT's original orders omitted consideration of the NCLAT's earlier ruling in M/s. Viavi Solutions India Private Limited & Ors. vs. Registrar of Companies, NCT Delhi and Haryana (Company Appeal (AT) 49 etc. of 2016, dated 28th February 2016), which laid down factors relevant to compounding offences; NCLT's rectification orders held that review cannot substitute for appeal and that the compounding fee was fixed per its judicial discretion considering the long period of defaults. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT dismissed the original compounding petitions by orders dated 26th September 2016; the Appellant sought rectification/review under Rule 154 of the NCLT Rules citing the alleged omission to consider the Viavi Solutions precedent, which NCLT dismissed by orders dated 28th April 2017; the Appellant appealed both the rectification dismissals and the original orders to NCLAT in these two connected appeals.
legal_issues: (i) Whether NCLT has the power to review its own final order/judgment (as distinct from mere rectification of clerical/arithmetical errors or accidental slips/omissions under Rule 154, or amendment of a mistake apparent from the record under Section 420(2)); (ii) whether an alleged failure by NCLT to consider or reference a cited precedent constitutes an 'omission' warranting rectification under Rule 154; (iii) whether NCLAT can entertain a challenge to the original NCLT orders dated 26th September 2016 given they were appealed well beyond the statutory limitation period under Section 421(3).
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Unlike a civil court's power of review under Order 47 Rule 1 CPC, NCLT possesses no general inherent power to review its own final order or judgment; its only powers in this regard are: (a) under Section 420(2), to rectify a 'mistake apparent from the record' and amend the order accordingly, within two years of the order; (b) under Rule 154, to correct clerical or arithmetical mistakes or errors arising from an accidental slip or omission; and (c) under Rule 155, general power to amend defects/errors in pleadings within thirty days of completion of pleadings. None of these provisions permit substituting one considered order for another merely because a party believes the reasoning was deficient. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The inherent power under Rule 11 of the NCLT Rules (to make orders necessary for meeting the ends of justice or preventing abuse of process) can only be exercised during the pendency of an application or appeal - not after final disposal, and not as a substitute for review of the Tribunal's own concluded order. An 'omission' correctable under Rule 154 must be a genuine accidental slip integral to the substance of the order (e.g., a clerical or arithmetical error); a Tribunal's non-reference to a cited judgment does not, by itself, constitute such an 'omission', since no Tribunal is obliged to expressly discuss every precedent cited by a party, whether relevant or irrelevant. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Compounding fees imposed under Section 441, exercised as a matter of judicial discretion after considering the length/extent of statutory defaults, are not disturbed by NCLAT merely because a party disagrees with the outcome or points to an uncited precedent, absent a genuine clerical/arithmetical error or accidental omission on the face of the record. Separately, appeals against original NCLT orders (as opposed to subsequent rectification orders) remain subject to the strict 90-day outer limit under Section 421(3) (45 days plus a further condonable 45 days), regardless of intervening rectification proceedings, and NCLAT has no jurisdiction to entertain such a challenge once that period has lapsed. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Since NCLT's non-reference to the Viavi Solutions precedent did not constitute a rectifiable 'omission', and since NCLT has no general power to review its own concluded orders, the rectification-dismissal orders dated 28th April 2017 were rightly upheld; separately, since more than 9.5 months had elapsed since the original orders dated 26th September 2016 (far exceeding the maximum 90-day window under Section 421(3)), NCLAT had no jurisdiction to entertain a challenge to those original orders on merits.
operative_order: Both impugned rectification orders dated 28th April 2017 upheld. The prayer to interfere with the original orders dated 26th September 2016 is rejected as time-barred under Section 421(3), NCLAT having no power to condone delay beyond the statutory 90-day outer limit. Both appeals (Company Appeal (AT) No. 206 of 2017 and No. 221 of 2017) dismissed; no order as to costs.
summary: APC Credit Rating's two compounding petitions under Section 441 of the Companies Act, 2013 (for defaults under the 1956 Act) were dismissed by NCLT in September 2016, with compounding fees fixed based on the long period of default. The company sought rectification/review under Rule 154 of the NCLT Rules, arguing NCLT had omitted to consider an earlier NCLAT precedent (Viavi Solutions) on compounding factors; NCLT dismissed these rectification applications in April 2017, and the company appealed both the rectification dismissals and the original orders to NCLAT. NCLAT held that NCLT has no general power to review its own concluded orders - only narrow powers to rectify clerical/arithmetical mistakes (Rule 154) or mistakes apparent from the record (Section 420(2)) - and that non-reference to a cited precedent does not constitute a rectifiable 'omission'. NCLAT also held it had no jurisdiction to entertain a challenge to the original September 2016 orders, since more than 9.5 months had passed, well beyond the statutory 90-day maximum window under Section 421(3) for filing such an appeal. Both appeals were dismissed.

case_title: Alpha & Omega Diagnostics (India) Ltd. vs Asset Reconstruction Company of India Ltd. & Ors.
bench: New Delhi (arising from NCLT Mumbai Bench, T.C.P. No. 1117/I&BP/NCLT/MB/MAH/2017)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Alpha & Omega Diagnostics (India) Ltd. is the Corporate Applicant/Corporate Debtor and Appellant; Asset Reconstruction Company of India Ltd. is the Financial Creditor/Respondent, along with other Respondents. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: the Appellant filed a Section 10 application for its own corporate insolvency resolution process; separately, personal properties of the Corporate Debtor's Promoters (specifically certain flats not owned by or reflected in the Corporate Debtor's balance sheet) had been given as security/collateral to banks in connection with recovery proceedings. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: not detailed in this order, which concerns only the scope of the moratorium following admission, not the underlying default amount. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: the Ld. Chief Metropolitan Magistrate had passed an order dated 11.04.2017 appointing a Court Commissioner to take over possession of the flats (belonging to the Promoters, not the Corporate Debtor); NCLT Mumbai Bench admitted the Section 10 application by impugned order dated 10th July 2017, subject to the qualification that moratorium would not extend to properties not owned by the Corporate Debtor. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: it was undisputed between the parties that the flats in question were not owned by the Corporate Debtor and were not reflected in its balance sheet, but rather constituted personal properties of the Promoters pledged as security to banks; this fact was raised during the NCLT hearing and not disputed by either side. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: the Appellant filed a Section 10 application before NCLT Mumbai Bench; NCLT admitted the application by order dated 10th July 2017, declaring moratorium under Section 14 but expressly clarifying that the moratorium would not extend to properties not owned by the Corporate Debtor (such as the Promoters' flats), appointing an Interim Resolution Professional; the Appellant, aggrieved only by this qualifying limitation on the scope of the moratorium, appealed to NCLAT seeking to have the moratorium extended to cover matters pending before the Debt Recovery Tribunal (DRT) and under the SARFAESI Act relating to such third-party/Promoter assets.
legal_issues: Whether the moratorium declared under Section 14 of the IBC upon admission of a Section 10 application extends to properties not owned by the Corporate Debtor (such as personal properties of its Promoters/directors pledged as security to creditors), or is confined strictly to the Corporate Debtor's own assets.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The moratorium under Section 14(1)(c) of the IBC, which prohibits action to foreclose, recover, or enforce any security interest created by the Corporate Debtor in respect of 'its' property, is confined strictly to property owned by the Corporate Debtor itself; it does not extend to assets - movable or immovable - belonging to third parties such as directors, promoters, or guarantors, even if such third-party assets have been pledged as security in connection with the Corporate Debtor's debts. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The word 'its' in Section 14(1)(c) is significant and must be given its plain, natural meaning without supplying any casus omissus or expanding its scope through ejusdem generis; consistent with this, Section 10(3) similarly confines the Corporate Applicant's disclosure obligations to 'its' own books of accounts. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Where it is undisputed that certain properties (e.g., Promoters' personal flats pledged as security) are neither owned by the Corporate Debtor nor reflected in its balance sheet, such properties fall outside the ambit of the Section 14 moratorium, and recovery/enforcement actions against them (including under the SARFAESI Act or before the DRT) may continue notwithstanding the moratorium; the SARFAESI Act would only be affected by the moratorium to the extent an action seeks to foreclose or recover property actually owned by the Corporate Debtor. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Since the Appellant sought its own insolvency resolution process (necessarily encompassing only the Corporate Debtor's own assets), NCLT correctly declared moratorium limited to the Corporate Debtor's own property and correctly excluded the Promoters' personal properties from its protective scope; no interference with this qualification was warranted (the Tribunal expressly reserved opinion on the position of guarantors, as distinct from the principal debtor).
operative_order: Appeal dismissed; the impugned order dated 10th July 2017 (admitting the Section 10 application subject to the qualification that moratorium is confined to the Corporate Debtor's own property) is upheld; no order as to costs.
summary: Alpha & Omega Diagnostics filed its own Section 10 insolvency application, which NCLT Mumbai admitted while expressly clarifying that the resulting Section 14 moratorium would not extend to certain flats pledged as security by the company's Promoters, since those properties were not owned by the Corporate Debtor and were not reflected in its balance sheet. The company appealed, seeking to have the moratorium cover related DRT and SARFAESI proceedings concerning those Promoter-owned assets. NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that the word 'its' in Section 14(1)(c) confines the moratorium strictly to property actually owned by the Corporate Debtor, and cannot be judicially expanded to protect third-party assets such as those of directors or promoters, even where pledged as security for the Corporate Debtor's obligations - though the Tribunal expressly left open the position regarding guarantors.

case_title: International Road Dynamics South Asia Pvt. Ltd. vs Reliance Infrastructure Ltd. and D.A. Toll Road Pvt. Ltd.
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 72 of 2017 and Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 77 of 2017
bench: New Delhi (arising from NCLT Mumbai Bench, Mumbai)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: International Road Dynamics South Asia Pvt. Ltd. is the Operational Creditor/Appellant in both connected appeals; Reliance Infrastructure Ltd. is the Corporate Debtor/Respondent in CA 72/2017; D.A. Toll Road Pvt. Ltd. is the Corporate Debtor/Respondent in CA 77/2017. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: against Reliance Infrastructure, the appellant's claims arose from three separate work orders/projects - the 'GF Toll Project' (total payments made by Corporate Debtor of Rs. 5,41,07,993, including a last payment of Rs. 1,06,55,322 on 17th May 2013, with Rs. 2,84,52,328 claimed as due), the 'DS Toll Project' (Rs. 28,31,430 claimed due), and the 'NK Toll Project'; against D.A. Toll Road, the claim concerned invoices for which the Corporate Debtor made periodic part-payments, with a reconciliation exercise between the parties. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: against Reliance Infrastructure, an aggregate claimed default of Rs. 2,84,52,328 (GF Toll) plus Rs. 28,31,430 (DS Toll) was combined in a single Section 9 application, with distinct dates of default for each work order (last payment for GF Toll made 17th May 2013); against D.A. Toll Road, the appellant claimed Rs. 65,22,971 outstanding, with the last payment made by the Corporate Debtor on 26th September 2013, and a reconciliation statement dated 13th August 2015 showing Rs. 25,03,900 as due, with a separate note referencing Rs. 40,19,071 in 'bills on hold' not yet reflected in the debtor's books. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: appellant issued a Section 8 demand notice to Reliance Infrastructure on 21st January 2017; NCLT Mumbai rejected the Section 9 application against Reliance Infrastructure by order dated 29th March 2017, and against D.A. Toll Road by order dated 3rd April 2017; both orders were appealed to NCLAT, decided together on 1st August 2017. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: for Reliance Infrastructure, the claims for GF Toll, DS Toll and NK Toll projects (each arising from separate work orders with distinct payment histories and default dates) were combined into a single joint claim without separately explaining each date of default; for D.A. Toll Road, a reconciliation statement dated 13th August 2015 was placed on record showing Rs. 25,03,900 as due, with a note by the debtor's employee (Ajay Sharma) referencing Rs. 40,19,071 in bills on hold not carried into the company's books, casting doubt on the claimed total default of Rs. 65,22,971. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: the appellant filed separate Section 9 applications against Reliance Infrastructure and D.A. Toll Road before NCLT Mumbai Bench; NCLT rejected the Reliance Infrastructure application by order dated 29th March 2017 (holding, among other things, that an Operational Creditor could pursue arbitration and that facts did not warrant invoking Section 9), and rejected the D.A. Toll Road application by order dated 3rd April 2017 (finding a genuine dispute as to claim quantum requiring elaborate inquiry, with part of the claim also potentially barred by limitation); the appellant preferred these two connected appeals to NCLAT.
legal_issues: (i) Whether the availability of an alternative arbitration remedy, or the solvency of the Corporate Debtor, is a valid ground to reject a Section 9 application; (ii) whether claims arising from multiple separate work orders/agreements, with distinct amounts and dates of default, can be combined into a single joint Section 9 application; (iii) whether a genuine dispute as to the quantum of claimed default (evidenced by a reconciliation statement and unresolved discrepancies) bars admission of a Section 9 application.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The existence of an alternative remedy of arbitration, or the fact that the Corporate Debtor is otherwise solvent, cannot by itself be a ground to reject an otherwise complete Section 9 application. However, claims arising from separate, distinct commercial agreements/work orders - each carrying its own separate cause of action, amount, and date of default - cannot be clubbed together into a single joint Section 9 application; doing so renders the application defective (as distinct from merely incomplete) and not maintainable, since each cause of action must be separately pursued and independently satisfy the statutory requirements. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: While the Tribunal need not make a definitive finding on whether the Limitation Act, 1963 applies to bar Section 9 applications, a claimant is nonetheless required to explain significant delay and laches - such as failing to approach any forum for over four years after the last payment was made on a claim - even where the applicability of limitation itself remains unresolved. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Where a reconciliation statement between the creditor and Corporate Debtor, along with unexplained internal notes referencing amounts not yet reflected in the debtor's books, casts genuine doubt on the precise quantum of the claimed default, this constitutes a real dispute requiring elaborate inquiry beyond the summary scope permitted under the IBC, and the application cannot be admitted; similarly, disputes as to non-completion of a project within time and counter-claims may be relevant, but require supporting documentation showing the dispute was raised prior to the Section 8 notice to be considered. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Since the Reliance Infrastructure application impermissibly combined claims from three separate work orders without explaining the multi-year delay from the last payment date, and since the D.A. Toll Road claim's exact quantum was genuinely disputed given the reconciliation discrepancies, neither application warranted interference; however, the appellant remains free to file separate, properly constituted applications for each distinct work order/contract, subject to limitation, delay/laches, and absence of dispute.
operative_order: Both appeals dismissed; the impugned orders dated 29th March 2017 (Reliance Infrastructure) and 3rd April 2017 (D.A. Toll Road) are upheld; the appellant is at liberty to move separate applications in respect of separate work orders/contracts if not barred by limitation or delay/laches and if no dispute exists, following the procedure under the IBC and Rules; no order as to costs.
summary: International Road Dynamics filed two Section 9 applications - one against Reliance Infrastructure combining claims from three separate toll road projects/work orders into a single application, and another against D.A. Toll Road Pvt. Ltd. for an amount whose exact quantum was disputed following a reconciliation exercise between the parties. NCLT Mumbai rejected both applications. On appeal, NCLAT held that while an arbitration clause or the debtor's solvency cannot alone justify rejecting a Section 9 application, combining distinct claims arising from separate work orders (each with its own default date and amount) into one joint application renders it defective and not maintainable; it also noted the appellant's unexplained multi-year delay in pursuing the GF Toll Project claim. For D.A. Toll Road, NCLAT agreed that a reconciliation statement and unresolved internal notes cast genuine doubt on the claimed default amount, requiring inquiry beyond the IBC's summary scope. Both appeals were dismissed, with liberty granted to file fresh, properly separated applications for each distinct contract.

case_title: Jindal Steel & Power Ltd. vs DCM International Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Jindal Steel & Power Ltd. is a tenant of the Respondent and the Appellant; DCM International Ltd. is the Corporate Debtor/Respondent, the landlord of premises occupied by the Appellant. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: the parties had entered into a Memorandum of Understanding relating to certain premises, with the Appellant occupying the premises as a tenant of the Corporate Debtor; the Appellant did not make any claim in respect of the provision of goods or services by it to the Corporate Debtor. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: no default amount or date is specified in this order, as the appeal turned entirely on the Appellant's eligibility to be classified as an Operational Creditor rather than on the merits of any claimed debt. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: NCLT dismissed the Appellant's Section 9 application by impugned order dated 6th October 2017; the appeal was decided by NCLAT on 28th November 2017. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: the existence of a Memorandum of Understanding between the parties regarding the tenanted premises was acknowledged, but no evidence of any operational debt (arising from provision of goods/services, or dues payable under law to the Central or State Government) owed by the Corporate Debtor to the Appellant was shown. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: the Appellant, as tenant, filed a Section 9 application against the Corporate Debtor/landlord before the Adjudicating Authority, which was dismissed by order dated 6th October 2017; the Appellant appealed to NCLAT.
legal_issues: Whether a tenant of a Corporate Debtor, whose claim arises from a Memorandum of Understanding relating to leased premises rather than from the provision of goods or services or statutory dues, qualifies as an 'Operational Creditor' under Section 5(20) read with Section 5(21) of the IBC, entitled to file an application under Section 9.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A person qualifies as an 'Operational Creditor' under Section 5(20) read with Section 5(21) of the IBC only if the debt claimed arises from the provision of goods or services (including employment) or from dues payable under law to the Central Government, State Government, or a local authority; a tenant's claim arising merely from a landlord-tenant relationship or a Memorandum of Understanding concerning leased premises, without any element of goods/services supplied by the claimant or statutory dues owed, does not constitute an 'operational debt'. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The existence of a Memorandum of Understanding between the parties regarding tenanted premises does not, by itself, transform a tenant's claim into an operational debt; the tenant must independently show that its claim falls within the specific categories defined under Section 5(21). 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Absent any claim by the Appellant relating to provision of goods or services to the Corporate Debtor, or dues under law payable to a government authority, the tenant cannot be treated as an Operational Creditor entitled to invoke Section 9, regardless of any contractual relationship (such as an MOU) between the parties concerning the premises. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Since the Appellant, as a tenant, made no claim falling within the statutory definition of operational debt, it did not qualify as an Operational Creditor, and the Adjudicating Authority correctly dismissed its Section 9 application.
operative_order: Appeal dismissed; no order as to costs.
summary: Jindal Steel & Power, a tenant of DCM International under a Memorandum of Understanding concerning certain premises, filed a Section 9 application against DCM International as Corporate Debtor, which NCLT dismissed. On appeal, NCLAT held that a tenant's claim arising merely from a landlord-tenant relationship or an MOU regarding premises - without any provision of goods or services by the claimant, or statutory dues owed by the Corporate Debtor - does not constitute an 'operational debt' under Section 5(21) of the IBC. Since the Appellant made no such qualifying claim, it did not fall within the definition of 'Operational Creditor' under Section 5(20), and its Section 9 application was rightly dismissed. The appeal was dismissed with no order as to costs.

case_title: M/s. Annapurna Infrastructure Pvt. Ltd. & Anr. vs M/s. SORIL Infra Resources Ltd.
bench: New Delhi (arising from NCLT Principal Bench, New Delhi, C.P. No. (IB)-22(PB)/2017)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: M/s. Annapurna Infrastructure Pvt. Ltd. and another are the Appellants (lessors), claiming to be Operational Creditors; M/s. SORIL Infra Resources Ltd. is the Corporate Debtor/Respondent (lessee). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: the Appellants leased premises to the Respondent under a Lease Deed dated 23rd November 2005, with rent payable by the Respondent; upon non-payment, the parties invoked the arbitration clause and, pursuant to a Delhi High Court order, Hon'ble Justice (Dr) Mukundakam Sharma (Retd.) was appointed Sole Arbitrator. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: the Arbitrator passed an award on 9th September 2016 granting the Appellants Rs. 2,67,52,283 for rent from 1.4.2008 to 22.3.2010 with 12% interest from 23.3.2010, Rs. 1,11,56,145 as damages equivalent to six months' rent, and future interest at 12% per annum until realization. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: the award was passed on 9th September 2016; Respondent's Section 34 application to set aside the award was dismissed on 19th December 2016; Appellants issued a Section 8 demand notice on 13th January 2017; Respondent replied on 27th January 2017 disputing the operational debt and citing a pending Section 37 appeal (FAO(OS)(COMM) 20 of 2017) against the Section 34 dismissal, along with pending execution proceedings before the Delhi High Court (listed for 12.5.2017); NCLT Principal Bench rejected the Section 9 application by order dated 24th March 2017. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: the arbitral award itself, the Section 34 dismissal order dated 19th December 2016, the Respondent's reply dated 27th January 2017 disputing the debt and citing the pending Section 37 appeal, and evidence of pending execution proceedings for enforcement of the award before the Delhi High Court. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appellants filed a Section 9 application before NCLT Principal Bench, New Delhi; NCLT rejected the application by order dated 24th March 2017, holding that a 'dispute' was pending (via the Section 37 appeal) and that the pendency of execution proceedings barred simultaneous invocation of the IBC as an alternative remedy; Appellants appealed to NCLAT.
legal_issues: (i) Whether an 'existence of dispute' under Section 8(2)(a) of the IBC persists where an arbitral award has been affirmed under Section 34 but an appeal under Section 37 of the Arbitration Act remains pending; (ii) whether pendency of execution proceedings to enforce an arbitral award bars an Operational Creditor from simultaneously invoking the IBC; (iii) whether a lessor claiming unpaid rent under a lease deed qualifies as an 'Operational Creditor' under Section 5(20) read with Section 5(21) of the IBC.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Under Section 5(6) read with Section 8(2)(a) of the IBC, 'existence of dispute' is constituted specifically by the pendency of a suit or arbitration proceeding relating to the debt - not by the pendency of a post-award challenge such as an application under Section 34 or an appeal under Section 37 of the Arbitration Act, since arbitration proceedings conclude upon the arbitral award under Section 32 of the Arbitration Act, and subsequent challenge proceedings are separate remedies, not a continuation of the arbitration itself. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Form 5 of the Adjudicating Authority Rules (Part V) expressly lists 'particulars of an order of a court, tribunal or arbitral panel adjudicating on the default' as a document/record of default for a Section 9 application, confirming that an arbitral award (even where a Section 34 or 37 challenge remains pending) constitutes valid evidence of debt and default under the IBC, consistent with the Tribunal's earlier ruling in Kirusa Software vs. Mobilox Innovations. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Insolvency Resolution Process is not a money suit for recovery or an execution proceeding for a decree/award (as distinct from Section 36 of the Arbitration Act, which governs execution); accordingly, the pendency of separate execution proceedings to enforce an arbitral award does not bar an Operational Creditor from independently invoking Section 9 of the IBC for the underlying default, and there is no 'single remedy' principle under the IBC analogous to Section 10 CPC that would preclude parallel pursuit of execution and insolvency proceedings. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Adjudicating Authority erred in treating the pending Section 37 appeal as an 'existing dispute' and in holding that pending execution proceedings barred the Section 9 application as an impermissible alternative/parallel remedy; however, since the Adjudicating Authority had not yet decided whether the lessor-Appellant, whose claim arose from unpaid rent under a lease deed, qualifies as an 'Operational Creditor' under Section 5(20)/5(21) (a claim requiring the debt to arise from provision of goods/services or statutory dues), that threshold question - along with completeness of the application - was left open for the Adjudicating Authority to determine on remand.
operative_order: Impugned order dated 24th March 2017 set aside; case remitted to NCLT, Principal Bench, New Delhi to decide (i) whether the 1st Appellant is an 'Operational Creditor' under Section 5(20)/5(21), and (ii) if so, whether the Section 9 application is complete for admission, granting seven days to cure defects if incomplete, per the proviso to Section 9; appeal allowed with these observations, without expressing any opinion on the operational-creditor and completeness questions, to be decided afresh after notice to parties, uninfluenced by the impugned order; no order as to costs.
summary: Lessors sought to trigger insolvency proceedings against their tenant, SORIL Infra Resources, based on an arbitral award for unpaid rent that had survived a Section 34 challenge, though a Section 37 appeal remained pending and execution proceedings were also underway. NCLT rejected the Section 9 application, holding a 'dispute' was still pending via the Section 37 appeal and that pursuing execution proceedings barred simultaneous recourse to the IBC. NCLAT held both grounds erroneous: arbitration proceedings conclude at the award stage under Section 32 of the Arbitration Act, so a pending post-award appeal does not constitute an 'existing dispute' under Section 8(2)(a); and the IBC's insolvency resolution process is not a recovery or execution mechanism, so pending execution proceedings for the same award do not bar a parallel Section 9 application. However, NCLAT declined to rule on whether the lessor qualified as an 'Operational Creditor' given rent arrears (a question NCLT had not reached), and remitted the case for that determination and for assessment of the application's completeness.

case_title: Mrs. Sonia Khosla (through L.R.) vs Mr. Sameer Kudsia & Ors.
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) No. 36 of 2016 along with Company Appeals (AT) Nos. 43 to 47 of 2016
bench: New Delhi (arising from NCLT New Delhi Bench, C.P. No. 114/2007, orders in C.A. Nos. 50, 51, 52, 53, 54 and 59/C-III/2016)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Mrs. Sonia Khosla (through legal representative) is the original Petitioner/Appellant, a Director and shareholder of the Respondent company; Mr. Sameer Kudsia and others (including Mr. Vikram Bakshi and family members) are Respondents, including a Chartered Accountant, an ex-Director, and an ex-Company Secretary named in various applications. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: the underlying dispute concerns a real estate development project in Village Mashobra/Chattiyan, governed by an Agreement dated 31st March 2006 between the 'Khosla Family' and 'VB and the company' (per Clause 29 of the Agreement, containing an arbitration clause), with allegations that Respondent No. 2 and associates diverted project lands, issued additional shares improperly, and changed the project's nature without Board approval. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: not applicable - this is an oppression and mismanagement dispute under Sections 397, 398, 402 and 403 of the Companies Act 1956, not a debt/default matter. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: the original Company Petition No. 114 of 2007 was filed before the erstwhile Company Law Board, transferred to NCLT New Delhi w.e.f. 1st June 2016 under Section 434(1)(a) of the Companies Act 2013; a Section 11 Arbitration Act application resulted in a Delhi High Court order dated 29th February 2008 appointing two arbitrators; the impugned NCLT orders under appeal were dated 20th October 2016 (CA No. 50/2016), 15th November 2016 (CA Nos. 51, 52, 53, 54/2016), and 5th December 2016 (CA No. 59/2016); the Company Petition remained pending for approximately 10 years with about 49 interlocutory applications pending as of the NCLAT hearing. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: the appellant sought interrogatories and later witness summons against the same three individuals (a Chartered Accountant, an ex-Director, and an ex-Company Secretary) in relation to an allegedly illegal allotment of 10,000 additional shares to the family of Respondent No. 2; NCLT found the interrogatory requests to be a roving, exhaustive-trial-like fishing expedition and rejected them; the appellant's subsequent review/recall application and repeated witness-summons applications targeting the same individuals were also rejected by NCLT as impermissible attempts to relitigate the same issue. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT rejected the appellant's interrogatory application (CA No. 50/2016) by order dated 20th October 2016; rejected the appellant's review/recall application (CA No. 51/2016) and a repeat witness-summons application (CA No. 53/2016) by order dated 15th November 2016 (also disposing of CA No. 54/2016, a Respondent application relating to disposal sequencing); and disposed of another application by order dated 5th December 2016 (CA No. 59/2016); the appellant filed these connected appeals challenging all these orders before NCLAT.
legal_issues: (i) Whether NCLT correctly rejected the appellant's application for interrogatories and subsequent repeat application to summon the same witnesses as an impermissible fishing expedition; (ii) whether NCLT had jurisdiction to review or recall its own orders; (iii) whether a long-pending Section 8 Arbitration and Conciliation Act application (filed in 2007) survives or becomes infructuous where a subsequent Section 11 application resulted in appointment of arbitrators by the High Court in 2008; (iv) the appropriate case-management approach for disposing of approximately 49 pending interlocutory applications accumulated over a decade in a single oppression-and-mismanagement petition.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A tribunal properly rejects interrogatory or witness-summons requests that amount to a roving, exhaustive fishing expedition (seeking communications, remunerations, private conversations, etc. of named individuals) rather than targeted, relevant inquiry, and a party cannot repeatedly relitigate the same request for the same witnesses/interrogatories after an earlier rejection by recharacterizing the request in a different procedural form. NCLT/Tribunals constituted under the Companies Act possess no inherent power to review or recall their own final orders absent express statutory conferral. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Where a Section 8 Arbitration and Conciliation Act application (seeking reference to arbitration) has been rendered moot by the subsequent invocation of Section 11 of the same Act (resulting in actual appointment of arbitrators by the High Court and commencement of arbitral proceedings), the earlier Section 8 application becomes infructuous and should be closed rather than left pending indefinitely; a Tribunal's failure to notice such a subsequent procedural development and account for it in disposing of connected applications constitutes an oversight warranting correction on appeal. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Following the Supreme Court's guidance in National Council for Cement & Building Materials, D.P. Maheshwari, and Revajeetu Builders on curbing dilatory litigation tactics (frivolous preliminary objections, indiscriminate amendment applications), a Tribunal should decide all issues together at final hearing rather than permit piecemeal, repeated interlocutory applications - especially belated amendment or impleadment applications filed years after the original petition - to indefinitely delay adjudication of the substantive petition; Section 422 of the Companies Act's mandate for expeditious disposal (within three months, or with recorded reasons and Presidential consent for extension) reinforces this approach. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: NCLT's rejections of the interrogatory application, the review/recall application, and the repeat witness-summons application were correctly decided and upheld; however, NCLT and the earlier Company Law Board erred in allowing the Section 8 Arbitration Act application to remain pending for a decade without noticing its own subsequent Section 11 proceedings had rendered it infructuous - that application (and connected applications) should be closed; numerous other long-pending, belated, or repetitive interlocutory applications (amendment petitions, impleadment applications, interim-relief applications duplicating final relief sought in the main petition, and repeated witness-summons applications) were similarly directed to be closed, with only the perjury-related Section 340 CrPC applications reserved for consideration at final hearing alongside the main petition, which was directed to be heard and disposed of expeditiously.
operative_order: The impugned orders dated 20th October 2016, 15th November 2016 and 5th December 2016 are upheld; the appeals are dismissed as to the grievances raised against them. Additionally, NCLAT directs: the Section 8 Arbitration Act application (CA No. 362 of 2007) and connected applications (CA Nos. 171/2008, and those in Counter Reference No. 822 and CA No. 52/2016) are held infructuous and to be closed by the Tribunal; various specified belated amendment, impleadment, clarification, review/recall, and repeat witness-summons applications (including CA Nos. 46/2016, 47/2016, 270/2009, 421/2009, 163/2008, 418/2009, 81/2014, 114/2014, 130/2014, 44/2016, and others) are to be closed/rejected by the Tribunal as detailed; certain interim-relief applications duplicating final reliefs sought in the main petition are also to be closed, to be considered only at final hearing if the petition succeeds; perjury-related Section 340 CrPC applications are reserved for consideration at final hearing together with the main Company Petition; the Tribunal is directed to complete hearing of the Company Petition expeditiously, preferably within one month, with parties directed to cooperate and avoid unnecessary adjournments. No order as to costs.
summary: In a decade-old oppression and mismanagement petition involving a real estate joint venture, the petitioner (through her legal representative) appealed several NCLT orders rejecting her repeated attempts to obtain interrogatories and witness summons against the same three individuals, and rejecting her application to review/recall an earlier order. NCLAT upheld all these rejections, finding the interrogatory requests to be an impermissible fishing expedition and the repeated witness-summons applications an improper attempt to relitigate a settled point, while confirming NCLT has no power to review its own orders. Separately, NCLAT noticed that a long-pending 2007 application under Section 8 of the Arbitration Act had become infructuous once arbitrators were actually appointed pursuant to a 2008 Section 11 application and Delhi High Court order - a development neither the Company Law Board nor NCLT had accounted for over the following decade. Invoking Supreme Court precedent against dilatory litigation tactics, NCLAT directed closure of numerous long-pending, repetitive, or belated interlocutory applications (amendment petitions, impleadment applications, and duplicative interim-relief requests) accumulated over ten years, reserved perjury-related applications for final hearing, and directed NCLT to expeditiously conclude the main petition within about a month.

case_title: Unimark Remedies Ltd. vs. Ashok Alco Chem Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant Unimark Remedies Ltd. (Corporate Debtor) and Respondent Ashok Alco Chem Ltd. (Creditor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Pending winding-up petition under Section 433(e) of the Companies Act, 1956 transferred from Bombay High Court to NCLT Mumbai Bench under Rule 5 of Companies (Transfer of Pending Proceedings) Rules, 2016. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Winding-up petition initiated based on alleged inability to pay debts under Section 433(e) of Companies Act, 1956; exact claimed default amount and date of default not specified in the appellate order. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Central Government issued transfer notification dated 2016-12-07 and substituted Rule 5 via notification dated 2017-06-29 granting time up to 2017-07-15 for compliance. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Substituted Rule 5 notification dated 2017-06-29 presented during proceedings and statement of parties confirming amicable settlement. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai dismissed petition on 2017-02-24 and refused recall on 2017-04-04 treating transferred petition under Section 9 of IBC; Appellant appealed both orders before NCLAT.
legal_issues: Whether a winding-up petition under Section 433(e) of the Companies Act, 1956 transferred under Section 434 of Companies Act, 2013 can automatically be treated as an application under Section 7, 9 or 10 of the IBC, 2016 under Rule 5 of Transfer Rules, and whether the impugned dismissal orders should be set aside in light of substituted Rule 5 and amicable settlement.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Winding-up petitions under Section 433(e) of the Companies Act, 1956 transferred under Section 434 of the Companies Act, 2013 cannot automatically be treated as applications under Section 7, 9, or 10 of the I&B Code without adhering to substituted statutory transfer rules and procedural requirements under Section 239. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 239(1) of I&B Code empowers framing rules regarding I&B Code but does not empower Central Government to transfer cases except under Section 434 of Companies Act, 2013; substituted Rule 5 of Transfer of Pending Proceedings Rules governs transferred winding-up petitions. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Strict compliance with substituted statutory notification requirements and evaluation of post-transfer settlement between parties. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The impugned orders passed under the invalidated earlier Rule 5 were unsustainable and set aside, with no remand needed due to amicable settlement between parties.
operative_order: Impugned orders dated 24th February 2017 and 4th April 2017 passed by NCLT Mumbai Bench are set aside. No remand ordered as parties amicably settled claims; Appellants directed to pay IRP costs as determined by NCLT if any amount is due. Appeal disposed of with no order as to costs.
summary: Unimark Remedies Ltd. appealed against NCLT Mumbai orders dismissing a transferred winding-up petition originally filed by Ashok Alco Chem Ltd. under Section 433(e) of Companies Act, 1956 and refusing recall. The transferred case had been treated as a Section 9 application under the 2016 Transfer Rules. NCLAT noted that Rule 5 was doubted and subsequently substituted by Central Government notification on June 29, 2017. Holding that Section 433(e) petitions cannot automatically convert to IBC applications without statutory power under Section 434, NCLAT set aside the impugned orders. Since parties amicably settled claims, the matter was not remanded, and the appeal was allowed.

case_title: Nirakar Dash & Ors. vs. Durgapur Bio Garden Private Limited & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants 1 to 6 (Nirakar Dash & others) and Appellant 7 are original shareholders/promoters holding 75% equity in Respondent No. 1 (Durgapur Bio Garden Pvt. Ltd.); Respondent No. 2 to 6 are managing shareholders accused of oppression. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Agricultural enterprise incorporated on 2002-12-13 with Appellants subscribing to 5,125 shares each (total 30,750 shares). 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Unlawful exclusion from company management and denial of membership rights; disputed share consideration cheques dated 2007-11-08 against alleged resignation letters dated 2007-03-28. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Appellants received notice from ASREC India Ltd. on 2014-11-15 regarding DRT proceedings and discovered alleged share transfers registered on 2006-05-05/2007-11-07 and Form 32 filings dated 2008-01-07 and 2009-08-25. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Appellants retained possession of original share certificates; Form-7(b) transfer forms lacked execution dates, company name, folio/share numbers, and stamp duty under Article 5(1)(a) Indian Stamp Act; annual returns up to 2012 continuously listed Appellants as directors. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appellants filed CP No. 57/2015 before CLB/NCLT Kolkata alleging oppression and mismanagement under Sections 397/398; NCLT dismissed petition on 2017-03-23 holding it time-barred under Section 113 Limitation Act.
legal_issues: Whether non-compliance with mandatory provisions of Section 108 of Companies Act, 1956 (Section 56 of Companies Act, 2013) invalidates alleged share transfers, and whether a petition alleging continuous oppression and mismanagement by illegal exclusion from shareholding and management is barred by limitation or laches when original share certificates remain in possession of petitioners.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Compliance with Section 108 of the Companies Act, 1956 (Section 56 of Companies Act, 2013) is mandatory for share transfers, and unlawful exclusion of valid share certificate holders relying on incomplete, unstamped, and suspicious transfer instruments constitutes a continuing cause of action for oppression and mismanagement not barred by limitation. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 108 of the 1956 Act requires proper, stamped, and fully executed instruments delivered with original share certificates; failure to fulfill these statutory requirements renders transfers void. Section 17 of Limitation Act applies where fraud and illegalities are concealed. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Suspicions and glaring contradictions on the face of transfer instruments, receipts, and statutory filings destroy the evidentiary value of claimed transfers. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The alleged share transfers and forced resignations were illegal and void, and NCLT erred in dismissing the petition on preliminary grounds of limitation.
operative_order: Impugned judgment of NCLT Kolkata quashed and set aside. Declared that no share transfer occurred from Appellants to Respondents 2 to 6. Quashed ROC filings dated 2009-08-25 and 2014-05-02 recording resignations/transfers. Respondents restrained from obstructing Appellants from participating in company affairs, and Respondents 3 to 6 restrained from interfering in company working. No order as to costs.
summary: Appellants, original shareholders holding 75% shares and original certificates of Durgapur Bio Garden Pvt. Ltd., appealed against NCLT Kolkata's dismissal of their petition under Sections 397/398 of Companies Act, 1956. NCLT had held the petition time-barred. Appellants discovered in 2014 that Respondents fraudulently claimed Appellants transferred shares and resigned in 2007. NCLAT held that Section 108 of the Companies Act, 1956 is mandatory. The alleged transfer forms lacked details, stamps, and share certificates. Holding that deprivation of shareholding rights constitutes a continuous cause of action and that Respondents committed oppression, NCLAT allowed the appeal, quashing the fraudulent transfers and ROC filings.

case_title: Aurosagar Estates Private Limited & Anr. vs. M.C. Davar Holdings Private Limited
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Respondent M.C. Davar Holdings Pvt. Ltd. (Petitioner) and Appellants Aurosagar Estates Pvt. Ltd. (Lessee/Company) and another. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Lease agreement and Inter-Corporate Deposits (ICDs) granted to Appellant Company, with alleged understanding to transfer shares of Appellant Company. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Non-payment of lease installments and failure to transfer shares of 1st Appellant company to AMP Group entities. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Petition under Section 241 filed on 2016-08-22; MA No. 90/2016 filed on 2016-10-04 seeking to amend petition by challenging Articles of Association amendment dated 2012-10-15. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Articles of Association amendment dated 2012-10-15 was known to Respondent and sought to be challenged beyond 3 years after filing of initial petition focused on lease defaults and AGM issues (2007–2015). 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai Bench allowed MA No. 90/2016 on 2017-03-10 permitting substantive amendment to introduce fresh cause of action; Appellants challenged this order before NCLAT.
legal_issues: Whether NCLT has power under Rule 155 of NCLT Rules, 2016 or Companies Act, 2013 to allow substantive amendments introducing a fresh, independent cause of action in a Section 241 petition, and whether Section 433 of Companies Act, 2013 applies Limitation Act, 1963 to bar amendments seeking to agitate a fresh cause of action beyond three years.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: NCLT does not possess wide power to allow substantive amendments to pleadings/prayers that introduce a fresh, distinct cause of action unrelated to original pleadings, especially when such fresh cause of action is barred by limitation under Section 433 of Companies Act, 2013 read with Article 113 of Limitation Act, 1963. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Rule 155 of NCLT Rules, 2016 limits amendment powers strictly to rectifying defects/errors within 30 days for determining real issues in existing proceedings; Section 433 mandatorily applies Limitation Act, 1963 to Tribunal proceedings 'as far as may be'. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Amendments introducing new facts/prayers must be evaluated against the 3-year limitation test from the date cause of action arose (Article 113, Limitation Act). 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The challenge to the Articles of Association amendment of 15th October 2012 was a fresh cause of action raised after three years, making it time-barred and beyond NCLT's jurisdiction to allow via amendment.
operative_order: Impugned order dated 10th March 2017 passed by NCLT Mumbai Bench set aside. NCLT directed to hear and decide the Section 241 petition expeditiously based strictly on original pleadings, reply, and rejoinder, with liberty to peruse documents related to original cause of action. No order as to costs.
summary: M.C. Davar Holdings Pvt. Ltd. filed a Section 241 petition under Companies Act, 2013 against Aurosagar Estates Pvt. Ltd. alleging oppression and mismanagement regarding lease defaults and ICDs. Later, through MA 90/2016, Respondent sought to amend the petition to challenge an amendment to Appellant's Articles of Association made on October 15, 2012. NCLT Mumbai allowed the amendment. On appeal, NCLAT held that Rule 155 of NCLT Rules, 2016 only permits correction of errors/defects, not substantive amendments introducing fresh causes of action. Applying Section 433 of Companies Act, 2013 and Article 113 of Limitation Act, NCLAT ruled the fresh cause of action was time-barred (>3 years old) and set aside NCLT's order.

case_title: MosmetroStroy (FZE) vs. BASF India Ltd. & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant MosmetroStroy (FZE) is the Corporate Debtor and Respondent M/s. BASF India Ltd. is the Operational Creditor[cite: 5]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: The Corporate Debtor purchased chemicals against invoices from the Operational Creditor[cite: 5]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Operational Creditor claimed an outstanding sum of Rs. 1,98,75,342[cite: 5]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Legal notices were issued on 19th August 2015 and 9th September 2015[cite: 5]. Central Government issued a transfer notification on 7th December 2016[cite: 5]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The Corporate Debtor had vacated its Chennai office in mid-May 2015 and returned to Russia[cite: 5]. No notice under Section 8(1) of the IBC was issued in Form-3 or 4 before treating the petition as a Section 9 application[cite: 5]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Original winding up petition (C.P.No. 495 of 2015) was filed before Madras High Court[cite: 5]. It was transferred to NCLT Chennai and admitted as a Section 9 IBC application on 1st September 2017 without providing the Corporate Debtor a proper opportunity to argue[cite: 5].
legal_issues: Whether a winding-up petition under Sections 433 and 434 of the Companies Act, 1956 transferred to the Adjudicating Authority can be treated as an application under Section 9 of the IBC without issuing a demand notice under Section 8(1) of the IBC or filing in Form-5[cite: 5].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A transferred winding-up petition cannot be treated as an application under Section 9 of the IBC unless the creditor complies with the mandatory requirements of the IBC, including the issuance of a demand notice and providing necessary information in the prescribed format[cite: 5]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Rule 5 of the Transfer Rules, 2016 requires the petitioner to submit all necessary information for admission under Sections 7, 8, or 9 of the IBC within sixty days; failure to do so results in the abatement of the petition[cite: 5]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal must verify if a valid Section 8(1) notice was issued and if Form-5 was duly completed with details like the proposed insolvency professional[cite: 5]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because no Section 8(1) notice was issued and Form-5 was not filed, the transferred petition could not be treated as a Section 9 application and stood abated under Rule 5 of the Transfer Rules[cite: 5].
operative_order: The impugned orders dated 1st September 2017 and 29th September 2017 passed by NCLT Chennai are set aside[cite: 5]. The application under Sections 433 and 434 of the Companies Act, 1956 is declared abated[cite: 5]. The Corporate Debtor is released from the rigour of law and allowed to function independently[cite: 5]. Liberty is granted to the Operational Creditor to issue a fresh Section 8 notice[cite: 5].
summary: The Operational Creditor initially filed a winding-up petition against the Corporate Debtor before the Madras High Court, which was transferred to NCLT Chennai and admitted under Section 9 of the IBC[cite: 5]. The Corporate Debtor appealed, arguing they were never served a demand notice under Section 8(1) of the IBC[cite: 5]. The NCLAT held that a transferred winding-up petition cannot be treated as a Section 9 application without strict compliance with IBC procedures, specifically the issuance of a demand notice and submission of required information under Rule 5 of the Transfer Rules, 2016[cite: 5]. Consequently, the NCLAT set aside the admission order, declared the original petition abated, and released the Corporate Debtor from the CIRP[cite: 5].

case_title: M/s. Sabari Inn Pvt. Ltd. vs. M/s. Rameesh Associates Pvt. Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant M/s. Sabari Inn Pvt. Ltd. is the Corporate Debtor and Respondent M/s. Rameesh Associates Pvt. Ltd. is the Operational Creditor[cite: 8]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: The Corporate Debtor entered into a contract with the Respondent Contractor[cite: 8]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The Operational Creditor claimed an outstanding sum of Rs. 12,06,508[cite: 8]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The Operational Creditor issued a legal notice on 7th September 2013[cite: 8]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The Corporate Debtor claims the entire amount was settled and paid[cite: 8]. No demand notice under Section 8(1) of the IBC was issued in Form-3 or 4 prior to the admission of the insolvency petition[cite: 8]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: A winding-up petition (C.P.No. 243 of 2015) was originally filed before the Madras High Court, transferred to NCLT Chennai, and admitted under Section 9 of the IBC on 20th June 2017 without granting the Corporate Debtor time to file a reply[cite: 8].
legal_issues: Whether a transferred winding-up petition can be treated and admitted as an application under Section 9 of the IBC without the Operational Creditor serving a demand notice under Section 8(1) of the IBC in the prescribed format[cite: 8].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Operational creditors must strictly comply with the statutory requirement of delivering a demand notice under Section 8(1) of the IBC in the prescribed format before a transferred winding-up petition can be admitted under Section 9[cite: 8]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Under Rule 5 of the Companies (Transfer of Pending Proceedings) Rules, 2016, petitioners must submit all information required for admission under the IBC; without the Section 8 notice and Form-5 details, the petition abates[cite: 8]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal must check the record for a valid Form-3 or Form-4 demand notice that informs the corporate debtor of the consequences of non-payment[cite: 8]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Since no Section 8(1) notice was issued and the required information in Form-5 was not submitted, the application stood abated and the admission order was illegal[cite: 8].
operative_order: The impugned order dated 20th June 2017 passed by NCLT Chennai is set aside[cite: 8]. The application under Sections 433 and 434 of the Companies Act, 1956 is declared abated[cite: 8]. The Corporate Debtor is released from the rigour of law and all actions of the Interim Resolution Professional are set aside[cite: 8].
summary: M/s. Rameesh Associates Pvt. Ltd. filed a winding-up petition against M/s. Sabari Inn Pvt. Ltd. before the Madras High Court, which was transferred to NCLT Chennai and admitted as a Section 9 application under the IBC[cite: 8]. The Corporate Debtor appealed, contending they never received a demand notice under Section 8(1) of the IBC[cite: 8]. The NCLAT observed that the Operational Creditor failed to issue the mandatory demand notice and did not provide the required details in Form-5 as mandated by the transfer rules[cite: 8]. Consequently, the NCLAT set aside the NCLT's admission order, declared the petition abated, and released the Corporate Debtor from the resolution process[cite: 8].

case_title: Vishwa Nath Singh vs. M/s. Visa Drugs & Pharmaceuticals Pvt. Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant Vishwa Nath Singh is the Director/shareholder of M/s. Swan Aluminiums Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor) and Respondent M/s. Visa Drugs & Pharmaceuticals Pvt. Ltd. is an erstwhile shareholder claiming to be a creditor[cite: 10]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: An unsecured loan/advance was given by the Respondent to the Corporate Debtor without any interest, following a Memorandum of Understanding executed on 18th February 2013[cite: 10]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The exact default amount is not specified, but it arose from an alleged unsecured loan shown in the balance sheet as on 5th December 2013[cite: 10]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Demand notices were sent on 11th August 2016, and the Corporate Debtor replied on 20th September 2016[cite: 10]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The balance sheets for 2014 and 2015 did not show any debt payable to the Respondent[cite: 10]. The unsecured loan was taken without any interest and lacked consideration for the time value of money[cite: 10]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Winding-up petitions were filed before the Punjab and Haryana High Court, transferred to NCLT Chandigarh, and admitted under Section 7 of the IBC on 4th September 2017[cite: 10].
legal_issues: Whether an unsecured loan given by a shareholder without any interest qualifies as a 'financial debt' under Section 5(8) of the IBC, allowing the lender to initiate CIRP as a 'financial creditor' under Section 7[cite: 10].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An interest-free unsecured loan lacking the element of time value of money does not constitute a 'financial debt' under the IBC, and the lender cannot be classified as a 'financial creditor'[cite: 10]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 5(8) of the IBC mandates that a financial debt must be disbursed against the consideration for the time value of money, typically involving the payment of interest or a similar commercial return[cite: 10]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal examines the loan terms to determine if there is a compensation mechanism for the time value of money; mere presence of a loan is insufficient[cite: 10]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Since there was no evidence that the money was borrowed against the payment of interest or time value of money, the Respondent is not a financial creditor, and the Section 7 application is not maintainable[cite: 10].
operative_order: The impugned orders dated 4th September and 18th September 2017 passed by NCLT Chandigarh are set aside[cite: 10]. The application under Sections 433 and 434 is declared abated and the Corporate Debtor is released from the resolution process to function independently[cite: 10].
summary: The Respondent, an erstwhile shareholder, filed a winding-up petition for an unpaid unsecured loan against the Corporate Debtor, which was transferred to NCLT Chandigarh and admitted as a Section 7 IBC application[cite: 10]. The Corporate Debtor's director appealed to the NCLAT[cite: 10]. The NCLAT observed that the loan in question was unsecured and interest-free, failing to meet the core requirement of 'financial debt' under Section 5(8) of the IBC, which requires disbursement against the consideration for the time value of money[cite: 10]. Consequently, the NCLAT ruled that the Respondent was not a 'financial creditor', set aside the NCLT's admission orders, and released the Corporate Debtor from the insolvency proceedings[cite: 10].

case_title: M/s. Therm Flow Engineers Private Limited & Ors. vs. Mr. Bhavesh Narumalani & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Petitioner Bhavesh Narumalani (25% initial shareholder) vs. M/s. Therm Flow Engineers Pvt. Ltd. (1st Respondent Company) and Respondent Nos. 2 & 3 (Managing Shareholders/Directors). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Equity shares of 1st Respondent Company issued and allotted to Respondent Nos. 4 to 11 without notice or offer to Petitioner, reducing Petitioner's shareholding from 25% to 8.33%. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Share capital increased from Rs. 1.00 lac to Rs. 2.00 lacs on 2009-12-21 and to Rs. 3.00 lacs on 2010-09-28; shares issued at Rs. 10 base value despite intrinsic fair value exceeding Rs. 3,000–5,900 per share (discount of over 99.7%). 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Allotment resolutions passed on 2010-01-29, 2011-01-18, and 2013-07-04; Petitioner discovered dilution upon receiving board meeting notices in June 2015. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: No notices of EGM or Board meetings were served on Petitioner; Annual Returns filed late; short-term borrowings taken from Narayanbhai Patel Group to purchase listed shares of Patel Air Temp Ltd. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Petitioner filed TP No. 106/397-398/NCLT/AHM/2016 before NCLT Ahmedabad; NCLT set aside share capital increases and allotments on 2017-03-15; both parties filed cross-appeals before NCLAT.
legal_issues: Whether the crucial date for testing maintainability under Section 399 of Companies Act is the date of alleged oppression when shareholding was illegally diluted, and whether allotment of shares to related parties at deep discounts without notice constitutes oppression.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: When a member's shareholding is illegally diluted below the 10% threshold without notice or opportunity, the petition's maintainability under Section 397/398 (Section 241) is evaluated as of the date the oppressive act occurred, not the date of petition filing. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Mandatory provisions of Companies Act and Articles requiring written notice for Board/General meetings cannot be bypassed; allotments without notice violate statutory rights. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Unsubstantiated claims of oral leave of absence or unproven service of notices fail to validate oppressive share issuance. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The dilution of shareholding via unnotified allotments at nominal prices constituted severe oppression, justifying setting aside the allotments and share transfers.
operative_order: Cross-appeals (Company Appeal (AT) No. 159 of 2017 and Company Appeal (AT) No. 198 of 2017) are dismissed. NCLT order setting aside increases in share capital, setting aside share allotments to Respondents 4 to 11, setting aside transfer of shares to Respondents 2 and 3, and ordering re-allotment of Respondent 12's shares is affirmed. No order as to costs.
summary: Bhavesh Narumalani held 25% equity in Therm Flow Engineers Pvt. Ltd., which was diluted to 8.33% through increases in share capital and allotments to Respondents 4 to 11 at Rs. 10/share despite fair values exceeding Rs. 3,000–5,900/share. NCLT Ahmedabad found this to be oppression and set aside the share capital increases and allotments. On appeal, NCLAT held that maintainability under Section 399 must be determined as of the date of oppression when dilution occurred. Affirming that allotments made without notice and at huge discounts constituted oppression, NCLAT dismissed both cross-appeals.

case_title: Upper India Steel Manufacturing and Engineering Co. Ltd. & Ors. vs. Gurlal Singh Grewal & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants Upper India Steel Manufacturing and Engineering Co. Ltd. & Ors. (Majority group/Company) and Respondents Gurlal Singh Grewal & Ors. (Petitioners/Minority group). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Minority shareholders filed CP No. 49/2007 alleging oppression, non-payment of dividend, reduction of directors, and excess remuneration under Section 314 of 1956 Act. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Claimed oppression through reduced representation and alleged excess salary under Section 314; NCLT ordered refund under Sec 314 and directed buyout of minority shares at fair value as on 2007-03-31 with compound interest at bank rate + 2%. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CP filed in April 2007 before CLB and transferred to NCLT Chandigarh under Sec 434(1)(a) of 2013 Act; NCLT judgment passed on 2017-03-01. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Minority group continued receiving dividends till 2011, held seats on the Board, and 1st Petitioner received full salary as Whole Time Director without contributing work. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT found no oppression but directed share buyout with compound interest and asset-based valuation; both parties appealed to NCLAT.
legal_issues: Whether NCLT has jurisdiction under Section 242 of Companies Act, 2013 to direct share buyouts, fix historical valuation dates, or grant compound interest when it explicitly finds that no case of oppression and mismanagement has been established.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Under Section 242 of the Companies Act, 2013, a tribunal derives jurisdiction to grant consequential directions (such as share buyouts or share transfers) ONLY IF it first arrives at a definite finding that the company's affairs are being conducted in an oppressive or prejudicial manner. 2.
