STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 242(1) & (2) requires a threshold finding of oppression/mismanagement to trigger statutory powers; absent such a finding, the tribunal lacks power to order share buyouts or interest. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Awarding compound interest at bank rate + 2% without statutory authority or specific prayer is unsustainable under Interest Act, 1978. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because petitioners failed to prove oppression and mismanagement, NCLT had no jurisdiction to order share buyouts, valuation, or interest.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) No. 150 of 2017 is allowed in part; directions regarding share buyout, share valuation date, payment of compound interest, and findings on dividend whittling are set aside. Findings rejecting oppression and mismanagement are upheld. Company Appeal (AT) No. 189 of 2017 is dismissed. No costs.
summary: Minority shareholders filed an oppression petition against Upper India Steel Manufacturing Co. Ltd. NCLT Chandigarh found that no case of oppression and mismanagement was established, but nevertheless ordered the majority to buy out the minority's shares based on 2007 valuation with compound interest. Both parties appealed. NCLAT held that under Section 242 of the Companies Act, 2013, the Tribunal has no jurisdiction to issue directions like share buyouts or grant compound interest unless a definite finding of oppression and mismanagement is first recorded. Consequently, NCLAT set aside the buyout and interest directions while affirming the dismissal of the oppression charges.

case_title: Nishal Rajsakha vs. BND Fashions Pvt. Ltd. & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant Nishal Rajsakha (Petitioner) and Respondents BND Fashions Pvt. Ltd. & Ors.[cite: 11] 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Claim of membership and shareholding rights in the 1st Respondent Company.[cite: 11] 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The specific default amount is not quantified; the core dispute centers on the appellant's unrecorded name in the register of members.[cite: 11] 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The NCLT order was passed on 10th March 2017.[cite: 11] 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The appellant's name was not recorded in the register of shareholders/members of the company.[cite: 11] 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Original Respondents 2 and 3 filed I.A.No 11/2016 challenging maintainability.[cite: 11] NCLT Ahmedabad dismissed the company petition (TP-136/2016) on 10th March 2017, holding the petitioner was not entitled to become a member.[cite: 11] Appellant subsequently appealed to NCLAT.[cite: 11]
legal_issues: Whether a composite petition under Sections 397 and 398 of the Companies Act, 1956 and Section 59 of the Companies Act, 2013 is maintainable when the petitioner's name is not entered in the register of members, and whether the Tribunal should decide the merits of a Section 59 claim if the main petition is dismissed as non-maintainable.[cite: 11]
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A petition alleging oppression and mismanagement is not maintainable if the petitioner is not a qualified member whose name is entered in the register of members.[cite: 11] Furthermore, a tribunal cannot adjudicate merits on connected statutory claims if the primary petition itself is not maintainable.[cite: 11] 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 399 of the Companies Act, 1956 (Section 244 of 2013 Act) strictly requires the applicant to be a qualified member to file under Sections 397 and 398 (Sections 241 and 242 of 2013 Act).[cite: 11] 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal strictly verified the register of members to determine locus standi before entertaining the merits of the allegations.[cite: 11] 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The petition under Sections 397 and 398 was not maintainable due to lack of membership, and consequently, the NCLT had no jurisdiction to give findings on the merits of the Section 59 claim.[cite: 11]
operative_order: The observations of NCLT Ahmedabad regarding the merits of the application under Section 59 of the Companies Act, 2013 are set aside.[cite: 11] The order dated 10th March 2017 is modified to that extent.[cite: 11] The application preferred by the appellant under Sections 397 and 398 is dismissed.[cite: 11] Appellant is given liberty to seek appropriate relief before a competent court.[cite: 11]
summary: Nishal Rajsakha appealed an NCLT Ahmedabad order dismissing his composite petition under Sections 397/398 of the 1956 Act and Section 59 of the 2013 Act against BND Fashions Pvt. Ltd.[cite: 11] The NCLT found he was not a member and therefore lacked standing.[cite: 11] NCLAT upheld the dismissal of the Sections 397/398 petition because his name was not in the register of members, failing Section 399 criteria.[cite: 11] However, NCLAT set aside NCLT's findings on the merits of the Section 59 claim, holding that if a petition is not maintainable, the Tribunal cannot decide its merits.[cite: 11]

case_title: M/s. Paharpur Cooling Towers Limited vs. Dalmia Cement (Bharat) Limited
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant M/s. Paharpur Cooling Towers Limited (Petitioner) and Respondent Dalmia Cement (Bharat) Limited.[cite: 12] 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Underlying corporate debt leading to a winding up petition.[cite: 12] 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Inability to pay debts under Section 433(e) of the Companies Act, 1956; specific amount not detailed in the appellate order.[cite: 12] 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The NCLT rejected the transfer application on 6th July 2017.[cite: 12] The Second Amendment Rules set a deadline of 15th July 2017 for compliance.[cite: 12] 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The Appellant relied on the First Amended Rules, which allowed a six-month extension for transferring cases, but the NCLT rejected the application for failing to take steps under Rule 5.[cite: 12] 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: A winding up petition was pending before the High Court and transferred.[cite: 12] The NCLT rejected the transfer application on 6th July 2017.[cite: 12] The NCLAT noted that the 15th July 2017 deadline under the Second Amendment had since passed, making a remand futile.[cite: 12]
legal_issues: Whether the NCLT erred in rejecting the transfer application on 6th July 2017 before the 15th July 2017 deadline introduced by the Second Amendment Rules, and whether relief can be granted after the statutory deadline has expired.[cite: 12]
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Even if an adjudicating authority prematurely rejects a transfer application before a statutory deadline, an appellate tribunal cannot grant further time to comply with transfer rules if the statutory deadline has already expired during the pendency of the appeal.[cite: 12] 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The Companies (Transfer of Pending Proceedings) Second Amendment Rules, 2017 mandated compliance for transferred winding-up petitions by 15th July 2017, after which non-compliant petitions abate.[cite: 12] 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal verified the chronological sequence of the impugned order (6th July) against the absolute statutory deadline (15th July).[cite: 12] 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Although the Appellant should have been allowed time until 15th July 2017, setting aside the impugned order would be of no avail because no further time could be granted beyond the expired deadline; instead, the Appellant must file a fresh IBC application.[cite: 12]
operative_order: The appeal is disposed of without setting aside the impugned order.[cite: 12] The Appellant is allowed to file a fresh application under Section 7 or Section 9 of the IBC in accordance with the second proviso to the Second Amendment Rule 5.[cite: 12] If filing under Section 9, a Section 8 notice must be provided.[cite: 12] The application cannot be dismissed on the ground of limitation.[cite: 12] No order as to costs.[cite: 12]
summary: M/s. Paharpur Cooling Towers Ltd. appealed against the NCLT's rejection of its transferred winding-up petition against Dalmia Cement (Bharat) Ltd. on 6th July 2017.[cite: 12] The NCLAT observed that under the Second Amendment Rules, the Appellant should have had until 15th July 2017 to comply.[cite: 12] However, because the 15th July deadline had already passed by the time of the appellate decision, the NCLAT concluded that setting aside the NCLT order would be futile as no further time could be granted.[cite: 12] The NCLAT disposed of the appeal by granting the Appellant liberty to file a fresh application under Section 7 or 9 of the IBC, protecting it from limitation objections.[cite: 12]

case_title: Transparent Technologies Pvt. Ltd. vs. Multi Trade
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant Transparent Technologies Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor) and Respondent Multi Trade (Operational Creditor).[cite: 13] 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Underlying commercial dispute resulting in an inability to pay debts.[cite: 13] 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Winding up petition based on inability to pay debts; specific default amount not mentioned.[cite: 13] 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Original winding up petition filed on 12th April 2016.[cite: 13] NCLT admission order passed on 17th August 2017.[cite: 13] 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The Operational Creditor did not issue a demand notice under Section 8(1) of the IBC, nor was a copy of Form 5 served on the Corporate Debtor.[cite: 13] 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Multi Trade filed a winding up petition before the Bombay High Court.[cite: 13] The matter was transferred to NCLT Mumbai, which treated it as a Section 9 IBC application and admitted it on 17th August 2017 based solely on the reply to the old Section 434 notice.[cite: 13] The Corporate Debtor appealed to NCLAT.[cite: 13]
legal_issues: Whether a transferred winding-up petition can be treated and admitted as an application under Section 9 of the IBC without the Operational Creditor serving a demand notice under Section 8(1) of the IBC and filing the requisite Form 5.[cite: 13]
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A transferred winding-up petition cannot be treated as a valid application under Section 9 of the IBC unless the creditor complies with mandatory statutory requirements, including the issuance of a Section 8(1) demand notice and the submission of required information in Form 5.[cite: 13] 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Rule 5 of the Companies (Transfer of Pending Proceedings) Rules, 2016 requires the petitioner to submit all necessary information for admission under Sections 7, 8, or 9 of the IBC; without this, the petition abates.[cite: 13] 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal found nothing on record to suggest that a Section 8(1) notice was issued and served or that Form 5 was filed, invalidating the NCLT's reliance on a reply to an old Section 434 notice.[cite: 13] 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Due to the absence of the mandatory Section 8 notice and requisite information under Rule 5, the application could not be admitted under Section 9 and must be dismissed.[cite: 13]
operative_order: The impugned order dated 17th August 2017 passed by NCLT Mumbai is set aside.[cite: 13] The application preferred by the Respondent is dismissed.[cite: 13] All actions taken by the Interim Resolution Professional, including the moratorium and freezing of accounts, are declared illegal and set aside.[cite: 13] The Corporate Debtor is released from all rigors of law to function independently.[cite: 13] No order as to costs.[cite: 13]
summary: Multi Trade filed a winding-up petition against Transparent Technologies Pvt. Ltd. before the Bombay High Court, which was transferred to NCLT Mumbai and admitted as a Section 9 IBC application.[cite: 13] The Corporate Debtor appealed, arguing that no demand notice under Section 8(1) of the IBC was issued and Form 5 was not filed.[cite: 13] The NCLAT held that under Rule 5 of the Transfer Rules, a transferred petition cannot be treated as a Section 9 application without strict compliance with IBC procedures, specifically the Section 8 demand notice and Form 5 submission.[cite: 13] Consequently, the NCLAT set aside the CIRP admission order and released the Corporate Debtor.[cite: 13]

case_title: MSP Paper Mill Pvt. Ltd. vs. Arjun Chemicals Pvt. Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant Mr. M.S. Palanivel (Ex-Director of Corporate Debtor MSP Paper Mill Pvt. Ltd.) and Respondent Arjun Chemicals Pvt. Ltd. (Operational Creditor).[cite: 15] 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Underlying commercial supply dispute; part of the payment was made when the matter was pending before the High Court.[cite: 15] 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Claim based on inability to pay debts under Section 433(e) of the 1956 Act; specific amount not detailed.[cite: 15] 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The NCLT admission order was passed on 28th July 2017.[cite: 15] 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The Respondent admitted that no demand notice under Section 8(1) of the IBC was issued in Form 3 or Form 4 prior to admission.[cite: 15] 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: A winding up petition was filed before the High Court, transferred to NCLT Chennai, and admitted as a Section 9 IBC application on 28th July 2017.[cite: 15] The ex-director of the Corporate Debtor appealed to NCLAT.[cite: 15]
legal_issues: Whether a transferred winding-up petition can be treated and admitted as an application under Section 9 of the IBC without the Operational Creditor serving a mandatory demand notice under Section 8(1) of the IBC.[cite: 15]
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Operational creditors must strictly comply with the statutory requirement of delivering a demand notice under Section 8(1) of the IBC before a transferred winding-up petition can be admitted under Section 9.[cite: 15] 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Rule 5 of the Companies (Transfer of Pending Proceedings) Rules, 2016 requires the submission of all necessary information, including the Section 8 notice and Form-5 details; failure renders the application incomplete and abated.[cite: 15] 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal relied on the Respondent's own admission that the mandatory Section 8(1) notice in Form 3 or Form 4 was never issued.[cite: 15] 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because no Section 8(1) notice was issued, the application was incomplete and stood abated, rendering the NCLT's admission order illegal.[cite: 15]
operative_order: The impugned order dated 28th July 2017 passed by NCLT Chennai is set aside.[cite: 15] The application under Section 433 of the Companies Act, 1956 is declared abated and dismissed.[cite: 15] All actions of the Interim Resolution Professional, including the moratorium, are set aside.[cite: 15] The Corporate Debtor is released to function independently.[cite: 15] Liberty is granted to the Respondent to issue a fresh Section 8 notice and file under Section 9 if there is debt, default, and no pre-existing dispute.[cite: 15] No order as to costs.[cite: 15]
summary: Arjun Chemicals Pvt. Ltd. filed a winding-up petition against MSP Paper Mill Pvt. Ltd., which was transferred to NCLT Chennai and admitted as a Section 9 application under the IBC.[cite: 15] An ex-director of the Corporate Debtor appealed, arguing that no demand notice under Section 8(1) of the IBC had been issued.[cite: 15] The Respondent conceded this fact.[cite: 15] Relying on Rule 5 of the Transfer Rules and precedent, the NCLAT held that an application without the mandatory Section 8 demand notice is incomplete.[cite: 15] Consequently, the NCLAT set aside the admission order, declared the petition abated, and released the Corporate Debtor from the CIRP, granting the Respondent liberty to initiate fresh proceedings.[cite: 15]

case_title: Mintri Tea Company Limited vs. Punjab National Bank
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant Mintri Tea Company Limited (Corporate Debtor) and Respondent Punjab National Bank (Financial Creditor)[cite: 16]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Underlying term loan and other credit facilities extended to the Corporate Debtor, which were subsequently restructured on 25th September 2013[cite: 16]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The Financial Creditor claimed a default of Rs. 10,37,69,840.06 in the IBC petition, compared to an earlier demand of Rs. 7,62,64,904.80 calculated five months prior on 6th February 2017[cite: 16]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: SARFAESI notice was issued demanding payment within 60 days prior to restructuring; the Section 7 IBC application was filed subsequently[cite: 16]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The Corporate Debtor did not deny the existence of the debt or the occurrence of the default, but challenged the Section 7 application solely on the basis of the mismatch in the calculated default amount[cite: 16]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Kolkata admitted the Section 7 application on 20th September 2017; the Corporate Debtor and its shareholders appealed to the NCLAT[cite: 16].
legal_issues: Whether a mismatch or dispute regarding the exact quantum of the claimed default amount is a valid ground to reject an application under Section 7 of the IBC when the existence of the debt and the occurrence of a default are undisputed[cite: 16].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Under Section 7 of the IBC, an application by a financial creditor must be admitted if the adjudicating authority is satisfied that a default has occurred and the debt is due; a dispute over the exact quantum of the debt does not bar admission[cite: 16]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 7(5) mandates admission upon satisfaction of default; relying on the Supreme Court's ruling in Innovative Industries Ltd., the debt need only be 'due' (payable in law and fact), and variations in claim calculations involving interest do not negate the underlying default[cite: 16]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal reviewed the records to confirm that the financial creditor's calculations included interest up to the date of filing, establishing that a debt was due and a default had objectively occurred[cite: 16]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because the Corporate Debtor did not dispute the occurrence of the default or the payability of the debt, the NCLT correctly admitted the application despite the mismatch in the claimed amounts[cite: 16].
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed[cite: 16]. The NCLT Kolkata's order admitting the Section 7 application and appointing the Interim Resolution Professional is affirmed[cite: 16]. No order as to costs[cite: 16].
summary: Punjab National Bank filed a Section 7 IBC application against Mintri Tea Company Limited. The Corporate Debtor appealed against the NCLT Kolkata's admission order, arguing that the default amount claimed (Rs. 10.37 Crores) mismatched an earlier demand (Rs. 7.62 Crores) made five months prior. The NCLAT held that under Section 7, the adjudicating authority merely needs to be satisfied that a debt is due and a default has occurred. Since the Corporate Debtor did not dispute the existence of the default itself, disputes over the exact quantum (due to interest calculations) do not prevent the admission of the insolvency petition. The appeal was dismissed[cite: 16].

case_title: K. Muthusamy vs. N. Sankaranarayana & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant K. Muthusamy (Respondent in original CLB petition) and Respondent N. Sankaranarayanan (Original 6th Respondent/Applicant for execution)[cite: 17]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Management of company affairs subject to a prior Company Law Board (CLB) decree dated 25th February 2009[cite: 17]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Non-execution of the CLB's 2009 order directing a Chartered Accountant to investigate financial transactions and submit a report[cite: 17]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Original CLB order passed on 2009-02-25; affirmed by Madras High Court on 2011-02-21; execution application later transferred to NCLT Chennai[cite: 17]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The Applicant (6th Respondent) filed for execution under Section 634A of the 1956 Act because the original CLB order had not been enforced; the Appellant contested the Applicant's locus standi as he was not the direct beneficiary of the order[cite: 17]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Chennai ruled the execution application was maintainable but premature, directing the Chartered Accountant to submit the report within two months, while granting liberty to file for execution later. The Appellant challenged this locus standi ruling before NCLAT[cite: 17].
legal_issues: Whether a party to a company petition who is not the direct beneficiary of the final order/decree has the locus standi to file an application for execution under Section 634A of the Companies Act, 1956 (now Section 424(3) of the Companies Act, 2013)[cite: 17].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Any party to a company petition, regardless of whether they are the petitioner, respondent, or direct beneficiary, has the locus standi to bring to the Tribunal's notice that its order has not been enforced and seek its execution[cite: 17]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 424(3) of the Companies Act, 2013 (formerly Section 634A of the 1956 Act) empowers the Tribunal to enforce its orders as decrees of a court; this provision does not restrict the right to seek enforcement solely to the beneficiary of the order[cite: 17]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal confirmed the party's status as a respondent in the original proceedings, establishing sufficient standing to seek enforcement of the court's prior unexecuted directives[cite: 17]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The 6th Respondent was entitled to file the execution application, and the NCLT correctly held that while the specific application was premature, the locus standi was valid and the underlying directives (CA report) must proceed[cite: 17].
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed[cite: 17]. The NCLT Chennai's order affirming the applicant's standing to file under Section 634A and directing the Chartered Accountant to submit the report is upheld[cite: 17]. No order as to costs[cite: 17].
summary: In an execution dispute tracing back to a 2009 Company Law Board order, the Appellant challenged the locus standi of a co-respondent who filed an execution application, arguing the co-respondent was not the beneficiary of the decree. NCLAT affirmed the NCLT's decision, holding that under Section 424(3) of the Companies Act, 2013 (formerly Section 634A of the 1956 Act), any party to the proceedings can notify the Tribunal of non-compliance and seek enforcement. While the NCLT found the specific execution application premature, NCLAT agreed that the co-respondent had standing and upheld the directive for the Chartered Accountant to submit the pending report[cite: 17].

case_title: Schweitzer Systemtek India Pvt. Ltd. vs. Phoenix ARC Pvt. Ltd. & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant Schweitzer Systemtek India Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Applicant/Debtor) and Respondent Phoenix ARC Pvt. Ltd. (Financial Creditor)[cite: 18]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Underlying corporate debt for which the promoter acted as a personal guarantor and provided property as security[cite: 18]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default prompting the Corporate Debtor to file a Section 10 application; specific default amount is not detailed in the appellate order[cite: 18]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: NCLT Mumbai admitted the Section 10 application and declared a moratorium on 3rd July 2017[cite: 18]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The Financial Creditor initiated SARFAESI proceedings and attached the movable and immovable properties of the personal guarantor (promoter); the Corporate Applicant sought to extend the IBC moratorium to protect these guarantor properties[cite: 18]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai admitted the Section 10 application but explicitly clarified that the moratorium under Section 14 does not apply to properties not owned by the Corporate Debtor (i.e., personal guarantor properties). The Corporate Applicant appealed this clarification to NCLAT[cite: 18].
legal_issues: Whether the moratorium declared under Section 14 of the IBC upon admission of a corporate insolvency resolution process prohibits recovery actions against the personal properties of a guarantor or third party attached under the SARFAESI Act[cite: 18].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The moratorium under Section 14(1)(c) of the IBC strictly applies only to the properties owned by the Corporate Debtor and does not protect the personal assets of a guarantor, promoter, or any third party from recovery actions[cite: 18]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The term "its" in Section 14(1)(c) specifically denotes property owned by the Corporate Debtor; applying the rule of literal interpretation and 'Noscitur a Sociis', properties beyond the ownership of the Corporate Debtor fall outside the ambit of the moratorium[cite: 18]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal determines the applicability of the moratorium by verifying whether the asset in question is reflected in the balance sheet as owned by the Corporate Debtor[cite: 18]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because the attached properties belonged to the personal guarantor and were not owned by the Corporate Debtor, the NCLT correctly excluded them from the protection of the Section 14 moratorium[cite: 18].
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed[cite: 18]. The NCLT Mumbai's order clarifying that the moratorium does not extend to the guarantor's property is upheld[cite: 18]. Parties are directed to bear their respective costs[cite: 18].
summary: The Corporate Debtor initiated its own insolvency under Section 10 of the IBC. While NCLT Mumbai admitted the application, it clarified that the Section 14 moratorium only protects the Corporate Debtor's properties and does not stop the Financial Creditor's SARFAESI actions against the personal guarantor's properties. The Corporate Debtor appealed, arguing the guarantor's assets should be protected. NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that the statutory language "its property" in Section 14 strictly limits the moratorium to assets owned by the Corporate Debtor and does not extend to third-party or guarantor assets[cite: 18].

case_title: Neelkanth Township and Construction Pvt. Ltd. vs. Urban Infrastructure Trustees Limited
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant Neelkanth Township and Construction Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor) and Respondent Urban Infrastructure Trustees Limited (Financial Creditor/Debenture Holder)[cite: 19]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Issuance of Debenture Certificates to the Respondent; some carried zero interest and others carried one percent interest[cite: 19]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Non-payment of the matured debentures; the debentures were due for redemption in the years 2011, 2012, and 2013[cite: 19]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The Section 7 IBC application was filed in 2017, which the Corporate Debtor argued was barred by the Limitation Act since maturity was in 2011-2013[cite: 19]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The Financial Creditor did not provide a record of default from an Information Utility but relied on other documents under Part V of Form-1; arbitration proceedings for the same cause of action were pending[cite: 19]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai admitted the Section 7 application on 21st April 2017. The Corporate Debtor appealed, challenging the completeness of the application, the financial debt status of the debentures, and raising the limitation bar[cite: 19].
legal_issues: Whether a Section 7 application is maintainable without an Information Utility record, whether debentures carrying zero or 1% interest qualify as 'financial debt' under Section 5(8), and whether the Limitation Act, 1963 applies to bar a claim for debentures matured in 2011-2013[cite: 19].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Debentures inherently qualify as financial debt under the IBC regardless of the interest rate; the absence of Information Utility records does not invalidate a petition if alternate evidence per Form-1 is provided; and the IBC is not a recovery proceeding, so the Limitation Act does not strictly bar initiation for matured, unpaid debts representing a continuous default[cite: 19]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 5(8)(c) explicitly includes any amount raised pursuant to the issue of debentures as 'financial debt'. Under Section 7(3)(a), if the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Board of India has not specified alternate records, the documents prescribed in Part V of Form-1 under the Adjudicating Authority Rules, 2016 suffice to prove default[cite: 19]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal found the debenture certificates and financial statements sufficient to prove the existence and non-payment of the debt, constituting a continuous default under Section 3(12)[cite: 19]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The debentures were issued against the time value of money, the default was continuous making the limitation argument inapplicable, and the application was complete based on Form-1 requirements, justifying the NCLT's admission order[cite: 19].
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed[cite: 19]. The NCLT Mumbai's order admitting the Section 7 application and declaring a moratorium is upheld[cite: 19]. No order as to costs[cite: 19].
summary: Urban Infrastructure Trustees Limited filed a Section 7 IBC application against Neelkanth Township and Construction Pvt. Ltd. for unpaid debentures matured in 2011-2013. The Corporate Debtor appealed the NCLT's admission, arguing the application lacked Information Utility records, the zero/1% interest debentures weren't 'financial debt', and the claim was time-barred. NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that debentures are explicitly classified as financial debt under Section 5(8)(c). Furthermore, the absence of Information Utility records does not render the petition incomplete if Form-1 requirements are met, and the Limitation Act does not bar the initiation of CIRP for a continuous default of debt[cite: 19].

case_title: Dharmendra Kumar Rathore & Anr. vs. Shri Bankhandi Nath Developers Pvt. Ltd. & Ors.
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) No. 72 of 2017 (and connected appeals 108 & 109 of 2017)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants Dharmendra Kumar Rathore & Anr. (Petitioners in connected CP) and Respondents Shri Bankhandi Nath Developers Pvt. Ltd. & Ors. (including original directors and third-party buyers)[cite: 20]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: An agreement to sell executed on 12th July 2011 to purchase land for Rs. 3,28,00,000, where the company paid an advance of Rs. 1,00,00,000[cite: 20]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Claimed oppression through illegal share transfers, fabricated resignations, and the unilateral parting of the company's equitable right to property resulting in third-party sale deeds on 15th November 2011[cite: 20]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Sale deeds were executed on 15th November 2011; Company Petitions were filed in 2012 and 2013; NCLT passed its order on 24th January 2017[cite: 20]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The Respondent directors transferred the equitable right to purchase the property to third parties without appellant consent and unilaterally returned a cheque of Rs. 55,00,000 from the third parties, citing "internal disputes," thereby depriving the company of funds[cite: 20]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Allahabad found both groups guilty of oppression, refused to set aside the sale deeds since third parties were involved, and appointed an independent 5th director. Both groups appealed to NCLAT[cite: 20].
legal_issues: Whether the NCLT can set aside registered sale deeds executed between a vendor and third parties under Section 242 of the Companies Act when the company only held an equitable right under an agreement to sell, and whether a director's unilateral refusal to accept funds owed to the company constitutes oppression[cite: 20].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A company tribunal acting under Section 242 cannot set aside registered sale deeds executed by a third-party vendor in favor of other third parties, as the company never held title to transfer; however, directors who unilaterally reject funds owed to the company act prejudicially to its interests and must compensate the company[cite: 20]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 242(f) and (g) of the 2013 Act cannot be invoked to cancel transfers of property that were not actually effected by the company itself, especially without the consent of the resisting third-party purchasers[cite: 20]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal relied on additional affidavits confirming that the Respondent director returned the third-party cheques on the pretext of company disputes, proving a deliberate act depriving the company of its rightful capital[cite: 20]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: While the NCLT correctly declined to cancel the sale deeds due to lack of jurisdiction over third-party titles, the Respondent director's unilateral refusal to accept the sale consideration caused prejudice, warranting a modification to impose compensatory interest[cite: 20].
operative_order: The appeals are disposed of with a modification to the NCLT order[cite: 20]. Respondent No. 2 is directed to ensure the returned money comes to the company's account and the Respondent directors are ordered to compensate the company with 12% interest p.a. on the outstanding amounts from 15th November 2011 until payment within one month[cite: 20]. The appointment of the independent 5th director is upheld[cite: 20]. Parties to bear their own costs[cite: 20].
summary: In cross-petitions for oppression and mismanagement regarding Shri Bankhandi Nath Developers Pvt. Ltd., NCLT Allahabad found both factions guilty, appointed an independent director, but refused to cancel a controversial land sale to third parties. On appeal, NCLAT agreed that under Section 242 of the Companies Act, the Tribunal lacks jurisdiction to cancel registered sale deeds executed by a third-party vendor to other third parties, as the company only held an agreement to sell. However, NCLAT found that a respondent director had oppressively returned cheques owed to the company from the third-party buyers due to "internal disputes." NCLAT modified the order, directing the respondent directors to return the funds to the company with 12% interest[cite: 20].

case_title: Hasmukh Bachubhai Baraiya vs. Symphony Ltd. & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant Hasmukh Bachubhai Baraiya (Shareholder) vs. 1st Respondent Symphony Ltd. and 5th Respondent[cite: 21]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Claim for duplicate share certificates in respect of 21,500 equity shares (Ledger Folio Nos. 021673 and 021674) and release of unclaimed dividends[cite: 21]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Shares alleged to have been misplaced around 1997 without any formal application or notice of loss filed for 20 years until September 2015[cite: 21]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Company informed appellant in November 2015 that shares were transferred to 5th Respondent in January 1998; petition filed under Sections 56, 58, and 59; civil suit filed in 2016; FIR lodged in May 2017[cite: 21]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Lack of evidence regarding the alleged misplacement of shares, tallies showing transferor signatures matched, and a pending civil suit since 2016 concerning title over 20,000 equity shares[cite: 21]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Ahmedabad Bench dismissed TP No. 116/2016 on 26th April 2017; appellant challenged the order before NCLAT[cite: 21].
legal_issues: Whether the Tribunal can compel a company to issue duplicate share certificates under Section 46(2) of the Companies Act, 2013 when there are disputed questions of fact regarding the loss of shares and a pending civil suit concerning title over the same shares[cite: 21].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Where there are serious bona fide disputes regarding the title/ownership of shares and pending civil litigation between parties, a tribunal will not exercise summary jurisdiction to direct the issuance of duplicate share certificates. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 46(2) of the Companies Act, 2013 provides for duplicate share issuance, but claims clouded by an unverified 20-year delay in reporting loss and active civil suits do not warrant relief. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The absence of contemporaneous evidence or timely reporting of lost shares, combined with an established transfer record and competing title claims, defeats the appellant's claim. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because of disputed facts, an unexplained 20-year delay, and a pending civil suit regarding share title, the NCLT rightly refused to grant relief.
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed with no order as to costs, with clarifications that a fresh cause of action may arise if the civil suit is decreed in favor of either party, and SEBI's independent investigations remain unaffected[cite: 21].
summary: Hasmukh Bachubhai Baraiya appealed against an NCLT Ahmedabad order dismissing his petition for duplicate share certificates and unclaimed dividends for 21,500 shares of Symphony Ltd[cite: 21]. The NCLT had rejected the claim due to a 20-year delay in reporting the loss, lack of supporting evidence, and a pending civil suit regarding title to the shares[cite: 21]. NCLAT affirmed the dismissal, holding that summary proceedings under the Companies Act cannot resolve disputed questions of title when a civil suit is already pending and the loss was never reported timely[cite: 21].

case_title: Sobha Limited vs. Pancard Clubs Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant Sobha Limited (Operational Creditor) and Respondent Pancard Clubs Ltd. (Corporate Debtor)[cite: 23]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: RCC construction agreements entered into between 1st November 2012 and 23rd September 2013 for projects at Baner, Pune and Durgapur, West Bengal[cite: 23]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Claimed dues of Rs. 2,00,15,969 for Baner and Rs. 2,84,48,027 for Durgapur, totaling over Rs. 4.80 crores[cite: 23]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Initial demand notice under Section 8(1) issued on 25th January 2017; subsequent application withdrawn and refiled after a fresh Section 8 notice[cite: 23]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Arbitration proceedings under Section 11 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 were invoked by the parties before the High Court prior to the service of the Section 8 notice[cite: 23]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai rejected the Section 9 application on 29th July 2017 due to the existence of a pre-existing dispute and SEBI restrictions; the Operational Creditor appealed to NCLAT[cite: 23].
legal_issues: Whether invocation of arbitration proceedings prior to the issuance of a demand notice under Section 8 of the IBC establishes a 'pre-existing dispute' sufficient to bar an application under Section 9[cite: 23].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The initiation or invocation of arbitration proceedings over invoice claims prior to the issuance of a Section 8 demand notice constitutes clear evidence of a 'pre-existing dispute', rendering a Section 9 application non-maintainable. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 9 of the IBC prohibits the admission of an operational insolvency application if a dispute existed prior to the receipt of the demand notice. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal verified court records showing that arbitration under Section 11 was filed prior to the Section 8 notice. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because arbitration proceedings were initiated before the Section 8 notice, a pre-existing dispute existed, making the Section 9 petition maintainable only if resolved, but correctly dismissed here.
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed with no order as to costs[cite: 23].
summary: Sobha Limited filed a Section 9 IBC application against Pancard Clubs Ltd. for unpaid construction dues[cite: 23]. NCLT Mumbai rejected the application on the grounds of a pre-existing dispute and SEBI orders restricting the company's assets[cite: 23]. On appeal, NCLAT held that while SEBI orders cannot nullify IBC proceedings or serve as a standalone ground to reject a petition, the application was nonetheless non-maintainable because arbitration proceedings had already been invoked by the parties prior to the Section 8 notice, establishing a pre-existing dispute[cite: 23]. The appeal was dismissed[cite: 23].

case_title: Sapphire Industrial Infrastructures Pvt. Ltd. & M/s. Precious Energy Services Ltd. & Ors. vs. Registrar of Companies, NCT of Delhi & Haryana
appeal_number: I.A. No. 337 of 2017 in Company Appeal (AT) No. 106 of 2017 & I.A. No. 338 of 2017 in Company Appeal (AT) No. 107 of 2017
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants Sapphire Industrial Infrastructures Pvt. Ltd. and M/s. Precious Energy Services Ltd. & Ors. versus Respondent Registrar of Companies, NCT of Delhi & Haryana[cite: 26]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Applications for compounding of offences under the Companies Act, 1956[cite: 26]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Fines imposed for alleged violations of Sections 149, 177, and 178 of the Companies Act, 1956[cite: 26]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Original common order passed on 30th May 2017; rectification applications (I.A. Nos. 337 and 338 of 2017) decided on 18th June 2017[cite: 26]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Clerical and typographical errors in the prior common order incorrectly cited violations of Section 149 and misallocated fines for Sections 177 and 178[cite: 26]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appellants filed interlocutory applications under Rules 11 and 31 of the NCLAT Rules, 2016 to rectify apparent clerical and typographical errors in the common order dated 30th May 2017[cite: 26].
legal_issues: Whether the Appellate Tribunal can recall and modify portions of its prior judgment under Rules 11 and 31 of the NCLAT Rules, 2016 to correct apparent clerical and typographical errors regarding statutory violations and fine allocations[cite: 26].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An appellate tribunal possesses inherent powers under procedural rules (such as Rules 11 and 31 of the NCLAT Rules, 2016) to rectify apparent clerical, typographical, or accidental errors in its orders. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Rules 11 and 31 permit the correction of judgments to reflect accurate statutory provisions and compounding applications actually pleaded and argued. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Concession by the opposing counsel (Registrar of Companies) acknowledging the typographical mistakes committed by the Tribunal in the original judgment. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because errors were apparent on the face of the record, the offending paragraphs containing incorrect fine allocations and statutory references must be recalled and substituted with accurate directions.
operative_order: I.A. Nos. 337 and 338 of 2017 are disposed of[cite: 26]. Paragraphs 18, 19, and 20 of the original order dated 30th May 2017 are recalled and substituted[cite: 26]. In Company Appeal (AT) No. 106 of 2017, a fine of Rs. 5 Lakhs on the company and Rs. 1 Lakh each on one director and three officers (total Rs. 9 Lakhs) is imposed for violation of Section 178(1)[cite: 26]. In Company Appeal (AT) No. 107 of 2017, a fine of Rs. 5 Lakhs on the company and Rs. 1 Lakh each on one director and two officers (total Rs. 8 Lakhs) is imposed for violation of Section 177, bringing the total sum to Rs. 17 Lakhs[cite: 26]. The underlying NCLT common order dated 13th February 2017 is set aside[cite: 26].
summary: Appellants filed interlocutory applications under Rules 11 and 31 of the NCLAT Rules, 2016 to correct clerical and typographical errors in a common order dated 30th May 2017 concerning compounding of offences under the Companies Act, 1956[cite: 26]. The Registrar of Companies conceded that mistakes occurred in assigning penalties for Sections 149, 177, and 178[cite: 26]. Acknowledging the errors apparent on the face of the record, the NCLAT recalled paragraphs 18, 19, and 20 of the original order, substituted them with correct fine allocations totaling Rs. 17 Lakhs for violations of Sections 177 and 178(1), and set aside the underlying NCLT order[cite: 26].

case_title: Mr. Senthil Kumar Karmegam vs. Dolphin Offshore Enterprises (Mauritius) Pvt. Ltd. & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant Mr. Senthil Kumar Karmegam (Director of Corporate Debtor Unison Engineering & Construction Private Ltd.) and Respondent Dolphin Offshore Enterprises (Mauritius) Pvt. Ltd. (Operational Creditor)[cite: 28]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate insolvency resolution process initiated based on an operational debt claim[cite: 28]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default on operational debt leading to a Section 9 application; specific monetary default amount not detailed in the order[cite: 28]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Demand notice issued by an advocate on 17th March 2017; NCLT Mumbai admission order passed on 20th June 2017[cite: 28]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The demand notice was issued by an advocate (Ms. Priyanka Patel) on behalf of the Operational Creditor rather than by the Operational Creditor itself or an authorized person holding a position with or in relation to it[cite: 28]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai admitted the Section 9 application in C.P. No. 594/I&BP/2017; the Director of the Corporate Debtor appealed the admission order to NCLAT[cite: 28].
legal_issues: Whether an advocate, lawyer, or third-party professional who holds no position with or in relation to the operational creditor can issue a valid demand notice under Section 8 of the IBC on behalf of the operational creditor[cite: 28].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An advocate, lawyer, chartered accountant, or company secretary who holds no position with or in relation to the operational creditor and lacks specific board authorization cannot issue a demand notice under Section 8 of the IBC. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 8 and Rule 5 of the Adjudicating Authority Rules require the demand notice to be issued by the operational creditor or an authorized person stating their position with/in relation to the creditor; a standard lawyer's notice does not suffice. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Review of the demand notice revealed it was issued purely by an external advocate without any evidence of holding a formal position within the operational creditor entity. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because the demand notice was legally defective being issued by an unauthorized advocate instead of in mandatory Form 3 or Form 4 by the operational creditor, the initiation of the resolution process was illegal and must be set aside.
operative_order: The appeal is allowed[cite: 28]. The impugned order dated 20th June 2017 passed by NCLT Mumbai in C.P. No. 594/I&BP/2017 is set aside[cite: 28]. All consequential orders, including the moratorium and appointment of the IRP, are declared illegal and set aside[cite: 28]. The Corporate Debtor is released from the rigors of law to function independently[cite: 28]. No order as to costs[cite: 28].
summary: Mr. Senthil Kumar Karmegam, Director of the Corporate Debtor, appealed against the NCLT Mumbai order admitting an operational insolvency application filed by Dolphin Offshore Enterprises (Mauritius) Pvt. Ltd[cite: 28]. The Appellant contended that the mandatory demand notice under Section 8 of the IBC was illegally issued by an external advocate rather than the Operational Creditor itself[cite: 28]. Relying on precedent (*Uttam Galva Steels Limited*), the NCLAT held that an advocate holding no position within the operational creditor entity cannot issue a Section 8 demand notice[cite: 28]. Consequently, the NCLAT set aside the admission order, dismissed the Section 9 application, and released the Corporate Debtor from insolvency proceedings[cite: 28].

case_title: Amod Amladi vs. Mrs. Sayali Rane & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant Amod Amladi (Investor of Citrus Check Inns Limited) versus Respondents Mrs. Sayali Rane & Anr. (Operational Creditor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Initiation of Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process (CIRP) against Citrus Check Inns Limited under Section 9 of the IBC. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Section 9 application admitted by the Adjudicating Authority; specific default amount not detailed in the order. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Admission order passed on 2nd May 2017; intervention petition rejected by NCLT on 3rd October 2017; appeal decided on 30th November 2017. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Allegations by the investor that the CIRP initiation was fraudulent and collusive, and that SEBI/SAT orders upheld by the Supreme Court were suppressed before the Adjudicating Authority. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appellant filed an intervention petition before NCLT Mumbai to recall the admission order; NCLT dismissed it on 3rd October 2017 holding it had no power to recall; Appellant challenged this order before NCLAT.
legal_issues: Whether an investor has the locus standi as an 'aggrieved person' to challenge a CIRP admission order, whether the Adjudicating Authority has the power to review or recall an order admitting an application under Section 9, and whether a time-barred challenge to an admission order is maintainable.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An investor of a corporate debtor is not an 'aggrieved person' entitled to appeal an admission order under Section 61, and the Adjudicating Authority does not possess the power of review or recall to dismiss a CIRP petition post-admission. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 61(2) imposes strict limitation periods for appeals against admission orders, and the I&B Code does not vest adjudicating authorities with recall powers for admission orders. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Examination of the appellant's status as an investor rather than a party with direct standing to contest the admission or seek a recall. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because investors must file claims before the IRP rather than challenge admission via recall or time-barred appeals, and the NCLT lacks recall jurisdiction, the appeal is not maintainable.
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed with no order as to costs. It is clarified that the impugned order and this judgment will not prevent the appellant investor from filing its claim before the Insolvency Resolution Professional.
summary: Amod Amladi, an investor of Citrus Check Inns Limited, appealed against an NCLT Mumbai order rejecting his intervention petition to recall a Section 9 CIRP admission order. The NCLAT held that an investor lacks locus standi as an 'aggrieved person' to challenge the admission order outside the statutory limitation period under Section 61(2), and the Adjudicating Authority has no power to review or recall an admission order once passed. Consequently, the NCLAT dismissed the appeal, clarifying that the proper remedy for the investor is to submit its claim before the Insolvency Resolution Professional.

case_title: Value Kine Interiors Pvt. Ltd. vs. Rattan India Power Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Value Kine Interiors Pvt. Ltd. (Operational Creditor) and Rattan India Power Ltd. (Corporate Debtor)[cite: 30]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Interior decoration and construction contract work[cite: 30]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Operational debt claimed; exact default amount not specified[cite: 30]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Demand notice issued under Section 8(1); reply disputing claim sent on 11th September 2017[cite: 30]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Correspondence from 2015 and 2016 (e.g., Oct 1, 2015, Feb 10, 2016, May 16, 2016, Mar 11, 2016) showing Corporate Debtor alleged incomplete work, abandonment, and resulting losses[cite: 30]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT New Delhi Bench rejected Section 9 application on 23rd October 2017 due to pre-existing dispute; Operational Creditor appealed to NCLAT[cite: 30].
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority was justified in rejecting the Section 9 application under the IBC on the ground of a pre-existing dispute between the operational creditor and the corporate debtor[cite: 30].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Under Section 9 of the IBC, if a pre-existing dispute is brought to notice via a valid notice of dispute, the application must be rejected[cite: 30]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 8(2)(a) and Section 9(5)(2)(d) mandate rejection when a plausible dispute exists, reading 'and' as 'or' to avoid legislative anomaly[cite: 30]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The dispute must be a plausible contention requiring investigation and not a feeble or spurious defense; correspondence showing uncompleted work and loss establishes a true dispute[cite: 30]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because contemporaneous letters established a genuine pre-existing dispute regarding incomplete work and losses, the Adjudicating Authority rightly rejected the application[cite: 30].
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed with no order as to costs[cite: 30].
summary: Value Kine Interiors Pvt. Ltd. appealed against the NCLT New Delhi Bench order rejecting its Section 9 insolvency application against Rattan India Power Ltd[cite: 30]. The NCLT had found an existence of a pre-existing dispute regarding incomplete work and abandonment[cite: 30]. Reviewing correspondence from late 2015 and early 2016, the NCLAT noted that the Corporate Debtor had consistently raised issues of uncompleted work and financial losses prior to the insolvency trigger[cite: 30]. Citing the Supreme Court's ruling in Mobilox Innovations, the NCLAT held that once a plausible pre-existing dispute is established, the Section 9 application must be rejected[cite: 30]. Accordingly, the NCLAT dismissed the appeal upholding the rejection[cite: 30].

case_title: Ramesh Chander Gupta vs. Punjab National Bank
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant Ramesh Chander Gupta (Suspended Director of Arcee Ispat Udyog Ltd., Corporate Debtor) and Respondent Punjab National Bank (Financial Creditor)[cite: 31]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Credit facilities and loan advanced by the Financial Creditor to the Corporate Debtor[cite: 31]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default on credit facilities leading to Section 7 application; exact default amount not detailed in the order[cite: 31]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Authorization letter issued on 28th March 2017; NCLT admission order passed on 30th August 2017[cite: 31]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Board resolutions dated 30th May 2002 and 30th October 2009 delegating general powers to bank officers to conduct legal proceedings, supplemented by an instrument dated 5th November 2015[cite: 31]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Chandigarh Bench admitted PNB's Section 7 application on 30th August 2017; Suspended Director appealed to NCLAT challenging the maintainability based on authorization[cite: 31].
legal_issues: Whether an application under Section 7 of the IBC is maintainable when filed by a bank officer authorized via general board resolutions rather than a specific power of attorney[cite: 31].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: While a pure power of attorney holder cannot file an IBC application, an officer of a financial institution authorized by general Board resolutions delegating legal representation and recovery powers acts as a valid authorized representative[cite: 31]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Form-1 and Section 7 require an 'authorized person' who states their position in relation to the financial creditor[cite: 31]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Examination of internal bank resolutions and delegation instruments to confirm that the filing officer possesses institutional authorization[cite: 31]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because bank officers authorized to sanction and recover loans possess valid institutional authorization to initiate Section 7 proceedings despite loose nomenclature, the application is maintainable[cite: 31].
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed and the order of admission under Section 7 is affirmed, with no order as to costs[cite: 31].
summary: Ramesh Chander Gupta, suspended director of Arcee Ispat Udyog Ltd., appealed against NCLT Chandigarh's order admitting Punjab National Bank's Section 7 application[cite: 31]. The Appellant contended that the application was not maintainable as it was filed by an unauthorized person[cite: 31]. Citing the precedent in Palogix Infrastructure, the NCLAT held that although power of attorney holders cannot initiate IBC proceedings, bank officers acting under general Board resolutions delegating legal powers are valid authorized representatives[cite: 31]. Finding that the senior manager was duly authorized to initiate recovery, the NCLAT dismissed the appeal and affirmed the admission order[cite: 31].

case_title: Mr. Praveen Shankaralyam vs. M/s Elan Professional Appliances Pvt. Ltd. & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant Praveen Shankaralyam (Petitioner/Removed Director) and Respondents M/s Elan Professional Appliances Pvt. Ltd. & Others[cite: 32]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate management and directorship disputes[cite: 32]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Removal from directorship on 1st December 2010; petition filed in September 2015 (after nearly 5 years)[cite: 32]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Cause of action accrued on 1st December 2010; petition filed in September 2015 and refiled in January 2015[cite: 32]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Records confirming notice of removal served to the appellant in December 2010 and correct address records maintained[cite: 32]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Principal Bench, New Delhi dismissed the company petition as barred by limitation and laches; Appellant appealed to NCLAT[cite: 32].
legal_issues: Whether a company petition under Sections 397 and 398 of the Companies Act, 1956 filed more than five years after removal from directorship is barred by limitation, delay, and laches[cite: 32].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Even where specific statutory limitation arguments under new enactments are debated, an applicant cannot escape dismissal of a company petition when there is an unexplained and inordinate delay of over five years amounting to laches[cite: 32]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Application of Section 433 of the Companies Act, 2013 and Article 113 of the Limitation Act, 1963 to equitable company petitions[cite: 32]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Verification of the date of removal (December 2010) against the date of petition filing (September 2015) alongside address confirmation[cite: 32]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because the appellant waited nearly five years after his removal to challenge it without valid excuse, the petition is barred by delay and laches[cite: 32].
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed with no order as to costs[cite: 32].
summary: Mr. Praveen Shankaralyam appealed against an NCLT Principal Bench order dismissing his company petition under Sections 397 and 398 of the 1956 Act[cite: 32]. The NCLT had dismissed the petition as barred by limitation and laches, noting that the appellant was removed as director in December 2010 but only filed his petition nearly five years later in September 2015[cite: 32]. The NCLAT held that regardless of technical arguments surrounding the Limitation Act, a petitioner cannot approach the tribunal after an inordinate and unexplained delay of five years[cite: 32]. Finding no merit in excuses regarding dividend mailing addresses, the NCLAT dismissed the appeal[cite: 32].

case_title: Anant Kajare vs. Eknath Aher & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant Anant Kajare (Investor of M/s Royal Twinkle Star Club Limited) and Respondents Eknath Aher & Anr. (Operational Creditor)[cite: 33]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process (CIRP) initiated against M/s Royal Twinkle Star Club Limited under Section 9 of the IBC[cite: 33]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Section 9 application admitted via consent order on 2nd May 2017; specific default amount not detailed[cite: 33]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Admission order passed on 2nd May 2017; NCLT rejection of recall petition on 3rd October 2017; appeal decided on 30th November 2017[cite: 33]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Investor allegations that the CIRP was initiated fraudulently in collusion with directors and that SEBI/SAT/Supreme Court orders were suppressed[cite: 33]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appellant filed an intervention petition before NCLT Mumbai to recall the 2nd May 2017 admission order; NCLT dismissed it on 3rd October 2017; Appellant appealed to NCLAT[cite: 33].
legal_issues: Whether an investor of a corporate debtor has locus standi as an 'aggrieved person' to challenge a CIRP admission order, and whether the Adjudicating Authority has the inherent power to review or recall its admission order[cite: 33].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An investor of a corporate debtor lacks locus standi to appeal a CIRP admission order outside the statutory limitation period, and adjudicating authorities possess no inherent power to review or recall admission orders post-admission[cite: 33]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 61(2) of the IBC sets strict limitation rules for appeals, and the I&B Code contains no provision empowering tribunals to recall admission orders[cite: 33]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Assessing the petitioner's legal standing as an investor rather than a primary disputing party with statutory standing to seek recall[cite: 33]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because investors must file claims before the IRP rather than seeking recall or filing time-barred appeals, and tribunals lack review powers, the appeal is not maintainable[cite: 33].
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed with no order as to costs, subject to the clarification that this order does not bar the investor from filing claims before the IRP[cite: 33].
summary: Anant Kajare, an investor in M/s Royal Twinkle Star Club Limited, appealed against an NCLT Mumbai order rejecting his intervention petition to recall a Section 9 CIRP admission order[cite: 33]. The Appellant claimed the insolvency was initiated collusively and fraudulently[cite: 33]. The NCLAT held that an investor is not an 'aggrieved person' entitled to challenge an admission order past the limitation period under Section 61(2) of the IBC[cite: 33]. Furthermore, the Adjudicating Authority lacks the power of review or recall once an insolvency application is admitted[cite: 33]. Dismissing the appeal, the NCLAT clarified that the investor's proper recourse is to submit claims before the IRP[cite: 33].

case_title: Asian Natural Resources (India) Limited & Anr. vs. IDBI Bank Limited
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants Asian Natural Resources (India) Limited and Bhatia Global Trading Limited (Corporate Debtors) and Respondent IDBI Bank Limited (Financial Creditor)[cite: 45]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Credit facilities and loan accounts extended to the corporate debtors by the bank consortium[cite: 45]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default on financial debt leading to Section 7 applications; NCLT Ahmedabad admitted the applications on 23rd May 2017[cite: 45]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Notices sent by speed post on 8th May 2017; fresh notices of hearing dispatched on 12th May 2017 and received by appellants on 15th May 2017[cite: 45]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Speed post receipts and delivery reports confirming service of notice, alongside inter-se consortium agreements dated 21st February 2009 and 17th March 2011 designating SBI as the lead bank[cite: 45]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Ahmedabad admitted the Section 7 applications on 23rd May 2017; Corporate Debtors appealed to NCLAT[cite: 45].
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority violated principles of natural justice by admitting insolvency applications without notice, and whether an inter-se consortium agreement designating a lead bank strips an individual financial creditor of its statutory right to file a Section 7 application under the IBC[cite: 45].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Inter-se agreements between member banks of a consortium cannot override or take away the independent statutory right conferred upon any financial creditor under Section 7 of the IBC to initiate corporate insolvency resolution processes[cite: 45]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 7(1) explicitly permits a financial creditor either by itself or jointly to file an application upon default, and this right is not abrogated by internal banking arrangements or consortium lead-bank structures[cite: 45]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Review of speed post delivery records confirming that notices were duly served on the corporate debtors prior to admission[cite: 45]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because service of notice was duly proven and inter-se agreements are non-binding on third-party corporate debtors and cannot override statutory IBC provisions, the challenges fail[cite: 45].
operative_order: Both appeals are dismissed with no order as to costs[cite: 45].
summary: Asian Natural Resources (India) Limited and Bhatia Global Trading Limited appealed against NCLT Ahmedabad orders admitting Section 7 IBC applications filed by IDBI Bank[cite: 45]. The Appellants contended that the orders violated natural justice due to lack of notice and argued that IDBI Bank had waived its right to act independently under inter-se consortium agreements designating the State Bank of India (SBI) as the lead bank[cite: 45]. The NCLAT dismissed the appeals, holding that delivery receipts proved notice was duly served, and inter-se agreements between lenders cannot override or curtail a financial creditor's independent statutory right to trigger insolvency under Section 7 of the IBC[cite: 45].

case_title: Rajinder Kapoor Proprietor R.K.Kapoor & Co. vs. Anil Kumar Interim Resolution Professional & Ors.[cite: 1]
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants are Rajinder Kapoor and Ashwini Kumar Prabhakar; Respondent is Anil Kumar[cite: 1]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate insolvency resolution process initiated against the corporate debtor[cite: 1]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Corporate insolvency resolution process initiated under the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016[cite: 1]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The thirty-day term of the Interim Resolution Professional expired, and the Adjudicating Authority passed an order on September 8, 2017[cite: 1]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The Committee of Creditors decided to remove the present Interim Resolution Professional and appoint another Insolvency Resolution Professional under Section 27 of the I&B Code[cite: 1]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appellants challenged the NCLT Chandigarh Bench order dated September 8, 2017 before the NCLAT[cite: 1].
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority is duty-bound to consider the replacement of an Interim Resolution Professional proposed by the Committee of Creditors under Section 27 of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016[cite: 1].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The Adjudicating Authority is duty-bound to consider the name of another Resolution Professional proposed by the Committee of Creditors or call for a name from the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Board of India[cite: 1]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 27 of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 empowers the committee of creditors to replace a resolution professional by a vote of seventy-five per cent of voting shares[cite: 1]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Verification that the Committee of Creditors has duly passed a resolution to replace the IRP/RP in accordance with statutory voting thresholds[cite: 1]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Adjudicating Authority must act in accordance with Section 27, and until a regular Insolvency Resolution Professional is appointed, the IRP shall perform day-to-day routine work strictly per the Code[cite: 1].
operative_order: Both appeals stand disposed of directing the Adjudicating Authority to consider the replacement of the Resolution Professional as proposed by the Committee of Creditors; until a regular IRP is appointed, the current IRP shall perform routine work strictly per the I&B Code, with no order as to costs[cite: 1].
summary: Appellants Rajinder Kapoor and Ashwini Kumar Prabhakar challenged the NCLT Chandigarh Bench order dated September 8, 2017, concerning the continuation of the Interim Resolution Professional (IRP) beyond thirty days[cite: 1]. The main issue was whether the Adjudicating Authority must replace the IRP when the Committee of Creditors (CoC) proposes a new Insolvency Resolution Professional under Section 27 of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016[cite: 1]. The NCLAT held that the Adjudicating Authority is duty-bound to consider the CoC's proposed replacement or seek names from the Board[cite: 1]. Consequently, the appellate tribunal disposed of the appeals, directing the Adjudicating Authority to pass appropriate orders while allowing the existing IRP to handle routine duties in the interim[cite: 1].

case_title: Shri Abnash Chander Mahajan & Ors. vs. Vikas Promoters Pvt. Ltd. & Ors.[cite: 2]
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants are Shri Abnash Chander Mahajan & Ors.; Respondents are Vikas Promoters Pvt. Ltd. & Ors.[cite: 2]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Company petition filed alleging oppression and mismanagement, fund diversion, siphoning, and undervaluation of company assets[cite: 2]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Claims relating to invalid share allotments, siphoned funds, diversion of interest-free loans, and valuation of shares for exit, with an estimated Mall value of approximately Rs. 100-111 crores[cite: 2]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Company Law Board passed an order on January 16, 2014; Auditor-cum-Valuer submitted a report on February 4, 2015; NCLT passed the impugned order on March 22, 2017[cite: 2]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Valuation report dated February 4, 2015, and an affidavit filed by respondents before the Debts Recovery Tribunal (DRT) showing the valuation of the Mall at Rs. 100 crores[cite: 2]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appellants filed Company Petition No. 110 (ND) 2009 under Sections 397/398 of the Companies Act, 1956, and NCLT Principal Bench passed an order on March 22, 2017 ordering fresh valuation, challenged in Company Appeal (AT) No. 131 of 2017[cite: 2].
legal_issues: Whether the Tribunal erred in directing a fresh valuation report without properly discussing the earlier valuation report dated February 4, 2015[cite: 2].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: When evaluating share valuation and corporate assets in oppression and mismanagement petitions, the tribunal must consider all relevant valuation materials, including prior valuation reports and affidavits filed by parties in other judicial forums[cite: 2]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Interpretation of powers under Sections 397 and 398 of the Companies Act, 1956 to grant relief against oppression and mismanagement and determine fair share value for exit[cite: 2]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Assessment of consistency between expert valuation reports and admissions made by parties in affidavits before judicial forums like the DRT[cite: 2]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: While the decision of the Tribunal to direct a fresh valuation is not interfered with, the Tribunal must consider the earlier valuation report, the fresh valuation report, and the respondents' affidavit before the DRT when determining share value[cite: 2].
operative_order: The appeal stands disposed of with directions that the Tribunal shall consider the valuation report dated February 4, 2015, the fresh valuation report, and the affidavit filed by respondents before the DRT while passing appropriate orders on share valuation within a specified timeframe, with no costs[cite: 2].
summary: Appellants challenged the NCLT Principal Bench order dated March 22, 2017, which ordered a fresh valuation in an oppression and mismanagement petition under Sections 397 and 398 of the Companies Act, 1956[cite: 2]. The core dispute involved the valuation of the company's Mall and whether the earlier February 4, 2015 valuation report should have been discarded[cite: 2]. The NCLAT declined to interfere with the directive for a fresh valuation but ruled that the Tribunal must consider the earlier valuation report, the new report, and an affidavit filed by respondents before the Debts Recovery Tribunal stating a Rs. 100 crore valuation[cite: 2]. The appeal was disposed of with these directions[cite: 2].

case_title: Rahul Rice Mills Pvt. Ltd. vs. Registrar of Companies, New Delhi[cite: 3]
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Rahul Rice Mills Pvt. Ltd.; Respondent is the Registrar of Companies, New Delhi[cite: 3]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Business of rice milling facing financial crisis during 2008-2011, leading to voluntary application for company strike-off under the Fast Track Exit Scheme, 2011[cite: 3]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Financial uncertainty and distress during the years 2008-09, 2009-10, and 2010-11[cite: 3]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Board of Directors applied for the Fast Track Exit Scheme on September 22, 2011; application received on October 18, 2011; NCLT passed the impugned order on April 21, 2017[cite: 3]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Annual returns for 2009-10, balance sheet as on March 31, 2010, Board resolution dated September 22, 2011, and subsequent consent letters and resolution dated November 27, 2015 seeking revival[cite: 3]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appellant filed Company Petition No. 171 of 2016 under Section 560(6) of the Companies Act, 1956 before NCLT Principal Bench, New Delhi, seeking restoration of the company, which was rejected on April 21, 2017[cite: 3].
legal_issues: Whether a company struck off its register upon a voluntary application under the Fast Track Exit Scheme, 2011 can be restored under Section 560(6) of the Companies Act, 1956 merely because the directors are now willing to infuse funds[cite: 3].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Once promoters voluntarily exercise discretion to strike off a company under an exit scheme, subsequent willingness of directors to infuse funds does not constitute sufficient ground under Section 560 for restoration[cite: 3]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 560(6) of the Companies Act, 1956 allows restoration of a struck-off company only when proper grounds and reasonable cause are demonstrated, not at the whim of erstwhile directors[cite: 3]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Examination of whether the company was transacting business or holding property after dissolution and whether valid statutory grounds for revival exist beyond mere change in financial capacity of promoters[cite: 3]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Tribunal's rejection of the restoration application was legally sound because the company was voluntarily dissolved under the Fast Track Exit Scheme, had no ongoing business or property, and the appeal must be dismissed[cite: 3].
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed with no order as to costs, upholding the NCLT order rejecting the restoration of the company under Section 560(6)[cite: 3].
summary: Rahul Rice Mills Pvt. Ltd. appealed against the NCLT New Delhi judgment dated April 21, 2017, which rejected its petition under Section 560(6) of the Companies Act, 1956 to restore the company on the ROC register[cite: 3]. The company had voluntarily opted for the Fast Track Exit Scheme, 2011 in September 2011 due to financial crises[cite: 3]. Years later, the erstwhile directors sought revival, offering to infuse funds[cite: 3]. The NCLAT affirmed the NCLT's decision, holding that a company voluntarily struck off by its management cannot be revived at whim under Section 560 simply because promoters' financial conditions have improved, especially when no business or property exists[cite: 3]. The appeal was dismissed[cite: 3].

case_title: South Asia Human Rights Documentation Centre Pvt. Ltd. & Ors. vs. Suhas Chakma & Anr.[cite: 4]
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants are South Asia Human Rights Documentation Centre Pvt. Ltd. & Ors.; Respondent No. 1 is Suhas Chakma; Respondent No. 2 is Mr. Vittal Rao[cite: 4]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Dispute regarding the alleged fraudulent and sham transfer of 50% shares held by Respondent No. 1 to Respondent No. 2 for an alleged cash consideration of Rs. 30,000 in May 2003[cite: 4]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Transfer of 50% shareholding without proper execution of share transfer forms and share certificates, claimed by appellants to have occurred in May 2003 and reflected in annual returns[cite: 4]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Shares allegedly transferred in May 2003; Respondent No. 1 discovered the non-inclusion as shareholder in December 2008 and February 2009 upon inspecting annual returns; NCLT passed the order on November 21, 2016[cite: 4]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Annual returns filed with ROC lacking specific transaction date and valid share transfer forms, absence of executed share transfer forms and share certificates, and Rs. 30,000 cash consideration receipt[cite: 4]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Respondent No. 1 filed a petition under Sections 397, 398, and 111 of the Companies Act, 1956 before NCLT New Delhi Bench as Company Petition No. 4(ND)2016, which was allowed on November 21, 2016, leading to Company Appeal (AT) No. 31 of 2017[cite: 4].
legal_issues: Whether the Tribunal erred in holding the share transfer of Respondent No. 1's shares to Respondent No. 2 as fraudulent and sham, and whether the petition was barred by limitation[cite: 4].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Annual returns without a definite date of transaction and lacking executed share transfer forms and share certificates cannot validate a disputed share transfer, and limitation is reckoned from the date of knowledge when records lack clear transaction dates[cite: 4]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Interpretation of provisions governing share transfers under the Companies Act, 1956 and the limitation period for filing oppression and mismanagement petitions when share transfers are concealed or lack contemporaneous documentation[cite: 4]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Strict evidentiary requirement requiring production of duly executed share transfer forms and share certificates, where reliance solely on vague annual returns without clear transaction dates fails to discharge the onus of proof[cite: 4]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Since the appellants failed to produce valid share transfer forms or establish a definite date of transfer, and the petition was filed within limitation from the date of knowledge (2008-2009), the NCLT's finding that the transfer was fraudulent and sham is upheld, and the appeal dismissed[cite: 4].
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed with no order as to costs, upholding the NCLT order setting aside the fraudulent share transfer and granting relief to Respondent No. 1[cite: 4].
summary: South Asia Human Rights Documentation Centre Pvt. Ltd. appealed against the NCLT New Delhi order dated November 21, 2016, which declared the transfer of 50% shares from Suhas Chakma to Vittal Rao as fraudulent and sham[cite: 4]. The appellants argued that the transfer occurred in May 2003 and was reflected in annual returns, making the petition time-barred[cite: 4]. The NCLAT held that annual returns lacking a specific transfer date or executed share transfer forms cannot substantiate a valid transfer[cite: 4]. Furthermore, because no definite transaction date was established in company records, limitation was rightly reckoned from the date of knowledge (2008-2009) when the petitioner discovered the anomaly[cite: 4]. The appeal was dismissed[cite: 4].

case_title: Lokhandwala Kataria Construction Pvt. Ltd. vs. Nisus Finance & Investment Manager LLP[cite: 5]
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Lokhandwala Kataria Construction Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor); Respondent is Nisus Finance & Investment Manager LLP (Financial Creditor)[cite: 5]. 2.
