COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Issuance of debentures by the Corporate Debtor to the Financial Creditor[cite: 5]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Dishonour of the first cheque issued for redemption of part of the debentures, constituting default[cite: 5]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Application under Section 7 admitted on June 15, 2017[cite: 5]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Dishonoured cheque for redemption of part of the debentures and an out-of-court settlement reached between parties after admission[cite: 5]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Adjudicating Authority (NCLT Mumbai) admitted the Section 7 application on June 15, 2017[cite: 5]. Corporate Debtor appealed to NCLAT relying on a post-admission settlement to seek withdrawal under Rule 11[cite: 5].
legal_issues: Whether an application under Section 7 of the IBC can be withdrawn on the basis of an out-of-court settlement after it has been admitted by the Adjudicating Authority, by invoking the inherent powers of the Appellate Tribunal[cite: 5].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Once a corporate insolvency resolution process application is admitted, it cannot be withdrawn on the basis of a settlement between the parties, and the process must proceed[cite: 5]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Rule 8 of the I&B (Application to Adjudicating Authority) Rules, 2016 allows withdrawal only before admission; inherent powers under Rule 11 of NCLAT Rules, 2016 have not been adopted for the I&B Code to allow post-admission withdrawal[cite: 5]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Admission of the Section 7 application locks in the process, making any subsequent bilateral settlement immaterial to the termination of the insolvency proceedings[cite: 5]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The appeal must be dismissed because the Tribunal cannot exercise inherent powers to allow withdrawal of an admitted Section 7 application based on a post-admission settlement[cite: 5].
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed with no order as to costs, upholding the admission of the CIRP[cite: 5].
summary: Lokhandwala Kataria Construction appealed the NCLT Mumbai order admitting a Section 7 IBC application filed by Nisus Finance due to a dishonored debenture redemption cheque[cite: 5]. The parties settled the dispute post-admission and sought to withdraw the application invoking NCLAT's inherent powers[cite: 5]. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, ruling that an admitted Section 7 application cannot be withdrawn based on a bilateral settlement because Rule 8 only permits pre-admission withdrawal and Rule 11 of NCLAT Rules has not been adopted for the IBC[cite: 5].

case_title: Sandeep Reddy & Anr. vs. Jaycon Infrastructure Ltd.[cite: 6]
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants are Sandeep Reddy & Anr.; Respondent is Jaycon Infrastructure Ltd. (Operational Creditor)[cite: 6]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: A sub-contract works agreement dated April 19, 2011, scheduled for completion by December 31, 2012[cite: 6]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Dispute over non-completion of work, as the Operational Creditor allegedly abandoned the works in May 2014 after completing only 78% of the agreement value[cite: 6]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Sub-contract dated April 19, 2011; alleged abandonment in May 2014; NCLT order passed on October 10, 2017[cite: 6]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Uncompleted contract works establishing a pre-existing dispute, and a subsequent written settlement reached between the parties[cite: 6]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Hyderabad admitted the Section 9 application on October 10, 2017 and appointed an IRP suo motu[cite: 6]. Appellants challenged this in NCLAT[cite: 6].
legal_issues: Whether a Section 9 application is maintainable if there is a pre-existing dispute prior to the Section 8 demand notice, and whether an Adjudicating Authority can suo motu appoint an IRP not suggested by the parties or the Board[cite: 6].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An application for insolvency by an operational creditor is not maintainable if a dispute regarding the underlying transaction existed prior to the issuance of the statutory demand notice[cite: 6]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Sections 8 and 9 of the I&B Code mandate the rejection of an insolvency application if a pre-existing dispute is established[cite: 6]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Uncontroverted facts showing failure to complete contractual works and abandonment before the demand notice establish a pre-existing dispute[cite: 6]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Section 9 application was fundamentally flawed due to a pre-existing dispute, rendering the admission order illegal, prompting the Appellate Tribunal to set aside the order and release the corporate debtor[cite: 6].
operative_order: The impugned order dated October 10, 2017 is set aside, the Section 9 application is dismissed, the corporate debtor is released to function independently, and no fees are payable to the IRP[cite: 6].
summary: Appellants challenged the NCLT Hyderabad order admitting a Section 9 application filed by Jaycon Infrastructure Ltd. and the suo motu appointment of an IRP[cite: 6]. The NCLAT noted that a dispute existed regarding the completion of sub-contract works long before the Section 8 demand notice was issued[cite: 6]. Furthermore, the parties had subsequently settled the matter[cite: 6]. The NCLAT held that the Section 9 application was not maintainable due to the pre-existing dispute, set aside the NCLT order, dismissed the insolvency application, and restored the company's management to its Board[cite: 6].

case_title: M/s. Jai Lakshmi Solvents (P) Ltd. & Ors. vs. M/s. Swadisht Oils Pvt. Limited[cite: 7]
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants are Operational Creditors (including M/s. J.R Agro Industries, M/s. Abhi Agro, M/s. Jai Lakshmi Solvents, M/s. Rungta Industries, M/s. Arohul Foods); Respondent is M/s. Swadisht Oils Pvt. Limited[cite: 7]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Multiple operational creditors filed applications under Section 9 of the IBC against the corporate debtor[cite: 7]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Unspecified operational debts leading to the filing of Section 9 applications[cite: 7]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: NCLT passed orders in March and May 2017 giving 7 days to cure defects; NCLAT passed order on May 15, 2017[cite: 7]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Adjudicating Authority's orders granting time to remove defects in the Section 9 applications[cite: 7]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT adjourned the applications to allow defect removal[cite: 7]. Appellants appealed to NCLAT arguing that the NCLT must pass an order within 14 days under Section 9[cite: 7].
legal_issues: Whether the 14-day period prescribed under Section 9(5) of the Insolvency & Bankruptcy Code, 2016 for the Adjudicating Authority to pass an order is mandatory or directory[cite: 7].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The statutory time limit prescribed for an Adjudicating Authority to admit or reject an insolvency application is procedural and directory in nature, not mandatory[cite: 7]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Sub-section (5) of Section 9 of the I&B Code, which stipulates a 14-day period for decision-making, is a directory procedural law as previously settled in the J.K. Jute Mills case[cite: 7]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: N/A as this was purely a procedural legal question[cite: 7]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because the 14-day timeline is directory, the Adjudicating Authority can grant time to remove defects beyond this period, and the appeals are disposed of accordingly[cite: 7].
operative_order: The appeals are disposed of without costs, allowing the appellants to complete the records within the time granted by the Adjudicating Authority to remove defects[cite: 7].
summary: Several operational creditors appealed against NCLT orders that adjourned their Section 9 insolvency applications to allow time for defect removal[cite: 7]. The appellants argued that the Adjudicating Authority was mandated to pass an order within 14 days under Section 9(5) of the IBC[cite: 7]. The NCLAT, relying on its precedent in J.K. Jute Mills Company Limited, ruled that the 14-day period is procedural and directory, not mandatory[cite: 7]. Consequently, the NCLAT disposed of the appeals, permitting the appellants to cure the defects within the time granted by the NCLT[cite: 7].

case_title: IVRCL Ltd vs. M/s IOT Utkal Energy Services Ltd & Others[cite: 8]
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is IVRCL Ltd (petitioner); Respondents include M/s IOT Utkal Energy Services Ltd and its nominee director Mr. Jatin Jamandas Mavani[cite: 8]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate dispute regarding oppression and mismanagement within the company[cite: 8]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Alleged acts of oppression and mismanagement occurring in a Board Meeting and EGM dated December 31, 2012[cite: 8]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Board meeting and EGM held on December 31, 2012; NCLT passed the impugned order on December 20, 2016[cite: 8]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Dispute over whether the appellant's representative attended and consented to resolutions at the December 31, 2012 meetings, which determined their knowledge of the events[cite: 8]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appellant filed an amendment application in CP No. 41/2013 to include facts about the December 2012 meetings[cite: 8]. NCLT Kolkata partially allowed it on December 20, 2016, impleading the director but refusing the amendment on facts due to alleged prior knowledge[cite: 8]. Appellants challenged this in NCLAT[cite: 8].
legal_issues: Whether a petitioner in an oppression and mismanagement company petition can amend the petition to include facts occurring prior to or during the pendency of the petition[cite: 8].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An amendment to introduce facts related to oppression and mismanagement can be allowed if the facts were unknown to the petitioner at the time of filing or occurred subsequently as consequential actions; however, known prior acts or completely fresh causes of action cannot be introduced via amendment[cite: 8]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Principles governing pleadings and amendments in oppression and mismanagement petitions under Sections 241 and 242 of the Companies Act, 2013[cite: 8]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Assessing the petitioner's prior knowledge of the events to determine if the suppression of facts precludes amendment[cite: 8]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Tribunal modified the NCLT order, directing it to allow the amendment only for unknown prior facts and connected subsequent developments, while excluding known prior facts or entirely new causes of action[cite: 8].
operative_order: The impugned order dated December 20, 2016 is modified, permitting the appellant to file an additional affidavit in consonance with the NCLAT's observations within 15 days, and directing NCLT to dispose of the petition expeditiously within one month[cite: 8].
summary: IVRCL Ltd appealed the NCLT Kolkata order that refused an amendment to its oppression and mismanagement petition to include events from a December 31, 2012 Board Meeting[cite: 8]. NCLT had reasoned the appellant already knew about those events[cite: 8]. The NCLAT modified the order, establishing guidelines for amendments: facts unknown at filing or connected subsequent developments may be added, whereas known prior facts or completely fresh causes of action cannot[cite: 8]. The Tribunal directed the appellant to file an additional affidavit conforming to these rules and ordered the NCLT to expedite the final hearing[cite: 8].

case_title: International Recreation & Amusement Ltd. vs. S.R. Construction[cite: 9]
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is International Recreation & Amusement Ltd. (Corporate Debtor); Respondent is S.R. Construction (Operational Creditor)[cite: 9]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Underlying operational debt dispute between the corporate debtor and operational creditor[cite: 9]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Unspecified operational default leading to the Section 9 application[cite: 9]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: NCLT passed the impugned order on April 28, 2017; Corporate Debtor gained knowledge on July 20, 2017, and filed the appeal on July 26, 2017[cite: 9]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Post-admission settlement of the dispute between the parties, and the undisputed fact that the admission order was passed ex-parte without notice to the corporate debtor[cite: 9]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Principal Bench admitted the Section 9 application on April 28, 2017 without notice[cite: 9]. The corporate debtor appealed to the NCLAT upon learning of the order from the IRP[cite: 9].
legal_issues: Whether an order admitting a Section 9 insolvency application is legally sustainable if passed without notice to the corporate debtor, in violation of the principles of natural justice[cite: 9].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An order initiating corporate insolvency resolution process passed without serving notice to the corporate debtor violates the principles of natural justice and is liable to be set aside[cite: 9]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 9 of the I&B Code must be read in consonance with natural justice requirements, requiring a hearing or notice before admission[cite: 9]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Uncontroverted admission by the respondent that the Adjudicating Authority passed the admission order without issuing notice to the corporate debtor[cite: 9]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The failure to provide notice rendered the admission order illegal, and coupled with the parties' subsequent settlement, the Section 9 application must be dismissed[cite: 9].
operative_order: The impugned order dated April 28, 2017 is set aside, the Section 9 application is dismissed, the corporate debtor is restored to its Board of Directors, and the appellant is directed to pay the IRP's fees[cite: 9].
summary: International Recreation & Amusement Ltd. appealed an NCLT Principal Bench order that admitted a Section 9 insolvency application filed by S.R. Construction[cite: 9]. The corporate debtor argued that the admission order was passed ex-parte without any notice, violating natural justice[cite: 9]. The operational creditor did not dispute this and confirmed the parties had settled[cite: 9]. The NCLAT held that the ex-parte admission violated natural justice, set aside the NCLT order, and dismissed the insolvency application[cite: 9]. The corporate debtor was restored to its Board, and directed to pay the IRP's fees[cite: 9].

case_title: BSE Ltd. vs. M/s Ricoh Company Ltd & Ors.[cite: 10]
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is BSE Ltd; Respondents are M/s Ricoh Company Ltd & Ors.[cite: 10]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Recapitalization and reduction of share capital of Ricoh Company Ltd.[cite: 10]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Corporate dispute over cancellation/reduction of share capital involving 1,09,59,792 shares held by NRP Group Limited[cite: 10]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Tribunal ordered Rs. 1123 crores to be brought in on August 24, 2016; Tribunal issued a clarification order on September 30, 2016[cite: 10]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: NCLT Mumbai order directing bringing in Rs. 1123 crores as share application money before cancellation of shares, and SEBI regulations governing listing obligations[cite: 10]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai passed an interim order clarifying that procedure under Sections 100-104 of the 1956 Act need not be followed since the order was under Section 242 of the 2013 Act. BSE Ltd appealed this in NCLAT[cite: 10].
legal_issues: Whether the NCLT can exempt a company from complying with Sections 100-104 of the Companies Act, 1956 and SEBI Regulations when ordering a reduction of share capital under Section 242 of the Companies Act, 2013[cite: 10].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: While SEBI regulations and the Companies Act must be read harmoniously, provisions of the Companies Act, 1956 regarding High Court confirmation for share capital reduction are redundant after the transfer of jurisdiction to the NCLT[cite: 10]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 434 of the Companies Act, 2013 and Section 242 interpreted alongside SEBI Act requirements; Sections 100-102 of the 1956 Act are no longer applicable as High Court powers have been divested[cite: 10]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Examination of the statutory transition of jurisdiction from High Courts to the NCLT and its effect on pending schemes[cite: 10]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLT erred in passing the clarification under Section 242(2)(c) as an interim order, but since High Court jurisdiction under Sections 100-102 is divested, those specific sections need not be followed, though other SEBI rules must be complied with[cite: 10].
operative_order: The appeal is allowed, setting aside the September 30, 2016 NCLT order, and directing respondents to follow mandatory SEBI Act provisions and regulations, except Sections 100 to 102 of the Companies Act, 1956, with no order as to costs[cite: 10].
summary: BSE Ltd appealed an NCLT Mumbai order which held that Ricoh Company Ltd need not follow the share capital reduction procedure under Sections 100-104 of the Companies Act, 1956, because the order was passed under Section 242 of the 2013 Act[cite: 10]. The NCLAT noted that while SEBI regulations are mandatory and must be harmonized with the Companies Act, the requirement of High Court confirmation under Sections 100-102 of the 1956 Act has become redundant due to the transfer of jurisdiction to the NCLT[cite: 10]. The NCLAT set aside the NCLT's clarification order but directed the company to follow all SEBI regulations minus the obsolete High Court confirmation steps[cite: 10].

case_title: Mr. Venumbaka Vijaya Sai Reddy & Ors. vs. Registrar of Companies, Hyderabad[cite: 11]
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants are former directors and company secretary of Jagati Publications Limited; Respondent is the Registrar of Companies, Hyderabad[cite: 11]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Violations related to financial reporting and statutory filings[cite: 11]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Non-attachment of Cash Flow Statements for 2007-08 and 2006-07; incorrect disclosure of issued capital (Rs. 81.91 Cr instead of Rs. 100 Cr); non-disclosure of related party transactions[cite: 11]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Inspection conducted between 2012-2015; preliminary finding letter issued July 30, 2015; NCLT orders passed June 5 and June 28, 2017[cite: 11]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: E-forms 23AC and ACA filed without cash flow statements, and balance sheets showing discrepancies in issued versus paid-up capital[cite: 11]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appellants filed compounding applications under Section 621A before the CLB, which were transferred to NCLT Hyderabad[cite: 11]. NCLT rejected some applications for alleged false submissions and allowed others but imposed multiplied penalties[cite: 11]. Appellants challenged this in the NCLAT[cite: 11].
legal_issues: Whether the NCLT was justified in rejecting compounding applications for first-time technical offences, and whether compounding fees could be multiplied by the number of years when the statute does not explicitly prescribe it as a continuing offence[cite: 11].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Compounding of first-time technical offences should generally be allowed unless mala fide intent is proven; compounding fees cannot exceed the maximum statutory penalty unless the statute explicitly defines the violation as a continuing offence with per-day fines[cite: 11]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Sections 211(7) and 217(5) of the Companies Act, 1956 prescribe fixed maximum penalties for each offence and do not contain provisions for per-day or recurring continuing penalties, unlike Section 168[cite: 11]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Review of balance sheets and compounding applications, finding no evidence of false submissions that warranted rejection by NCLT, alongside ROC's admission that these were first-time defaults[cite: 11]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLT erred in rejecting compounding for lack of intent/false submissions and erred in multiplying the compounding fees beyond the maximum statutory limits for non-recurring offences[cite: 11].
operative_order: The appeals are allowed, the impugned NCLT orders are set aside, and compounding is permitted for all appellants with specific statutory maximum compounding fees (Rs. 10,000 or Rs. 20,000 depending on the section) directed to be paid from their personal accounts[cite: 11].
summary: Former directors of Jagati Publications Limited appealed NCLT Hyderabad orders that rejected their compounding applications under Section 621A of the Companies Act, 1956 or imposed excessive penalties[cite: 11]. The offences involved technical lapses like failing to attach cash-flow statements or minor misstatements in share capital[cite: 11]. The NCLAT found that the NCLT incorrectly rejected applications on unfounded grounds of false submissions and unlawfully multiplied the penalty amount by 10 years for other offences[cite: 11]. The Tribunal clarified that Sections 211 and 217 do not prescribe continuing penalties[cite: 11]. The NCLAT allowed the appeals, permitting compounding with statutory maximum fines[cite: 11].

case_title: Axis Bank Ltd. vs. Dinkar T. Venkatsubramanian[cite: 12]
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Axis Bank Ltd (Financial Creditor); Respondent is Dinkar T. Venkatsubramanian (Resolution Professional for JODPL Pvt. Ltd.)[cite: 12]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Claim of the financial creditor during the corporate insolvency resolution process[cite: 12]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Dispute regarding the acceptance of a financial creditor's claim[cite: 12]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Committee of Creditors (CoC) meeting was held on November 3, 2017[cite: 12]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Minutes of the Committee of Creditors meeting dated November 3, 2017, demonstrating the acceptance of the appellant's claim[cite: 12]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appellant filed an appeal regarding its claim but subsequently sought to withdraw it after the Interim Resolution Professional and CoC accepted the claim during the pendency of the appeal[cite: 12].
legal_issues: Whether the appeal should be permitted to be withdrawn following the CoC's acceptance of the financial creditor's claim[cite: 12].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An appeal may be withdrawn if the core grievance of the appellant has been resolved by the Committee of Creditors during the pendency of the appeal[cite: 12]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: N/A[cite: 12]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Reliance on the minutes of the CoC meeting confirming the resolution of the dispute[cite: 12]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Tribunal permitted the withdrawal of the appeal upon taking the CoC minutes on record, thereby disposing of the matter[cite: 12].
operative_order: The appeal is disposed of as withdrawn, with the minutes of the Committee of Creditors of JODPL Pvt. Ltd. kept on record, and no order as to costs[cite: 12].
summary: Axis Bank Ltd. filed an appeal against the Resolution Professional of JODPL Pvt. Ltd. regarding the treatment of its claim as a financial creditor[cite: 12]. During the pendency of the appeal, the Committee of Creditors held a meeting on November 3, 2017, where a decision was taken to accept the financial creditor's claim[cite: 12]. Consequently, the appellant's counsel requested to withdraw the appeal[cite: 12]. The NCLAT permitted the withdrawal, took the CoC meeting minutes on record, and disposed of the appeal with no costs[cite: 12].

case_title: Agroh Infrastructure Developers Pvt Ltd vs. Narmada Construction (Indore) P Ltd[cite: 13]
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Agroh Infrastructure Developers Pvt Ltd (Corporate Debtor); Respondent is Narmada Construction (Indore) P Ltd (Operational Creditor)[cite: 13]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Underlying operational debt dispute between the corporate debtor and the operational creditor[cite: 13]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Unspecified operational default leading to the issuance of a statutory demand notice[cite: 13]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Demand notice issued on April 4, 2017, and served on April 8, 2017; NCLT admitted the application on May 18, 2017[cite: 13]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Postal Department track record showing service of the demand notice, and the undisputed fact that the NCLT passed the admission order without issuing notice to the Corporate Debtor[cite: 13]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Operational Creditor filed a Section 9 application which was admitted by NCLT Ahmedabad on May 18, 2017, without notice to the Corporate Debtor. The Appellant appealed to NCLAT[cite: 13].
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority can admit an application under Section 9 of the IBC without giving prior notice of hearing to the corporate debtor, thereby violating principles of natural justice[cite: 13].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An order admitting an insolvency application passed without issuing notice to the corporate debtor violates the principles of natural justice and is liable to be set aside[cite: 13]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 9 of the IBC, read with natural justice principles, mandates that a corporate debtor be given an opportunity to be heard before CIRP is initiated[cite: 13]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The respondent did not dispute the fact that no notice was issued by the Adjudicating Authority prior to admission[cite: 13]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The ex-parte admission of the Section 9 application was illegal. Since the parties subsequently settled the dispute and agreed to withdraw the application, the NCLAT set aside the admission order and terminated the CIRP[cite: 13].
operative_order: The impugned order dated May 18, 2017, is set aside, the CIRP actions are declared illegal, and the corporate debtor is released from the rigour of law to function independently. The operational creditor is allowed to withdraw the application and is directed to pay the fees of the Interim Resolution Professional[cite: 13].
summary: Agroh Infrastructure Developers Pvt Ltd challenged the NCLT Ahmedabad order admitting a Section 9 insolvency application filed by Narmada Construction[cite: 13]. The appellant argued that the NCLT admitted the petition without issuing any prior notice, thus violating natural justice[cite: 13]. The NCLAT noted that while the statutory demand notice was properly served, the NCLT failed to provide a hearing before admission[cite: 13]. Given this procedural flaw and the fact that the parties had subsequently settled the matter, the NCLAT set aside the CIRP initiation, restored the company to its Board of Directors, and permitted the operational creditor to withdraw the application[cite: 13].

case_title: Mother Pride Dairy India Pvt. Ltd. vs. Portrait Advertising & Marketing Pvt. Ltd.[cite: 14]
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Mother Pride Dairy India Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor); Respondent is Portrait Advertising & Marketing Pvt. Ltd. (Operational Creditor)[cite: 14]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Underlying operational debt dispute between the advertising agency and the dairy company[cite: 14]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Unspecified operational default leading to the Section 9 application[cite: 14]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: NCLT Principal Bench admitted the application on June 27, 2017. Settlement occurred post-admission[cite: 14]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Post-admission settlement agreement and payment made between the Operational Creditor and Corporate Debtor[cite: 14]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Principal Bench admitted the Section 9 application on June 27, 2017. Appellant challenged the admission in NCLAT seeking withdrawal based on the subsequent settlement[cite: 14].
legal_issues: Whether an application under Section 9 of the IBC can be withdrawn on the basis of a settlement reached after the application has already been admitted by the Adjudicating Authority[cite: 14].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Once an insolvency application is admitted, it cannot be withdrawn even by the applicant creditor based on a bilateral settlement, because the proceeding becomes an in rem process where other creditors are entitled to raise claims[cite: 14]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Rule 8 of the Insolvency & Bankruptcy (Adjudicating Authority) Rules, 2016 permits withdrawal only before admission; post-admission, Sections 15 and 18 of the IBC take effect, mandating public announcement and collation of all creditors' claims[cite: 14]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Undisputed fact that the settlement occurred after the admission order was passed by the NCLT[cite: 14]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Appellate Tribunal refused to interfere with the admission order solely on the ground of a post-admission settlement, holding that withdrawal is legally impermissible at this stage, though the corporate debtor may settle all claims for potential closure[cite: 14].
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed with no costs. The Tribunal clarified that if the corporate debtor satisfies the claims of all other creditors, the IRP may bring it to the NCLT's notice for potential closure of the resolution process in accordance with law[cite: 14].
summary: Mother Pride Dairy India Pvt. Ltd. appealed the NCLT Principal Bench order dated June 27, 2017, which admitted a Section 9 insolvency application filed by Portrait Advertising[cite: 14]. The appellant sought to set aside the order on the ground that the parties had settled the dispute and payment had been made after the admission[cite: 14]. The NCLAT held that under Rule 8, an application can only be withdrawn before admission[cite: 14]. Once admitted, the CIRP is an in rem proceeding affecting all creditors under Sections 15 and 18[cite: 14]. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal but noted that if all creditors' claims are satisfied, the Adjudicating Authority could consider closing the CIRP[cite: 14].

case_title: BSE Ltd. vs. M/s Ricoh Company Ltd & Ors.[cite: 10]
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is BSE Ltd; Respondents are M/s Ricoh Company Ltd & Ors.[cite: 10]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Recapitalization and reduction of share capital of Ricoh Company Ltd.[cite: 10]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Corporate dispute over cancellation/reduction of share capital involving 1,09,59,792 shares held by NRP Group Limited[cite: 10]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Tribunal ordered Rs. 1123 crores to be brought in on August 24, 2016; Tribunal issued a clarification order on September 30, 2016[cite: 10]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: NCLT Mumbai order directing bringing in Rs. 1123 crores as share application money before cancellation of shares, and SEBI regulations governing listing obligations[cite: 10]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai passed an interim order clarifying that procedure under Sections 100-104 of the 1956 Act need not be followed since the order was under Section 242 of the 2013 Act. BSE Ltd appealed this in NCLAT[cite: 10].
legal_issues: Whether the NCLT can exempt a company from complying with Sections 100-104 of the Companies Act, 1956 and SEBI Regulations when ordering a reduction of share capital under Section 242 of the Companies Act, 2013[cite: 10].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: While SEBI regulations and the Companies Act must be read harmoniously, provisions of the Companies Act, 1956 regarding High Court confirmation for share capital reduction are redundant after the transfer of jurisdiction to the NCLT[cite: 10]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 434 of the Companies Act, 2013 and Section 242 interpreted alongside SEBI Act requirements; Sections 100-102 of the 1956 Act are no longer applicable as High Court powers have been divested[cite: 10]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Examination of the statutory transition of jurisdiction from High Courts to the NCLT and its effect on pending schemes[cite: 10]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLT erred in passing the clarification under Section 242(2)(c) as an interim order, but since High Court jurisdiction under Sections 100-102 is divested, those specific sections need not be followed, though other SEBI rules must be complied with[cite: 10].
operative_order: The appeal is allowed, setting aside the September 30, 2016 NCLT order, and directing respondents to follow mandatory SEBI Act provisions and regulations, except Sections 100 to 102 of the Companies Act, 1956, with no order as to costs[cite: 10].
summary: BSE Ltd appealed an NCLT Mumbai order which held that Ricoh Company Ltd need not follow the share capital reduction procedure under Sections 100-104 of the Companies Act, 1956, because the order was passed under Section 242 of the 2013 Act[cite: 10]. The NCLAT noted that while SEBI regulations are mandatory and must be harmonized with the Companies Act, the requirement of High Court confirmation under Sections 100-102 of the 1956 Act has become redundant due to the transfer of jurisdiction to the NCLT[cite: 10]. The NCLAT set aside the NCLT's clarification order but directed the company to follow all SEBI regulations minus the obsolete High Court confirmation steps[cite: 10].

case_title: Mr. Venumbaka Vijaya Sai Reddy & Ors. vs. Registrar of Companies, Hyderabad[cite: 11]
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants are former directors and company secretary of Jagati Publications Limited; Respondent is the Registrar of Companies, Hyderabad[cite: 11]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Violations related to financial reporting and statutory filings[cite: 11]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Non-attachment of Cash Flow Statements for 2007-08 and 2006-07; incorrect disclosure of issued capital (Rs. 81.91 Cr instead of Rs. 100 Cr); non-disclosure of related party transactions[cite: 11]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Inspection conducted between 2012-2015; preliminary finding letter issued July 30, 2015; NCLT orders passed June 5 and June 28, 2017[cite: 11]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: E-forms 23AC and ACA filed without cash flow statements, and balance sheets showing discrepancies in issued versus paid-up capital[cite: 11]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appellants filed compounding applications under Section 621A before the CLB, which were transferred to NCLT Hyderabad[cite: 11]. NCLT rejected some applications for alleged false submissions and allowed others but imposed multiplied penalties[cite: 11]. Appellants challenged this in the NCLAT[cite: 11].
legal_issues: Whether the NCLT was justified in rejecting compounding applications for first-time technical offences, and whether compounding fees could be multiplied by the number of years when the statute does not explicitly prescribe it as a continuing offence[cite: 11].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Compounding of first-time technical offences should generally be allowed unless mala fide intent is proven; compounding fees cannot exceed the maximum statutory penalty unless the statute explicitly defines the violation as a continuing offence with per-day fines[cite: 11]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Sections 211(7) and 217(5) of the Companies Act, 1956 prescribe fixed maximum penalties for each offence and do not contain provisions for per-day or recurring continuing penalties, unlike Section 168[cite: 11]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Review of balance sheets and compounding applications, finding no evidence of false submissions that warranted rejection by NCLT, alongside ROC's admission that these were first-time defaults[cite: 11]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLT erred in rejecting compounding for lack of intent/false submissions and erred in multiplying the compounding fees beyond the maximum statutory limits for non-recurring offences[cite: 11].
operative_order: The appeals are allowed, the impugned NCLT orders are set aside, and compounding is permitted for all appellants with specific statutory maximum compounding fees (Rs. 10,000 or Rs. 20,000 depending on the section) directed to be paid from their personal accounts[cite: 11].
summary: Former directors of Jagati Publications Limited appealed NCLT Hyderabad orders that rejected their compounding applications under Section 621A of the Companies Act, 1956 or imposed excessive penalties[cite: 11]. The offences involved technical lapses like failing to attach cash-flow statements or minor misstatements in share capital[cite: 11]. The NCLAT found that the NCLT incorrectly rejected applications on unfounded grounds of false submissions and unlawfully multiplied the penalty amount by 10 years for other offences[cite: 11]. The Tribunal clarified that Sections 211 and 217 do not prescribe continuing penalties[cite: 11]. The NCLAT allowed the appeals, permitting compounding with statutory maximum fines[cite: 11].

case_title: Axis Bank Ltd. vs. Dinkar T. Venkatsubramanian[cite: 12]
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Axis Bank Ltd (Financial Creditor); Respondent is Dinkar T. Venkatsubramanian (Resolution Professional for JODPL Pvt. Ltd.)[cite: 12]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Claim of the financial creditor during the corporate insolvency resolution process[cite: 12]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Dispute regarding the acceptance of a financial creditor's claim[cite: 12]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Committee of Creditors (CoC) meeting was held on November 3, 2017[cite: 12]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Minutes of the Committee of Creditors meeting dated November 3, 2017, demonstrating the acceptance of the appellant's claim[cite: 12]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appellant filed an appeal regarding its claim but subsequently sought to withdraw it after the Interim Resolution Professional and CoC accepted the claim during the pendency of the appeal[cite: 12].
legal_issues: Whether the appeal should be permitted to be withdrawn following the CoC's acceptance of the financial creditor's claim[cite: 12].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An appeal may be withdrawn if the core grievance of the appellant has been resolved by the Committee of Creditors during the pendency of the appeal[cite: 12]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: N/A[cite: 12]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Reliance on the minutes of the CoC meeting confirming the resolution of the dispute[cite: 12]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Tribunal permitted the withdrawal of the appeal upon taking the CoC minutes on record, thereby disposing of the matter[cite: 12].
operative_order: The appeal is disposed of as withdrawn, with the minutes of the Committee of Creditors of JODPL Pvt. Ltd. kept on record, and no order as to costs[cite: 12].
summary: Axis Bank Ltd. filed an appeal against the Resolution Professional of JODPL Pvt. Ltd. regarding the treatment of its claim as a financial creditor[cite: 12]. During the pendency of the appeal, the Committee of Creditors held a meeting on November 3, 2017, where a decision was taken to accept the financial creditor's claim[cite: 12]. Consequently, the appellant's counsel requested to withdraw the appeal[cite: 12]. The NCLAT permitted the withdrawal, took the CoC meeting minutes on record, and disposed of the appeal with no costs[cite: 12].

case_title: Agroh Infrastructure Developers Pvt Ltd vs. Narmada Construction (Indore) P Ltd[cite: 13]
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Agroh Infrastructure Developers Pvt Ltd (Corporate Debtor); Respondent is Narmada Construction (Indore) P Ltd (Operational Creditor)[cite: 13]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Underlying operational debt dispute between the corporate debtor and the operational creditor[cite: 13]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Unspecified operational default leading to the issuance of a statutory demand notice[cite: 13]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Demand notice issued on April 4, 2017, and served on April 8, 2017; NCLT admitted the application on May 18, 2017[cite: 13]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Postal Department track record showing service of the demand notice, and the undisputed fact that the NCLT passed the admission order without issuing notice to the Corporate Debtor[cite: 13]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Operational Creditor filed a Section 9 application which was admitted by NCLT Ahmedabad on May 18, 2017, without notice to the Corporate Debtor. The Appellant appealed to NCLAT[cite: 13].
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority can admit an application under Section 9 of the IBC without giving prior notice of hearing to the corporate debtor, thereby violating principles of natural justice[cite: 13].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An order admitting an insolvency application passed without issuing notice to the corporate debtor violates the principles of natural justice and is liable to be set aside[cite: 13]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 9 of the IBC, read with natural justice principles, mandates that a corporate debtor be given an opportunity to be heard before CIRP is initiated[cite: 13]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The respondent did not dispute the fact that no notice was issued by the Adjudicating Authority prior to admission[cite: 13]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The ex-parte admission of the Section 9 application was illegal. Since the parties subsequently settled the dispute and agreed to withdraw the application, the NCLAT set aside the admission order and terminated the CIRP[cite: 13].
operative_order: The impugned order dated May 18, 2017, is set aside, the CIRP actions are declared illegal, and the corporate debtor is released from the rigour of law to function independently. The operational creditor is allowed to withdraw the application and is directed to pay the fees of the Interim Resolution Professional[cite: 13].
summary: Agroh Infrastructure Developers Pvt Ltd challenged the NCLT Ahmedabad order admitting a Section 9 insolvency application filed by Narmada Construction[cite: 13]. The appellant argued that the NCLT admitted the petition without issuing any prior notice, thus violating natural justice[cite: 13]. The NCLAT noted that while the statutory demand notice was properly served, the NCLT failed to provide a hearing before admission[cite: 13]. Given this procedural flaw and the fact that the parties had subsequently settled the matter, the NCLAT set aside the CIRP initiation, restored the company to its Board of Directors, and permitted the operational creditor to withdraw the application[cite: 13].

case_title: Mother Pride Dairy India Pvt. Ltd. vs. Portrait Advertising & Marketing Pvt. Ltd.[cite: 14]
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Mother Pride Dairy India Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor); Respondent is Portrait Advertising & Marketing Pvt. Ltd. (Operational Creditor)[cite: 14]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Underlying operational debt dispute between the advertising agency and the dairy company[cite: 14]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Unspecified operational default leading to the Section 9 application[cite: 14]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: NCLT Principal Bench admitted the application on June 27, 2017. Settlement occurred post-admission[cite: 14]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Post-admission settlement agreement and payment made between the Operational Creditor and Corporate Debtor[cite: 14]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Principal Bench admitted the Section 9 application on June 27, 2017. Appellant challenged the admission in NCLAT seeking withdrawal based on the subsequent settlement[cite: 14].
legal_issues: Whether an application under Section 9 of the IBC can be withdrawn on the basis of a settlement reached after the application has already been admitted by the Adjudicating Authority[cite: 14].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Once an insolvency application is admitted, it cannot be withdrawn even by the applicant creditor based on a bilateral settlement, because the proceeding becomes an in rem process where other creditors are entitled to raise claims[cite: 14]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Rule 8 of the Insolvency & Bankruptcy (Adjudicating Authority) Rules, 2016 permits withdrawal only before admission; post-admission, Sections 15 and 18 of the IBC take effect, mandating public announcement and collation of all creditors' claims[cite: 14]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Undisputed fact that the settlement occurred after the admission order was passed by the NCLT[cite: 14]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Appellate Tribunal refused to interfere with the admission order solely on the ground of a post-admission settlement, holding that withdrawal is legally impermissible at this stage, though the corporate debtor may settle all claims for potential closure[cite: 14].
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed with no costs. The Tribunal clarified that if the corporate debtor satisfies the claims of all other creditors, the IRP may bring it to the NCLT's notice for potential closure of the resolution process in accordance with law[cite: 14].
summary: Mother Pride Dairy India Pvt. Ltd. appealed the NCLT Principal Bench order dated June 27, 2017, which admitted a Section 9 insolvency application filed by Portrait Advertising[cite: 14]. The appellant sought to set aside the order on the ground that the parties had settled the dispute and payment had been made after the admission[cite: 14]. The NCLAT held that under Rule 8, an application can only be withdrawn before admission[cite: 14]. Once admitted, the CIRP is an in rem proceeding affecting all creditors under Sections 15 and 18[cite: 14]. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal but noted that if all creditors' claims are satisfied, the Adjudicating Authority could consider closing the CIRP[cite: 14].

case_title: P.K. Ores Private Limited vs. Tractors India Private Limited[cite: 15]
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is P.K. Ores Private Limited (Corporate Debtor); Respondent is Tractors India Private Limited (Operational Creditor)[cite: 15]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Repair and installation of a Caterpillar Engine (CAT 6.6) by the Operational Creditor for the Corporate Debtor[cite: 15]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Operational Creditor claimed an unpaid debt of Rs. 9,76,095/-. The Corporate Debtor alleged a counter-loss of Rs. 2 crores due to negligence and non-supply of spares[cite: 15]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Demand notice sent on January 17, 2017; pre-existing dispute raised via correspondence in November and December 2016; NCLT admission order passed on April 3, 2017[cite: 15]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Letter dated November 16, 2016 from the Corporate Debtor complaining about the faulty engine and claiming damages, predating the Section 8 demand notice[cite: 15]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Kolkata admitted the Section 9 application on April 3, 2017 without issuing notice to the Corporate Debtor. The Corporate Debtor challenged this ex-parte admission before the NCLAT[cite: 15].
legal_issues: Whether the NCLT can admit a Section 9 insolvency application without issuing a prior notice to the corporate debtor, and whether a dispute raised regarding the quality of services before the issuance of the demand notice bars the application[cite: 15].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An order admitting a corporate insolvency resolution process application without issuing notice to the corporate debtor violates the principles of natural justice and must be set aside. Additionally, raising a substantive dispute regarding the quality of goods or services prior to the demand notice constitutes a pre-existing dispute barring Section 9 applications[cite: 15]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 424 of the Companies Act, 2013 mandates adherence to natural justice, making prior notice essential for Sections 7 and 9 of the IBC. Section 5(6) read with Section 8(2) of the IBC encompasses disputes regarding the quality of goods raised before a competent authority or through communications prior to the statutory notice[cite: 15]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Assessment of pre-demand correspondence (November 16, 2016 letter) demonstrating that the Corporate Debtor had raised substantive issues about the engine's functionality and claimed financial losses well before the Section 8 notice was issued[cite: 15]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Since the Adjudicating Authority admitted the petition ex-parte in violation of natural justice, and the record proved the existence of a pre-existing dispute regarding service quality, the admission order was illegal and the petition not maintainable[cite: 15].
operative_order: The impugned NCLT order dated April 3, 2017 is set aside. The CIRP proceedings, including the appointment of the IRP and the moratorium, are declared illegal. The Corporate Debtor is released to function independently, and the Financial/Operational Creditor is directed to pay the IRP's fees. The appeal is allowed with no order as to costs[cite: 15].
summary: P.K. Ores Private Limited challenged the NCLT Kolkata's ex-parte admission of a Section 9 insolvency petition filed by Tractors India Private Limited[cite: 15]. The NCLAT found that the NCLT violated natural justice by failing to issue a notice before admission[cite: 15]. Furthermore, pre-demand correspondence from November 2016 showed that the corporate debtor had formally complained about the quality of the repaired Caterpillar engine and claimed counter-damages, constituting a valid pre-existing dispute under Section 5(6) of the IBC[cite: 15]. The NCLAT consequently set aside the admission order, dismissed the petition, and restored the corporate debtor's management[cite: 15].

case_title: M/s. Cinepolis India Pvt Ltd. & Ors vs. Registrar of Companies, NCT of Delhi & Haryana[cite: 16]
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants are M/s. Cinepolis India Pvt Ltd. & Ors.; Respondent is the Registrar of Companies, NCT of Delhi & Haryana[cite: 16]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate compliance failure regarding the timely filing of Annual Returns and financial statements[cite: 16]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Non-compliance with statutory filing requirements for the financial year ended March 31, 2013, attracting penalties under Sections 92, 137, 96, and 129 of the Companies Act, 2013[cite: 16]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Financial year ended March 31, 2013; NCLT order passed on March 7, 2017[cite: 16]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Appellants admitted the default and filed for compounding. It was undisputed that no prosecution was pending before any Special Court for these offences[cite: 16]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appellants filed a compounding application under Section 441 of the Companies Act, 2013 before the NCLT New Delhi. The NCLT dismissed it on March 7, 2017, directing them to file before the Special Court. Appellants appealed to NCLAT[cite: 16].
legal_issues: Whether the NCLT has the jurisdiction to compound offences under Section 441 of the Companies Act, 2013 that are punishable with imprisonment or fine, when no prosecution is pending before a Special Court[cite: 16].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The Tribunal has the statutory jurisdiction to compound offences punishable with alternative penalties of 'fine or imprisonment' without seeking permission from a Special Court, provided no prosecution is currently pending before such a court[cite: 16]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 441(6) of the Companies Act, 2013 prohibits the Tribunal from compounding offences punishable only with imprisonment, or imprisonment and fine. However, for offences carrying an alternative punishment (imprisonment OR fine), the Tribunal exercises parallel jurisdiction to compound[cite: 16]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Examination of the penal clauses of Sections 92, 137, 96, and 129 to confirm that the punishments prescribed are alternative (fine or imprisonment) and verifying that no Special Court was seized of the matter[cite: 16]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLT incorrectly declined jurisdiction. Because the statutes prescribe alternative punishments and no Special Court case was pending, the Tribunal was fully empowered to hear and decide the compounding application on merits[cite: 16].
operative_order: The impugned order dated March 7, 2017 is set aside. The case is remitted back to the NCLT New Delhi Bench to decide the quantum of penalty to be imposed after calling for a report from the Registrar of Companies, with no order as to costs[cite: 16].
summary: M/s Cinepolis India Pvt Ltd. appealed an NCLT New Delhi order that returned its compounding application for failing to submit annual returns, directing them to approach a Special Court[cite: 16]. The NCLAT clarified the scope of Section 441 of the Companies Act, 2013, noting that the Tribunal is prohibited from compounding offences punishable with mandatory imprisonment[cite: 16]. However, for offences carrying alternative punishments ('imprisonment or fine'), the Tribunal possesses parallel jurisdiction to compound without Special Court permission, provided no prosecution is pending[cite: 16]. Consequently, the NCLAT set aside the NCLT's order and remitted the matter for deciding the compounding penalty on merits[cite: 16].

case_title: Mrs. Proddaturi Malathi vs. SRP Logistics Pvt Ltd & Ors.[cite: 17]
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Mrs. Proddaturi Malathi (Shareholder/Director); Respondents are SRP Logistics Pvt Ltd and its other directors/shareholders, primarily Mr. Sekhar Pendam and Mrs. Salalitha Parsha[cite: 17]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Dispute over the increase in authorized/paid-up share capital and the disproportionate allotment of shares in a closely held private company[cite: 17]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Alleged illegal allotment of shares reducing the appellant's shareholding from 49.99% to 14.29% without following statutory pre-emptive rights[cite: 17]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Disputed share allotments took place in September 2015 and November 2016. EOGM for the appellant's removal was scheduled for April 10, 2017. NCLT passed the impugned order on April 27, 2017[cite: 17]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Corporate records indicating the drastic dilution of the appellant's shareholding and EOGM notices seeking her removal without assigning reasons[cite: 17]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appellant filed an oppression and mismanagement petition under Sections 59, 241, 242, and 244 before the NCLT Hyderabad. NCLT disposed of the petition on April 27, 2017 solely by setting aside her removal as a director, ignoring the share allotment issues. Appellant challenged this piecemeal disposal[cite: 17].
legal_issues: Whether the Tribunal erred in disposing of an oppression and mismanagement petition by addressing only the issue of a director's removal while failing to adjudicate substantive allegations regarding illegal share allotments and dilution of shareholding under Section 62 of the Companies Act, 2013[cite: 17].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: In a petition alleging systemic oppression and mismanagement, the Tribunal is obligated to adjudicate upon all substantive core issues raised, such as illegal share allotments and violation of pre-emptive rights, and cannot dispose of the matter by merely addressing ancillary issues like director removal[cite: 17]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 62 of the Companies Act, 2013 is applicable to private companies, imposing a mandatory fiduciary duty on directors to offer further issue of shares to existing shareholders proportionately to prevent oppressive dilution of their stake[cite: 17]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Assessment of the NCLT's failure to return findings on the alleged disproportionate share allotments, compliance with the Ministry's notifications, and the alleged mala fide intent to reduce the appellant's shareholding from 49.99% to 14.29%[cite: 17]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLT's piecemeal approach of selectively deciding the director removal issue while ignoring the core oppression allegations regarding share capital was inappropriate, necessitating a remand for a comprehensive adjudication on merits[cite: 17].
operative_order: The matter is remanded back to the NCLT Hyderabad to deal with all issues raised in the petition on their merits. As an interim measure, any Board Resolution passed for the removal of the appellant from the post of Director shall not be given effect until the NCLT disposes of the case[cite: 17].
summary: Appellant Mrs. Proddaturi Malathi challenged an NCLT Hyderabad order which disposed of her oppression and mismanagement petition by merely setting aside her removal as a director, while ignoring her primary grievance about the illegal allotment of shares that reduced her stake in SRP Logistics Pvt Ltd from 49.99% to 14.29%[cite: 17]. The NCLAT noted that Section 62 of the Companies Act, 2013 applies to private companies, thereby protecting the pre-emptive rights of existing shareholders against oppressive dilution[cite: 17]. The NCLAT held that the NCLT failed to exercise its jurisdiction properly by ignoring these core oppression issues, and remanded the matter back for a full adjudication on merits, with interim protection for the appellant's directorship[cite: 17].

case_title: Anra Pharmaceuticals Pvt. Ltd. & Ors vs. A. Ramasubbu[cite: 18]
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants are Anra Pharmaceuticals Pvt. Ltd. & Ors.; Respondent is A. Ramasubbu[cite: 18]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Internal corporate dispute leading to prayers for winding up and nullification of sale/mortgage deeds[cite: 18]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Respondent sought winding up of the company and liquidation of its properties[cite: 18]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Petition originally filed before CLB in March 2016; transferred to NCLT; NCLT passed the impugned order on June 20, 2017[cite: 18]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The original petition invoked Sections 397, 398, 433, 439, and 450 of the Companies Act, 1956 before the CLB[cite: 18]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: A composite petition for oppression/mismanagement and winding up was filed before the CLB. Upon its transfer to the NCLT under Section 434, the NCLT rejected the appellants' maintainability objections and treated the winding-up prayer as an application under Section 9 of the IBC. Appellants challenged this conversion in the NCLAT[cite: 18].
legal_issues: Whether the NCLT can treat a winding-up petition filed originally before the Company Law Board under Section 433 of the Companies Act, 1956 as an application under Section 9 of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016[cite: 18].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A winding-up petition under the Companies Act, 1956 was not legally maintainable before the Company Law Board (CLB). Consequently, upon transfer to the NCLT, such a legally flawed petition cannot be converted into an insolvency application under the IBC[cite: 18]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 434 of the Companies Act, 2013 and Rule 5 of the Companies (Transfer of Pending Proceedings) Rules, 2016 stipulate that only valid winding-up petitions transferred from a High Court can be treated as IBC applications. The CLB inherently lacked jurisdiction over winding-up matters[cite: 18]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Verification of the forum where the petition was originally instituted (the CLB) to determine if it possessed the statutory jurisdiction to entertain winding-up prayers under the 1956 Act[cite: 18]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because the CLB had no jurisdiction over winding-up prayers, the NCLT fundamentally erred in converting the petition into a Section 9 IBC proceeding. The Tribunal is only competent to hear the transferred petition on the grounds of oppression and mismanagement[cite: 18].
operative_order: The NCLT order dated June 20, 2017 is set aside. Liberty is granted to the NCLT to try the transferred petition exclusively under Sections 397 and 398 of the Companies Act, 1956 (now Section 241 of the 2013 Act) in accordance with law, with no order as to costs[cite: 18].
summary: Anra Pharmaceuticals Pvt. Ltd. appealed against an NCLT order which treated a transferred Company Law Board (CLB) petition for winding up as a Section 9 application under the IBC[cite: 18]. The NCLAT noted that under the Companies Act, 1956, the CLB had no jurisdiction to entertain winding-up petitions; such jurisdiction vested exclusively with High Courts[cite: 18]. Thus, the statutory rules permitting the conversion of pending winding-up petitions into IBC applications apply strictly to matters transferred from High Courts, not the CLB[cite: 18]. The NCLAT set aside the NCLT order and directed that the petition be heard solely on the grounds of oppression and mismanagement[cite: 18].

case_title: Kole Investment and Trading Company Private Limited & Ors. vs. Mrs. Sulochana Neelkanth Kalyani & Ors.[cite: 19]
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) No. 389 of 2017 & Company Appeal (AT) No. 391 of 2017[cite: 19]
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants are Kole Investment and Trading Company Pvt Ltd & Ors (investment companies) and Gaurishankar N. Kalyani & Rohini G. Kalyani; Respondent No. 1 is Mrs. Sulochana Neelkanth Kalyani (Original Petitioner No. 7)[cite: 19]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Dispute over the control of a family trust and the associated investment companies holding significant shareholding in the flagship company, Kalyani Consultants Pvt Ltd[cite: 19]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Contested removal of the original petitioner's name from the share register and subsequent board resolutions attempting to transmit shares by operation of law to circumvent a High Court decree[cite: 19]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: High Court rectification order passed on June 7, 2016; disputed Board Resolution dated August 26, 2016; NCLT Company Petition filed on August 29, 2016; NCLT impugned order dated October 18, 2017[cite: 19]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: High Court judgement restoring the petitioner's shares, a subsequent Board Resolution allegedly circumventing this order via transmission by operation of law, and pending contempt petitions in the High Court[cite: 19]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Petitioner filed an oppression and mismanagement petition before NCLT Mumbai. Appellants challenged the maintainability, arguing the petitioner was stripped of her shares by the August 2016 resolution. NCLT rejected the maintainability applications, leading to these appeals in the NCLAT[cite: 19].
legal_issues: Whether a petitioner can maintain an oppression and mismanagement petition under Section 241/244 of the Companies Act, 2013 when the controlling directors purportedly transmitted her shares to themselves by 'operation of law' to circumvent a prior judicial rectification order[cite: 19].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: When a petitioner holds a valid judicial order or decree for the rectification of the register of members in their favor, the company cannot defeat their statutory right to maintain an oppression and mismanagement petition by artificially removing their name from the register through questionable board resolutions[cite: 19]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Interpreting Section 244 of the Companies Act, 2013 alongside the doctrine of derivative action, when wrongdoers in control of a company act mala fide to dilute the shareholding of a majority shareholder despite judicial orders, the aggrieved shareholder retains locus standi[cite: 19]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Juxtaposing the prior High Court order restoring the petitioner's shares against the subsequent Board Resolution stripping them away via a novel claim of transmission under the Trusts Act, revealing a mala fide attempt to overreach the court's decree[cite: 19]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLT correctly rejected the maintainability applications because the petitioner possessed a valid legal right and locus standi derived from the prior judicial decrees, making the oppression petition maintainable[cite: 19].
operative_order: Both appeals are dismissed with heavy costs of Rs. 1,00,000/- each saddled on the individual appellants (Rohini Gaurishankar Kalyani and Gaurishankar Neelkanth Kalyani), payable from their personal accounts to Respondent No. 1[cite: 19].
summary: Appellants challenged the NCLT Mumbai order which held that Mrs. Sulochana N. Kalyani's oppression and mismanagement petition was maintainable[cite: 19]. The appellants argued she was not a shareholder due to an August 2016 Board Resolution that purportedly transmitted her shares to them by 'operation of law'[cite: 19]. The NCLAT noted that she had previously won a High Court order declaring earlier transfers void and restoring her shares[cite: 19]. The August 2016 resolution was a mala fide attempt by the wrongdoers to circumvent that judicial decree[cite: 19]. The NCLAT held that her right to maintain the petition under Section 244 of the Companies Act, 2013 could not be defeated by such artificial maneuvers. Both appeals were dismissed with heavy costs[cite: 19].

case_title: Wiki Kids Limited & Avantel Ltd vs. Regional Director & Ors.[cite: 20]
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant No. 1 is Wiki Kids Limited (Transferor Company) and Appellant No. 2 is Avantel Ltd (Transferee Company); Respondents include Regional Director, Registrar of Companies, Official Liquidator, BSE Limited, and SEBI[cite: 20]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: A proposed Scheme of Amalgamation to merge the transferor company into the transferee company, both of which share common promoters[cite: 20]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The transferor company had no commercial operations for 13 years and a net worth of approximately Rs. 22.32 lakhs, but the share exchange ratio provided an approximate value of Rs. 12 crores to its promoters[cite: 20]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: High Court directed meetings were held on January 27, 2017, and the NCLT rejected the scheme on July 13, 2017[cite: 20]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: An independent valuation report and fairness opinion containing heavy disclaimers about relying on management's future projections, coupled with the absence of past commercial revenue and a missing Cash Flow Statement[cite: 20]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The second motion petitions were filed before NCLT Hyderabad, which rejected the scheme on July 13, 2017, observing it primarily benefited the promoters and lacked public interest. The companies subsequently appealed to the NCLAT[cite: 20].
legal_issues: Whether the NCLT has the jurisdiction to reject a scheme of amalgamation approved by shareholders and statutory authorities on the ground that the valuation disproportionately favors the common promoters and is not in the public interest[cite: 20].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The Tribunal possesses the duty and jurisdiction to ensure a scheme of amalgamation is just and fair to all shareholders and serves the public interest; it can reject a scheme if it is a device to grant undue financial advantage solely to common promoters based on speculative future projections[cite: 20]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The NCLT's supervisory jurisdiction over amalgamations under Sections 230-232 of the Companies Act, 2013 requires it to evaluate the broad fairness of the scheme to prevent unjust enrichment, without needing to mathematically audit every detail[cite: 20]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Evaluating the stark contrast between the transferor's negligible historical performance/net worth (Rs. 22.32 lakhs) and the massive projected valuation (Rs. 12 crores) allocated to the common promoters[cite: 20]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Since the scheme was clearly designed to give an immediate, unjustified windfall to the common promoters based on contingent future revenues rather than substantive past performance, the NCLT's rejection of the scheme was fully justified and the appeal must be dismissed[cite: 20].
operative_order: The appeal is rejected with no order as to costs, upholding the NCLT's decision to dismiss the Scheme of Amalgamation[cite: 20].
summary: Wiki Kids Limited and Avantel Ltd appealed against an NCLT Hyderabad order that rejected their proposed Scheme of Amalgamation[cite: 20]. Despite securing requisite approvals from shareholders and facing no formal objections from statutory authorities like SEBI or BSE, the NCLT found the scheme heavily skewed to benefit the common promoters[cite: 20]. The transferor company had no commercial revenue for 13 years and a net worth of Rs. 22.32 lakhs, yet the share exchange ratio granted a Rs. 12 crore benefit to its promoters based entirely on future projections[cite: 20]. The NCLAT upheld the NCLT's decision, affirming that the Tribunal must assess the broad fairness of a scheme to protect stakeholders and prevent unjust promoter enrichment[cite: 20].

case_title: World Book Company Pvt. Ltd vs. World Book India Pvt. Ltd. & Ors.[cite: 21]
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is World Book Company Pvt. Ltd.; Respondent No. 1 is World Book India Pvt. Ltd.[cite: 21]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate dispute regarding the incorporation and use of an allegedly identical or deceptively similar trademark and trade name 'World Book'[cite: 21]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The foreign entity 'World Book Inc.' filed a trademark infringement suit against the Appellant and successfully secured an interim injunction against its use of the name[cite: 21]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Respondent No. 1 was incorporated on August 24, 2012; the High Court injunction was granted against the Appellant on May 27, 2013; NCLT passed the impugned order on March 22, 2017[cite: 21]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: A pending Trade Mark Infringement Suit (CS(COMM) 1372/2016) before the Delhi High Court wherein an active interim injunction explicitly restrained the Appellant from using the trademark 'WORLD BOOK'[cite: 21]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The Appellant filed an application under Section 7(7) of the Companies Act, 2013 before NCLT Principal Bench seeking the removal of Respondent No. 1's name and prosecution for fraud. NCLT dismissed it with Rs. 25,000 costs, noting the High Court injunction. The Appellant appealed to the NCLAT[cite: 21].
legal_issues: Whether an application under Section 7(7) of the Companies Act, 2013 to strike off a respondent company's name for deceptive incorporation is maintainable when the applicant itself has been judicially injuncted from using the disputed trademark[cite: 21].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An applicant cannot maintain a petition under the Companies Act to penalize another company for deceptive use of a corporate name or trademark if the applicant itself has been judicially injuncted from utilizing that very trademark[cite: 21]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 7(7) of the Companies Act, 2013, which provides remedies against incorporation through false or deceptive information, cannot be invoked by a party whose locus to claim rights over the trade name is suspended pending a civil suit injunction[cite: 21]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Consideration of the Delhi High Court's interim injunction order dated May 27, 2013, which explicitly barred the Appellant from using the 'WORLD BOOK' mark or any deceptively similar corporate name[cite: 21]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because the Appellant was actively restrained by the High Court from using the trade name in dispute, it lacked the standing to seek the Respondent's removal or prosecution for using the same name, rendering the NCLT's dismissal fully justified[cite: 21].
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed with no order as to costs, upholding the NCLT's dismissal of the petition and the imposition of Rs. 25,000 in costs[cite: 21].
summary: World Book Company Pvt. Ltd. appealed against the NCLT Principal Bench's dismissal of its petition under Section 7(7) of the Companies Act, 2013[cite: 21]. The appellant sought the removal of Respondent 'World Book India Pvt. Ltd.' from the ROC register, alleging fraudulent incorporation using a deceptively similar name[cite: 21]. However, a foreign entity, 'World Book Inc.', had previously secured an interim injunction from the Delhi High Court restraining the appellant from using the 'WORLD BOOK' trademark[cite: 21]. The NCLAT held that since the appellant was judicially injuncted from using the trademark in a pending civil suit, it could not maintain a petition to penalize the respondent for using that same mark[cite: 21]. The appeal was dismissed[cite: 21].

case_title: Pankaj Khandelia & Anr vs. Khandelia Oil and General Mills Pvt. Ltd. & Ors.[cite: 22]
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants are Pankaj Khandelia & Anr. (Original Petitioners); Respondents are Khandelia Oil and General Mills Pvt. Ltd. & Ors.[cite: 22]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Alleged wrongful transfer of the petitioners' shares in the respondent company resulting in oppression and mismanagement[cite: 22]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Dispute over the validity of a share transfer executed beyond the prescribed two-month statutory period[cite: 22]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Division bench recorded differences on September 30, 2016; Third Member passed a decision on June 2, 2017; Final impugned order dismissing the petition passed on June 27, 2017[cite: 22]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Undisputed procedural irregularities where dissenting opinions of the division bench, the framing of the points of difference, and the third Member's decision were all recorded purely on the administrative side without open court pronouncement[cite: 22]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: A Division Bench of NCLT Chandigarh disagreed and recorded their dissent administratively on September 30, 2016. The matter was administratively referred to a third Member, who decided the case on June 2, 2017, again administratively. A final order was pronounced in open court on June 27, 2017. Appellants challenged these procedural lapses in the NCLAT[cite: 22].
legal_issues: Whether the procedure adopted by the NCLT of recording dissenting opinions, framing points of difference, and issuing a third Member's decision on the administrative side without open court pronouncement violates the principles of natural justice and Sections 419 and 420 of the Companies Act, 2013[cite: 22].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: All judicial decisions—including dissenting opinions, points of difference framed for third-member referral, and third-member judgments—must be pronounced in an open court to comply with the principles of natural justice and transparency[cite: 22]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 419(5) and Section 420(3) of the Companies Act, 2013 require judicial decisions to be delivered transparently. The mandate to give parties a reasonable opportunity of being heard logically extends to pronouncing all judgments and points of difference in an open court and supplying copies to the parties[cite: 22]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Examination of the admitted procedural facts confirming that crucial judicial steps, including the dissent and the third member's judgment, were executed on the administrative side without listing for formal pronouncement[cite: 22]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLT's actions flagrantly violated procedural law and the rules of natural justice. Consequently, the third member's decision and the final majority order were declared illegal, set aside, and the matter was remanded for a proper open-court referral process[cite: 22].
operative_order: The impugned order dated June 27, 2017, and the third Member's decision dated June 2, 2017, are set aside. The case is remitted to the President of the NCLT Principal Bench to provide certified copies of the differences to the parties and refer the matter to a new third Member for a fresh hearing and appropriate open-court order[cite: 22].
summary: The Appellants challenged the dismissal of their oppression and mismanagement petition by the NCLT Chandigarh Bench on severe procedural grounds[cite: 22]. A Division Bench had disagreed on the matter, but their dissenting opinions and the points of difference were recorded on the administrative side without open court pronouncement[cite: 22]. The matter was then sent to a third Member, whose decision was also not pronounced in open court[cite: 22]. A final order was subsequently passed based on this flawed process[cite: 22]. The NCLAT held that under Sections 419 and 420 of the Companies Act, 2013, all judicial decisions, dissents, and terms of reference must be pronounced in an open court to satisfy natural justice[cite: 22]. The NCLAT allowed the appeals, set aside the irregular orders, and remanded the matter to the NCLT President for a fresh referral to a new third Member[cite: 22].

case_title: Pawan Dubey & Anr vs J.B.K. Developers Private Limited[cite: 23]
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants are Pawan Dubey & Anr. (Flat Buyers/Allottees); Respondent is J.B.K. Developers Private Limited (Corporate Debtor/Builder)[cite: 23]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Booking of a residential flat (Flat No. IRIS-102) under a construction-linked payment plan governed by a builder-buyer allotment letter dated November 1, 2012[cite: 23]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Delay in handing over possession after the 30-month period expired, leading the Appellants to claim a refund of Rs. 25,97,940 plus interest[cite: 23]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Allotment letter issued on Nov 1, 2012; the 30-month possession period expired on April 30, 2015. A Section 8 notice was sent on Jan 23, 2017, and the NCLT order was passed on March 31, 2017[cite: 23]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The Letter of Allotment specifying conditions for refund (such as a 15% deduction on cancellation) which conflicted directly with the appellants' demand for a full refund plus 18%/19% interest[cite: 23]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The flat buyers filed a Section 9 application claiming to be Operational Creditors. The NCLT Principal Bench dismissed the petition on March 31, 2017, ruling they were not Operational Creditors. The buyers appealed to the NCLAT[cite: 23].
legal_issues: Whether an allottee or purchaser of a residential flat qualifies as an 'Operational Creditor' under Section 5(20) and 5(21) of the IBC to trigger the corporate insolvency resolution process under Section 9[cite: 23].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Purchasers of immovable property (such as flats or commercial sites) do not supply goods or provide services, and thus do not fall within the exhaustive statutory definition of 'Operational Creditor' under the IBC[cite: 23]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 5(21) of the IBC strictly restricts 'operational debt' to claims arising from the provision of goods, services, employment, or statutory dues. It does not encompass general debt or financial advances made for purchasing real estate[cite: 23]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Examination of the allotment letter's terms which demonstrated an advance for real estate acquisition, not the provision of goods or services. The Tribunal also noted the variance in the claimed default amount versus the contractual refund clauses[cite: 23]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because flat buyers do not supply goods or services, they cannot invoke Section 9 as Operational Creditors. Therefore, the insolvency application was fundamentally non-maintainable, necessitating the dismissal of the appeal[cite: 23].
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed with no order as to costs, upholding the NCLT's finding that flat purchasers are not Operational Creditors under the IBC[cite: 23].
summary: Pawan Dubey and another, who had booked a residential flat with J.B.K. Developers, appealed the NCLT Principal Bench's dismissal of their Section 9 IBC application[cite: 23]. The buyers sought a refund of their advance along with interest due to delayed possession, arguing that the IBC was meant to cover all creditors[cite: 23].
