The NCLAT rejected this broad interpretation, clarifying that 'operational debt' under Sections 5(20) and 5(21) of the IBC strictly relates to the provision of goods, services, employment, or government dues[cite: 23]. Since flat purchasers do not supply goods or services, they cannot be classified as 'Operational Creditors' to initiate insolvency proceedings under Section 9[cite: 23]. The NCLAT upheld the NCLT's decision and dismissed the appeal[cite: 23].

case_title: Philips India Limited vs. Goodwill Hospital & Research Centre Ltd.[cite: 24]
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 14 of 2017 & No. 15 of 2017[cite: 24]
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Philips India Limited (Operational Creditor); Respondents are Goodwill Hospital & Research Centre Ltd. and Karma Healthcare Private Limited (Corporate Debtors)[cite: 24]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Comprehensive Annual Maintenance Contracts (CAMC) for medical equipment (Allura Xper FD 20C and Brilliance 64) entered into between the parties[cite: 24]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Non-payment of maintenance dues under the CAMC by the corporate debtors, leading to the initiation of Section 9 IBC applications[cite: 24]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Winding-up notice under Section 433 of the Companies Act was issued on March 9, 2016. A reply outlining deficiency in service was sent on March 30, 2016. NCLT dismissed the Section 9 applications on March 2, 2017[cite: 24]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The reply dated March 30, 2016, specifically denied liability and highlighted the Operational Creditor's failure to provide timely and adequate maintenance services, causing severe financial loss to the hospitals[cite: 24]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The NCLT Principal Bench rejected the Section 9 applications, finding a pre-existing dispute based on the March 2016 reply. The Operational Creditor appealed to the NCLAT, arguing that 'dispute' under Section 5(6) must be strictly confined to a pending suit or arbitration[cite: 24].
legal_issues: Whether the definition of 'dispute' under Section 5(6) of the IBC is exhaustively limited to a pending suit or arbitration proceeding, or whether it includes a substantive dispute regarding the quality of services raised prior to the issuance of a Section 8 demand notice[cite: 24].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The term 'dispute' under Section 5(6) of the IBC is inclusive, not exhaustive, and is not strictly confined to pending suits or arbitration proceedings. A substantive objection regarding service quality raised prior to the Section 8 notice qualifies as a pre-existing dispute barring Section 9 applications[cite: 24]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Reading Sections 8(2) and 5(6) of the IBC together, the word 'includes' in Section 5(6) illustrates but does not restrict the types of disputes. The existence of a dispute can be discerned from prior communications or notices before any formal judicial or arbitral body[cite: 24]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Evaluating the Corporate Debtors' March 30, 2016 reply to the winding-up notice, which explicitly detailed deficient services, unattended machinery, and resulting financial loss, clearly establishing a bona fide pre-existing dispute[cite: 24]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Since the Corporate Debtors had raised a genuine dispute about the quality of service long before the Section 8 demand notice was issued, the NCLT rightly rejected the Section 9 applications, and the appeals must be dismissed[cite: 24].
operative_order: Both appeals are dismissed with no order as to costs, upholding the NCLT's rejection of the Section 9 insolvency applications[cite: 24].
summary: Philips India Limited filed two appeals against the NCLT Principal Bench's dismissal of its Section 9 IBC applications against Goodwill Hospital and Karma Healthcare[cite: 24]. The NCLT found a pre-existing dispute based on the hospitals' reply to a prior winding-up notice, wherein they alleged deficient maintenance of medical equipment[cite: 24]. The appellant argued that under Section 5(6) of the IBC, a 'dispute' must strictly mean a pending suit or arbitration[cite: 24]. The NCLAT, applying its precedent in Kirusa Software, held that the definition of a dispute is inclusive[cite: 24]. A substantive complaint regarding the quality of services raised before the issuance of the Section 8 demand notice constitutes a valid pre-existing dispute[cite: 24]. Consequently, the NCLAT affirmed the NCLT's dismissal of the insolvency applications[cite: 24].

case_title: D. Muthukumar vs. A. Premkumar & Another[cite: 25]
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is D. Muthukumar; Respondents are A. Premkumar & Another[cite: 25]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Real estate business joint venture and investments in M/s. K.K. Flats[cite: 25]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Alleged unpaid loans and investments[cite: 25]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Statutory winding up notice issued on October 25, 2014; NCLT order passed on August 21, 2017[cite: 25]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Income tax returns, ledger books, and cheques indicating that the appellant had made repayments and categorizing the debt as unsecured loans rather than financial debt[cite: 25]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: A winding up petition under Section 433(e) & (f) of the Companies Act, 1956 was transferred to NCLT Chennai, which treated it as a Section 7 IBC application and admitted it. The Appellant challenged this in the NCLAT[cite: 25].
legal_issues: Whether a transferred winding up petition can be automatically treated and admitted as a Section 7 IBC application without the applicant providing the requisite Form-1 information and proving their status as a 'Financial Creditor'[cite: 25].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Transferred winding-up proceedings cannot be automatically admitted under the IBC unless the applicant complies with the procedural requirements of providing statutory forms and records of default[cite: 25]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Rule 5 of the Transfer of Pending Proceedings Rules, 2016 requires the submission of all information mandated for admission under Section 7, 8, or 9 of the IBC, including Form-1 details[cite: 25]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Assessment of whether the applicant supplied the required Form-1 information, records from an information utility, and evidence that the disbursed amount constituted 'time value of money' under Section 5(8)[cite: 25]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLT erred by admitting the application without verifying the respondent's status as a 'Financial Creditor' and without the required Form-1 details, rendering the admission bad in law[cite: 25].
operative_order: The impugned order is set aside, the transferred application stands abated, the corporate debtor is released from the resolution process, and the appellant is directed to pay the IRP fees[cite: 25].
summary: Appellant D. Muthukumar challenged the NCLT Chennai's decision to treat a transferred winding up petition filed by A. Premkumar as a Section 7 IBC application and admit it[cite: 25]. The NCLAT noted that the respondents had not submitted the required information under Form-1, nor proved that the debt was a 'financial debt' disbursed against the time value of money[cite: 25]. Holding that transferred winding-up petitions must still comply with IBC procedural prerequisites before admission, the NCLAT set aside the NCLT's order, abated the application, and released the corporate debtor[cite: 25].

case_title: M/S. Meyer Apparel Ltd. & Anr vs. M/S. Surbhi Body Products Pvt. Ltd[cite: 26]
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 33 of 2017 & No. 34 of 2017[cite: 26]
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants are M/S. Meyer Apparel Ltd. & Anr (Corporate Debtor); Respondents are M/S. Surbhi Body Products Pvt. Ltd. and M/s. Godolo & Godolo Exports Pvt. Ltd. (Operational Creditors)[cite: 26]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Purchase and supply of interlining and linen items[cite: 26]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Operational debts claimed of Rs. 2,13,570 and Rs. 11,68,834 respectively[cite: 26]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Winding up notices issued in March 2015; disputes raised via letters in September 2015; NCLT admission order passed on April 7, 2017[cite: 26]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Correspondence from 2015 asserting inferior quality of goods, a prior winding-up petition before the High Court, and a civil suit for recovery filed by the corporate debtor[cite: 26]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Chandigarh admitted the Section 9 applications despite the corporate debtor raising quality disputes. The Corporate Debtor appealed to the NCLAT, and parties also filed a joint petition for disposal based on a settlement[cite: 26].
legal_issues: Whether a Section 9 IBC application is maintainable when there is a pre-existing dispute regarding the quality of goods raised by the corporate debtor prior to the issuance of the Section 8 demand notice[cite: 26].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An application for corporate insolvency resolution under Section 9 is not maintainable if a bona fide dispute regarding the quality of goods existed prior to the demand notice[cite: 26]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 5(6) of the IBC defining 'dispute' is inclusive and not exhaustive, and when read harmoniously with Section 8(2), it encompasses disputes raised over the quality of goods even outside pending suits or arbitrations[cite: 26]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Review of correspondence from 2015 and prior winding-up/civil litigation proving the corporate debtor had formally contested the quality of goods supplied long before the IBC notice was issued[cite: 26]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because a valid pre-existing dispute regarding quality existed, the NCLT lacked jurisdiction to admit the Section 9 applications, rendering the admission orders illegal[cite: 26].
operative_order: The impugned NCLT orders are set aside, the CIRP actions are declared illegal, and the proceedings are closed. The corporate debtor is released to function independently, and the appellant is directed to pay the IRP's fees[cite: 26].
summary: M/S. Meyer Apparel Ltd. appealed against NCLT Chandigarh orders admitting Section 9 IBC applications filed by two operational creditors[cite: 26]. The appellant argued that a pre-existing dispute existed regarding the inferior quality of the supplied goods, which had been raised via notices and litigation in 2015, well before the IBC demand notices[cite: 26]. The NCLAT, affirming that the definition of 'dispute' under Section 5(6) of the IBC is inclusive, held that prior complaints about goods quality constitute a valid pre-existing dispute[cite: 26]. Consequently, the NCLAT set aside the admission orders, closed the insolvency proceedings, and restored the corporate debtor's management[cite: 26].

case_title: Shri Praveen Kumar Singh vs. Medinimata Agro Products Pvt Ltd[cite: 27]
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants are Shri Praveen Kumar Singh and Shri Lalit Kumar Singh; Respondents are Medinimata Agro Products Pvt Ltd and others[cite: 27]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Joint acquisition of a rice mill (auction unit) from UPFC and subsequent internal shareholding arrangements[cite: 27]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Dispute over the transfer of the appellants' 52% shareholding to the respondents[cite: 27]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Share transfers executed on September 9, 2016; Appellants resigned on November 12, 2006; NCLT passed the impugned order on April 4, 2017[cite: 27]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Share transfer forms signed by appellants, resignation letters, and bank records showing encashment of Rs. 13 lakhs as consideration for the shares[cite: 27]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appellants filed a petition under Sections 397/398 of the Companies Act, 1956 alleging oppression and fraudulent share transfer. NCLT Kolkata dismissed the petition, finding the share transfer valid and no oppression. Appellants appealed to NCLAT[cite: 27].
legal_issues: Whether a petition for oppression and mismanagement is maintainable when the petitioners have already transferred their shares for consideration, and whether oral allegations of forgery can override documentary evidence of such transfer[cite: 27].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An oppression and mismanagement petition is not maintainable if the petitioners are no longer shareholders on the date of filing the petition, having validly transferred their shares[cite: 27]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Under Sections 91 and 92 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872, oral assertions claiming forgery cannot be admitted to contradict terms of a contract or disposition of property when primary documentary evidence (such as signed transfer forms and proof of payment) exists and no vitiating facts are proven[cite: 27]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Evaluating the documentary proof of share transfer forms, resignation letters, and account payee cheques totaling Rs. 13 lakhs encashed by the appellants, against their unsubstantiated oral claims of forgery[cite: 27]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLT correctly concluded that the appellants willingly transferred their shares for consideration, meaning they were no longer shareholders and had no standing to claim oppression[cite: 27].
operative_order: The NCLAT declined to interfere with the NCLT order and dismissed the appeal with no order as to costs[cite: 27].
summary: Appellants Shri Praveen Kumar Singh and Shri Lalit Kumar Singh appealed against an NCLT Kolkata order dismissing their oppression and mismanagement petition[cite: 27]. The appellants alleged their 52% shareholding in Medinimata Agro Products was fraudulently transferred via forged documents[cite: 27]. The NCLAT upheld the NCLT's finding that the appellants had voluntarily signed share transfer forms and resignation letters, and had encashed Rs. 13 lakhs as consideration[cite: 27]. Citing the Indian Evidence Act, the Tribunal ruled that unsubstantiated oral claims of forgery cannot override solid documentary evidence[cite: 27]. Since the appellants were no longer shareholders, the petition was non-maintainable and the appeal was dismissed[cite: 27].

case_title: Bihar State Industrial Development Corporation Limited vs. Asiatic Oxygen Ltd. & Ors.[cite: 28]
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) No. 127 of 2017 & No. 151 of 2017[cite: 28]
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants/Respondents are Bihar State Industrial Development Corporation Limited and Asiatic Oxygen Ltd.; the joint venture company is Bihar Air Products Limited[cite: 28]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Management and shareholding dispute in a joint venture company where the state corporation sought to exit and sell its shares[cite: 28]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Dispute over the state corporation attempting to sell its shares to an outsider (M/s. Anjaneya Ispat Limited) without offering them to the joint venture partner first[cite: 28]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Company Law Board order passed on June 30, 2009; NCLT passed the impugned order on February 22, 2017[cite: 28]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The CLB previously ruled the corporation's failure to offer shares to its partner was oppressive. The state corporation subsequently decided not to sell its shares to the third party[cite: 28]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Asiatic Oxygen filed a petition under Section 397/398. The CLB ruled in its favor in 2009. The matter later transferred to NCLT Kolkata, which in 2017 found a 'deadlock' and ordered an independent valuation and buyout. Both parties appealed this NCLT order[cite: 28].
legal_issues: Whether a Tribunal can order a mandatory valuation and buyout of shares based on a perceived 'deadlock' when the primary act of anticipated oppression (the sale of shares to a third party) has been abandoned by the respondent[cite: 28].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: When the specific action that constituted the anticipated oppression is withdrawn or abandoned, the cause of action for oppression no longer subsists, and drastic equitable remedies like mandatory buyouts are unwarranted[cite: 28]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Under Section 402 of the Companies Act, 1956, remedies for oppression and mismanagement, including buyout orders in cases of deadlock, must be grounded in an ongoing or subsisting grievance[cite: 28]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Taking judicial notice of the state corporation's formal declaration that it had decided not to sell its shares to any third party and had not effectuated the disputed 2007 tender[cite: 28]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Since the state corporation unequivocally withdrew its intent to sell shares to the third party, the foundational oppression claim ceased to exist, rendering the NCLT's order for valuation and buyout erroneous[cite: 28].
operative_order: The impugned NCLT Kolkata order dated February 22, 2017 is set aside, and the appeals are disposed of with no order as to costs, as the cause of oppression no longer subsists[cite: 28].
summary: Appeals were filed against an NCLT Kolkata order that directed an independent valuation and buyout of shares in a joint venture, Bihar Air Products Limited, citing a 'deadlock'[cite: 28]. Asiatic Oxygen Ltd. had originally complained that its partner, Bihar State Industrial Development Corporation, oppressively tried to sell its shares to an outsider[cite: 28]. During the NCLAT proceedings, the state corporation confirmed it had abandoned its plan to sell its shares to any third party[cite: 28]. The NCLAT held that because the anticipated oppression was withdrawn, the cause of action no longer subsisted[cite: 28]. Consequently, the NCLAT set aside the NCLT's buyout order and disposed of the appeals[cite: 28].

case_title: Shriram EPC Limited vs. Rio Glass Solar SA[cite: 29]
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Shriram EPC Limited (Corporate Debtor); Respondent is Rio Glass Solar SA (Operational Creditor, a Spanish company)[cite: 29]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: International commercial dealings resulting in an operational debt[cite: 29]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Unpaid operational debt claimed by the foreign operational creditor[cite: 29]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Demand notice issued on May 5, 2017; NCLT admission order passed on August 10, 2017[cite: 29]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Section 8 notice issued by 'Advani & Co.', a law firm; Section 9 application signed by advocates holding a Power of Attorney; and a default certificate issued by 'CaixaBank', which is not a recognized Indian financial institution under the IBC[cite: 29]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Chennai admitted the Section 9 application. The Corporate Debtor challenged the maintainability of the petition before the NCLAT based on procedural defects[cite: 29].
legal_issues: Whether a Section 9 application is maintainable when the Section 8 demand notice is issued by a law firm, the application is signed by a Power of Attorney holder, and the required certificate from a financial institution under Section 9(3)(c) is not from a recognized Indian financial institution[cite: 29].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A corporate insolvency application is non-maintainable if the statutory demand notice is issued by a third-party lawyer/law firm, the application is filed by a Power of Attorney holder, or the mandatory certificate under Section 9(3)(c) is not provided by a recognized financial institution[cite: 29]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Form-3 and Form-4 under the Adjudicating Authority Rules require the demand notice to be issued by a person holding a position in or relation to the operational creditor; moreover, the IBC is a complete code that overrides the Power of Attorney Act[cite: 29]. Section 9(3)(c) is mandatory[cite: 29]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Verification of the notice signed by 'Advani & Co.', the Form-5 signed by advocates acting as PoA holders, and the default certificate issued by a foreign bank (CaixaBank) unacknowledged under the IBC[cite: 29]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The operational creditor failed to comply with multiple mandatory statutory prerequisites (proper notice issuer, proper signatory, and valid default certificate), rendering the Section 9 application inherently defective and the admission order illegal[cite: 29].
operative_order: The impugned NCLT order is set aside, the Section 9 application is dismissed, the corporate debtor is released from the CIRP, and the appellant is directed to pay the IRP's fees, with no order as to costs[cite: 29].
summary: Shriram EPC Limited appealed against an NCLT Chennai order admitting a Section 9 IBC application filed by Rio Glass Solar SA, a Spanish company[cite: 29]. The NCLAT found multiple fatal procedural defects: the Section 8 demand notice was issued by a law firm rather than an authorized officer of the operational creditor; the Section 9 application was signed by advocates acting as Power of Attorney holders (impermissible under IBC); and the default certificate was from a foreign bank (CaixaBank) not recognized as a financial institution under the Code[cite: 29]. Reaffirming that these statutory requirements are mandatory, the NCLAT set aside the admission order, dismissed the application, and released the corporate debtor[cite: 29].

case_title: Leo Duct Engineers & Consultants Ltd vs Canara Bank
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Leo Duct Engineers & Consultants Ltd. is the Corporate Applicant and Corporate Debtor[cite: 1]. Canara Bank and Standard Chartered Bank are the Financial Creditors[cite: 1]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: The transaction involves financial debts secured by guarantees and the immovable properties of the directors[cite: 1]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The specific default amount is not mentioned, but the occurrence of default is admitted[cite: 1]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The Financial Creditors had already set the wheel in motion under the SARFAESI Act before the Section 10 petition was evaluated[cite: 1]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The Adjudicating Authority noted that the petition was complete, in the required format (Form 6), and provided all requisite details of creditors, debts, and default[cite: 1]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The Corporate Applicant filed under Section 10 before NCLT Mumbai, which dismissed it on 22nd June 2017 on the ground that admitting the petition and imposing a moratorium would stall the pending SARFAESI proceedings and abuse the process of law[cite: 1].
legal_issues: Whether the pendency of recovery proceedings under the SARFAESI Act or DRT Act can be a valid ground for the Adjudicating Authority to reject a complete application filed by a Corporate Applicant under Section 10 of the IBC[cite: 1].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An application for corporate insolvency resolution process cannot be rejected on the ground of pending recovery proceedings under other statutes if the statutory requirements of the Code are fulfilled[cite: 1]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 10 of the IBC does not empower the Adjudicating Authority to go beyond the records prescribed under Section 10 and Form 6, subject only to the ineligibility conditions prescribed under Section 11 of the Code[cite: 1]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: If the Adjudicating Authority is satisfied that a debt exists, a default has occurred, the application is complete, and the applicant is not ineligible under Section 11, it has no option but to admit the application[cite: 1]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The bench concluded that pendency of action under Section 13(4) of the SARFAESI Act or Section 19 of the DRT Act constitutes an unrelated fact and cannot be a ground to reject a Section 10 application on the premise of suppression of facts[cite: 1].
operative_order: The impugned order dated 22nd June 2017 passed by the NCLT Mumbai Bench is set aside[cite: 1]. The case is remitted back to the Adjudicating Authority to admit the application under Section 10 after notice to the parties, provided there is no defect, and to allow time for defect removal if necessary[cite: 1]. No order as to costs[cite: 1].
summary: Leo Duct Engineers filed a Section 10 IBC application which NCLT Mumbai dismissed, citing that it was a tactic to stall pending SARFAESI Act proceedings initiated by the Financial Creditors[cite: 1]. The NCLAT allowed the appeal, holding that the Adjudicating Authority cannot look beyond the requirements of Section 10, Form 6, and ineligibility under Section 11 of the IBC[cite: 1]. Pending SARFAESI or DRT proceedings are not valid grounds for rejecting a complete Section 10 application[cite: 1]. The matter was remitted for admission[cite: 1].

case_title: Mr. Vyomesh M. Shah & Anr vs Vinca Developer Pvt. Limited & Anr
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Mr. Vyomesh M. Shah & Anr are Appellants (Hubtown promoters)[cite: 2]. Vinca Developer Pvt. Ltd. (Respondent 1), FMO (Respondent 2/Foreign Investor), Nominee Directors (Respondents 3 & 4), Hubtown Ltd (Respondent 5/Guarantor), and ITSL (Respondent 10/Debenture Trustee) are the respondents[cite: 2]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: FMO invested Rs. 418 crores in Vinca via Compulsorily Convertible Debentures and equity under a Nov 2009 Subscription Agreement, which Vinca then invested into its subsidiaries 'Amazia' and 'Rubix' via Optionally Partially Convertible Debentures (OPCDs)[cite: 2]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Amazia and Rubix defaulted on payment obligations under the OPCDs, leading the Debenture Trustee to enforce security[cite: 2]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The Subscription Agreement was dated 20th November 2009, and the Debenture Trust Deeds were dated 1st December 2009[cite: 2]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Article 60(d) of Vinca's Articles of Association explicitly deemed Appellants to have a conflict of interest on OPCD matters, granting sole decision-making power to Nominee Directors[cite: 2]. A Supreme Court order dated 15 Nov 2016 found the transaction was prima facie not violative of FEMA[cite: 2]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appellants filed CP No. 39/Mah/2016 alleging oppression and mismanagement, which NCLT Mumbai dismissed on Jan 17, 2017, imposing a Rs. 50,000 cost[cite: 2].
legal_issues: Whether the actions of the Nominee Directors instructing the Debenture Trustee to enforce security and recover dues under OPCDs without Board consent constituted oppression and mismanagement under Section 241 of the Companies Act, 2013[cite: 2].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Enforcing valid contractual rights and securities through authorized nominee directors does not constitute oppression or mismanagement[cite: 2]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The Tribunal interpreted Article 60(d) of the Articles of Association to conclude that Nominee Directors had the sole right to instruct the Debenture Trustee on OPCD matters due to the Appellants' conflict of interest, distinguishing this from general 'Reserved Matters' under Article 63[cite: 2]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal relied on the Supreme Court's prior finding that the investment structure was not a colorable device to circumvent FEMA, confirming that realization of securities benefited the company[cite: 2]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Appellants were attempting to obstruct the legitimate receipt of funds by the company upon enforcement of securities, and thus no case of oppression or mismanagement was made out[cite: 2].
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed for lack of merit[cite: 2]. There shall be no order as to costs[cite: 2].
summary: Appellants challenged an NCLT order dismissing their oppression and mismanagement petition against Vinca Developer and foreign investor FMO[cite: 2]. Appellants claimed FMO's nominee directors oppressively bypassed the Board to enforce securities on defaulting subsidiaries[cite: 2]. NCLAT dismissed the appeal, ruling that the Articles of Association explicitly granted nominee directors the sole right to act on OPCD matters due to the Appellants' conflict of interest[cite: 2]. Enforcing valid contractual securities to recover debts is not oppressive[cite: 2].

case_title: Shanta Prasad Chakravarty vs M/S. Bochapathar Tea Estate Private Ltd
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants are the Original Petitioners/shareholders[cite: 3]. Respondent 1 is the Company (Bochapathar Tea Estate Pvt. Ltd.)[cite: 3]. Respondents 5 & 6 are the Statutory Auditors (P.K. Goenka, Jyoti Prasad Kanoi)[cite: 3]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Audit of the company's Annual Financial Statement[cite: 3]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The Company allegedly defaulted on making PF contributions for workers, which the auditors allegedly suppressed in the financial report[cite: 3]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The contested financial report was for the Financial Year 2014-15[cite: 3]. The original petition was filed in November 2016[cite: 3]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The auditors admitted an error in the Annual Financial Report but stated they corrected it in the subsequent Tax Audit Report, had already resigned, and faced an ongoing ICAI investigation initiated by the Appellants[cite: 3]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appellants filed CP No. 1/2016 before NCLT Guwahati alleging oppression and mismanagement[cite: 3]. The auditors filed I.A. No. 07/2017 to be deleted from the array of parties, which NCLT granted[cite: 3].
legal_issues: Whether statutory auditors are necessary or proper parties in a petition for oppression and mismanagement filed under Sections 241 and 242 of the Companies Act, 2013[cite: 3].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Statutory auditors are not necessary parties to a petition for oppression and mismanagement, as such acts are averred against the company, board of directors, or shareholders, not the auditors[cite: 3]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: While Section 245 of the Companies Act (Class Action) allows for claiming damages against an auditor, a petition filed strictly under Sections 241 and 242 cannot import the remedies of Section 245 without following its specific procedural requirements[cite: 3]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Because the auditors had already resigned and a parallel investigation by the ICAI was ongoing, joining them in the NCLT petition would lead to a multiplicity of proceedings and potential conflict of decisions[cite: 3]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT held that the NCLT correctly deleted the statutory auditors from the array of parties because allegations against them do not fall within the framework of Sections 241 and 242[cite: 3].
operative_order: The impugned order deleting the statutory auditors from the array of parties is upheld[cite: 3]. The company appeal is dismissed with no order as to costs[cite: 3].
summary: Shareholders of Bochapathar Tea Estate filed an oppression and mismanagement petition against the company and joined the statutory auditors for allegedly suppressing PF payment defaults[cite: 3]. The NCLT deleted the auditors from the party list, prompting this appeal[cite: 3]. The NCLAT upheld the NCLT's decision, clarifying that oppression and mismanagement claims under Sections 241 and 242 of the Companies Act apply to the company and management, not statutory auditors[cite: 3]. Actions against auditors must follow the specific procedures of Section 245 (Class Action), which was not invoked here[cite: 3].

case_title: Jk Jute Mill Mazdoor Morcha vs Juggilal Kamlapa Jute Mills Co. Ltd
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is JK Jute Mill Mazdoor Morcha (a registered Trade Union)[cite: 4]. Respondent is Juggilal Kamlapa Jute Mills Co. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor)[cite: 4]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Claim relates to unpaid employment dues of workmen including wages, salaries, bonus, provident fund, and gratuity[cite: 4]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Total dues to the members of the intervenors were claimed to be more than Rs. 113.8 lacs[cite: 4]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The Section 9 petition was allegedly filed before the expiry of the prescribed 10 days from the date of receipt of the demand notice[cite: 4]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The Corporate debtor was under a lockout[cite: 4]. Pending civil suits and writ petitions indicated pre-existing disputes regarding the dues[cite: 4]. An MoU dated 18 October 2008 existed for rescheduling repayment[cite: 4]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The Trade Union filed a Section 9 application (CP No. 36/ALD/2017) before NCLT Allahabad, which rejected it on 28th April 2017 holding it not maintainable[cite: 4].
legal_issues: Whether an application under Section 9 of the IBC is maintainable at the instance of a Workmen's Association or Trade Union acting as an 'operational creditor'[cite: 4].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A Trade Union or Workmen's Association does not qualify as an operational creditor and cannot file a joint insolvency petition on behalf of its members[cite: 4]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 5(20) and 5(21) of the IBC require an operational creditor to have supplied goods or services[cite: 4]. A Trade Union itself does not render services to the corporate debtor, thus no operational debt is owed directly to it[cite: 4]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Individual workmen have separate causes of action, separate claim amounts, and separate dates of default[cite: 4]. A consolidated application by a union fails the procedural requirement of individual demand notices under Section 8 and Form 5[cite: 4]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: While individual workmen can file Section 9 applications for defaults exceeding Rs. 1 Lakh, a Trade Union cannot maintain a joint Section 9 petition as it does not hold an operational debt[cite: 4].
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed, upholding the NCLT's rejection of the Section 9 application filed by the Trade Union[cite: 4]. No order as to costs[cite: 4].
summary: A registered Trade Union filed a Section 9 IBC application on behalf of workmen against Juggilal Kamlapa Jute Mills for unpaid wages and benefits[cite: 4]. The NCLT rejected the petition[cite: 4]. On appeal, the NCLAT upheld the rejection, ruling that a Trade Union does not fall within the definition of an operational creditor under Section 5(20) of the IBC because it does not directly provide services to the corporate debtor[cite: 4]. Furthermore, the NCLAT held that joint petitions are not maintainable under Section 9, as each workman has a distinct claim and date of default, requiring individual demand notices[cite: 4].

case_title: Shri Sanjivbhai Kirtibhai Patel & Ors vs M/S Biocare Remedies Private Limited & Ors
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants/Petitioners were the original 100% shareholders (sellers) of Biocare Remedies Pvt. Ltd.[cite: 5]. Respondent 2 is the buyer who assumed management[cite: 5]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: An MoU dated 22.11.2001 where Appellants agreed to sell 100% shareholding to Respondent 2 for Rs. 50 lakhs[cite: 5]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Out of Rs. 50 lakhs, Rs. 33.05 lakhs was paid[cite: 5]. Cheques for the remaining Rs. 16.95 lakhs were dishonoured[cite: 5]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The MoU was signed on 22.11.2001, the first dilution allotment occurred on 01.09.2002, and the petition was filed on 28.10.2013[cite: 5]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Appellants' shareholding was systematically reduced from 100% to 49.91% between 2002 and 2012 by increasing authorized capital and allotting shares to Respondent 2's group without notice to Appellants[cite: 5]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Ahmedabad (TP No. 58) held this to be oppression and ordered Respondents to pay the balance Rs. 16.95 lakhs at 12% interest from the 2013 petition date, prompting cross-appeals to NCLAT[cite: 5].
legal_issues: Whether increasing authorized share capital and allotting further shares to the buyer's group without notice to the original shareholders constitutes oppression, and what the appropriate equitable relief should be under Section 402[cite: 5].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Increasing authorized share capital and allotting new shares exclusively to the majority group without notifying existing minority shareholders constitutes an act of oppression[cite: 5]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 402 of the Companies Act, 1956 confers wide discretionary powers on the Tribunal to pass orders contrary to strict agreements to end the matters complained of and do substantial justice in the company's interest[cite: 5]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal found oppression based on lack of notice, but balanced this against the fact that setting aside the allotments would detrimentally reverse 15 years of corporate operations managed by the buyers[cite: 5]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Equitable justice required enforcing the buyout as per the MoU but compensating the oppressed sellers with a higher, compounded interest rate on the unpaid consideration from the date of default rather than cancelling the allotments[cite: 5].
operative_order: NCLAT modified the NCLT order: Respondent 2 is directed to pay Rs. 16,95,000 to the Appellants with 15% interest compounded annually from 25.11.2002 until payment[cite: 5]. Upon payment, Appellants must deposit their original share certificates for transfer to the Respondents[cite: 5]. No order as to costs[cite: 5].
summary: The original promoters of Biocare Remedies sold 100% of their shares via a 2001 MoU for Rs. 50 Lakhs[cite: 5]. After paying part of the amount, the buyers dishonoured cheques for the remaining Rs. 16.95 Lakhs[cite: 5]. Meanwhile, the buyers diluted the original promoters' shareholding to 49.91% without notice[cite: 5]. NCLT found oppression but ordered the buyers to pay the balance with 12% interest from 2013[cite: 5]. NCLAT agreed that cancelling the allotments would harm the company after 16 years[cite: 5]. However, invoking wide powers under Section 402, NCLAT modified the relief, directing the buyers to pay the balance with 15% compounded interest from the date of default in 2002[cite: 5].

case_title: Raj Hari Eswaran vs M/s. CMI India Pvt. Ltd. & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Raj Hari Eswaran is the Appellant and a promoter/shareholder of the Corporate Debtor[cite: 6]. M/s. CMI India Pvt. Ltd. is the 1st Respondent and Operational Creditor[cite: 6]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: The Corporate Debtor placed purchase orders during 2012-14 with the Operational Creditor for the supply of cables, which required a 36-month warranty[cite: 6]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The Operational Creditor claimed an outstanding sum of Rs. 7,88,54,073 plus interest[cite: 6]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The Operational Creditor issued a legal notice on 15th September 2016, to which the Corporate Debtor replied denying liability on 17th October 2016[cite: 6]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The Corporate Debtor explicitly disputed the debt pre-litigation due to the Operational Creditor's inability to provide the agreed warranty[cite: 6]. The Operational Creditor never issued a demand notice under Section 8 of the IBC before its winding-up petition was treated as a Section 9 application[cite: 6]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The Operational Creditor filed a winding-up petition before the Madras High Court which was transferred to NCLT Chennai[cite: 6]. NCLT treated it as a Section 9 application and admitted it on 12th October 2017[cite: 6].
legal_issues: Whether a pending winding-up petition transferred to the NCLT can be admitted as a Section 9 IBC application without the operational creditor issuing a mandatory demand notice under Section 8 of the IBC or providing Form 5 information[cite: 6].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A transferred winding-up petition abates if the operational creditor fails to comply with the statutory prerequisites of the IBC, specifically the issuance of a prior demand notice and submission of required information[cite: 6]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Rule 5 of The Companies (Transfer of Pending Proceedings) Rules, 2016 strictly requires the petitioner to submit all necessary information for admission under the IBC within 60 days[cite: 6]. For a Section 9 application, this mandates serving a demand notice under Section 8(1) in Form 3 or 4 and filing the application in Form 5[cite: 6]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Since it was undisputed that no Section 8 notice was issued and the Form 5 details were omitted, the tribunal found the transferred application fatally incomplete[cite: 6]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The failure to provide the mandated information within 60 days triggered the proviso to Rule 5 of the Transfer Rules, meaning the application under Sections 433 and 434 of the Companies Act, 1956 stood abated[cite: 6].
operative_order: The NCLAT set aside the impugned order dated 12th October 2017 and dismissed the application as abated[cite: 6]. The Corporate Debtor was released from the CIRP and its Board of Directors allowed to function independently[cite: 6]. The Operational Creditor was granted liberty to issue a fresh Section 8 notice[cite: 6].
summary: An Operational Creditor's winding-up petition was transferred from the High Court to NCLT Chennai, which admitted it as a Section 9 IBC application[cite: 6]. The Corporate Debtor's promoter appealed[cite: 6]. The NCLAT allowed the appeal, ruling that the Operational Creditor failed to issue the mandatory Section 8 demand notice and did not submit the required information in Form 5 as stipulated by the Transfer Rules, 2016[cite: 6]. Consequently, the petition abated and the CIRP was quashed[cite: 6].

case_title: M/s MRF Limited and Others vs M/s Oriental Insurance Company Ltd. & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: M/s MRF Limited is the 1st Appellant/Company[cite: 7]. Oriental Insurance Company Ltd. is the 1st Respondent/Claimant, Sanchit Financial is the 2nd Respondent/Broker, and Morgan Stanley Asset Management Inc is the 3rd Respondent/Registered Shareholder[cite: 7]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: The broker executed a trade for the sale of 50 MRF shares on 22nd February 1996, which were subsequently lost before delivery to the NSE[cite: 7]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The insurer claimed title and sought duplicate share certificates for the 50 missing shares after settling the broker's claim[cite: 7]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Shares were lost in March 1996; MRF refused to stop the transfer on 28th May 1996[cite: 7]. A civil suit was filed in 1997, dismissed for default in 2014, and the Section 59 petition was filed in 2015[cite: 7]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: MRF had already transferred the shares to Morgan Stanley on 28th March 1996[cite: 7]. The Respondents filed a civil suit to declare title which was dismissed for non-prosecution twice, effectively abandoning their claim[cite: 7]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The Insurer filed a petition under Section 59 of the Companies Act, 2013 before NCLT Chennai, which directed MRF to issue duplicate shares on 10th February 2017[cite: 7]. MRF appealed[cite: 7].
legal_issues: Whether a petition for rectification of the register of members under Section 59 of the Companies Act, 2013 is maintainable after an unexplained delay of 19 years and the abandonment of a civil suit seeking a declaration of title[cite: 7].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A petition for rectification of a share register is not maintainable if it is barred by inordinate delay, laches, and the prior abandonment of a civil claim for declaration of title over the same shares[cite: 7]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Although the Limitation Act and Section 433 of the Companies Act 2013 may not strictly apply to Section 59 petitions filed prior to 1st June 2016, the equitable principles of delay and laches remain applicable, referencing the time limits previously prescribed under Section 111 of the Companies Act, 1956[cite: 7]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal found that the claimant was informed of the share transfer to a third party in May 1996 but sat on its rights for 19 years[cite: 7]. The dismissal of its civil suit for non-prosecution evidenced an abandonment of the title claim[cite: 7]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Seeking a declaration of title disguised as a rectification petition after abandoning the original civil suit and delaying for 19 years without valid explanation is impermissible[cite: 7].
operative_order: The NCLAT set aside the impugned order dated 10th February 2017 passed by the NCLT Chennai Bench[cite: 7]. The appeal is allowed with no order as to costs[cite: 7].
summary: Oriental Insurance sought rectification of MRF Ltd's register to claim 50 shares lost by a broker in 1996[cite: 7]. NCLT Chennai allowed the Section 59 petition[cite: 7]. NCLAT allowed MRF's appeal and set aside the order, ruling that the insurer's petition was barred by an unexplained 19-year delay and laches[cite: 7]. Furthermore, the insurer had effectively abandoned its claim to title by allowing a prior civil suit on the exact same subject to be dismissed for default[cite: 7].

case_title: Shri Surinder Kumar Virdi vs Beavers Leather Pvt Ltd. & Ors
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Shri Surinder Kumar Virdi is the Appellant, a minority shareholder (36.50%) and director[cite: 8]. Beavers Leather Pvt Ltd is Respondent No. 1 (Company), while Respondents 2 to 4 are the majority shareholders[cite: 8]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: The company was non-operating and generated income solely by leasing a 5000 sq. yard property to M.A. Traders for Rs. 1,00,000 per month[cite: 8]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The majority shareholders drew an annual remuneration of Rs. 2,10,000 and Rs. 1,50,000 despite the company having no active business, while paying zero dividends to the minority[cite: 8]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The Appellant was removed as a director in an EOGM on 7th May 2015[cite: 8]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The EOGM removing the Appellant was convened without the mandatory 21 days' notice[cite: 8]. The NCLT factually found that the majority was drawing remuneration while ignoring the minority's interests[cite: 8]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The Appellant filed an oppression petition before NCLT Chandigarh, which concluded the company was in a 'mess' and ordered an independent valuation to facilitate the Appellant's exit[cite: 8]. The Appellant challenged this forced exit[cite: 8].
legal_issues: Whether it is equitable in an oppression and mismanagement case to force an illegally ousted minority shareholder to exit the company without granting them the first right to purchase the majority's shares at a discounted valuation[cite: 8].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The law cannot be weaponized to incentivize oppressors by allowing them to illegally oust a minority shareholder and then force a buyout of the minority's shares at a valuation depressed by their own mismanagement[cite: 8]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Sections 100 and 101 of the Companies Act regarding EOGM notices are mandatory; non-compliance renders a director's removal null and void[cite: 8]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The act of drawing remuneration in a non-operating company that only earns rental income, while withholding dividends and illegally ousting the minority director, firmly established siphoning of funds and oppression[cite: 8]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: To prevent unfair advantage, the oppressed minority must be reinstated and granted the first right to buy out the oppressing majority at a discounted price to compensate for the past oppression[cite: 8].
operative_order: The NCLAT modified the NCLT's order[cite: 8]. The Appellant is restored as a director until an exit occurs[cite: 8]. Respondents are directed to quote an acquisition value per share within one month[cite: 8]. The Appellant is granted the first right to purchase the majority's shareholding at a 10% discount to the quoted rate[cite: 8]. Respondents are barred from drawing future remuneration during the interregnum[cite: 8].
summary: A minority shareholder appealed an NCLT order that directed his forced exit despite finding the majority guilty of oppression, siphoning funds through unjustified remuneration, and illegally removing him as a director[cite: 8]. NCLAT modified the order, holding that oppressors must not be incentivized by forcing the minority out[cite: 8]. The NCLAT restored the appellant's directorship and granted him the first right to buy out the majority shareholders at a 10% discount to compensate for the oppression[cite: 8].

case_title: A.D. Electro Steel Co. Pvt. Ltd. & Anr vs Anil Steels
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: A.D. Electro Steel Co. Pvt. Ltd. & Anr are the Appellants and Corporate Debtors[cite: 9]. Anil Steels is the Respondent and Operational Creditor[cite: 9]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: The transaction involved the supply of Buffer Plunger (Wagon) Casting and Buffer Casing (Wagon) Casting[cite: 9]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The creditor claimed default on an operational debt (exact sum unspecified in the order) which the creditor's counsel later admitted had been paid[cite: 9]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The Operational Creditor issued a Section 138 Negotiable Instruments Act notice on 15th June 2016, and the Corporate Debtor replied on 28th June 2016[cite: 9]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: In its 28th June 2016 reply, the Corporate Debtor explicitly raised disputes regarding the supply quantities and violations of agreement terms, evidencing a dispute pre-dating the IBC demand notice[cite: 9]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The Operational Creditor filed a Section 9 application which NCLT Kolkata admitted on 7th September 2017, appointing an Interim Resolution Professional[cite: 9]. The Corporate Debtor appealed this admission[cite: 9].
legal_issues: Whether an application under Section 9 of the IBC is maintainable when there is documentary evidence of a pre-existing dispute raised by the Corporate Debtor before the issuance of the statutory demand notice[cite: 9].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An application for Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process under Section 9 must be rejected if there is a pre-existing dispute regarding the operational debt that was communicated to the creditor prior to the demand notice[cite: 9]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Applying the Supreme Court's precedent in Mobilox Innovations, Section 8(2)(a) is interpreted to mean that a dispute need not be pending in a formal suit or arbitration; the mere existence of a dispute prior to the demand notice is sufficient to halt the insolvency process[cite: 9]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The NCLAT assessed the pre-IBC correspondence, specifically the reply dated 28th June 2016 to the NI Act notice, and determined it constituted clear evidence of a pre-existing dispute over the goods supplied[cite: 9]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because a pre-existing dispute was established and undisputed by the Operational Creditor, the Section 9 application was fundamentally not maintainable[cite: 9].
operative_order: The NCLAT set aside the impugned order dated 7th September 2017 passed by NCLT Kolkata and dismissed the Section 9 application[cite: 9]. All actions taken by the IRP were declared illegal, and the Corporate Debtor was released from the CIRP to function independently[cite: 9]. No order as to costs[cite: 9].
summary: NCLT Kolkata admitted a Section 9 IBC application filed by Anil Steels against A.D. Electro Steel[cite: 9]. The Corporate Debtor appealed to NCLAT, relying on correspondence from June 2016 that demonstrated a clear dispute regarding the supply of castings long before the IBC notice was issued[cite: 9]. Following the Supreme Court's Mobilox precedent, NCLAT held that the pre-existing dispute rendered the insolvency petition not maintainable, allowed the appeal, and released the Corporate Debtor from the CIRP[cite: 9].

case_title: Nand Lal Bhatia & Ors vs Kuldeep Kaul & Ors
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) No. 134 of 2017 along with Nos. 135 & 136 of 2017
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Nand Lal Bhatia & Ors are the Appellants (Bhatia Group)[cite: 11]. Kuldeep Kaul & Ors are the Respondents (Kaul Group)[cite: 11]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: The parties engaged in joint management and shareholding of the HBE Group of Companies, including Horizon Broadcast Electronics Pvt. Ltd. (HBEPL)[cite: 11]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: An independent auditor assessed a liability of Rs. 9,31,67,979 and USD 4,30,564 payable by the Appellants to the Respondents, leading the Tribunal to order an interim part-payment of Rs. 1 Crore[cite: 11]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The original Company Petition (CP No. 38 of 2015) was filed on 19th May 2015[cite: 11]. The challenged interim order was passed on 24th March 2017[cite: 11]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Both factions filed cross-petitions alleging the other siphoned business into newly incorporated, competing entities[cite: 11]. By consent, an independent auditor was appointed, who submitted a revised valuation report on 8th February 2017[cite: 11]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: On 24th March 2017, the NCLT Principal Bench passed an interim order directing the Appellants to deposit Rs. 1 Crore to test their bona-fides before hearing their objections to the valuation report[cite: 11]. The Appellants challenged this interim direction before the NCLAT[cite: 11].
legal_issues: Whether the NCLT had the justification to pass an interim order directing the Appellants to deposit Rs. 1 Crore to test their bona-fides prior to adjudicating their objections to the valuation report in an oppression and mismanagement dispute[cite: 11].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An appellate tribunal should refrain from interfering with interim, equitable arrangements ordered by a lower tribunal, particularly when the main petition has been pending for an extended period and the interim deposit is minor compared to the total disputed liability[cite: 11]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 422 of the Companies Act, 2013 mandates the expeditious disposal of petitions, ideally within 90 days[cite: 11]. Entertaining appeals against reasonable interim directions frustrates this statutory objective and needlessly prolongs litigation[cite: 11]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The NCLAT observed that the Rs. 1 Crore deposit ordered by the NCLT was significantly less than the Rs. 9.31 Crores determined by the independent valuer[cite: 11]. Consequently, the interim direction was deemed a fair measure to test bona-fides rather than an unjust punitive burden[cite: 11]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT concluded that the interim order was justified to ensure smooth operations and required no appellate interference, remitting the matter for expedited final disposal[cite: 11].
operative_order: The NCLAT declined to interfere with the impugned order dated 24th March 2017[cite: 11]. The case is remitted to the NCLT, Principal Bench, New Delhi, to decide the main petition in accordance with the law after taking the valuation reports into consideration[cite: 11]. The appeals are disposed of with no order as to costs[cite: 11].
summary: The Appellants and Respondents filed cross-petitions for oppression and mismanagement regarding the HBE Group of Companies[cite: 11]. The NCLT appointed an independent auditor by consent[cite: 11]. Before finalizing the valuation report, the NCLT passed an interim order directing the Appellants to pay Rs. 1 Crore to test their bona-fides, which the Appellants challenged[cite: 11]. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that the interim payment was reasonable given it was a fraction of the valuer's assessed liability (over Rs. 9 Crores)[cite: 11]. The NCLAT declined to interfere and remitted the matter to the NCLT for expedited final disposal[cite: 11].

case_title: Silvertone Constructions Private Limited vs Eastern Manufacturing Private Limited
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants are Silvertone Constructions Pvt. Ltd. and Jupiter Finvest Pvt. Ltd[cite: 12]. Respondent 1 is Eastern Manufacturing Pvt. Ltd., and Respondent 7 is Sunbeam Vanijya Pvt. Ltd[cite: 12]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: A Conversion Agreement dated 29th May 2009 regarding the use of the company's jute mill and the installation of new machinery[cite: 12]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The Appellants alleged that the Jute Mill was fraudulently transferred to Respondent 7 to deprive the Appellants of their 53.40% shareholding premium[cite: 12]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The disputed Conversion Agreement was executed on 29th May 2009, and the original Company Petition was filed in 2012[cite: 12]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Despite a slight variation in nomenclature between "The Eastern Manufacturing Company Limited" and "Eastern Manufacturing Private Limited", statutory records such as the CIN, registered address, and historical MOA confirmed they were the same entity[cite: 12]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Respondent 7 filed C.A. No. 448 of 2012 for deletion from the array of parties, which NCLT Kolkata allowed on 3rd July 2017, leading to this appeal[cite: 12].
legal_issues: Whether a party can be deleted from an oppression and mismanagement petition based on a minor discrepancy in the nomenclature of the respondent company it contracted with, despite statutory documents establishing their identity[cite: 12].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A necessary party cannot be struck from the array of respondents solely due to a minor typographical error in the company's name if statutory records sufficiently establish its true identity[cite: 12]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The petitioner is the "Dominus Litus"; if a respondent claims improper array, they bear the onus to prove their presence is unnecessary for the effective adjudication of the dispute[cite: 12]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal must rely on substantive statutory indicators like the CIN, registered address, and Annual Returns rather than bare nomenclature variations to determine corporate identity[cite: 12]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because the documentary evidence proved Respondent 1 was the exact entity that contracted with Respondent 7, Respondent 7 was a proper and necessary party whose deletion would prejudicially affect the Appellants[cite: 12].
operative_order: The appeal is allowed, and the impugned order deleting Respondent 7 is set aside[cite: 12]. Respondent 7 is directed to pay costs of Rs. 50,000 to the Appellants[cite: 12]. The Tribunal is ordered to dispose of the Company Petition expeditiously[cite: 12].
summary: Silvertone Constructions appealed an NCLT order that deleted Respondent 7 from an oppression petition because of a mismatch in the contracting company's name ("Company Ltd" vs "Private Ltd")[cite: 12]. The NCLAT allowed the appeal, ruling that statutory filings like the CIN and registered address proved they were the same juristic entity[cite: 12]. Consequently, Respondent 7 was a necessary party to the dispute[cite: 12].

case_title: T. Sreemannarayana vs Magnifico Minerals Pvt. Ltd. & Ors
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is T. Sreemannarayana, a shareholder/Director of the Corporate Debtor, Sai Balaji Sponge Iron India Pvt. Ltd[cite: 13]. The 1st Respondent is Magnifico Minerals Pvt. Ltd., the Operational Creditor[cite: 13]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: A contract for which the Corporate Debtor issued post-dated cheques that were subsequently dishonoured[cite: 13]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The Operational Creditor claimed an outstanding default amount of Rs. 4,25,10,464[cite: 13]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: A winding-up legal notice was issued on 10th December 2015[cite: 13]. The NCLT passed the ex-parte admission order on 22nd June 2017[cite: 13]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Following the transfer of the winding-up petition to the NCLT, the Operational Creditor entirely failed to issue a demand notice in Form 3 or 4 under Section 8(1) of the IBC, and failed to file Form 5[cite: 13]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: A winding-up petition transferred from the High Court to NCLT Hyderabad was admitted ex-parte as a Section 9 IBC application on 22nd June 2017, which the Appellant challenged[cite: 13].
legal_issues: Whether a transferred winding-up petition can be validly admitted under Section 9 of the IBC if the operational creditor fails to issue the mandatory Section 8 demand notice and submit Form 5 information within 60 days of the transfer[cite: 13].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A transferred winding-up petition stands abated by operation of law if the operational creditor fails to fulfill the mandatory statutory prerequisites under the IBC, such as issuing a prior demand notice and submitting the required forms[cite: 13]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The proviso to Rule 5 of the Companies (Transfer of Pending Proceedings) Rules, 2016 strictly mandates that petitioners must submit all required information for admission under the IBC within 60 days, failing which the petition shall abate[cite: 13]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal noted it was undisputed that no Section 8(1) notice was issued and Form 5 details were omitted, rendering the application fatally defective[cite: 13]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because the Operational Creditor failed to provide the mandated IBC details and demand notice, the transferred petition could not proceed and stood abated[cite: 13].
operative_order: The NCLAT set aside the ex-parte impugned order dated 22nd June 2017 and dismissed the Operational Creditor's application as abated[cite: 13]. The Corporate Debtor was released from the CIRP, and no order as to costs was made[cite: 13].
summary: A winding-up petition against Sai Balaji Sponge Iron was transferred to NCLT and admitted ex-parte under Section 9 of the IBC[cite: 13]. The NCLAT reversed this decision, holding that the Operational Creditor had failed to issue the mandatory Section 8 demand notice and file the required Form 5 information within 60 days of transfer[cite: 13]. Consequently, the petition abated under Rule 5 of the Transfer Rules, 2016, and the CIRP was quashed[cite: 13].

case_title: Vashisht Kumar Goyal vs M/S Rishi Infratech Pvt Ltd. & Ors
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Vashisht Kumar Goyal is the Appellant[cite: 14]. M/s Rishi Infratech Pvt Ltd. is Respondent 1/Petitioner, Mahamaya Exports Pvt. Ltd. is the target company, and Amit Kumar (Appellant's brother) is the newly added Respondent 6[cite: 14]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Rishi Infratech acquired 34,20,000 equity shares, representing 30% of Mahamaya Exports, between 2014 and 2015[cite: 14]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Rishi Infratech alleged denial of AGM notices, refusal of inspection of statutory records, fictitious entries, and a secretive change of the corporate office[cite: 14]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The share transfers occurred in Nov 2014 and Aug 2015[cite: 14]. The NCLT allowed the amendment application on 10th February 2017[cite: 14]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Following a CLB order, the Respondents disclosed a Register of Contracts which revealed secret agreements executed with Amit Kumar on 21.12.2015 without notifying the Petitioners[cite: 14]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Rishi Infratech filed an oppression petition and later moved to amend it to include facts discovered via the CLB's document production order[cite: 14]. NCLT allowed this amendment, which the Appellant challenged[cite: 14].
legal_issues: Whether a petitioner in an oppression and mismanagement case can amend the original petition to incorporate subsequent events and newly discovered facts extracted through an interim disclosure order[cite: 14].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An amendment to a company petition is permissible if it brings on record facts and subsequent events related to oppression that the petitioner only discovered after filing the original petition[cite: 14]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: While entirely fresh, unrelated causes of action require a separate petition, consequential actions or newly discovered facts connected to existing allegations of mismanagement are perfectly permissible as amendments for substantive justice[cite: 14]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal noted that information regarding the disputed contracts and meetings was extracted solely through the CLB's prior disclosure order, proving the petitioner lacked this knowledge initially[cite: 14]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: To ensure substantive justice and proper disposal, the NCLT correctly permitted the amendment incorporating facts that emerged from the mandated disclosure of records[cite: 14].
operative_order: The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, upholding the NCLT's order dated 10th February 2017 that allowed the amendment and impleadment[cite: 14]. Both parties were directed to bear their own costs[cite: 14].
summary: Rishi Infratech filed an oppression petition against Mahamaya Exports[cite: 14]. After the CLB ordered the production of company records, Rishi Infratech discovered secret contracts and moved to amend its petition[cite: 14]. The NCLT allowed the amendment[cite: 14]. The NCLAT dismissed the Appellant's challenge, ruling that amendments incorporating connected subsequent events or newly discovered evidence are necessary for substantive justice in oppression cases[cite: 14].

case_title: M/S. Ksheeraabd Constructions Pvt. Ltd vs M/S. Vijay Nirman Company Pvt. Ltd
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Ksheeraabd Constructions Pvt. Ltd. is the Appellant and Corporate Debtor[cite: 15]. Vijay Nirman Company Pvt. Ltd. is the Respondent and Operational Creditor[cite: 15]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: An underlying contract led to disputes which were subsequently adjudicated by an Arbitral Tribunal[cite: 15]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The Operational Creditor claimed a debt based on a crystallized Arbitral Award, while the Corporate Debtor claimed a counter-claim of Rs. 19 crores[cite: 15]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The Arbitral Award was passed on 21st January 2017[cite: 15]. The Section 9 application was admitted on 29th August 2017[cite: 15]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The Corporate Debtor had filed an application under Section 34 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 to set aside the arbitral award prior to the IBC proceedings[cite: 15]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Hyderabad admitted the Section 9 IBC petition filed by the Operational Creditor[cite: 15]. The Corporate Debtor appealed, arguing that the pending Section 34 challenge constituted a "pre-existing dispute"[cite: 15].
legal_issues: Whether the pendency of an application to set aside an arbitral award under Section 34 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 constitutes an "existence of dispute" that precludes the admission of a Section 9 application under the IBC[cite: 15].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The pendency of a challenge to an arbitral award under Section 34 of the Arbitration Act does not constitute a pre-existing dispute under the IBC, and cannot stall a Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process under Section 9[cite: 15]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 238 of the IBC has an overriding effect over the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996[cite: 15]. Under Form-5 of the IBC Rules, an order of an arbitral panel adjudicating a default is explicitly treated as a "record of Operational Debt", not a pending dispute[cite: 15]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: While an ongoing arbitration before an award is passed constitutes a dispute, an arbitral award that has already adjudicated the default serves as concrete evidence of debt under the IBC framework, regardless of its delayed executability under Section 36 of the Arbitration Act[cite: 15]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Corporate Debtor cannot rely on a pending Section 34 application to evade insolvency proceedings, as the arbitral award itself solidifies the debt under the overriding mandate of the IBC[cite: 15].
operative_order: The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, upholding the NCLT's admission order dated 29th August 2017[cite: 15]. No order was made as to costs[cite: 15].
summary: NCLT Hyderabad admitted a Section 9 IBC application against Ksheeraabd Constructions based on a debt crystallized by an Arbitral Award[cite: 15]. The Corporate Debtor appealed, arguing that its pending Section 34 challenge to the award constituted a pre-existing dispute[cite: 15]. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, ruling that under the overriding effect of the IBC, an arbitral award is a statutory "record of operational debt", and a pending Section 34 challenge cannot be used to stall insolvency proceedings[cite: 15].

case_title: M/S. Bhash Software Labs Pvt. Ltd vs M/S. Mobme Wireless Solutions Ltd
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Bhash Software Labs Pvt. Ltd. is the Appellant/Corporate Debtor[cite: 16]. Mobme Wireless Solutions Ltd. is the Respondent/Operational Creditor[cite: 16]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: An Agreement dated 3rd January 2015 wherein the Operational Creditor provided bulk SMS services to the Corporate Debtor[cite: 16]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The Operational Creditor demanded Rs. 75,76,380 for services provided from November 2015 to February 2016[cite: 16]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The Operational Creditor issued a winding-up notice on 25th August 2016, to which the Corporate Debtor replied on 23rd September 2016[cite: 16]. NCLT passed the admission order on 1st June 2017[cite: 16]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The Corporate Debtor's September 2016 reply explicitly disputed the debt, citing poor service quality and abrupt termination[cite: 16]. The IBC demand notice was sent to an incorrect address and returned unserved[cite: 16]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Chennai admitted the Section 9 petition ex-parte without issuing notice to the Corporate Debtor[cite: 16]. The Corporate Debtor appealed to the NCLAT[cite: 16].
legal_issues: Whether a Section 9 IBC application can be admitted ex-parte without serving notice to the Corporate Debtor, and whether a prior documented complaint regarding service quality invalidates the application[cite: 16].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An Adjudicating Authority must issue a limited notice to the Corporate Debtor before admitting an insolvency petition to satisfy natural justice and verify the existence of a default or dispute[cite: 16]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: A dispute under the IBC includes any documented complaint raised prior to the Section 8 demand notice regarding the quality of goods/services, and is not strictly confined to pending formal suits or arbitrations[cite: 16]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The NCLAT found that the demand notice was sent to the wrong address, and the NCLT failed to mandate a fresh notice[cite: 16]. Furthermore, the September 2016 reply to the winding-up notice clearly documented a genuine, pre-existing dispute regarding service quality[cite: 16]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because the NCLT violated natural justice by admitting the petition ex-parte, and because a genuine pre-existing dispute was proven, the Section 9 application was fundamentally flawed and not maintainable[cite: 16].
operative_order: The NCLAT set aside the impugned ex-parte order dated 1st June 2017 and dismissed the Section 9 application[cite: 16]. The Corporate Debtor was released from the CIRP, and the Operational Creditor was directed to bear the IRP's fees[cite: 16].
summary: NCLT Chennai admitted a Section 9 IBC petition against Bhash Software Labs ex-parte[cite: 16]. Bhash Software appealed, arguing it never received the demand notice and had a pre-existing dispute[cite: 16]. The NCLAT allowed the appeal, ruling that the NCLT violated natural justice by not serving notice[cite: 16]. Additionally, correspondence from 2016 proved a genuine pre-existing dispute regarding the quality of SMS services, rendering the insolvency petition not maintainable[cite: 16].
