STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 238 of the IBC has an overriding effect over the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996[cite: 15]. Under Form-5 of the IBC Rules, an order of an arbitral panel adjudicating a default is explicitly treated as a "record of Operational Debt", not a pending dispute[cite: 15]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: While an ongoing arbitration before an award is passed constitutes a dispute, an arbitral award that has already adjudicated the default serves as concrete evidence of debt under the IBC framework, regardless of its delayed executability under Section 36 of the Arbitration Act[cite: 15]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Corporate Debtor cannot rely on a pending Section 34 application to evade insolvency proceedings, as the arbitral award itself solidifies the debt under the overriding mandate of the IBC[cite: 15].
operative_order: The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, upholding the NCLT's admission order dated 29th August 2017[cite: 15]. No order was made as to costs[cite: 15].
summary: NCLT Hyderabad admitted a Section 9 IBC application against Ksheeraabd Constructions based on a debt crystallized by an Arbitral Award[cite: 15]. The Corporate Debtor appealed, arguing that its pending Section 34 challenge to the award constituted a pre-existing dispute[cite: 15]. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, ruling that under the overriding effect of the IBC, an arbitral award is a statutory "record of operational debt", and a pending Section 34 challenge cannot be used to stall insolvency proceedings[cite: 15].

case_title: M/S. Bhash Software Labs Pvt. Ltd vs M/S. Mobme Wireless Solutions Ltd
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Bhash Software Labs Pvt. Ltd. is the Appellant/Corporate Debtor[cite: 16]. Mobme Wireless Solutions Ltd. is the Respondent/Operational Creditor[cite: 16]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: An Agreement dated 3rd January 2015 wherein the Operational Creditor provided bulk SMS services to the Corporate Debtor[cite: 16]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The Operational Creditor demanded Rs. 75,76,380 for services provided from November 2015 to February 2016[cite: 16]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The Operational Creditor issued a winding-up notice on 25th August 2016, to which the Corporate Debtor replied on 23rd September 2016[cite: 16]. NCLT passed the admission order on 1st June 2017[cite: 16]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The Corporate Debtor's September 2016 reply explicitly disputed the debt, citing poor service quality and abrupt termination[cite: 16]. The IBC demand notice was sent to an incorrect address and returned unserved[cite: 16]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Chennai admitted the Section 9 petition ex-parte without issuing notice to the Corporate Debtor[cite: 16]. The Corporate Debtor appealed to the NCLAT[cite: 16].
legal_issues: Whether a Section 9 IBC application can be admitted ex-parte without serving notice to the Corporate Debtor, and whether a prior documented complaint regarding service quality invalidates the application[cite: 16].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An Adjudicating Authority must issue a limited notice to the Corporate Debtor before admitting an insolvency petition to satisfy natural justice and verify the existence of a default or dispute[cite: 16]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: A dispute under the IBC includes any documented complaint raised prior to the Section 8 demand notice regarding the quality of goods/services, and is not strictly confined to pending formal suits or arbitrations[cite: 16]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The NCLAT found that the demand notice was sent to the wrong address, and the NCLT failed to mandate a fresh notice[cite: 16]. Furthermore, the September 2016 reply to the winding-up notice clearly documented a genuine, pre-existing dispute regarding service quality[cite: 16]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because the NCLT violated natural justice by admitting the petition ex-parte, and because a genuine pre-existing dispute was proven, the Section 9 application was fundamentally flawed and not maintainable[cite: 16].
operative_order: The NCLAT set aside the impugned ex-parte order dated 1st June 2017 and dismissed the Section 9 application[cite: 16]. The Corporate Debtor was released from the CIRP, and the Operational Creditor was directed to bear the IRP's fees[cite: 16].
summary: NCLT Chennai admitted a Section 9 IBC petition against Bhash Software Labs ex-parte[cite: 16]. Bhash Software appealed, arguing it never received the demand notice and had a pre-existing dispute[cite: 16]. The NCLAT allowed the appeal, ruling that the NCLT violated natural justice by not serving notice[cite: 16]. Additionally, correspondence from 2016 proved a genuine pre-existing dispute regarding the quality of SMS services, rendering the insolvency petition not maintainable[cite: 16].

case_title: Black Pearl Hotels Pvt. Ltd vs Planet M Retail Ltd
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Black Pearl Hotels Pvt. Ltd. is the Appellant and Operational Creditor[cite: 28]. Planet M Retail Ltd is the Respondent and Corporate Debtor[cite: 28]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: A Business Conducting Agreement dated 1st February 2008 to run a music concept store in exchange for a monthly minimum guaranteed fee[cite: 28]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Claimed outstanding dues of Rs. 3,92,38,405 dating back to October 2011[cite: 28]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The Section 8 demand notice was issued in 2017, and a reply denying the claim was received on 18th March 2017[cite: 28]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The Corporate Debtor stopped payment in September 2011[cite: 28]. A prior arbitration application was dismissed on 4th March 2014 without liberty to proceed, while a separate Section 9 Arbitration Act application was withdrawn with liberty[cite: 28]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The Operational Creditor filed a Section 9 IBC application which the NCLT Mumbai dismissed on 4th May 2017 as barred by limitation, leading to this appeal[cite: 28].
legal_issues: Whether an application under Section 9 of the IBC is barred by the Limitation Act, 1963 if the underlying debt defaulted in 2011, but the statutory right to apply under the IBC accrued only upon its enactment[cite: 28].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The right to apply under the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 accrues solely from the date the Code came into force, meaning an application filed within three years of that enactment date cannot be barred by limitation[cite: 28]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Under Article 137 of the Limitation Act, 1963, the three-year limitation period begins to run when the right to apply accrues[cite: 28]. Because the IBC came into effect on 1st December 2016, the right to apply under Section 9 accrued strictly on that date[cite: 28]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Adjudicating Authority erred by calculating the limitation period from the date of the commercial default in 2011 rather than the date the statutory remedy under the IBC was created[cite: 28]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Section 9 application, having been filed in early 2017, was well within three years from 1st December 2016 and therefore was not barred by limitation[cite: 28].
operative_order: The NCLAT set aside the impugned order dated 4th May 2017 passed by NCLT Mumbai[cite: 28]. The case is remitted for admission after issuing notice and hearing the parties[cite: 28]. The Adjudicating Authority is directed to allow time to remove any defects if the application is incomplete[cite: 28]. The appeal is allowed with no order as to costs[cite: 28].
summary: The Operational Creditor filed a Section 9 application against Planet M Retail Ltd for unpaid fees stemming from a 2008 agreement, with defaults starting in 2011[cite: 28]. NCLT Mumbai dismissed the petition as barred by limitation because the default occurred over three years prior[cite: 28]. The NCLAT allowed the appeal and set aside the dismissal, holding that the right to apply under the IBC accrued only on 1st December 2016, when the Code came into force[cite: 28]. Thus, an application filed shortly after the IBC's enactment falls within the three-year period prescribed by Article 137 of the Limitation Act, 1963[cite: 28].

case_title: Achenbach Buschhutten Cmbh & Co vs Arcotech Ltd
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Achenbach Buschhutten GmbH & Co. is a German company acting as the Operational Creditor/Appellant[cite: 29]. Arcotech Ltd. is the Corporate Debtor/Respondent[cite: 29]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Claim for an operational debt arising under an agreement containing an arbitration clause[cite: 29]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Operational debt defaulted by the Corporate Debtor[cite: 29]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The Section 9 application was rejected by NCLT Chandigarh on 25th May 2017[cite: 29]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The Appellant submitted a 'confirmation of receipt of payment' letter from a foreign bank, 'Sparkasse Siegen', instead of a certificate from an Indian statutory financial institution[cite: 29]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Chandigarh rejected the Section 9 application, citing both the existence of an arbitration clause as a dispute and non-compliance with the financial institution certificate requirement[cite: 29]. The Appellant challenged this rejection[cite: 29].
legal_issues: Whether a certificate from a foreign bank that does not qualify as a 'Financial Institution' under Section 3(14) of the IBC fulfills the mandatory requirement of Section 9(3)(c) for initiating CIRP[cite: 29].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An operational creditor must provide a certificate of non-payment from a 'Financial Institution' strictly as defined under the IBC; certificates from unrecognized foreign banks are legally invalid[cite: 29]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 3(14) of the IBC defines 'financial institution' referencing scheduled banks under Section 45-I of the RBI Act, Section 2(72) of the Companies Act, or institutions explicitly notified by the Central Government[cite: 29]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal noted that filing the certificate under Section 9(3)(c) is mandatory, not merely directory[cite: 29]. Because 'Sparkasse Siegen' fits none of the statutory definitions, the document supplied failed to meet the mandatory legal standard[cite: 29]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Although a mere arbitration clause does not constitute a pre-existing dispute, the Section 9 application was correctly dismissed due to the absence of a mandatory certificate from a statutorily recognized Financial Institution[cite: 29].
operative_order: The NCLAT found no merit in the appeal and dismissed it, upholding the NCLT's rejection of the Section 9 application[cite: 29]. No order as to costs was passed[cite: 29].
summary: A German Operational Creditor filed a Section 9 application against Arcotech Ltd., which NCLT Chandigarh rejected[cite: 29]. The NCLT cited the existence of an arbitration clause and the failure to provide a valid financial institution certificate[cite: 29]. The NCLAT clarified that a mere arbitration clause does not constitute a pre-existing dispute[cite: 29]. However, it dismissed the appeal because the appellant submitted a certificate from 'Sparkasse Siegen', a foreign bank not recognized as a 'Financial Institution' under Section 3(14) of the IBC, thereby violating the mandatory requirement of Section 9(3)(c)[cite: 29].

case_title: M/S. J.P. Engineers Pvt. Ltd vs M/S. Indo Alusys Industries Ltd
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: M/s. J.P. Engineers Pvt. Ltd. is the Appellant/Operational Creditor[cite: 30]. M/s. Indo Alusys Industries Ltd. is the Respondent/Corporate Debtor[cite: 30]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Claim based on invoices for goods and services provided[cite: 30]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The claim included amounts owed to another firm allegedly taken over by the Operational Creditor[cite: 30]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The demand notice was issued by an advocate on 9th May 2017[cite: 30]. The NCLT rejected the petition on 5th September 2017[cite: 30]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The Corporate Debtor had disputed the claim by a letter dated 4th March 2017 (prior to the IBC notice) stating the invoice numbers did not match[cite: 30]. The Section 8 demand notice was issued by an external Advocate who held no position in relation to the Operational Creditor[cite: 30]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT New Delhi rejected the Section 9 application because the demand notice was issued by a lawyer and due to a pre-existing dispute[cite: 30]. The Operational Creditor appealed to the NCLAT[cite: 30].
legal_issues: Whether a demand notice under Section 8 of the IBC can be validly issued by an Advocate without holding any position within the Operational Creditor, and whether prior correspondence rejecting mismatched invoices constitutes a pre-existing dispute[cite: 30].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A demand notice under Section 8 of the IBC must be issued by the Operational Creditor or an authorized person holding a position in relation to the Operational Creditor; additionally, prior correspondence disputing invoices constitutes a valid pre-existing dispute barring CIRP[cite: 30]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 8, read with Forms 3 and 4, mandates that the person signing the notice must state their formal position in relation to the Operational Creditor[cite: 30]. An external advocate acting merely as counsel does not satisfy this strict statutory requirement[cite: 30]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The subsequent ratification of the advocate's action by the Board of Directors does not cure the defect because the notice must strictly adhere to the IBC's specific formats at the time of issuance[cite: 30]. Furthermore, the 4th March 2017 letter clearly established a dispute regarding mismatched invoices prior to the demand notice[cite: 30]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Section 9 application was fundamentally flawed due to a defectively issued demand notice and the concrete existence of a pre-existing dispute, justifying its dismissal[cite: 30].
operative_order: The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, upholding the NCLT's order dated 5th September 2017 rejecting the Section 9 application[cite: 30]. No order as to costs was passed[cite: 30].
summary: The Operational Creditor filed a Section 9 IBC application against Indo Alusys Industries Ltd, which the NCLT rejected[cite: 30]. The NCLAT upheld the rejection on two grounds[cite: 30]. First, the mandatory Section 8 demand notice was defectively issued by an external advocate who did not hold any position within the Operational Creditor, a flaw that cannot be cured by subsequent ratification[cite: 30]. Second, documentary evidence showed that the Corporate Debtor had raised a genuine dispute regarding mismatched invoices in March 2017, prior to the issuance of the IBC notice, rendering the application unmaintainable[cite: 30].

case_title: Balaji Enterprise vs Gammon India Limited & Ors
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Balaji Enterprise is the Appellant/Operational Creditor[cite: 31]. Gammon India Limited is the Respondent/Corporate Debtor[cite: 31]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Claim for operational debt arising from agreements containing arbitration clauses[cite: 31]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Claim based on unpaid operational debt[cite: 31]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The Operational Creditor issued a notice invoking arbitration under Section 21 of the Arbitration Act on 5th January 2017[cite: 31]. NCLT Mumbai dismissed the Section 9 application on 19th July 2017[cite: 31]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Prior to issuing the Section 8 demand notice under the IBC, the Operational Creditor itself initiated formal arbitration proceedings against the Corporate Debtor[cite: 31]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai dismissed the Section 9 IBC application because the Operational Creditor's own invocation of arbitration established the existence of a pre-existing dispute under Section 5(6) of the IBC[cite: 31]. The Appellant challenged the dismissal[cite: 31].
legal_issues: Whether the invocation of arbitration proceedings by the Operational Creditor itself prior to issuing a demand notice under Section 8 constitutes a pre-existing 'dispute' under Section 5(6) of the IBC that bars the initiation of CIRP[cite: 31].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Formal arbitration proceedings are deemed to commence on the date the request to refer the dispute to arbitration is received, and such pending arbitration constitutes a 'dispute' precluding the admission of an insolvency petition[cite: 31]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Under Section 21 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, arbitration commences upon receipt of the notice[cite: 31]. Consequently, under Section 5(6) of the IBC, this pending arbitration definitively qualifies as a 'dispute' relating to the existence of a debt[cite: 31]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Since the Operational Creditor issued an arbitration notice on 5th January 2017, prior to the IBC demand notice, arbitration proceedings had legally commenced[cite: 31]. It defies logic for the creditor to claim ignorance of the very dispute it initiated[cite: 31]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The existence of pending arbitration proceedings invoked by the creditor squarely falls under the definition of a dispute, barring the admission of the Section 9 application[cite: 31].
operative_order: The NCLAT disposed of the appeal by declining to interfere with the NCLT's dismissal order dated 19th July 2017[cite: 31]. However, liberty was granted to the Appellant to move the appropriate forum for agreements lacking an arbitration clause[cite: 31]. No order as to costs[cite: 31].
summary: Balaji Enterprise filed a Section 9 IBC application against Gammon India, which the NCLT dismissed because the creditor had already initiated arbitration proceedings prior to the IBC demand notice[cite: 31]. The NCLAT affirmed the dismissal, ruling that under Section 21 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, arbitration commences when the notice is received[cite: 31]. This pending arbitration squarely falls under the definition of a 'dispute' under Section 5(6) of the IBC, preventing the admission of the insolvency petition[cite: 31].

case_title: Rachit Suresh Gangar & Ors. vs Triveni Bialleti Industries Private Limited & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants are Rachit Suresh Gangar & Ors. (original petitioners)[cite: 32]. Respondents are Triveni Bialleti Industries Private Limited & Ors[cite: 32]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Internal corporate management dispute leading to an oppression and mismanagement petition[cite: 32]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The appellants alleged they were illegally removed as Directors in 2011 and further alleged in 2016 that company property was sold without notice or an Extra Ordinary General Meeting[cite: 32]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The original removal occurred in 2011, while the subsequent alleged property sale happened during the petition's pendency around 1st June 2016[cite: 32]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The Tribunal explicitly found that the appellants failed to prove their oppression case in all respects[cite: 32]. However, taking note of the company's continuous losses and a pending demerger before the Bombay High Court, the NCLT still directed a fair valuation exit for the petitioners on 'just and equitable' grounds[cite: 32]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai dismissed the oppression petition on merits but ordered the respondents to provide an exit to the petitioners[cite: 32]. The Appellants appealed, and the Respondents conceded that the exit direction lacked jurisdiction[cite: 32].
legal_issues: Whether a Tribunal has the jurisdiction under Section 242 of the Companies Act, 2013 to grant equitable relief and mandate a shareholder exit after definitively concluding that the petitioners failed to prove any act of oppression or mismanagement[cite: 32].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The Tribunal cannot exercise its remedial powers to grant equitable relief or direct a shareholder buyout if it explicitly finds that the allegations of oppression and mismanagement have not been proven[cite: 32]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 242 of the Companies Act, 2013 limits the Tribunal's power to pass orders to situations where oppression or mismanagement is substantively established; invoking 'just and equitable' grounds merely to bring a dispute to a logical end is ultra vires absent this foundational finding[cite: 32]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Since the NCLT explicitly recorded that the petitioners completely failed to prove their case, the statutory prerequisite for invoking Section 242 was absent[cite: 32]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT held that the Tribunal exceeded its jurisdiction by ordering an exit valuation despite dismissing the oppression claims, thus requiring the setting aside of the specific exit direction[cite: 32].
operative_order: The NCLAT upheld the NCLT's finding that the appellants failed to prove their case but set aside the direction ordering the respondents to provide an exit to the petitioners on fair valuation[cite: 32]. The appeal was disposed of with no order as to costs, leaving the appellants at liberty to file a fresh petition for subsequent causes of action if statutorily qualified[cite: 32].
summary: Appellants challenged an NCLT Mumbai order dismissing their oppression and mismanagement petition against Triveni Bialleti Industries[cite: 32]. The NCLT found the appellants completely failed to prove their case, yet it directed the respondents to provide an exit to the appellants on "just and equitable" grounds due to company losses[cite: 32]. The NCLAT set aside the exit direction, ruling that the NCLT lacks jurisdiction under Section 242 of the Companies Act, 2013 to grant equitable relief or mandate a shareholder exit once it definitively concludes that no oppression or mismanagement occurred[cite: 32].

case_title: Pawan Kumar & Ors vs Newtech Agro Products Pvt. Ltd. & Ors
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants are Pawan Kumar & Ors., minority shareholders holding 37.45% equity[cite: 33]. Respondents are Newtech Agro Products Pvt. Ltd. & Ors[cite: 33]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: The dispute involves the internal transfer of 29,000 equity shares between respondent groups and the overall allotment of increased share capital[cite: 33]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The appellants alleged that share transfers executed in 2006 and during an AGM on 29.05.2008 were fraudulent and violated the Articles of Association[cite: 33]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The contested transfers occurred in 2006 and 2008, while the oppression petition was filed in 2010[cite: 33]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The NCLT found the 2008 transfers suspect because the company failed to produce AGM notices or minute books, indicating a violation of the Articles of Association[cite: 33]. However, five of the six individuals who received the shares were never impleaded as parties to the petition[cite: 33]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Chandigarh dismissed the petition, citing severe delay, laches, and the fatal non-joinder of necessary parties (the un-impleaded transferees)[cite: 33]. The Appellants appealed to the NCLAT[cite: 33].
legal_issues: Whether a Tribunal can set aside allegedly illegal and fraudulent share transfers in an oppression and mismanagement petition when the petitioners have failed to implead the transferees as necessary parties[cite: 33].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An adjudicatory body cannot reverse share transfers or grant relief that adversely impacts specific individuals if those individuals are not impleaded as necessary parties to the proceedings[cite: 33]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The equitable relief mechanisms under Sections 397/398 and 402/403 of the Companies Act, 1956 are strictly subject to the principles of natural justice; affected parties cannot be condemned or stripped of their shares unheard[cite: 33]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Despite establishing that the 2008 share transfers likely violated the Articles of Association due to missing documentation, the Tribunal could not grant relief because the appellants neglected for seven years to implead five of the six direct beneficiaries of the transfer[cite: 33]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The petition was rightfully dismissed due to the fatal non-joinder of necessary parties and unexplainable laches by the petitioners[cite: 33].
operative_order: The NCLAT disposed of the appeal by refusing to interfere with the NCLT's dismissal order[cite: 33]. Recognizing a corporate deadlock, the NCLAT granted the Appellants the liberty to negotiate an honorable exit from the company based on an appropriate valuation of shares, assets, and goodwill[cite: 33]. No order as to costs[cite: 33].
summary: Appellants holding 37.45% shares in Newtech Agro Products challenged an NCLT order that dismissed their oppression petition regarding allegedly illegal share transfers made in 2008[cite: 33]. While the NCLT noted that the transfers likely violated the Articles of Association, it dismissed the case because the appellants inexplicably failed to implead the actual transferees as necessary parties[cite: 33]. The NCLAT upheld the dismissal, affirming that share transfers cannot be set aside without hearing the affected transferees[cite: 33]. The NCLAT also upheld findings on delay and laches but granted the appellants liberty to negotiate a fair exit from the deadlocked company[cite: 33].

case_title: Mr. P.B. Amolik & Ors vs The Bombay Diocesan Trust Association Private Limited & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants are Mr. P.B. Amolik & Ors. Respondents are The Bombay Diocesan Trust Association Private Limited & Ors[cite: 34]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Management of a Section 25 non-profit company which is simultaneously registered as a public charitable trust[cite: 34]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Appellants were removed from their positions as directors and trustees due to criminal activities and breach of trust[cite: 34]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The Charity Commissioner ordered the removal of the appellants as trustees on 17th December 2012[cite: 34]. NCLT Mumbai dismissed their subsequent oppression petition on 19th December 2016[cite: 34]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The Charity Commissioner's order removing the appellants under Section 41D of the Bombay Public Trusts Act (BPT Act) reached finality after their appeals to the City Civil Court and Bombay High Court failed[cite: 34]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appellants filed an oppression petition against their removal as directors before the NCLT[cite: 34]. NCLT Mumbai dismissed it based on res judicata because the Charity Commissioner had already adjudicated their removal[cite: 34]. The Appellants appealed to NCLAT[cite: 34].
legal_issues: Whether an oppression and mismanagement petition under Sections 397/398 of the Companies Act seeking reinstatement as a director is barred by res judicata if the petitioners were already lawfully removed as trustees of the same entity by the Charity Commissioner under the Bombay Public Trusts Act[cite: 34].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: When an entity operates dually as a charitable trust and a non-profit company, a competent authority's final order removing individuals from the trust operates as res judicata against parallel proceedings seeking their reinstatement as company directors[cite: 34]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: For a Section 25 company that doubles as a public trust, the roles of the Board of Directors and Trustees are legally inseparable and unified for the purposes of management and duty performance[cite: 34]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Since the Charity Commissioner's removal order for criminal activities and breach of trust had been unsuccessfully challenged and reached finality, the NCLT correctly applied the doctrine of res judicata pro veritate accipitur, preventing the issue from being retried from a corporate angle[cite: 34]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Granting relief under Sections 397/398 is discretionary; reinstating individuals facing pending criminal cases who were already legally stripped of trusteeship would harm the entity's charitable interests[cite: 34].
operative_order: The NCLAT found no merit in the appeal and dismissed it, upholding the NCLT's decision to dismiss the oppression petition on the grounds of res judicata[cite: 34]. No order as to costs was made[cite: 34].
summary: The Appellants were removed as directors and trustees of a Section 25 company (also registered as a public trust) following criminal charges[cite: 34]. The Charity Commissioner formally removed them as trustees under the Bombay Public Trusts Act, an order which reached finality[cite: 34]. The Appellants then filed an oppression petition before the NCLT seeking reinstatement as directors, which was dismissed on principles of res judicata[cite: 34]. The NCLAT affirmed the dismissal, ruling that the roles of director and trustee in such an entity are legally inseparable[cite: 34]. Since the Charity Commissioner's removal order was final, parallel relief under the Companies Act, 1956 could not be granted[cite: 34].

case_title: Mr. Karthikk Elangovan vs M/S. Metal Gems And Anr
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Mr. Karthikk Elangovan is the Appellant and Shareholder of the Corporate Debtor (M/s. Saranya Forging & Engineers India Pvt. Ltd.)[cite: 35]. M/s. Metal Gems is the 1st Respondent and Operational Creditor[cite: 35]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Supply of copper rods and related products by the Operational Creditor during 2012 and 2013[cite: 35]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Claim for unpaid operational debt arising from the allegedly supplied goods[cite: 35]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: A winding-up notice was sent on 1st June 2015. After transfer to the NCLT, the admission order initiating CIRP was passed on 22nd September 2017[cite: 35]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Pre-existing disputes were explicitly raised by the Corporate Debtor regarding the substandard quality of the goods via emails in 2013 and a formal reply in December 2014[cite: 35]. Post-transfer, the Operational Creditor failed to issue a Section 8 IBC demand notice or submit Form 5[cite: 35]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: A pending winding-up petition was transferred to NCLT Chennai, which treated it as a Section 9 IBC application and admitted it[cite: 35]. The Appellant challenged the admission[cite: 35].
legal_issues: Whether a pending winding-up petition transferred to the NCLT can be validly admitted under Section 9 of the IBC if the operational creditor failed to issue the mandatory Section 8 demand notice and submit Form 5 information[cite: 35].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Transferred winding-up petitions abate by operation of law if the operational creditor fails to fulfill the mandatory statutory prerequisites under the IBC, primarily the issuance of a Section 8 demand notice[cite: 35]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Rule 5 of the Companies (Transfer of Pending Proceedings) Rules, 2016 strictly mandates that the petitioner must submit all required IBC information (including Form 5 and the Form 3/4 demand notice) within 60 days of the transfer notification, failing which the petition shall abate[cite: 35]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: It was undisputed that no Section 8 demand notice was issued by the Operational Creditor and the Form 5 details were omitted, rendering the application statutorily defective[cite: 35]. Additionally, documentary evidence showed a clear pre-existing dispute regarding substandard goods[cite: 35]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The failure to issue the mandatory demand notice and supply required information meant the petition abated under the Transfer Rules, requiring the NCLAT to set aside the admission order[cite: 35].
operative_order: The NCLAT set aside the impugned admission order dated 22nd September 2017 and declared that the application under Sections 433 and 434 of the Companies Act, 1956 stands abated[cite: 35]. The Corporate Debtor was released from CIRP[cite: 35]. No order as to costs was passed[cite: 35].
summary: A winding-up petition against Saranya Forging & Engineers was transferred to NCLT Chennai, which admitted it as a Section 9 IBC application[cite: 35]. A shareholder of the corporate debtor appealed, arguing that no Section 8 demand notice was issued and a pre-existing dispute over goods quality existed[cite: 35]. The NCLAT allowed the appeal, ruling that under Rule 5 of the Transfer Rules 2016, an operational creditor must submit a Section 8 demand notice and file the requisite Form 5 within 60 days of the transfer[cite: 35]. Failure to comply results in the automatic abatement of the petition[cite: 35]. Consequently, the CIRP admission was quashed and the company released[cite: 35].

case_title: Labdhi Enterprises vs Baramati Agro Pvt. Limited
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Labdhi Enterprises is the Appellant and Operational Creditor[cite: 36]. Baramati Agro Pvt. Limited is the Respondent and Corporate Debtor[cite: 36]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Supply of goods for which invoices were raised and allegedly received without dispute[cite: 36]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The operational creditor claimed a default of Rs. 27,97,696 payable since 27th April 2010[cite: 36]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The debt became payable on 27th April 2010[cite: 36]. NCLT Mumbai dismissed the transferred petition on 30th June 2017[cite: 36]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: NCLT dismissed the application primarily because the debt was due in 2010 with no acknowledgement within three years, rendering it time-barred[cite: 36]. Concurrently, the appellant had not submitted all required IBC information post-transfer as per Rule 5[cite: 36]. 6. legal_issues: Whether a transferred winding-up petition treated as a Section 9 IBC application can be dismissed strictly as time-barred under the Limitation Act for a 2010 default, and the procedural effect of failing to submit IBC-specific information post-transfer[cite: 36].

Whether a transferred winding-up petition treated as a Section 9 IBC application can be dismissed strictly as time-barred under the Limitation Act for a 2010 default, and the procedural effect of failing to submit IBC-specific information post-transfer[cite: 36].

STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: While the Limitation Act, 1963 does not strictly bar CIRP initiation, the doctrine of laches applies; stale claims should not be entertained unless the delay is explained or there is a continuing cause of action[cite: 36]. case_title: Prabhakar Processors Pvt Ltd & Ors vs Kusumdevi Tibrewal & Ors
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Prabhakar Processors Pvt Ltd & Ors are the Appellants[cite: 38]. Kusumdevi Tibrewal & Ors are the Respondents (Original Petitioners)[cite: 38]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: An alleged Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) dated 16th April 2011 to transfer shares between the Tibrewal group and the Appellants[cite: 38]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The Respondents filed a petition alleging oppression and mismanagement, which the Appellants countered by claiming the Respondents had already sold their shares via the MOU[cite: 38]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The MOU was dated 16th April 2011[cite: 38]. The NCLT Ahmedabad passed its preliminary order on 2nd January 2017[cite: 38]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The Respondents (Petitioners) never signed the MOU themselves; it was signed by relatives[cite: 38]. No formal transfer procedure under the Companies Act or Articles of Association was followed, and no entry was made in the company's register reflecting a transfer of shares[cite: 38]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The Appellants challenged the maintainability of the oppression petition before NCLT Ahmedabad, arguing the Respondents were no longer shareholders due to the MOU[cite: 38]. The NCLT ruled the Respondents retained standing, prompting this appeal[cite: 38].
legal_issues: Whether petitioners maintain locus standi as shareholders to file an oppression and mismanagement petition when an unexecuted Memorandum of Understanding exists to transfer their shares, but the shares have not been legally transferred in the company's register[cite: 38].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An individual remains a shareholder with the right to sue for oppression and mismanagement until their shares are legally and formally transferred and registered in the name of another party in the company's records[cite: 38]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The statutory definition of a "relative" under Section 2(41) read with Section 6 of the Companies Act, 1956 cannot be applied to bind a non-signatory shareholder to a private contract (MOU) transferring shares[cite: 38]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Since the Petitioners did not personally sign the MOU, and no formal transfer procedure was executed in accordance with law (i.e., no entry made in the company register), the mere existence of the MOU did not extinguish their legal shareholder status[cite: 38]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because the shares were not legally transferred, the Respondents maintained the required shareholding to have locus standi under Sections 397 and 398 of the Companies Act, 1956[cite: 38].
operative_order: The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, upholding the NCLT's judgment dated 2nd January 2017 regarding the maintainability of the petition[cite: 38]. The NCLAT clarified that this order does not prevent the Appellants from registering the transfer in the future if it is found genuine and in accordance with the law[cite: 38]. No order as to costs[cite: 38].
summary: Respondents filed an oppression petition against Prabhakar Processors[cite: 38]. The Appellants challenged their standing, claiming the Respondents had already agreed to transfer their shares via a 2011 MOU signed by their relatives[cite: 38]. case_title: Dilip Kumar Ari vs M/S. Matrikalyan Nursing Home Private Limited & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Dilip Kumar Ari is the Appellant/Original Petitioner[cite: 39]. M/s. Matrikalyan Nursing Home Private Limited is the 1st Respondent Company, and the 2nd Respondent is the allottee of the disputed shares[cite: 39]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Increase in the company's share capital from 11,100 shares to 17,800 shares, and the subsequent allotment of 6,700 shares to the 2nd Respondent[cite: 39]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The Appellant challenged the Board's decision to increase share capital and allot shares to the 2nd Respondent[cite: 39]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The disputed Board meeting and share allotment occurred on 31st July 2008[cite: 39]. The oppression petition was filed more than six years later[cite: 39]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The Tribunal found that the 6,700 shares were allotted to the 2nd Respondent with the explicit consent of the Appellant[cite: 39]. A related civil suit (T.S.No. 3322 of 2007) regarding asset entitlement was pending in the City Civil Court, Calcutta[cite: 39]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The Appellant filed an oppression and mismanagement petition before NCLT Kolkata[cite: 39]. On 18th August 2017, the NCLT dismissed the petition on the ground of delay, leading to this appeal[cite: 39].
legal_issues: Whether a delay of over six years in filing an oppression and mismanagement petition regarding a share allotment can be condoned on the ground that the petitioner was concurrently pursuing a civil suit regarding company assets[cite: 39].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The pendency of a civil suit concerning asset entitlement cannot be used to justify or condone an inordinate delay in filing a statutory petition for oppression and mismanagement before the Company Law Tribunal[cite: 39]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Reliefs under Sections 397/398 of the Companies Act, 1956 deal specifically with the oppressive conduct of corporate affairs, which is fundamentally distinct from civil property disputes litigated in regular civil courts[cite: 39]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Since the disputed share allotment occurred in 2008 with the Appellant's own consent, and the petition was filed over six years later, the claim was fatally stale[cite: 39]. The pending 2007 civil suit did not cover the specific allegations of oppression, making it an invalid excuse for the delay[cite: 39]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLT correctly dismissed the petition on the ground of severe delay and laches, as the Appellant offered no valid justification for waiting over six years to challenge an action he had initially consented to[cite: 39].
operative_order: The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, upholding the NCLT Kolkata's order dated 18th August 2017. No order was made as to costs[cite: 39].
summary: The Appellant challenged a 2008 Board decision that increased share capital and allotted 6,700 shares to the 2nd Respondent[cite: 39]. case_title: D.R. Sharma vs Roshanlal Duneja
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: D.R. Sharma is the Appellant (Transferor)[cite: 40]. Roshanlal Duneja is the Respondent[cite: 40]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: The Appellant sold shares to SBI Capital Market Limited on 5th April 1991, but the company's transfer agency refused to register the transfer due to a signature mismatch[cite: 40]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The company refused to register the share transfer[cite: 40]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The initial refusal occurred shortly after April 1991[cite: 40]. The second formal refusal was on 6th January 1995[cite: 40]. The appellant filed a civil suit in 2000 (dismissed prior to 2012) and the NCLT petition in 2014[cite: 40]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The transfer agency repeatedly rejected the transfer (in 1991 and 1995) because the appellant's signature differed from the recorded specimen[cite: 40]. The Appellant engaged in prolonged correspondence and a failed civil suit before finally approaching the NCLT 19 years later[cite: 40]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The Appellant filed a petition under Sections 58 and 59 of the Companies Act, 2013 before NCLT Ahmedabad[cite: 40]. The NCLT dismissed it as barred by limitation, leading to this appeal[cite: 40].
legal_issues: Whether an appeal challenging a company's refusal to register a transfer of shares is maintainable when filed before the Tribunal 19 years after the company's formal refusal, despite the appellant intervening with a civil suit and correspondence[cite: 40].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An appeal against a company's refusal to register a share transfer is barred by limitation and the doctrine of laches if the aggrieved party fails to approach the appropriate Tribunal within the statutorily prescribed timeframe following the refusal[cite: 40]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 58(4) of the Companies Act, 2013 (and formerly Section 111 of the 1956 Act) mandates strict limitation periods (60 to 90 days, or 2 to 4 months) for challenging a refusal to transfer shares[cite: 40]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal noted that the explicit refusal to transfer the shares occurred at the latest by 6th January 1995[cite: 40]. The Appellant's reliance on a failed civil suit filed in 2000 and extensive correspondence over two decades could not cure the statutorily barred claim[cite: 40]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: A 19-year delay between the refusal to register the transfer and the filing of the petition constitutes severe, unexplained laches, justifying the Tribunal's dismissal of the petition on the ground of limitation[cite: 40].
operative_order: The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, upholding the NCLT's decision that the petition was barred by limitation due to unexplained long delay and laches[cite: 40]. No order as to costs was made[cite: 40].
summary: The Appellant sold shares in 1991, but the company refused to register the transfer because of a signature mismatch, explicitly confirming this refusal in 1995[cite: 40]. After pursuing correspondence and a failed civil suit, the Appellant filed a petition under Sections 58 and 59 of the Companies Act, 2013 before the NCLT in 2014[cite: 40]. The NCLT dismissed the petition as time-barred[cite: 40]. The NCLAT affirmed the dismissal, ruling that the strict limitation periods under the Companies Act for challenging a transfer refusal cannot be bypassed, and a 19-year delay constitutes severe and unexplained laches[cite: 40].

case_title: AMREX Marketing Pvt. Ltd. & Anr. vs B&A Packaging (India) Ltd
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: AMREX Marketing Pvt. Ltd. & Anr. are the Appellants[cite: 41]. B&A Packaging (India) Ltd. is the Respondent Company[cite: 41]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: The Appellants acquired shares in the Respondent company in excess of the 5% threshold without making the requisite disclosures under SEBI Takeover Regulations[cite: 41]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The Appellants violated Regulation 29(1) of the SEBI (Substantial Acquisition of Shares and Takeovers) Regulations, 2011[cite: 41]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The Respondent company claimed to have discovered the illegal acquisition on 12.06.2013 and filed the Section 111-A petition shortly after on 10.07.2013[cite: 41]. NCLT Kolkata passed its final order on 17th January 2017[cite: 41]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The SEBI Adjudicating Authority had already penalized the Appellants under Section 15-A(b) of the SEBI Act for the violation[cite: 41]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The Respondent filed a petition under Section 111-A of the Companies Act, 1956[cite: 41]. NCLT Kolkata ordered the Appellants to return the excess shares for a buy-back by the company[cite: 41]. The Appellants appealed[cite: 41].
legal_issues: Whether the Company Law Tribunal has the power under Section 111-A(3) of the Companies Act, 1956 to order a mandatory buy-back of shares acquired in violation of SEBI Takeover Regulations, even if SEBI has already imposed a penalty for the same violation[cite: 41].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The Company Law Tribunal possesses independent jurisdiction under Section 111-A(3) to rectify the register and undo the mischief of an illegal share acquisition, parallel to and distinct from SEBI's power to impose penal fines[cite: 41]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: While SEBI punishes regulatory violations (Section 15A(b) of the SEBI Act), Section 111-A(3) of the Companies Act empowers the Tribunal to take corrective action, such as directing the parties to hand over the illegally acquired shares, to restore the status quo and undo the mischief[cite: 41]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Since it was an undisputed fact that the Appellants had violated SEBI regulations (evidenced by the SEBI penalty), the Tribunal was fully justified in ordering equitable restitution[cite: 41]. The limitation defense failed because the petition was filed within a month of the company discovering the illegal acquisition[cite: 41]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The imposition of a SEBI penalty does not absolve the acquirer of the illegal shares; the Tribunal must ensure the excess shares are returned to the company via a compensated buy-back to cure the illegality[cite: 41].
operative_order: The NCLAT found no illegality in the NCLT's order directing the Appellants to hand over the excess shares and the Respondent to pay the buy-back price[cite: 41]. The appeal was dismissed with no order as to costs[cite: 41].
summary: The Appellants illegally acquired shares in B&A Packaging in excess of 5%, violating SEBI Takeover Regulations[cite: 41]. SEBI fined the Appellants for this violation[cite: 41]. Subsequently, the company petitioned the NCLT under Section 111-A of the Companies Act, 1956[cite: 41]. The NCLT ordered the Appellants to hand over the excess shares for a mandatory buy-back by the company at market value[cite: 41]. The Appellants appealed, arguing the petition was time-barred and SEBI had already punished them[cite: 41]. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, ruling that SEBI's penal powers and the Tribunal's corrective powers under Section 111-A are distinct; while SEBI punishes the act, the Tribunal must undo the mischief by ordering the return of the illegally acquired shares[cite: 41].

PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The Appellant filed a petition under Sections 58 and 59 of the Companies Act, 2013 before NCLT Ahmedabad[cite: 40]. legal_issues: Whether an appeal challenging a company's refusal to register a transfer of shares is maintainable when filed before the Tribunal 19 years after the company's formal refusal, despite the appellant intervening with a civil suit and correspondence[cite: 40].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An appeal against a company's refusal to register a share transfer is barred by limitation and the doctrine of laches if the aggrieved party fails to approach the appropriate Tribunal within the statutorily prescribed timeframe following the refusal[cite: 40]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 58(4) of the Companies Act, 2013 (and formerly Section 111 of the 1956 Act) mandates strict limitation periods (60 to 90 days, or 2 to 4 months) for challenging a refusal to transfer shares[cite: 40]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal noted that the explicit refusal to transfer the shares occurred at the latest by 6th January 1995[cite: 40]. The Appellant's reliance on a failed civil suit filed in 2000 and extensive correspondence over two decades could not cure the statutorily barred claim[cite: 40]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: A 19-year delay between the refusal to register the transfer and the filing of the petition constitutes severe, unexplained laches, justifying the Tribunal's dismissal of the petition on the ground of limitation[cite: 40].
operative_order: The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, upholding the NCLT's decision that the petition was barred by limitation due to unexplained long delay and laches[cite: 40]. No order as to costs was made[cite: 40].
summary: The Appellant sold shares in 1991, but the company refused to register the transfer because of a signature mismatch, explicitly confirming this refusal in 1995[cite: 40]. After pursuing correspondence and a failed civil suit, the Appellant filed a petition under Sections 58 and 59 of the Companies Act, 2013 before the NCLT in 2014[cite: 40]. The NCLT dismissed the petition as time-barred[cite: 40]. The NCLAT affirmed the dismissal, ruling that the strict limitation periods under the Companies Act for challenging a transfer refusal cannot be bypassed, and a 19-year delay constitutes severe and unexplained laches[cite: 40].

case_title: AMREX Marketing Pvt. Ltd. & Anr. vs B&A Packaging (India) Ltd
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: AMREX Marketing Pvt. Ltd. & Anr. are the Appellants[cite: 41]. B&A Packaging (India) Ltd. is the Respondent Company[cite: 41]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: The Appellants acquired shares in the Respondent company in excess of the 5% threshold without making the requisite disclosures under SEBI Takeover Regulations[cite: 41]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The Appellants violated Regulation 29(1) of the SEBI (Substantial Acquisition of Shares and Takeovers) Regulations, 2011[cite: 41]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The Respondent company claimed to have discovered the illegal acquisition on 12.06.2013 and filed the Section 111-A petition shortly after on 10.07.2013[cite: 41]. NCLT Kolkata passed its final order on 17th January 2017[cite: 41]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The SEBI Adjudicating Authority had already penalized the Appellants under Section 15-A(b) of the SEBI Act for the violation[cite: 41]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The Respondent filed a petition under Section 111-A of the Companies Act, 1956[cite: 41]. NCLT Kolkata ordered the Appellants to return the excess shares for a buy-back by the company[cite: 41]. The Appellants appealed[cite: 41].
legal_issues: Whether the Company Law Tribunal has the power under Section 111-A(3) of the Companies Act, 1956 to order a mandatory buy-back of shares acquired in violation of SEBI Takeover Regulations, even if SEBI has already imposed a penalty for the same violation[cite: 41].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The Company Law Tribunal possesses independent jurisdiction under Section 111-A(3) to rectify the register and undo the mischief of an illegal share acquisition, parallel to and distinct from SEBI's power to impose penal fines[cite: 41]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: While SEBI punishes regulatory violations (Section 15A(b) of the SEBI Act), Section 111-A(3) of the Companies Act empowers the Tribunal to take corrective action, such as directing the parties to hand over the illegally acquired shares, to restore the status quo and undo the mischief[cite: 41]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Since it was an undisputed fact that the Appellants had violated SEBI regulations (evidenced by the SEBI penalty), the Tribunal was fully justified in ordering equitable restitution[cite: 41]. The limitation defense failed because the petition was filed within a month of the company discovering the illegal acquisition[cite: 41]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The imposition of a SEBI penalty does not absolve the acquirer of the illegal shares; the Tribunal must ensure the excess shares are returned to the company via a compensated buy-back to cure the illegality[cite: 41].
operative_order: The NCLAT found no illegality in the NCLT's order directing the Appellants to hand over the excess shares and the Respondent to pay the buy-back price[cite: 41]. The appeal was dismissed with no order as to costs[cite: 41].
summary: The Appellants illegally acquired shares in B&A Packaging in excess of 5%, violating SEBI Takeover Regulations[cite: 41]. SEBI fined the Appellants for this violation[cite: 41]. Subsequently, the company petitioned the NCLT under Section 111-A of the Companies Act, 1956[cite: 41]. The NCLT ordered the Appellants to hand over the excess shares for a mandatory buy-back by the company at market value[cite: 41]. The Appellants appealed, arguing the petition was time-barred and SEBI had already punished them[cite: 41]. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, ruling that SEBI's penal powers and the Tribunal's corrective powers under Section 111-A are distinct; while SEBI punishes the act, the Tribunal must undo the mischief by ordering the return of the illegally acquired shares[cite: 41].

case_title: Jaynarayan Pusaram Karwa vs Mukund Subhash Karwa[cite: 1]
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellants are Original Respondents 2 to 4 representing the JPK Group, while the Respondents are Original Petitioners 1 to 9 representing the SPK Group, alongside Respondent No. 10, Krishidhan Seeds Private Limited[cite: 1]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: A family arrangement through an MOU dated 13.02.2013 was executed to divide properties, liabilities, and the flagship company between two rival family factions[cite: 1]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: There is no financial default claimed, as the core dispute centers on allegations of oppression and mismanagement[cite: 1]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The original company petition was filed on 18.02.2014, followed by an arbitral award on 31.07.2014 that sought to resolve the distribution of assets[cite: 1]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Key evidence included the MOU, the subsequent arbitral award allotting the respondent company to the appellants, and reports by a court-appointed observer detailing financial irregularities, such as writing off Rs. 79.6 million as doubtful advances[cite: 1]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The original petition for oppression and mismanagement resulted in the NCLT appointing an interim administrator on 12.09.2017 to protect the company pending finalization of the arbitral award, a decision the appellants challenged[cite: 1].
legal_issues: Whether the NCLT had the jurisdiction and justification to pass interim protective orders, including appointing an interim administrator, without recording a conclusive finding of oppression and mismanagement while an arbitral award was pending challenge[cite: 1].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A tribunal possesses the inherent jurisdiction to order interim protective measures regarding company management to safeguard corporate interests pending the final judicial resolution of a related arbitral award[cite: 1]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The tribunal interpreted its powers to grant relief under oppression and mismanagement provisions as active and necessary because the arbitral award distributing the company's assets had not reached finality due to a pending challenge under Section 34 of the Arbitration Act[cite: 1]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The tribunal evaluated the overarching factual matrix—including long-standing disputes, non-implementation of the MOU, and documented financial irregularities—finding sufficient grounds to intervene protectively without demanding conclusive proof of oppression at the interim stage[cite: 1]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT ruled that the NCLT judiciously exercised its discretion to protect the company based on the factual record, rendering it inappropriate to interfere with the interim arrangement until the arbitral award is finalized[cite: 1].
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed with costs quantified at Rs. 1 lac to be paid jointly or severally by the three appellants to respondents 1 to 7[cite: 1].
summary: In a dispute between two family groups over the management of Krishidhan Seeds Private Limited, the appellants challenged an NCLT order appointing an interim administrator[cite: 1]. The NCLT implemented this interim measure due to allegations of financial irregularities and a pending judicial challenge to an arbitral award that had allotted the company to the appellants[cite: 1]. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that the NCLT correctly exercised its discretion to protect the company's assets and balance equities while the arbitral award's finality remained contested[cite: 1].

case_title: M/s. Shree Shrine Engineering & Marketing Company Pvt. Ltd. vs The Registrar of Companies, Gujarat[cite: 2]
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is M/s. Shree Shrine Engineering & Marketing Company Pvt. Ltd., and the Respondent is the Registrar of Companies, Gujarat[cite: 2]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: No commercial transaction is involved; the dispute relates strictly to statutory filing non-compliance[cite: 2]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: There is no financial default amount; the default concerns an offense committed under Section 129(2) of the Companies Act, 2013[cite: 2]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The violation pertained to the Companies Act, 2013, which came into effect on 1st April 2014, leading to the compounding order on 9th February 2017[cite: 2]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The primary evidence was the existence of a separate, distinct application preferred by the Appellant under Section 621A specifically for compounding the offense under Section 129 of the Companies Act, 2013, which contradicted their claim that it was merely an amendment to an older petition[cite: 2]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The NCLT Ahmedabad compounded the offense by imposing a fine of Rs. 1 lac on Mr. Ashok Kumar, a Director of the Appellant company, which the Appellant challenged on the grounds that they should not be penalized twice for what they considered a continuous issue[cite: 2].
legal_issues: Whether the NCLT erred in imposing a distinct compounding fine for a violation under Section 129 of the Companies Act, 2013, when the appellant argued the application was merely an amendment to an earlier compounding petition concerning a different statutory provision[cite: 2].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Separate statutory violations warrant separate compounding applications and corresponding fines, and an independent application for a distinct statutory violation cannot be legally treated merely as an amendment to an earlier petition[cite: 2]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The tribunal strictly interpreted the penal action prescribed under Section 129(7) of the Companies Act, 2013, which mandates imprisonment up to one year or a fine ranging from fifty thousand to five lakh rupees, or both[cite: 2]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The bench relied on the procedural record which clearly established that the appellant had filed a distinct, standalone application for the Section 129 violation, completely nullifying the defense that it was a simple amendment[cite: 2]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT concluded there was no reason to interfere with the NCLT's order because the Rs. 1 lac fine imposed was perfectly aligned with the statutory limits for the distinct offense committed, leading to the dismissal of the appeal[cite: 2].
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed in the absence of any merit, with no order as to costs[cite: 2].
summary: M/s. Shree Shrine Engineering appealed an NCLT order that imposed a Rs. 1 lac compounding fine on its director for violating Section 129(2) of the Companies Act, 2013[cite: 2]. The appellant argued that this was essentially a duplicate penalty, claiming the application was just an amendment to an earlier petition concerning Section 166 of the Companies Act, 1956[cite: 2]. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, noting that the appellant had explicitly filed a separate compounding application for the Section 129 violation, and the imposed fine was well within the statutory limits[cite: 2].

case_title: Aseem Gupta vs ROC Delhi and Haryana[cite: 3]
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is Aseem Gupta, a former director of a company, and the Respondents are ROC Delhi and Haryana along with SEBI[cite: 3]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: The dispute stems from the issuance of a company prospectus and the alleged misappropriation of funds from unsuspecting investors[cite: 3]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: There is no financial debt default; the issue involves statutory violations under Sections 63 and 68 of the Companies Act, 1956, relating to misstatements in a prospectus[cite: 3]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The underlying timeline of the prospectus is unspecified, but the compounding application was initially rejected by the NCLT on 17th March 2017[cite: 3]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: SEBI presented evidence that the appellant was a signatory to the prospectus through an attorney, making him liable for the misstatements, while the appellant contended he never attended board meetings or signed documents directly[cite: 3]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The appellant applied for compounding under Section 621A of the 1956 Act, which the NCLT rejected on 17.03.2017; upon appeal, the NCLAT identified that the tribunal lacked statutory jurisdiction to compound the offense without Special Court permission[cite: 3].
legal_issues: Whether the NCLT possessed the legal competence to compound offenses under Sections 63 and 68 of the Companies Act, 1956, which carry punishments of fine or imprisonment, without obtaining the prior permission of the Special Court[cite: 3].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An adjudicating tribunal strictly lacks the jurisdiction to compound offenses punishable by imprisonment or fine without first obtaining the explicit permission of the Special Court[cite: 3]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The NCLAT interpreted Section 441(6)(a) of the Companies Act, 2013, holding that any offense compoundable under the Act involving imprisonment or fine mandates Special Court approval, superseding the procedures of the 1956 Act[cite: 3]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The tribunal reviewed the statutory penalty tied to the alleged violations and determined, as a matter of pure law, that the mandatory procedural prerequisite of Special Court permission was absent[cite: 3]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT concluded it could not interfere with the NCLT's refusal to compound the offense because the NCLT was statutorily incompetent to do so without Special Court permission, resulting in the appellant withdrawing the appeal[cite: 3].
operative_order: The appeal is disposed of, granting the appellant permission to withdraw the appeal with liberty to approach the Special Court to obtain permission to prefer a compounding application under Section 441 of the Companies Act, 2013[cite: 3].
summary: Aseem Gupta, a former director, appealed the NCLT's refusal to compound alleged statutory offenses regarding misstatements in a company prospectus under Sections 63 and 68 of the Companies Act, 1956[cite: 3]. SEBI opposed the compounding to protect duped investors, while Gupta claimed he was merely a scapegoat who had not directly participated[cite: 3]. The NCLAT declined to interfere, ruling that under Section 441(6) of the Companies Act, 2013, the Tribunal lacks the competence to compound offenses punishable by imprisonment or fine without prior permission from the Special Court, prompting the appellant to withdraw the appeal[cite: 3].

case_title: Seema Gupta vs Supreme Infrastructure India Ltd & Ors[cite: 4]
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant, Seema Gupta, is the Operational Creditor, and the Respondent, Supreme Infrastructure India Ltd, is the Corporate Debtor[cite: 4]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: The exact nature of the transaction is unstated, but the relationship forms an operational debt[cite: 4]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The specific default amount and the date of default are not recorded in the order[cite: 4]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The Section 9 IBC application was rejected by the NCLT on 10th March 2017 due to procedural non-compliance[cite: 4]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: It was an undisputed evidentiary fact that the Operational Creditor failed to issue a demand notice under Section 8 of the IBC, relying instead on a previously issued winding-up notice under the Companies Act, 1956[cite: 4]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The NCLT Mumbai rejected the Section 9 application at the threshold due to the absence of a Section 8 notice, prompting the appellant to argue that an older notice under Sections 433 and 434 of the Companies Act, 1956 should be sufficient[cite: 4].
legal_issues: Whether a statutory winding-up notice issued under the Companies Act, 1956 can serve as a valid legal substitute for the mandatory demand notice required under Section 8 of the IBC for initiating a Section 9 application[cite: 4].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The issuance of a specific demand notice under Section 8 of the IBC is an inflexible mandatory prerequisite for initiating a corporate insolvency resolution process as an operational creditor under Section 9[cite: 4]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The tribunal strictly interpreted Sections 8 and 9 of the IBC, ruling that a Section 9 petition explicitly requires the expiry of ten days from the delivery of a Section 8 demand notice, invalidating the substitution of older Companies Act notices[cite: 4]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The tribunal applied a strict procedural compliance test, determining that the absolute absence of a properly formatted Section 8 notice procedurally barred the initiation of the Section 9 application[cite: 4]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT concluded that giving prior notice under Section 8 of the IBC is mandatory, and since it was completely bypassed, the adjudicating authority correctly rejected the application[cite: 4].
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed as the tribunal found no merit in it[cite: 4].
summary: Operational creditor Seema Gupta appealed the NCLT Mumbai's dismissal of her Section 9 IBC application against Supreme Infrastructure India Ltd[cite: 4]. The application had been rejected because Gupta failed to issue the mandatory Section 8 demand notice, arguing instead that a prior winding-up notice under the Companies Act, 1956 was sufficient[cite: 4]. Relying on established precedent, the NCLAT affirmed that issuing a specific notice under Section 8 of the IBC is a strict mandatory prerequisite for a Section 9 petition and dismissed the appeal for lack of merit[cite: 4].

case_title: Thoughtbuzz India Private Limited & Ors. vs Registrar of Companies, NCT of Delhi and Haryana[cite: 5]
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellants are Thoughtbuzz India Private Limited and its directors, Deepak Mittal and Irfan Ejaz Khan, and the Respondent is the Registrar of Companies, NCT of Delhi and Haryana[cite: 5]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: There is no commercial transaction; the issue revolves around statutory non-compliance and the compounding of those offenses[cite: 5]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The default relates to violations of Sections 92, 96, and 129 of the Companies Act, 2013, for which the ROC initially recommended total fines of Rs. 23.5 lakhs per director and Rs. 18.5 lakhs on the company[cite: 5]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The default periods occurred between 2015 and 11.09.2017[cite: 5]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The primary evidentiary record was the ROC's report recommending high penalty amounts for admitted statutory defaults across multiple sections of the Companies Act[cite: 5]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The NCLT allowed the compounding application but significantly reduced the ROC's recommended fines (from Rs. 18.5 lakhs to 3.5 lakhs for the company, and from Rs. 23.5 lakhs to 4.5 lakhs per director); however, the Appellants still appealed the reduced amounts but failed to appear at the hearing[cite: 5].
legal_issues: Whether the NCLAT should interfere with the quantum of compounding fines imposed by the NCLT for statutory defaults under the Companies Act, 2013, when the Appellants failed to appear to prosecute their appeal[cite: 5].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An appeal challenging the quantum of a statutory compounding fine can be rightfully dismissed for non-prosecution and on merits when the appellant fails to appear and the lower tribunal has already exercised its discretion leniently[cite: 5]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The bench implicitly validated the NCLT's discretionary power under Section 441 of the Companies Act, 2013 to significantly reduce compounding fines from the maximum amounts recommended by the ROC[cite: 5]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The tribunal reviewed the procedural record showing the substantial reduction in fines already granted by the NCLT and found no factual or legal basis to grant further leniency, especially given the appellants' absence[cite: 5]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT concluded that the appeal lacked merit and the appellants were in default of appearance, warranting the outright dismissal of the appeal[cite: 5].
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed both on the counts of default and on merit, with no order as to costs[cite: 5].
summary: Thoughtbuzz India Private Limited and its directors appealed an NCLT order regarding the compounding of offenses under Sections 92, 96, and 129 of the Companies Act, 2013[cite: 5]. The NCLT had heavily reduced the fines recommended by the ROC, bringing the company's fine down from Rs. 18.5 lakhs to Rs. 3.5 lakhs, and the directors' fines from Rs. 23.5 lakhs to Rs. 4.5 lakhs[cite: 5]. Despite this leniency, the appellants appealed but repeatedly failed to appear for the hearing, leading the NCLAT to dismiss the appeal for both default and lack of merit[cite: 5].

case_title: Shri Hem Raj Singh vs Naraingarh Distillery Limited[cite: 7]
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant, Shri Hem Raj Singh, was the promoter and Managing Director, while the Respondents include Naraingarh Distillery Limited (Respondent No. 1), Baldev Singh Kang (Respondent No. 2), and other subsequent shareholders[cite: 7]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: The parties were involved in the joint running of a distillery business and quasi-partnership, with the Appellant initially holding 19.2% equity[cite: 7]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: There is no financial default; the dispute centers on the illegal removal of the Appellant from the Managing Director post and the unlawful dilution of his shareholding to 1.12%[cite: 7]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: An EGM was convened on 31.05.2006 to remove the Appellant; later, the Company Law Board (CLB) passed a status quo order regarding shareholding on 11.09.2007[cite: 7]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The evidentiary record demonstrated that newspaper publications for the EGM notice incorrectly named a different company (Naraingarh Sugar Mills Limited), and Annual Returns from 2012 proved that the Respondents transferred shares and altered directorships in blatant violation of the 2007 CLB status quo order[cite: 7]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The NCLT Chandigarh originally dismissed the Appellant's petition for oppression and mismanagement, prompting the Appellant to seek relief from the NCLAT[cite: 7].
legal_issues: Whether the removal of a Managing Director via an improperly noticed EGM and the subsequent dilution of his shareholding in direct violation of a tribunal's status quo order constitutes actionable oppression and mismanagement[cite: 7].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Conducting an Extraordinary General Meeting to remove a director without proper statutory notice and subsequently transferring shares in direct violation of an active tribunal status quo order constitutes grave oppression and mismanagement[cite: 7]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 284 of the Companies Act, 1956 mandates strict and specific notice for the removal of a director; generalized newspaper publications bearing the wrong company name entirely fail to satisfy this statutory requirement[cite: 7]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal scrutinized the Annual Returns and undisputed facts of the Appellant's incarceration, concluding that the EGM notice was fatally defective and the share transfers were indisputably executed in contempt of the status quo order[cite: 7]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT definitively held that the Respondents' actions were oppressive and illegal, warranting the quashing of the NCLT order and the full restoration of the Appellant's original position and shareholding[cite: 7].
operative_order: The appeal is allowed; the impugned NCLT order is quashed and set aside; the transfer and additional allotment of shares to Respondents 5 to 9 are quashed; the appointment of Respondents 5 to 7 as Directors is quashed; and the status quo regarding directorship and shareholding pattern as of 11.09.2007 is fully restored[cite: 7].
summary: Shri Hem Raj Singh appealed against an NCLT Chandigarh order dismissing his petition for oppression and mismanagement against Naraingarh Distillery Limited[cite: 7]. The appellant alleged he was illegally removed as Managing Director while incarcerated, without proper statutory notice, and his shareholding was unlawfully diluted from 19.2% to 1.12% in direct violation of a 2007 Company Law Board status quo order[cite: 7]. The NCLAT allowed the appeal, finding that the newspaper notices for the EGM were invalid because they named the wrong company[cite: 7]. Furthermore, transferring shares despite an active status quo order constituted grave mismanagement[cite: 7]. Consequently, the NCLAT set aside the NCLT's dismissal, quashed the illegal share allotments and director appointments, and restored the original status quo regarding the company's shareholding pattern[cite: 7].

case_title: Sri. D Savan Kumar & Ors vs M/S. The Aryan Industries Pvt. Ltd., Ors[cite: 8]
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellants in the cross-appeals include the Original Petitioners (Shri T. Nand Kishore Singh) and Original Respondents (Shri Dundoo Shirish and Sri D Savan Kumar) against M/S The Aryan Industries Pvt. Ltd[cite: 8]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: A partnership firm floated the company in 1943, but it became completely defunct in 1963, leasing its plant to clear state financial loans[cite: 8]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: There is no financial debt default; the dispute involves ancient allegations of forged share transfers, illegal board inductions, and mismanagement[cite: 8]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: All alleged acts of oppression occurred between 1963 and 1998, but the original company petition was not filed until 2006[cite: 8]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The primary evidentiary finding was the extreme, unexplained delay in filing the petition in 2006 for grievances dating back to 1963-1998, compounded by the existence of multiple parallel civil suits and arbitration proceedings[cite: 8]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The NCLT Hyderabad ruled that the petition was barred by limitation and laches, but paradoxically exercised powers under Section 402 of the Companies Act, 1956 to supersede the board and order the auction of company properties, leading both sides to appeal[cite: 8].
legal_issues: Whether a Tribunal possesses the jurisdiction to issue sweeping equitable directions regarding a company's management and assets under Section 402 of the Companies Act, 1956, after expressly concluding that the underlying petition is barred by limitation and laches[cite: 8].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A tribunal is strictly precluded from exercising equitable jurisdiction to pass substantive orders or directions regarding a company's affairs once it has definitively concluded that the underlying petition is not maintainable due to limitation or laches[cite: 8]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The NCLAT interpreted Section 402 of the Companies Act, 1956 (and Section 242 of the 2013 Act) as being strictly contingent upon a valid, maintainable petition; these powers cannot be invoked independently in a time-barred suit[cite: 8]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The NCLAT applied the test of limitation, observing that because all alleged oppressive acts occurred between 1963 and 1998, the 2006 petition was hopelessly delayed and legally devoid of merit for equitable relief[cite: 8]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT concluded that the NCLT grossly exceeded its jurisdiction by issuing directions under Section 402 after dismissing the petition on maintainability grounds, thereby necessitating the quashing of those directions[cite: 8].
operative_order: The impugned order dated 31st March 2017 is set aside insofar as it relates to paragraph 29; the Company Petition is dismissed for having been filed after long delay and laches, and both appeals are disposed of with no order as to costs[cite: 8].
summary: Cross-appeals were filed by both petitioners and respondents challenging an NCLT Hyderabad order regarding M/S The Aryan Industries Pvt. Ltd[cite: 8]. The NCLT had found the original petition for oppression and mismanagement—based on events spanning 1963 to 1998—to be non-maintainable due to extreme delay and laches[cite: 8]. Despite this, the NCLT invoked Section 402 of the Companies Act, 1956, to supersede the company's board and order the sale of its properties[cite: 8]. The NCLAT set aside these directions, ruling that a tribunal lacks the jurisdiction to issue such substantive equitable orders once it has definitively held the underlying petition to be barred by limitation[cite: 8]. Consequently, the NCLAT dismissed the original company petition entirely and disposed of the appeals[cite: 8].

case_title: Pec Ltd vs Sri Gangadhara Steels Limited[cite: 9]
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant, PEC Ltd. (a Government of India Enterprise), is the Financial Creditor, and the Respondents are M/s. Sree Ramakrishna Alloys Ltd. and M/s. SriGangadhara Steels Limited (Corporate Debtors)[cite: 9]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: PEC Ltd. provided financial assistance and margin money via an ILC to the Corporate Debtors to procure M.S. Billets, charging a 1% trade margin and 14.5% interest for delayed payments[cite: 9]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default amounts stood at Rs. 15,16,26,907 for Sree Ramakrishna Alloys Ltd. and Rs. 7,43,89,467 for SriGangadhara Steels Limited as of 6th March 2017[cite: 9]. 4.
