STATUTORY TIMELINES: The underlying financial agreements were executed on 24th February 2014 and 19th May 2014; the NCLT passed its admission orders on 29th August 2017[cite: 9]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The agreements expressly detailed a 12.5% margin money requirement, a pledge of stock to PEC, and a 14.5% interest rate per annum on delayed payments, confirming a disbursement for the time value of money[cite: 9]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The Appellant filed insolvency applications under Section 7 of the IBC, but the NCLT admitted them by unilaterally treating them as Section 9 applications, thereby classifying the Appellant as an Operational Creditor[cite: 9].
legal_issues: Whether an Adjudicating Authority has the jurisdiction to unilaterally convert an insolvency application filed under Section 7 of the IBC into a Section 9 application and treat a Financial Creditor as an Operational Creditor[cite: 9].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An Adjudicating Authority lacks the jurisdiction to unilaterally convert a Section 7 application into a Section 9 application, as the two provisions require distinct statutory forms and procedural prerequisites, such as the mandatory prior demand notice under Section 8[cite: 9]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The NCLAT strictly interpreted Sections 5(7) and 5(8) of the IBC, affirming that financial assistance disbursed with a stipulated interest rate for delayed payments strictly constitutes a 'financial debt' disbursed against the time value of money[cite: 9]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal evaluated the core commercial agreements, identifying explicit clauses for a 14.5% interest rate and stock pledges, which unequivocally proved the debts were financial rather than operational[cite: 9]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT concluded that PEC Ltd. is a Financial Creditor and the NCLT committed a jurisdictional error in treating the Form-1 applications as Form-5 applications under Section 9, requiring a modification of the admission orders[cite: 9].
operative_order: Both appeals are allowed; the impugned NCLT orders are modified to treat the applications for all purposes as applications under Section 7 of the IBC, directing the Interim Resolution Professionals to treat the Appellant as a Financial Creditor and include it in the Committee of Creditors[cite: 9].
summary: PEC Ltd. appealed against NCLT orders admitting its insolvency applications against Sree Ramakrishna Alloys Ltd. and SriGangadhara Steels Limited[cite: 9]. The NCLT admitted the applications but erroneously treated PEC Ltd.—which filed under Section 7 of the IBC—as an Operational Creditor under Section 9[cite: 9]. PEC Ltd. argued this unlawfully deprived it of a seat on the Committee of Creditors[cite: 9]. The NCLAT allowed the appeals, clarifying that financial assistance bearing a 14.5% interest rate for delays strictly constitutes a financial debt disbursed for the time value of money[cite: 9]. The NCLAT ruled that an Adjudicating Authority lacks jurisdiction to unilaterally convert a Section 7 application into a Section 9 application[cite: 9]. Consequently, the NCLAT restored PEC Ltd.'s status as a Financial Creditor[cite: 9].

case_title: Surgi Aid Lifecare Private Limited vs Shri Rahuldev Vyas[cite: 10]
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellants are Surgi Aid Lifecare Pvt. Ltd. (Respondent No. 1) and its directors Chetan Nemlawala and Shammi Nemlawala, while the Respondent/Original Petitioner is Shri Rahuldev Vyas[cite: 10]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: A company was incorporated in 2010 to take over a proprietorship concern owned by the Petitioner, with an agreement for equal 1/3rd shareholding among the three individuals[cite: 10]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: There is no financial default; the dispute involves a corporate conflict over the appointment of a third director and a subsequent rights issue generated to meet a Rs. 14.54 Lakh financial shortfall[cite: 10]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The company was incorporated on 26.04.2010; the disputed director was appointed on 08.10.2013; the Company Petition was filed on 15.11.2016; and rights shares were issued on 26.12.2016[cite: 10]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Evidence showed the Petitioner voluntarily abstained from company affairs since 2012, secretly operated competing businesses, diverted Rs. 11.34 Lakhs to his personal account, and failed to update his registered address[cite: 10]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The NCLT Ahmedabad found no oppression or mismanagement by the Appellants but nonetheless set aside the director's appointment and the 2016 rights issue, and ordered the company to buy out the Petitioner's shares[cite: 10].
legal_issues: Whether a Tribunal can grant equitable relief, such as setting aside a director's appointment and cancelling a rights issue, under Sections 241 and 242 of the Companies Act, 2013, when it explicitly finds the petitioner approached with unclean hands, extreme laches, and failed to prove oppression[cite: 10].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A party who approaches a company tribunal with unclean hands, extreme delay, and laches, and completely fails to establish oppression or mismanagement, is legally barred from receiving any equitable relief under Sections 241 and 242[cite: 10]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The NCLAT strictly interpreted the boundaries of equitable intervention, holding that substantive interference in internal corporate decisions (such as a Section 62 rights issue) mandates a foundational finding of oppression or mismanagement[cite: 10]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal assessed the petitioner's overall conduct, finding conclusive evidence of his prolonged voluntary absence, unauthorized diversion of company funds, and operation of competing businesses, thereby completely failing the test of equitable conduct[cite: 10]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT concluded that the NCLT grossly erred in setting aside the director's appointment and the rights issue when there was no finding of oppression, confirming that internal board decisions to manage financial crunches are valid corporate actions[cite: 10].
operative_order: The appeal is allowed, the NCLT's impugned order is quashed and set aside, the original Company Petition is dismissed, and the original Petitioner is directed to pay costs of Rs. 1 Lakh to the Appellant Company[cite: 10].
summary: Surgi Aid Lifecare Private Limited and its directors appealed an NCLT Ahmedabad order granting equitable relief to the original petitioner, Shri Rahuldev Vyas[cite: 10]. Although the NCLT found that Vyas failed to prove oppression, had unclean hands, and had voluntarily abandoned company affairs since 2012, it still set aside a director's appointment and a 2016 rights issue[cite: 10]. The NCLAT allowed the appeal and dismissed the original petition, ruling that equitable relief under Sections 241 and 242 of the Companies Act, 2013 cannot be granted to a petitioner with unclean hands and severe laches[cite: 10]. The NCLAT affirmed that an internal board decision to issue rights shares to resolve a financial crunch is legally valid and cannot be annulled without establishing oppression[cite: 10].

case_title: M/S. Unitech Limited vs Registrar Of Companies, Delhi And...[cite: 11]
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is M/s. Unitech Limited (the Corporate Debtor), and the Respondent is the Registrar of Companies, Delhi and Haryana, along with affected depositors[cite: 11]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: The company actively accepted fixed deposits from the public and individual investors but subsequently failed to honor the repayment of the matured principal and interest[cite: 11]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The company defaulted on repaying matured public deposits amounting to more than Rs. 500 crores for the periods covering 2012, 2013, and up to March 2014[cite: 11]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The company failed to clear its dues before 31st March 2015 as mandated by the Companies Act, 2013, leading to the NCLT dismissing its petition for a time extension on 4th July 2016[cite: 11]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The evidentiary record established that despite explicit judicial undertakings to sell unencumbered land parcels (in Kochi, Varanasi, etc.) and recover refunds from state corporations, the company failed to deposit any generated funds into the designated repayment bank account over a three-year period[cite: 11]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: After the NCLT dismissed the company's plea for further time to repay depositors, the company appealed to the NCLAT; however, the NCLAT vacated its interim stay due to the company's delaying tactics and directed the ROC to initiate penal action[cite: 11].
legal_issues: Whether a defaulting company that has persistently failed to repay matured public deposits of over Rs. 500 crores is entitled to further extensions of time under Section 74(2) of the Companies Act, 2013, when it has consistently failed to honor its judicial undertakings to generate repayment funds[cite: 11].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A corporate entity cannot indefinitely postpone the repayment of matured public deposits by seeking successive statutory time extensions from the Tribunal without demonstrating genuine, actionable efforts or honoring its explicit judicial undertakings to generate funds[cite: 11]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 74(2) of the Companies Act, 2013 confers discretionary power on the Tribunal to extend the repayment timeline, but this discretion is explicitly barred for a company engaging in blatant delaying tactics without returning any money to its depositors[cite: 11]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal scrutinized the company's compliance record and concluded that the complete failure to deposit even a single rupee into the designated account over three years, despite clear undertakings, constituted an absolute lack of genuine intent to repay[cite: 11]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT definitively ruled that the appellant's chronic failure to repay depositors warranted no further equitable extensions, justifying the vacation of the stay and a direct order to the Registrar of Companies to initiate penal prosecution under Section 74(3)[cite: 11].
operative_order: The interim stay order is vacated, the appeal is disposed of, and the Registrar of Companies is explicitly directed to pursue a case under Section 74(3) of the Companies Act, 2013 before the Special Court against the appellant, with no order as to costs[cite: 11].
summary: M/s. Unitech Limited appealed a NCLT order that refused to grant further time for the repayment of over Rs. 500 crores in matured public deposits[cite: 11]. Despite numerous opportunities and explicit undertakings given to the CLB, NCLT, and NCLAT to sell unencumbered land and deposit the proceeds into a designated account, the company failed to deposit any funds[cite: 11]. The NCLAT refused to grant any further extensions, highlighting the company's severe delaying tactics, and directed the Registrar of Companies to immediately initiate penal prosecution under Section 74(3) of the Companies Act, 2013[cite: 11].

case_title: M/S. Aruna Hotels Limited vs Mr. N. Krishnan[cite: 12]
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is M/s. Aruna Hotels Limited (Corporate Debtor), and the Respondents (Mr. N. Krishnan, Mr. D. Ramjee, Mr. C. Ganapathy) are ex-employees acting as Operational Creditors[cite: 12]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: The operational debt is rooted in an employer-employee relationship and pertains to the alleged non-payment of salary arrears, gratuity, and leave salary[cite: 12]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Respondent D. Ramjee claimed a specific default amount of Rs. 2,60,68,883, comprising arrears of salary along with gratuity and leave salary[cite: 12]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The demand notices were issued by the respondents' advocate on 27th February 2017, and the NCLT admitted the primary insolvency application on 13th June 2017[cite: 12]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: It was an undisputed evidentiary fact that the mandatory Section 8 demand notices were issued and signed exclusively by an advocate/lawyer on behalf of the ex-employees, rather than in the prescribed Form-3 or Form-4 directly by the creditors[cite: 12]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The NCLT Chennai admitted the Section 9 insolvency application for D. Ramjee and directed the other employees to approach the Interim Resolution Professional, prompting the Corporate Debtor to appeal on the grounds of defective statutory demand notices[cite: 12].
legal_issues: Whether a statutory demand notice issued by an advocate or lawyer on behalf of an operational creditor, without utilizing the prescribed Form-3 or Form-4, constitutes a legally valid notice for initiating corporate insolvency resolution proceedings under Section 8 of the IBC[cite: 12].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A demand notice under Section 8 of the IBC must be strictly issued in the prescribed statutory format (Form-3 or Form-4) by the Operational Creditor or an authorized person holding a position in relation to the creditor, and a general notice issued by an advocate is legally invalid[cite: 12]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 8, read strictly with Rule 5 of the Adjudicating Authority Rules, mandates that the demand notice clearly warn the Corporate Debtor of the severe consequences of default (i.e., initiation of insolvency), an effect that a standard lawyer's notice fails to statutorily achieve[cite: 12]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal examined the physical notices and determined they were uniformly issued by an advocate who lacked any specific internal position or authorization from the operational creditors, rendering the notices procedurally defective under the IBC framework[cite: 12]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT concluded that the Section 9 insolvency applications were fundamentally non-maintainable due to the fatally defective Section 8 notices, thereby requiring the reversal of the NCLT's admission order and the release of the Corporate Debtor[cite: 12].
operative_order: The appeals are allowed; the NCLT Chennai's common order dated 13th June 2017 is set aside, the appointment of the IRP and the moratorium are declared illegal, the Section 9 applications are dismissed, and the Corporate Debtor is released to function independently[cite: 12].
summary: M/s. Aruna Hotels Limited appealed the NCLT Chennai's order admitting insolvency proceedings filed by three ex-employees claiming unpaid salaries and gratuity[cite: 12]. The NCLAT found that the mandatory Section 8 demand notices were improperly issued by an advocate rather than being issued in the prescribed Form-3 or Form-4 by the operational creditors themselves[cite: 12]. Relying on its own precedent, the NCLAT ruled that an advocate's notice cannot substitute the statutory format required under the IBC[cite: 12]. Consequently, the NCLAT set aside the insolvency admission, dismissed the Section 9 applications, and completely released the Corporate Debtor from the moratorium[cite: 12].

case_title: Belfin Spa vs Cima Shyam Springs Private Limited[cite: 13]
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellants are Belfin Spa (an Italian company) and its Italian citizens, Mr. Sergio Bellazzi and Ms. Rita Bellazi, while the Respondents are Cima Shyam Springs Private Limited and its related directors/entities[cite: 13]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: No specific underlying commercial transaction is detailed, as the matter solely concerns the procedural validity of a Power of Attorney used to file the appeal[cite: 13]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: There is no financial default amount; the default at issue is a 10-day procedural delay in filing the appeal against the NCLT's order[cite: 13]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The NCLT order was issued on 5th May 2017, the appeal was filed on 20th June 2017, the Power of Attorney was formally apostilled on 22nd June 2017, and it was formally accepted by the agent on 28th June 2017[cite: 13]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The core evidence comprised three Power of Attorney documents executed by the Italian appellants on 19th June 2017, certified by a public notary in Italy, and transmitted electronically to their Indian agent to urgently file the appeal[cite: 13]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The Appellants filed an application for the condonation of a 10-day delay, which the Respondents opposed by arguing the appeal was defective since the Indian agent's Power of Attorney was not formally apostilled and accepted on the exact date of filing[cite: 13].
legal_issues: Whether an appeal filed by an agent using an electronically transmitted, notary-certified Power of Attorney from foreign principals is legally valid if the formal apostille and the agent's written acceptance are completed shortly after the filing date[cite: 13].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An act performed by an authorized agent on behalf of a principal can be subsequently ratified by the principal, and such ratification relates back to the original date of the act, effectively curing procedural defects regarding the formal completion of authority documents[cite: 13]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The Tribunal applied the general principles of agency and contract law, establishing that technical procedural requirements (such as the specific date of an apostille) should not be weaponized to defeat substantive justice, especially for foreign litigants[cite: 13]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal evaluated the Italian notary's certificate dated 19th June 2017 and determined it irrefutably proved the principals' immediate intent to confer authority on their agent, an act they subsequently ratified without objection[cite: 13]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT concluded that discarding the appeal based on a minor technicality regarding the apostille date would be manifestly unjust, as the principals had clearly authorized and later ratified the filing, justifying the condonation of the 10-day delay[cite: 13].
operative_order: The short delay of 10 days in filing the appeal is condoned, allowing the appeal to proceed[cite: 13].
summary: Belfin Spa, an Italian company, filed an appeal against an NCLT Ahmedabad order with a brief 10-day delay[cite: 13]. The respondents contested the appeal's validity, arguing that the Indian agent who filed it lacked a fully apostilled and formally accepted Power of Attorney on the exact date of filing[cite: 13]. The NCLAT rejected this highly technical objection, noting that the foreign principals had signed and notarized the documents in Italy a day prior to filing and subsequently ratified the agent's actions[cite: 13]. Emphasizing that substantive justice should not be derailed by minor procedural technicalities, the NCLAT condoned the delay and allowed the appeal to proceed[cite: 13].

case_title: Bharti Defence And Infrastructure Limited vs Edelweiss Asset Reconstruction Company Limited[cite: 14]
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is Bharti Defence And Infrastructure Limited (Corporate Debtor), and the Respondent is Edelweiss Asset Reconstruction Company Limited (Financial Creditor)[cite: 14]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: The financial debt arises from significant loan facilities subjected to a Corporate Debt Restructuring (CDR) package and a Master Restructuring Agreement, which were secured by extensive pledges of shares[cite: 14]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: While the specific numeric amount is not stated, a massive financial default occurred, triggering the complete revocation of the CDR package and the issuance of a formal loan recall notice[cite: 14]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The CDR package officially failed by August 2014, IDBI Bank issued a loan recall notice on 5th August 2015, and the NCLT admitted the Section 7 application on 6th June 2017[cite: 14]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The Financial Creditor submitted substantial alternative evidence of default in Form 1, including the CDR failure letter, the loan recall notice, letters invoking share pledges, and relevant Bombay High Court orders confirming the non-payment[cite: 14]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The NCLT Mumbai admitted the Section 7 insolvency application; however, the Corporate Debtor appealed, arguing the application was legally defective because the default was not registered with an 'Information Utility' under Section 7(3)(a)[cite: 14].
legal_issues: Whether a Section 7 insolvency application is maintainable if the record of default is not registered with an 'Information Utility', but is instead supported by other substantial evidentiary documents provided in Form 1 of the Adjudicating Authority Rules[cite: 14].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The initiation of corporate insolvency proceedings under Section 7 does not strictly require the record of default to be sourced from an 'Information Utility' if the Financial Creditor provides sufficient alternative documentary evidence of default as prescribed by the relevant rules[cite: 14]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The Tribunal interpreted Section 7(3)(a) alongside Section 239 of the IBC, ruling that Part V of Form-1 (which permits 'other record or evidence of default') is legally sufficient to prove default, particularly when Information Utilities are not fully operationalized[cite: 14]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal evaluated the Financial Creditor's submissions—such as the loan recall notice, CDR failure letters, share pledge invocations, and High Court orders—and found them to be overwhelmingly sufficient evidence to prove the existence of financial debt and default[cite: 14]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT concluded that the NCLT Mumbai correctly admitted the Section 7 application because it was complete in all respects according to Form 1 and the evidence of default was unequivocally established, rendering the appeal meritless[cite: 14].
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed, upholding the NCLT's admission of the insolvency application and the moratorium orders, with no order as to costs[cite: 14].
summary: Bharti Defence And Infrastructure Limited challenged an NCLT Mumbai order admitting a Section 7 insolvency application filed by Edelweiss Asset Reconstruction Company[cite: 14]. The Corporate Debtor argued that the application was legally invalid because the default was not recorded with an Information Utility as outlined in the IBC[cite: 14]. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that in the absence of fully functional Information Utilities, alternative documentary evidence prescribed in Form 1—such as loan recall notices, CDR failure letters, and High Court orders—is perfectly valid and entirely sufficient to prove default and initiate the corporate insolvency process[cite: 14].

case_title: K. Srinivasa Rao vs Rajarajeswari[cite: 15]
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellants include M/s. Amaravathi Textiles Pvt. Ltd. and various transferee shareholders (e.g., K. Srinivasa Rao), while Respondent No. 1, Sri Rajarajeswari, is the original petitioner[cite: 15]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: The dispute centers around the internal transfer of 1,92,550 shares on 11th March 2010 and another 2,00,050 shares on 22nd July 2010 among existing members and non-members of the private company[cite: 15]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: There is no financial default; the central issue pertains to the allegedly illegal transfer of shares executed without offering them to existing shareholders in violation of the Articles of Association[cite: 15]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The disputed share transfers were executed in March and July of 2010, the original petition was filed under the Companies Act, 1956, and the NCLAT ultimately rejected the appeals on 23rd October 2017[cite: 15]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The evidence decisively showed that no mandatory transfer notice was served on existing shareholders under Article 12, and the appellants failed completely to produce crucial 2010 Board Minutes to prove the transfers were authorized under an alternative provision[cite: 15]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The NCLT Hyderabad declared the share transfers illegal for violating the company's Articles of Association and directed the rectification of the Register of Members, prompting the transferee shareholders to appeal[cite: 15].
legal_issues: Whether a Tribunal can legally invalidate share transfers and order the rectification of the member register when the transferees fail to produce authorizing board minutes and no prior transfer notice was served on existing shareholders as mandated by the Articles of Association[cite: 15].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Share transfers in a private company executed without serving the mandatory pre-emption transfer notice to existing shareholders, as explicitly required by its Articles of Association, are illegal and voidable, necessitating rectification of the register[cite: 15]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 111 of the Companies Act, 1956 (now Section 59 of the 2013 Act) empowers the Tribunal to direct the rectification of a member register if a share transfer flagrantly violates the explicit notice procedures enshrined in the company's governing Articles[cite: 15]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal drew an adverse inference against the appellants for their complete failure to produce the crucial Board Minutes from 2010 that allegedly authorized the transfers, confirming that the transfers lacked valid corporate approval[cite: 15]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT concluded that the NCLT was entirely justified in setting aside the share transfers due to the proven violation of Article 12 and the appellants' severe evidentiary failures, rendering the appeals meritless[cite: 15].
operative_order: The appeals are rejected, and the NCLT's direction requiring the company to rectify the Register of Members within 10 days is firmly upheld[cite: 15].
summary: Various shareholders and M/s. Amaravathi Textiles Pvt. Ltd. appealed against NCLT Hyderabad orders that invalidated the transfer of nearly 4 lakh shares executed in 2010[cite: 15]. The original petitioner, Sri Rajarajeswari, successfully proved that these transfers occurred without providing the mandatory transfer notice to existing shareholders, directly violating Article 12 of the company's Articles of Association[cite: 15]. The NCLAT rejected the appeals, noting that the appellants completely failed to produce crucial board minutes to defend or authorize the transfers[cite: 15]. Consequently, the NCLAT upheld the NCLT's order to rectify the Register of Members and nullify the illegal transfers[cite: 15].

case_title: Mbs It Institute Pvt. Ltd vs Rof Infratech And Housing Pvt. Ltd[cite: 16]
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant, MBS IT Institute Pvt. Ltd., is the Transferor Company, and the Respondent, ROF Infratech and Housing Pvt. Ltd., is the Transferee Company[cite: 16]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: The companies executed a mutually agreed Scheme of Amalgamation to merge their corporate entities[cite: 16]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: There is no financial default; the legal dispute strictly concerns the legal effective date of the sanctioned amalgamation scheme[cite: 16]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The scheme originally stipulated an appointed date of 1st April 2014, but the NCLT sanctioned it with a unilaterally altered effective date of 28th April 2017[cite: 16]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The core evidence was the text of the Scheme of Amalgamation itself, which explicitly defined the 'Appointed Date' as 1st April 2014, alongside clearance letters confirming the absence of any outstanding tax demands against the companies[cite: 16]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The NCLT sanctioned the amalgamation but arbitrarily shifted the appointed date to the date of its final order, prompting the companies to appeal to restore the original date[cite: 16].
legal_issues: Whether a Tribunal possesses the jurisdiction to unilaterally alter the explicitly stipulated 'appointed date' in a Scheme of Amalgamation to the date of its final order solely due to procedural delays in judicial disposal[cite: 16].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A Tribunal cannot arbitrarily shift the mutually agreed appointed date of a corporate amalgamation scheme to a subsequent date without substantive legal or factual justification[cite: 16]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 232(6) of the Companies Act, 2013 strictly mandates that an amalgamation scheme shall clearly indicate an appointed date and shall legally be deemed effective from that exact date, completely barring the Tribunal from imposing a subsequent date absent valid cause[cite: 16]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal evaluated the scheme's text and found no substantive justification (such as hidden tax liabilities or regulatory breaches) to alter the mutually agreed 1st April 2014 date[cite: 16]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT concluded that judicial delay is not a valid ground to alter an appointed date, modifying the NCLT's order to rightfully restore 1st April 2014 as the appointed date[cite: 16].
operative_order: The impugned NCLT order is modified to treat 1st April 2014 as the appointed date, and the appeal is disposed of with no order as to costs[cite: 16].
summary: MBS IT Institute and ROF Infratech challenged an NCLT order that sanctioned their amalgamation scheme but altered the appointed date from 1st April 2014 to 28th April 2017[cite: 16]. The NCLAT held that under Section 232(6) of the Companies Act, 2013, the Tribunal cannot arbitrarily shift the appointed date due to unavoidable delays in the court's disposal process[cite: 16]. Finding no substantive reason to alter the mutually agreed timeline, the NCLAT modified the order to restore 1st April 2014 as the official appointed date[cite: 16].

case_title: Steel Konnect (India) Private Limited vs M/S Hero Fincorp Limited[cite: 17]
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is Steel Konnect (India) Private Limited (Corporate Debtor), and the Respondent is M/S Hero Fincorp Limited (Financial Creditor)[cite: 17]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: The dispute stems from an unpaid financial debt owed by the Corporate Debtor to the Respondent, a non-banking financial company[cite: 17]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The specific default amount is unstated in the order, but a clear default of financial debt was proven[cite: 17]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The Section 7 IBC application was admitted by the NCLT on 19th April 2017[cite: 17]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The Financial Creditor submitted a certified statement of accounts alongside CIBIL records of default, which the Corporate Debtor challenged as insufficient for lacking formal Information Utility registration or Bankers Book Evidence[cite: 17]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The NCLT Ahmedabad admitted the Section 7 application; the Corporate Debtor subsequently appealed, claiming violations of natural justice and questioning its own suspended Board's locus to file the appeal[cite: 17].
legal_issues: Whether the suspended Board of Directors of a Corporate Debtor retains the locus standi to file an appeal under Section 61 of the IBC against an insolvency admission order, and whether alternative evidence is sufficient to prove default[cite: 17].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The suspended Board of Directors of a Corporate Debtor inherently retains the locus standi to file an appeal against the initiation of insolvency proceedings[cite: 17]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 17 of the IBC suspends the Board's powers to manage daily affairs, but it does not strip them of their status as aggrieved persons capable of appealing under Section 61, especially since the Interim Resolution Professional cannot logically appeal their own appointment[cite: 17]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal evaluated the procedural history, determining that because the Corporate Debtor was physically present and heard before the admission, any technical lack of formal notice was harmless and did not violate natural justice[cite: 17]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT concluded that while the Corporate Debtor has the locus to appeal through its suspended Board, the appeal must be dismissed on its merits because sufficient alternative evidence of default (CIBIL records) was legally provided[cite: 17].
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed, with the parties directed to bear their respective costs[cite: 17].
summary: Steel Konnect appealed the NCLT Ahmedabad's admission of a Section 7 insolvency application filed by Hero Fincorp[cite: 17]. The Financial Creditor challenged the suspended Board's locus to file the appeal[cite: 17]. The NCLAT ruled that the suspended Board retains the legal right to appeal under Section 61 of the IBC, as an Interim Resolution Professional cannot reasonably challenge their own appointment[cite: 17]. However, the NCLAT dismissed the appeal on its merits, finding no violation of natural justice and accepting the provided CIBIL records as sufficient legal evidence of default[cite: 17].

case_title: J.P. Srivastava & Sons (Rampur) Pvt. Ltd vs Gwalior Sugar Company Ltd[cite: 18]
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellants/Petitioners are J.P. Srivastava & Sons (Rampur) Pvt. Ltd. and associated individuals, and the Respondents are Gwalior Sugar Company Ltd. and its management[cite: 18]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: The underlying dispute involves the valuation and forced transfer of 5137 equity shares and various preference shares following a judicial settlement agreement[cite: 18]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: There is no financial default; the issue centers strictly on enforcing a share transfer at a judicially determined value of Rs. 6000 per share[cite: 18]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The original Company Law Board order was passed on 7th May 1996, fixing the valuation date as 30th June 1996, and the Supreme Court finalized the matter on 9th December 2014[cite: 18]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The evidence consisted of binding judicial orders from the CLB, High Court, and Supreme Court establishing the share value at Rs. 6000, which the Appellants attempted to illegally reopen by citing the subsequent release of 4759.69 acres of ceiling land[cite: 18]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: After decades of intense litigation, the NCLT Ahmedabad directed the Appellants to deposit the original share scripts for transfer based on the finalized valuation, prompting the Appellants to challenge the enforcement order[cite: 18].
legal_issues: Whether a Tribunal can enforce a finalized consent order for share transfer under Section 634(A) of the Companies Act, 1956, and whether alleged subsequent events can reopen a judicially confirmed share valuation[cite: 18].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Once a consent order regarding share valuation reaches absolute finality through the Supreme Court, it cannot be reopened or recalculated to account for subsequent corporate events[cite: 18]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 634(A) of the Companies Act, 1956 grants the Tribunal the explicit inherent power to enforce final orders by issuing specific procedural directions, such as mandating the physical deposit of share scripts[cite: 18]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal strictly relied on the litigation history, determining that because the Appellants explicitly accepted the Rs. 6000 valuation before the High Court, they were legally estopped from weaponizing the subsequent land release to demand a fresh valuation[cite: 18]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT concluded that the NCLT correctly exercised its enforcement powers to mandate the share transfer, definitively closing the valuation dispute that had been finalized by the Supreme Court[cite: 18].
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed with no order as to costs, fully upholding the NCLT's direction to deposit the share scripts for transfer[cite: 18].
summary: J.P. Srivastava & Sons appealed an NCLT Ahmedabad order directing them to surrender their share scripts in Gwalior Sugar Company Ltd. for transfer at a previously determined value of Rs. 6000 per share[cite: 18]. The appellants argued that the recent release of 4759 acres of company land from ceiling laws should retroactively increase the share valuation[cite: 18]. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, ruling that the share valuation had reached absolute finality through prior Supreme Court and High Court orders[cite: 18]. Consequently, the NCLT possessed the authority under Section 634(A) of the Companies Act, 1956 to enforce the transfer without reopening the valuation[cite: 18].

case_title: Ravi Mahajan vs Sunrise 14 A/S, Denmark[cite: 19]
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant, Ravi Mahajan, represents the Corporate Debtor (M/s. Muskaan Power Infrastructure Limited), and the Respondent, Sunrise 14 A/S, Denmark, is a foreign Financial Creditor[cite: 19]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: The debt originates from a trade finance facility agreement resulting in multiple loan disbursements to the Corporate Debtor[cite: 19]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The claimed default amount was USD 190,210, with the specific dates of default listed as 16th June 2016 and 24th August 2016[cite: 19]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The NCLT Chandigarh admitted the Section 7 application on 28th July 2017 and subsequently appointed the IRP on 3rd August 2017[cite: 19]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The core evidence revealed that the application (Form-1) filed by the Financial Creditor entirely lacked an enclosed 'record of default' from an Information Utility or IBBI-specified evidence, and was improperly signed by an advocate lacking a formal position with the creditor[cite: 19]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The NCLT admitted the insolvency application despite the missing statutory default records, prompting the Corporate Debtor to appeal the admission[cite: 19].
legal_issues: Whether a Section 7 insolvency application is maintainable if it completely lacks the mandatory 'record of default' and is filed by an advocate who does not hold a formal, authorized position with the Financial Creditor[cite: 19].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An insolvency application under Section 7 is fatally defective and completely non-maintainable if it fails to enclose a mandatory statutory record of default or is filed by an unauthorized legal representative[cite: 19]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 7(3)(a) of the IBC mandates the inclusion of a record of default; this is an inflexible statutory requirement, not an empty formality that can be bypassed or cured through purposive interpretation[cite: 19]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal strictly examined Part V of the submitted Form-1 and determined it was entirely devoid of the required default records and was unlawfully signed by an advocate holding no formal relation to the creditor[cite: 19]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT concluded that the Adjudicating Authority committed a grave error in entertaining the defective application, necessitating the complete dismissal of the insolvency proceedings[cite: 19].
operative_order: The impugned orders are set aside, the Section 7 application is dismissed, the Corporate Debtor is released from the rigors of the IBC, and the appeal is allowed[cite: 19].
summary: Ravi Mahajan appealed the NCLT Chandigarh's admission of a Section 7 insolvency application filed by a Danish company, Sunrise 14 A/S[cite: 19]. The NCLAT discovered that the creditor's application failed entirely to include any statutory 'record of default' as mandatorily required under Section 7(3)(a) of the IBC[cite: 19]. Furthermore, the application was improperly filed by an advocate who held no official position or authorization with the creditor[cite: 19]. Consequently, the NCLAT set aside the admission, dismissed the insolvency application, and completely released the Corporate Debtor from the moratorium[cite: 19].

case_title: Radeyshyam Mandwani vs Santosh Devcon Pvt. Ltd[cite: 20]
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellants (Radeyshyam Mandwani and Mukesh Matta) were directors holding 49% shares, while the Respondents include Santosh Devcon Pvt. Ltd. and majority shareholder Sunil Mandwani (51%)[cite: 20]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: The dispute involves the alleged fraudulent hijacking of a going concern via forged director resignations and illegal share allotments[cite: 20]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: There is no financial default; the issue relates exclusively to corporate hijacking and the filing of forged statutory forms (DIR-12)[cite: 20]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The alleged forged resignations were filed in December 2014, and the NCLT indefinitely stayed the subsequent Company Petition on 29th March 2017[cite: 20]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The Appellants provided substantial evidence of pre-existing disputes, including formal warning letters sent to statutory auditors and the ROC regarding a planned fraudulent takeover, directly preceding the filing of the disputed DIR-12 forms[cite: 20]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The NCLT Ahmedabad indefinitely stayed the Company Petition until three related criminal trials for forgery were concluded, an action the Appellants strongly challenged[cite: 20].
legal_issues: Whether a Tribunal can indefinitely stay a Company Petition involving an ongoing corporate concern pending the outcome of related criminal trials for forgery, despite the statutory mandate for expeditious disposal[cite: 20].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A Company Petition concerning the active management and hijacking of a going concern cannot be indefinitely stayed pending criminal proceedings, as it defeats the statutory mandate for swift corporate adjudication[cite: 20]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 422 of the Companies Act, 2013 explicitly requires the Tribunal to dispose of petitions expeditiously (ideally within three months), entirely precluding indefinite stays based on parallel criminal trials[cite: 20]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal noted that assessing the validity of a resignation is not merely about criminal forgery; it heavily requires evaluating strict corporate compliance under Section 168 (e.g., board notices, agendas), an assessment the NCLT is fully competent to perform independently[cite: 20]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT concluded the NCLT erred in staying the petition, as idling the company's adjudication irreparably harms justice and violates the Companies Act's strict timeline objectives[cite: 20].
operative_order: The impugned NCLT order is quashed and set aside, with a strict direction to the NCLT to decide the Company Petition at the earliest on its own merits, with no order as to costs[cite: 20].
summary: The appellants challenged an NCLT Ahmedabad order that indefinitely stayed their Company Petition against Santosh Devcon Pvt. Ltd. until related criminal forgery trials were resolved[cite: 20]. The appellants alleged they were ousted as directors through forged resignation letters to facilitate a corporate hijacking[cite: 20]. The NCLAT quashed the stay, emphasizing that Section 422 of the Companies Act, 2013 mandates expeditious disposal of corporate disputes[cite: 20]. The NCLAT ruled that the Tribunal must independently assess the statutory compliance of the resignations under Section 168, rather than forcing the ousted directors to wait years for a criminal verdict[cite: 20].

case_title: Smartcity (Kochi) Infrastructure Pvt. Ltd. vs Synergy Property Development Services Private Limited and Another
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is Smartcity (Kochi) Infrastructure Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor) and the Respondent is M/s. Synergy Property Development Services Pvt. Ltd. (Operational Creditor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: The parties engaged in a contract for Project Management Consultancy (PMC) services which the Operational Creditor allegedly discontinued and abandoned. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Unpaid dues claimed under the operational contract, though the core dispute centers on procedural defects and pre-existing disputes rather than admitted default metrics. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The demand notice under Section 8 was issued by a law firm ('JUSTLAW') on 20th April, 2017, and the Corporate Debtor replied on 18th May, 2017. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: A letter dated 12th November, 2016 from the Corporate Debtor explicitly notified the Operational Creditor that they had unilaterally abandoned the work, causing project delays and losses, thus evidencing a pre-existing dispute. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The original petition was filed before the NCLT Chennai Bench (CP/484(IB)/CB/2017), which admitted the application under Section 9 on 9th June, 2017, appointed an IRP, and declared a moratorium.
legal_issues: 1. Whether a demand notice under Section 8 of the IBC issued by a law firm/advocate holding no position with or relation to the Operational Creditor is legally valid. 2. Whether there was an existence of a dispute prior to the issuance of the Section 8 demand notice rendering the Section 9 application non-maintainable.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An advocate, lawyer, or law firm in the absence of any authority of the Board of Directors and holding no position with or in relation to the operational creditor cannot issue a valid demand notice under Section 8 of the IBC. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 8 and Rule 5 require the person authorized to act on behalf of the operational creditor to state their position with or in relation to the operational creditor, distinguishing a statutory demand notice from an ordinary lawyer's notice. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The court evaluated the written communications between the parties prior to the demand notice to determine if clear assertions of non-completion and abandonment of work constituted a bona fide pre-existing dispute. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because the demand notice was legally invalid having been issued by an unauthorized law firm and a pre-existing dispute regarding project abandonment was clearly established prior to notice, the NCLT's admission order under Section 9 is illegal and must be set aside.
operative_order: The impugned order dated 9th June, 2017 passed by the Adjudicating Authority, Chennai Bench is set aside. The application under Section 9 of the IBC is dismissed. All consequential actions, including the appointment of the IRP, moratorium, and freezing of accounts, are declared illegal and set aside. The Corporate Debtor is released from all rigours of law and restored to independent management by its Board of Directors. The Adjudicating Authority shall fix the IRP's fee for the period functioned, to be paid by the Respondent. No order as to costs.
summary: This appeal challenged an NCLT Chennai Bench order admitting a Section 9 application under the IBC filed by M/s. Synergy Property Development Services Pvt. Ltd. against Smartcity (Kochi) Infrastructure Pvt. Ltd. The NCLAT allowed the appeal on two primary grounds: first, the Section 8 demand notice was legally invalid because it was issued by a law firm ('JUSTLAW') that held no position with or relation to the Operational Creditor and lacked proper board authorization; second, a bona fide dispute regarding the abandonment of work and project delays existed prior to the issuance of the demand notice. Consequently, the NCLAT set aside the initiation of the corporate insolvency resolution process, dismissed the Section 9 petition, and released the Corporate Debtor from insolvency proceedings.

case_title: M/s. Gowthami Solvent Oils Private Limited & Ors. vs Mrs M. Bharathi Rao
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Mrs. M. Bharathi Rao (Respondent/Petitioner, minority shareholder) vs M/s. Gowthami Solvent Oils Private Limited & Ors. (Appellants/Corporate Entity). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Original shareholding investment where the Respondent subscribed to 350 equity shares of Rs.100 each in 1974. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Claimed unlawful reduction of the Respondent's shareholding from 2.12% to 0.2655% and non-allotment of 5250 shares across rights issues in 1991-92, 1995-96, and 2004-05. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Rights issues occurred between 1991 and 2005; Petitions were filed in Consumer Commission (1997), Civil Court (2000), CLB (2000); Central Govt permission to file CP granted on November 16, 2012; Company Petition filed on February 2, 2013. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Shareholding records demonstrating a reduction to 0.2655%, and the official Central Government approval letter dated 16th November 2012 allowing the Respondent to pursue the case. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Hyderabad allowed the CP 13/2013 on March 14, 2017, directing the allotment of shares. The Appellants challenged the NCLT order at the NCLAT strictly on the grounds of delay and laches for reopening 1991-92 matters.
legal_issues: Whether the company petition for oppression and mismanagement filed in 2013 concerning events from 1991-92 was barred by the doctrine of delay and laches.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Delay in filing a petition for oppression and mismanagement can be condoned if the petitioner diligently and continuously pursued remedies before alternative judicial forums or was awaiting mandatory statutory permissions. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 399(4) of the Companies Act 1956 empowers the Central Government to authorize minority shareholders holding less than 10% to file a petition under Sections 397/398, and the time consumed to obtain this specific statutory approval is a valid justification for delay. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The tribunal evaluates the continuity of litigation (bona fide attempts in other forums like Consumer Courts and Civil Courts) and statutory hurdles to determine if a satisfactory explanation for the lapse of time exists. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT concluded that the respondent sufficiently explained the delay due to pursuing litigation in the Consumer Commission, Civil Court, and CLB, coupled with her wait for Central Government permission. The appeal was dismissed.
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed with no order as to costs, upholding the NCLT's direction to allot 5250 rights issue shares and payment of costs by the Appellants.
summary: In a dispute involving M/s. Gowthami Solvent Oils Private Limited and Mrs. M. Bharathi Rao, the appellant company challenged an NCLT order directing the allotment of rights issue shares to the respondent to restore her original shareholding percentage, arguing the claim was barred by delay since the events occurred in 1991-92. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, noting the respondent continuously pursued remedies before the Consumer Commission, Civil Courts, and the CLB. Furthermore, because her shareholding fell below the 10% threshold required under Section 399 of the Companies Act, 1956, she had to obtain Central Government approval, granted in 2012, before filing the 2013 petition. The tribunal found this to be a valid explanation for the delay.

case_title: M/s Gopala Polyplast Ltd. & Ors vs Registrar Of Companies, Ahmedabad
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: M/s. Gopala Polyplast Ltd., its Managing Director, and Full Time Director (Appellants/Defaulters) vs Registrar of Companies, Ahmedabad (Respondent). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Compliance requirement for a public limited company to appoint a full-time Company Secretary. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Non-appointment of a full-time Company Secretary for a span of 1674 days (April 1, 2004, to October 31, 2008). 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: MCA informed the company of the contravention on September 22, 2008. The company appointed a Secretary in November 2008. RoC issued a show-cause notice on June 19, 2012. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: RoC report indicating a paid-up share capital of Rs. 14.77 crores, acknowledging that no similar offence was compounded in the last 3 years, and that the default was due to oversight, not willful defiance. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Ahmedabad, via order dated September 30, 2016, compounded the offence at Rs. 400 per day (total Rs. 6,69,600 each for 3 applicants). Appellants filed an appeal seeking a reduction in the penalty based on precedents.
legal_issues: Whether the compounding fine of Rs. 400 per day imposed by the NCLT for a non-willful violation of Section 383-A of the Companies Act, 1956 was disproportionate and should be reduced in alignment with established tribunal precedents.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: In compounding corporate offences, tribunals must maintain consistency in the imposition of fines by taking into account relevant factors, grounds of default, and comparative precedents set in similar cases. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: While Section 383-A(1A) of the Companies Act 1956 prescribes a maximum fine of Rs. 500 per day for non-compliance, the compounding authority under Section 621-A holds the discretion to reduce this amount proportionately based on the severity and intent behind the violation. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The assessment for reducing compounding fees involves verifying whether the default was willful, whether it was promptly rectified upon notice, the financial standing of the company, and absence of repeat offences. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT concluded that since the default was a non-willful oversight, no similar prior offences were committed, and rectification occurred promptly upon MCA notice, the fine should be reduced to Rs. 100 per day to maintain consistency with prior CLB/NCLT orders.
operative_order: The NCLT order is modified. The compounding fee is reduced to Rs. 100 per day per applicant. Each of the three appellants is directed to pay Rs. 1,67,400, resulting in a total fine of Rs. 5,02,200.
summary: In M/s Gopala Polyplast Ltd. vs Registrar of Companies, the appellants challenged the NCLT Ahmedabad's order imposing a compounding fine of Rs. 400 per day per applicant (totaling Rs. 6,69,600 each) for failing to appoint a full-time Company Secretary for 1674 days under Section 383-A of the Companies Act, 1956. The appellants argued the violation was an oversight and sought parity with precedents where lesser fines were levied. The NCLAT allowed the appeal, emphasizing that tribunals must maintain consistency in compounding similar offences. Recognizing the default was not willful and was immediately rectified upon notice, the NCLAT reduced the penalty to Rs. 100 per day, resulting in a revised fine of Rs. 1,67,400 per appellant.

case_title: Mr. Vijay Vasant Dhavle vs M/s. Dolce Pharmaceuticals Private Limited and Others
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Mr. Vijay Vasant Dhavle (Appellant/Petitioner) vs M/s. Dolce Pharmaceuticals Private Limited (Respondent No. 1) and Mr. Gopalkumar Prabhakumar Nair & Mrs. Rakhi Gopalkumar Nair (Respondent Nos. 4 & 5). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Rectification of the Register of Members to remove the names of Respondent Nos. 4 and 5, alongside a challenge to the Appellant's removal as a Director. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The alleged illegal inclusion of Respondent Nos. 4 and 5 in the company's register since 2010. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The initial petition (CP 25/2012) was filed in 2012 and dismissed on May 20, 2013. The EoGM removing the Appellant as Director occurred on February 21, 2015. The second petition was filed in 2015. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: A conclusive prior order by the Company Law Board dated May 20, 2013, which had already dismissed the exact same prayer to remove Respondent Nos. 4 and 5 on the grounds of a 7-year delay and laches. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai, via order dated May 1, 2017, rejected the prayer to remove R4 and R5 on the basis of limitation/res judicata, but kept the issue regarding the appellant's removal as Director (2015 EoGM) pending. The Appellant challenged the partial rejection.
legal_issues: Whether a fresh petition seeking relief that was previously dismissed on the grounds of delay and laches is barred from being re-adjudicated in the absence of a fresh cause of action.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: While the dismissal of a prior application on technical grounds (such as limitation) does not strictly operate as res judicata for all purposes, a subsequent petition for identical relief cannot be maintained without a fresh, independent cause of action. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Under Section 59 of the Companies Act, 2013, seeking rectification of a member register is impermissible if a competent forum has previously dismissed the identical claim due to delay and laches, and no new intervening facts exist. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The adjudicating authority must examine whether any subsequent or fresh cause of action has arisen since the prior dismissal; if not, the claim remains barred by the original finding of laches. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT concluded that since the prayer to remove the names of the 4th and 5th Respondents was already dismissed in 2012 due to delay and laches, no subsequent relief could be granted for the exact same cause of action, warranting the dismissal of the appeal.
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed with no order as to costs. The question regarding the validity of the EoGM dated 21st February 2015 is left open for determination by the NCLT.
summary: Mr. Vijay Vasant Dhavle appealed an NCLT Mumbai order that rejected his prayer to remove two members from the register of M/s. Dolce Pharmaceuticals under Section 59 of the Companies Act, 2013. The NCLT noted that the appellant's identical claim had previously been dismissed by the Company Law Board in 2013 for delay and laches. While the appellant argued that dismissal on limitation does not constitute res judicata, the NCLAT clarified that although technical dismissal is not res judicata, a subsequent petition for the same relief without a fresh cause of action is not maintainable. Consequently, the NCLAT dismissed the appeal, while leaving the pending issue of the appellant's removal as a director for the NCLT to determine.

case_title: M/s. Hotel Gaudavan Pvt. Ltd. & Ors. vs Alchemist Asset Reconstruction Co. Ltd. & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Alchemist Asset Reconstruction Co. Ltd. (Financial Creditor) vs M/s. Hotel Gaudavan Pvt. Ltd. & Ors. (Corporate Debtor/Appellants) and Mr. Harendra Singh Rathore. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Underlying financial default leading to the initiation of a corporate insolvency resolution process by an asset reconstruction company. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Unspecified financial default resulting in the NCLT's admission of a Section 7 insolvency petition and imposition of a moratorium on March 31, 2017. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Insolvency petition admitted on March 31, 2017. Corporate Debtor subsequently invoked arbitration. NCLT passed adverse contempt orders against directors on June 29, 2017. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: An explicit Supreme Court order dated Oct 23, 2017, quashing the post-moratorium arbitration and criminal FIRs initiated by the Corporate Debtor, terming them desperate attempts to impede the strictly time-bound CIRP. Furthermore, the appellants repeatedly failed to appear before the NCLAT. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Post-CIRP admission, the Corporate Debtor initiated multiple parallel proceedings (Writ Petition, SLPs, Arbitration, Criminal FIRs) to derail the IRP. NCLT found the directors in contempt. The appellants filed three appeals against these NCLT orders but continually sought adjournments and eventually failed to appear.
legal_issues: Whether appeals against CIRP admission and contempt orders can be sustained when the corporate debtor has continuously failed to appear and concurrently initiated unlawful post-moratorium proceedings that were struck down by the Supreme Court.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The initiation or continuation of parallel judicial proceedings, such as arbitration or criminal FIRs, calculated to impede the Resolution Professional after the declaration of an insolvency moratorium, is non est in law. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 14(1)(a) of the IBC imposes a strict, absolute bar on the institution or continuation of pending suits or proceedings, explicitly interdicting new arbitration actions against a Corporate Debtor once an insolvency petition is admitted. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal relies on the binding findings of the Supreme Court validating the absolute nature of the Section 14 moratorium, coupled with the appellants' repeated non-appearance, which evinces an abuse of process. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Given the Supreme Court's definitive ruling invalidating the parallel arbitration/criminal proceedings and the appellants' continuous failure to appear, the NCLAT dismissed all three appeals outright and imposed punitive costs for the blatant abuse of the judicial process.
operative_order: All three appeals are dismissed. A cost of Rs. 25,000 is imposed on each of the appellants (Harendra Singh Rathore, Lokendra Singh Rathore, Deependra Singh Rathore, and Ms. Mohan Kanwar), payable within thirty days.
summary: Three appeals were filed by M/s. Hotel Gaudavan Pvt. Ltd. and its directors against NCLT orders admitting a Section 7 insolvency petition by Alchemist Asset Reconstruction Co. Ltd. and subsequent contempt orders. Following the CIRP admission and moratorium on March 31, 2017, the corporate debtor's directors unlawfully initiated arbitration and criminal proceedings against the Resolution Professional. The Supreme Court had previously quashed these parallel proceedings, declaring them non est in law under Section 14(1)(a) of the IBC and noting a 'very sorry state of affairs.' Relying on the Supreme Court's ruling and citing continuous non-appearance by the appellants' counsel, the NCLAT dismissed all three appeals and imposed a cost of Rs. 25,000 on each of the directors for abusing the judicial process.

case_title: Shyam Industries Ltd. vs R. L. Steel Energy Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: R. L. Steel Energy Ltd. (Respondent/Operational Creditor) vs Shyam Industries Ltd. (Appellant/Corporate Debtor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Supply of goods or services resulting in an operational debt owed by the Corporate Debtor. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default in payment of operational dues prompting the issuance of statutory demand notices in early 2017. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Section 8 demand notices were issued on January 15, 2017, and February 18, 2017. NCLT Ahmedabad admitted the Section 9 petition on May 24, 2017. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The formal demand notices under Section 8(1) of the IBC were issued by an external legal firm, 'RT Legal, Advocates & Consultants', who lacked direct Board authorization and held no official position within the Operational Creditor's organization. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Ahmedabad admitted the Operational Creditor's Section 9 application on May 24, 2017. The Corporate Debtor appealed, arguing that the Section 8 demand notice was defectively issued by a third-party law firm, nullifying the foundation of the Section 9 petition.
legal_issues: Whether a statutory demand notice under Section 8 of the IBC issued by an advocate or legal firm holding no position with or in relation to the operational creditor is legally valid to maintain a Section 9 petition.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A statutory demand notice under the insolvency framework cannot be validly issued by an external lawyer or professional firm unless they hold a specific position relative to the operational creditor and possess explicit authorization from the Board of Directors. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 8 of the IBC read with Rule 5 requires that an authorized representative issuing the demand notice (Form-3 or Form-4) must expressly state their position with or in relation to the operational creditor. A standard lawyer's notice does not satisfy the strict compliance required by the Code. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The tribunal examines the face of the demand notice to verify the signatory's identity, demanding proof of an organizational position or direct Board authorization linking the signatory to the operational creditor. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because the Section 8 notices were issued by a legal firm holding no internal position with the respondent and lacking Board authorization, the notices were invalid, rendering the subsequent Section 9 petition unmaintainable.
operative_order: The NCLT admission order is set aside, and the Section 9 application is dismissed. The Corporate Debtor is released from the CIRP and moratorium. The Operational Creditor is directed to pay the fees of the Interim Resolution Professional.
summary: Shyam Industries Ltd. challenged an NCLT Ahmedabad order admitting a Section 9 insolvency petition filed by R. L. Steel Energy Ltd. The appellant argued that the statutory demand notices under Section 8 of the IBC, dated January 15 and February 18, 2017, were improperly issued by a law firm rather than the Operational Creditor or an authorized internal officer. Citing the precedent in Uttam Galva Steels Limited, the NCLAT held that an advocate or external professional cannot issue a Section 8 notice unless they hold a specific position relative to the operational creditor and possess explicit board authorization. Consequently, the NCLAT ruled the demand notices invalid, set aside the admission order, dismissed the Section 9 application, and released the corporate debtor from the resolution process.

case_title: Jord Engineers India Ltd. vs Valia & Company
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Valia & Company (Operational Creditor / Respondent) vs Jord Engineers India Ltd. (Corporate Debtor / Appellant). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Supply of goods, specifically Iron, Steel, and Raw Material, between 2011 and 2012. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default in payment against goods amounting to Rs. 4,72,28,431 along with interest of Rs. 10,70,493 for delayed payment. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: A demand notice was issued on April 26, 2017. NCLT Mumbai admitted the Section 9 application on July 31, 2017. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The demand notice was issued by an advocate (Amir Arsiwala) based on a general letter of retainer dated February 10, 2017, and it was not issued in the mandatory Form 3 or Form 4. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai admitted the Section 9 application and ordered a moratorium on July 31, 2017. The Corporate Debtor appealed, arguing that the Section 8 demand notice issued by an external lawyer was defective and thus the petition was not maintainable.
legal_issues: Whether a statutory demand notice under Section 8 of the IBC issued by an advocate holding no formal position with the operational creditor, and not in the prescribed Form 3 or 4, is legally valid to maintain a Section 9 application.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An advocate or external lawyer cannot validly issue a statutory demand notice under Section 8 of the IBC on behalf of an operational creditor unless they hold a specific position with or in relation to the operational creditor. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 8 read with Rule 5 of the Adjudicating Authority Rules mandates that the demand notice must be strictly in Form-3 or Form-4 and issued by a person expressly stating their 'position with or in relation to the Operational Creditor.' A standard lawyer's notice does not fulfill this strict statutory mandate. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal must examine the demand notice to verify if it strictly conforms to Form 3/4 and if the signatory inherently holds a position relative to the operational creditor beyond a mere legal retainer. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT concluded that since the demand notice was issued by a retained advocate holding no structural position in relation to the Operational Creditor, and omitted the mandatory statutory forms, it was invalid. Consequently, the Section 9 petition was unmaintainable.
operative_order: The NCLT admission order is set aside. The Section 9 application is dismissed, the corporate debtor is released from the CIRP and moratorium, and the operational creditor is directed to pay the fees of the Interim Resolution Professional.
summary: Jord Engineers India Ltd. appealed the NCLT Mumbai's decision admitting a Section 9 insolvency petition filed by Valia & Company. The core dispute centered on the validity of the Section 8 demand notice, which was issued by the operational creditor's retained advocate rather than an internal officer, and failed to utilize the mandatory Form 3 or 4. Citing its precedent in Uttam Galva Steels Limited, the NCLAT ruled that an external lawyer lacking a structural position with the operational creditor cannot validly issue a Section 8 notice. The tribunal held the notice legally defective, set aside the CIRP admission order, dismissed the insolvency petition, and fully restored the corporate debtor's management.

case_title: Zapp India Ltd. vs Maheshwar Textiles & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Maheshwar Textiles & Anr. (Operational Creditor / Respondent) vs Zapp India Ltd. (Corporate Debtor / Appellant). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Unspecified operational debt arising from standard commercial operations. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default in payment of operational dues prompting the issuance of a statutory demand notice. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Demand notice was issued on May 29, 2017. NCLT New Delhi admitted the Section 9 application on July 20, 2017. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The demand notice was issued strictly by an advocate (Saurabh Sharma) acting as legal counsel, completely devoid of any evidence demonstrating Board authorization or an internal corporate position with the operational creditor. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT New Delhi admitted the Section 9 application on July 20, 2017. The Corporate Debtor challenged the admission at the NCLAT, primarily arguing the defectiveness of the Section 8 notice issued by an external lawyer.
legal_issues: Whether a statutory demand notice under Section 8 of the IBC issued by an advocate lacking Board authorization and holding no position with the operational creditor is sufficient to maintain a Section 9 insolvency petition.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A demand notice under the IBC is defective and invalid if issued by an external advocate or lawyer who lacks explicit Board authorization and holds no position with or in relation to the operational creditor. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 8, when read alongside Rule 5 of the Adjudicating Authority Rules, strictly requires that the authorized signatory issuing Form-3 or Form-4 must possess and state their 'position with or in relation to the Operational Creditor.' A conventional lawyer's notice bypasses these strict statutory forms. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Adjudicating Authority must scrutinize the demand notice and its accompanying authorization to confirm whether the legal professional issuing the notice genuinely holds an internal organizational position relative to the operational creditor. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because the notice was issued by an advocate with no verifiable Board authorization or internal position with Maheshwar Textiles, it could not be treated as a valid Section 8 notice, rendering the Section 9 petition unmaintainable in law.
operative_order: The NCLT New Delhi order dated July 20, 2017, is set aside. The Section 9 application is dismissed, the corporate debtor is immediately released from the CIRP, and the appellant is directed to pay the fees of the Interim Resolution Professional.
summary: Zapp India Ltd. challenged an NCLT New Delhi order admitting a Section 9 insolvency petition filed by Maheshwar Textiles & Anr. The appellant argued that the mandatory Section 8 demand notice was invalidly issued by an external advocate. Consistent with its precedent in Uttam Galva Steels Limited, the NCLAT agreed, reiterating that a statutory demand notice must be issued in Form-3 or Form-4 by an individual who actively holds a position with or in relation to the operational creditor, backed by Board authorization. Since the advocate issuing the notice lacked this standing, the NCLAT deemed the notice invalid, set aside the CIRP admission, and dismissed the insolvency petition.

case_title: Inox Wind Ltd. vs Jeena & Co.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Jeena & Co. (Operational Creditor / Respondent) vs Inox Wind Ltd. (Corporate Debtor / Appellant). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Operational debts accrued in the normal course of business. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Temporary default in operational dues, which the corporate debtor successfully paid off entirely during the pendency of the appellate proceedings. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: NCLT Chandigarh admitted the Section 9 petition ex-parte on July 5, 2017, and appointed the IRP on July 11, 2017. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The respondent expressly admitted before the appellate tribunal that the NCLT passed the admission order without issuing any prior notice to the Corporate Debtor. Additionally, a claim by an ex-employee (Shailendra Puri) was amicably settled during the appellate hearing. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Chandigarh admitted the CIRP ex-parte on July 5, 2017. The Corporate Debtor appealed, asserting an egregious violation of the principles of natural justice and providing proof of its solvency and settlement of all dues.
legal_issues: Whether an Adjudicating Authority can lawfully admit an insolvency application under Section 9 of the IBC without issuing prior notice to the Corporate Debtor, thereby bypassing the principles of natural justice.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An Adjudicating Authority is strictly prohibited from admitting an insolvency application and initiating CIRP without issuing prior notice and affording the corporate debtor a fair hearing. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 424 of the Companies Act, 2013, heavily heavily integrated into IBC proceedings, mandates that the Adjudicating Authority must rigidly follow the principles of natural justice, precluding ex-parte admissions of insolvency petitions. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The appellate tribunal evaluates procedural propriety by verifying the case records to ascertain whether a formal notice of hearing was successfully served on the corporate debtor before the admission order was passed. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT concluded that the NCLT's admission of the Section 9 petition without issuing prior notice to the Corporate Debtor was a direct violation of natural justice (citing Innoventive Industries Ltd). Consequently, the admission orders were rendered illegal and inherently void.
operative_order: The NCLT orders dated July 5 and July 11, 2017, are set aside. The Section 9 application proceedings are closed, the corporate debtor is released from the rigors of the CIRP with immediate effect, and the appellant is ordered to pay the IRP's fees.
summary: Inox Wind Ltd. appealed the NCLT Chandigarh's ex-parte admission of a Section 9 insolvency petition filed by Jeena & Co. The appellant argued that the NCLT blatantly violated the principles of natural justice by admitting the petition without issuing any prior notice. The respondent admitted this procedural failure and acknowledged that the appellant, a solvent company, had already settled all outstanding dues. Referencing the precedent set in Innoventive Industries Ltd, which mandates strict adherence to natural justice under Section 424 of the Companies Act, 2013, the NCLAT set aside the CIRP admission orders. The NCLAT closed the insolvency proceedings and restored the corporate debtor's independent management.

case_title: Kumar Jyoti Ranjan and Ms Priyanka Kumari (Directors of JAP Infratech Pvt Ltd) vs Innovation House Industries Pvt Ltd
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Innovation House Industries Pvt Ltd (Operational Creditor / Respondent) vs JAP Infratech Pvt Ltd (Corporate Debtor), represented by its Directors Mr. Kumar Jyoti Ranjan and Ms Priyanka Kumari (Appellants). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Underlying operational transactions leading to an unpaid debt. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default in operational dues necessitating a statutory demand notice prior to CIRP initiation. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Demand notice was issued on February 28, 2017. NCLT admitted the petition on July 27, 2017, and appointed an IRP on October 4, 2017. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The demand notice was explicitly issued by an external law firm, 'Corporate Legal Partners' (Mr. Vikas Kumar, Advocate). The respondent presented a Board Resolution dated Feb 13, 2017, purportedly authorizing the advocates, which the appellant fiercely contested as a forged document. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT New Delhi admitted the Section 9 application on July 27, 2017. The directors of the Corporate Debtor appealed, challenging the legal validity of the demand notice issued by an external law firm.
legal_issues: Whether a statutory demand notice under Section 8 of the IBC is valid when issued by an external law firm, irrespective of a purported Board Resolution authorizing the firm, if the law firm holds no direct internal position with the operational creditor.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A demand notice issued by an external law firm on behalf of an operational creditor is inherently invalid under the IBC if the firm does not hold a distinct internal structural position with or in relation to the operational creditor. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 8 read with Rule 5 strictly dictates that the demand notice in Form-3 or Form-4 must declare the authorized signatory's 'position with or in relation to the operational creditor'. External legal counsel, despite authorization, do not satisfy this statutory criterion. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Regardless of disputes over the authenticity of Board Resolutions authorizing external lawyers, the Tribunal fundamentally assesses whether the legal firm holds a genuine internal 'position with or in relation to' the corporate entity. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT bypassed the dispute regarding the forged resolution, concluding that because the law firm 'Corporate Legal Partners' held no structural position with the operational creditor, the demand notice was fatally defective, rendering the Section 9 petition unmaintainable.
operative_order: The NCLT's admission order dated July 27, 2017, and all consequential orders are set aside. The Section 9 application is dismissed, the corporate debtor is immediately released from the CIRP, and the appellant is directed to pay the Resolution Professional's fees.
summary: The directors of JAP Infratech Pvt Ltd challenged NCLT New Delhi's orders admitting a Section 9 insolvency petition filed by Innovation House Industries Pvt Ltd. The appellants argued that the Section 8 demand notice was defectively issued by an external law firm, 'Corporate Legal Partners.' Although the respondent produced a Board Resolution purportedly authorizing the lawyers, the NCLAT relied on the Uttam Galva Steels Limited precedent, ruling that an external law firm holding no structural position with or in relation to the operational creditor cannot validly issue a Section 8 notice. Consequently, the NCLAT bypassed the dispute over the resolution's authenticity, deemed the petition unmaintainable, set aside the CIRP admission, and restored the corporate debtor's management.

case_title: Centech Engineers Private Limited & Anr vs Omicron Sensing Private Limited
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Centech Engineers Private Limited & Anr (Corporate Debtor/Appellants) vs Omicron Sensing Private Limited (Operational Creditor/Respondent). 2.
