COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Underlying operational transactions resulting in a dispute over dues. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Alleged unpaid operational debt, which was notably paid off subsequently. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: NCLT Mumbai admitted the CIRP application on July 6, 2017. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The demand notice under Section 8 of the IBC was issued not by the operational creditor, but by an external Advocate's firm named 'SPS & Associates' without any proof of being authorized by or holding a position with the operational creditor. Additionally, the operational creditor admitted during the appeal that the due amount had already been paid by the corporate debtor. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai admitted the Section 9 petition on July 6, 2017. The Corporate Debtor appealed, challenging the validity of the demand notice and noting that the dues were settled.
legal_issues: Whether a demand notice under Section 8 of the IBC issued by an external Advocate's Associate, who does not hold any position with or in relation to the operational creditor, is legally valid to maintain a Section 9 petition.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An external lawyer or advocate cannot validly issue a statutory demand notice on behalf of an operational creditor unless they hold a specific position with or in relation to the operational creditor. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 8 of the IBC read with Rule 5 of the Adjudicating Authority Rules requires the demand notice in Form-3 or Form-4 to expressly state the signatory's position with or relation to the operational creditor; a standard lawyer's notice does not suffice. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal must examine the demand notice to verify if it strictly conforms to statutory forms and if the signatory holds an internal organizational position relative to the operational creditor. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT held that because the notice was given by an 'Associate of Advocates' lacking any proven position with the operational creditor, and because the dues were already settled, the Section 8 notice was invalid and the NCLT order must be set aside.
operative_order: The impugned order dated 6th July 2017 is set aside. The Section 9 application is dismissed, the corporate debtor is released from the rigour of CIRP, and the respondent is directed to pay the fees of the Interim Resolution Professional.
summary: In Centech Engineers Private Limited vs Omicron Sensing Private Limited, the corporate debtor appealed an NCLT Mumbai order admitting a Section 9 insolvency petition. The corporate debtor argued that the Section 8 demand notice was invalidly issued by an external advocate firm ('SPS & Associates') rather than the operational creditor itself. Furthermore, the operational creditor conceded that the outstanding dues had already been paid by the corporate debtor. Relying on the precedent in Macquarie Bank Limited, the NCLAT ruled that a Section 8 notice issued by an external lawyer holding no internal position with the operational creditor is invalid. Consequently, the NCLAT allowed the appeal, set aside the CIRP admission, and restored the corporate debtor's management.

case_title: Akash Ganga Builders Private Limited vs Registrar Of Companies, NCT Of Delhi & Haryana
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Akash Ganga Builders Private Limited (Appellant/Company) vs Registrar of Companies, NCT of Delhi & Haryana (Respondent). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Statutory compliance concerning the filing of annual returns, balance sheets, and maintaining minimum paid-up capital. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Non-filing of annual returns and balance sheets for a 13-year period (2000 to 2012), and specifically a continuous default from 2008 to 2011 even after judicial leniency. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The company was first struck off; the High Court of Delhi passed a conditional restoration order in 2013 granting 8 weeks for compliance. ROC issued another notice on Feb 11, 2015, and struck off the company again on May 29, 2015. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Affidavits confirmed the appellant failed to file returns for 2008 to 2011 and blamed web-site issues, their CA, and the death of one of the two directors. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Following the second striking off in 2015, the appellant petitioned NCLT New Delhi for restoration. NCLT rejected the petition on June 30, 2017, due to persistent non-compliance. The appellant appealed to the NCLAT.
legal_issues: Whether a company struck off under Section 560(5) of the Companies Act, 1956 for prolonged statutory non-compliance is entitled to restoration when it repeatedly fails to utilize prior judicial opportunities to rectify the defaults.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Repeated and prolonged failure to file statutory returns, coupled with a failure to utilize prior judicial leniency, negates any equitable ground for the restoration of a struck-off company's name. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Under Section 560(6) of the Companies Act, 1956, restoration requires the petitioner to demonstrate that the company was carrying on business at the time of striking off, or that it is otherwise 'just' that the company be restored. Internal administrative excuses do not satisfy the 'just' threshold. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal assesses whether the company adduced substantial evidence of ongoing business operations or valid external impossibilities preventing compliance; internal excuses like director deaths or web-site issues are considered day-to-day matters. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT concluded that since the appellant failed to file returns for 2008 to 2011 despite a prior High Court order, and failed to prove it was carrying on business or show 'just' grounds for restoration, the ROC's action and the NCLT's dismissal were valid.
operative_order: The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, upholding the NCLT's order and the Registrar of Companies' decision to strike off the appellant company. No order as to costs.
summary: In Akash Ganga Builders Private Limited vs Registrar of Companies, the appellant company challenged an NCLT order refusing to restore its name to the register. The company had initially been struck off for not filing returns for 13 years, but obtained a conditional restoration from the Delhi High Court in 2013. Despite this opportunity, it persistently failed to file returns for 2008-2011, leading the ROC to strike it off again in 2015. The appellant blamed technical issues and the death of a director. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that internal administrative issues are not acceptable excuses for prolonged non-compliance and that the appellant failed to establish 'just' grounds for restoration under Section 560(6) of the Companies Act, 1956.

case_title: M/s. Bhagwan Motors Pvt. Ltd vs Harshad V. Vora
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Harshad V. Vora (Operational Creditor/Respondent) vs M/s. Bhagwan Motors Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor/Appellant). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Supply of goods leading to an outstanding operational debt. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default in payment for goods supplied. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Demand notices were issued on March 12, 2017, and April 18, 2017. NCLT admitted the petition on June 6, 2017. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The Section 8 demand notices were issued by an advocate's firm, 'Shri Rajeshwer K. Gupta & Co.', via a power of attorney, omitting to mention the advocate's internal position or relationship with the operational creditor as required by statutory forms. Furthermore, the NCLT had directed the operational creditor to serve notice of the admission hearing rather than issuing the notice itself. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Ahmedabad admitted the Section 9 application on June 6, 2017. The Corporate Debtor appealed, arguing a violation of natural justice (no notice by Adjudicating Authority) and invalidity of the demand notice.
legal_issues: 1. Whether an Adjudicating Authority can delegate the issuance of a pre-admission hearing notice to the operational creditor. 2. Whether a Section 8 demand notice issued by an advocate via a Power of Attorney, without stating an internal position with the operational creditor, is valid.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An Adjudicating Authority is duty-bound to independently issue notice to a corporate debtor before admitting an insolvency petition; delegating this to the applicant violates natural justice. Furthermore, a statutory demand notice cannot be issued by an external lawyer. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 8 read with Rule 5 requires the demand notice in Form-3 or Form-4 to declare the authorized signatory's 'position with or in relation to the operational creditor'. An advocate operating under a Power of Attorney does not meet this strict compliance standard. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal inspects the demand notice to verify if the mandatory structural relationship is declared, and reviews the case record to ensure the Adjudicating Authority itself issued the pre-admission notice. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT set aside the admission order on two grounds: the NCLT improperly directed the operational creditor to serve the hearing notice (violating Innoventive Industries precedent), and the Section 8 notice was invalidly issued by an external advocate (violating Uttam Galva Steels precedent).
operative_order: The NCLT's admission order dated June 6, 2017, is set aside. The Section 9 application is dismissed, the corporate debtor is immediately released from the CIRP, and the respondent is directed to pay the fees of the Interim Resolution Professional.
summary: M/s. Bhagwan Motors Pvt. Ltd. appealed against an NCLT Ahmedabad order admitting a Section 9 insolvency petition filed by Harshad V. Vora. The appellant argued that the NCLT violated natural justice by not issuing a pre-admission notice and that the Section 8 demand notice was defectively issued by an advocate. The NCLAT allowed the appeal on dual grounds. First, relying on the Innoventive Industries precedent, it held that the Adjudicating Authority must issue the notice itself rather than delegating it to the petitioner. Second, applying the Uttam Galva Steels precedent, it ruled that a Section 8 notice issued by an external lawyer holding no structural position with the operational creditor is invalid. The NCLAT set aside the CIRP admission and restored the corporate debtor's management.

case_title: Mass Metals Pvt. Ltd vs Sunflag Iron & Steel Co. Ltd
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Sunflag Iron & Steel Co. Ltd (Operational Creditor/Respondent) vs Mass Metals Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor/Appellant). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: An underlying debt resulting in a winding-up petition under Section 434(1)(a) of the Companies Act, which was later treated as a Section 9 IBC application. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Unpaid operational dues. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The demand notice was issued on March 17, 2017. NCLT admitted the petition on May 24, 2017. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The Section 8 demand notice was issued by Ankur S. Kulkarni, an Advocate on Record of the Supreme Court, with no evidence of Board authorization or any internal position with the operational creditor. Furthermore, the pre-admission notice of hearing was issued by the operational creditor via Speed Post/email on NCLT's directions, not by the Adjudicating Authority itself. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT New Delhi admitted the Section 9 application on May 24, 2017. The Corporate Debtor appealed, citing a violation of natural justice and invalidity of the demand notice.
legal_issues: 1. Whether a statutory demand notice under Section 8 issued by an Advocate on Record is valid. 2. Whether an Adjudicating Authority can admit a petition without independently issuing a limited notice to the corporate debtor.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A Section 8 demand notice issued by an external lawyer is invalid. Additionally, the Adjudicating Authority is bound to independently issue a limited notice to the corporate debtor before admitting an insolvency case to ascertain the existence of default or disputes. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Under Section 8 and Rule 5, the demand notice must be in Form-3 or Form-4 and issued by someone holding a position with or in relation to the operational creditor. An external advocate does not meet this requirement. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal reviews the issuer of the demand notice for structural linkage to the creditor, and checks the judicial record to verify if the Adjudicating Authority itself issued a pre-admission hearing notice. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT set aside the admission order, finding that the Section 8 notice was invalidly issued by an advocate (following Uttam Galva) and that the NCLT failed to afford proper opportunity by not independently issuing a pre-admission notice to the corporate debtor (following Innoventive Industries).
operative_order: The impugned order dated 24th May 2017 is set aside. CP No.16/2017 is dismissed. The corporate debtor is released from the CIRP, and the appellant is directed to pay the fees of the Interim Resolution Professional.
summary: Mass Metals Pvt. Ltd. appealed an NCLT New Delhi order admitting a Section 9 insolvency petition filed by Sunflag Iron & Steel Co. Ltd., which had been transferred from a winding-up proceeding. The appellant contended that the NCLT did not issue a pre-admission notice and that the statutory demand notice was invalidly issued by an Advocate on Record. The NCLAT allowed the appeal, heavily relying on prior precedents. It held that under the Uttam Galva ruling, a Section 8 notice issued by an external lawyer without holding an internal position with the creditor is legally void. Furthermore, referencing Innoventive Industries, it found that the Adjudicating Authority failed to independently issue a limited notice to the corporate debtor, thereby violating natural justice. The NCLAT set aside the CIRP admission.

case_title: Ellora Paper Mills Limited & Anr vs Ajithnath Steels Pvt. Ltd
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Ajithnath Steels Pvt. Ltd. (Financial Creditor/Respondent) vs Ellora Paper Mills Limited & Anr (Corporate Debtor/Appellants). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: A financial arrangement where the corporate debtor was required to pay back an amount within a specified period with interest accruing in case of default. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default in repaying the principal along with the continuously accruing monthly interest. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The IBC came into force on December 1, 2016. NCLT Mumbai admitted the petition on July 19, 2017. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The financial creditor demonstrated that interest accrued every month, constituting a continuous cause of action, thereby negating claims of laches or a stale debt. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai admitted the Section 7 application on July 19, 2017. The Corporate Debtor appealed, contending the application was barred by limitation under the Limitation Act.
legal_issues: Whether a Section 7 insolvency petition can be rejected on the ground of limitation if there is a continuous cause of action (accruing monthly interest) and whether the right to apply under the IBC accrues from the date the Code came into effect.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The Limitation Act, 1963, is not strictly applicable to the initiation of Corporate Insolvency Resolution Processes, but the doctrine of delay and laches applies to prevent stale claims. However, if there is a continuing cause of action, or the right to apply under the Code accrued recently (i.e., Dec 1, 2016), the petition is not barred by limitation. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Even if Article 137 of the Limitation Act were applied hypothetically, the right to apply for a CIRP under Sections 7, 9, or 10 of the IBC accrued only on December 1, 2016, when the Code came into force, making early petitions immune to a direct 3-year limitation bar on the application itself. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Adjudicating Authority must examine if there is a continuing cause of action (like continuous interest accrual) or if there are unexplained laches rendering the claim stale. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT concluded that since interest accrued monthly (a continuous cause of action) and the right to apply under the IBC accrued on December 1, 2016, the Section 7 petition was not barred by limitation. The NCLT's admission order was upheld.
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed. The NCLT Mumbai order admitting the Section 7 petition is upheld. No order as to costs.
summary: Ellora Paper Mills Limited appealed an NCLT Mumbai order admitting a Section 7 insolvency petition filed by Ajithnath Steels Pvt. Ltd. The appellant primarily argued that the financial creditor's claim was barred by limitation. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, referencing its precedent in M/s Speculum Plast Pvt. Ltd. The Tribunal noted that while the Limitation Act does not strictly apply to the initiation of CIRP, the doctrine of delay and laches is relevant for stale claims. However, in this case, the continuous monthly accrual of interest constituted a continuing cause of action. Furthermore, the right to apply under the IBC only accrued on December 1, 2016, meaning the petition could not be rejected as time-barred.

case_title: Bhupendra Patel & Anr. vs Hotel Satyaketu Pvt. Ltd. & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Bhupendra Patel & Anr. (Appellants/Petitioners) vs Hotel Satyaketu Pvt. Ltd. & Ors. (Respondents)[cite: 15]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Appellants were original partners in a firm that converted to a company in 2002[cite: 15]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Alleged illegal removal of names from the register of members and unauthorized transfer of shares in 2012[cite: 15]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The firm converted to a company on September 16, 2002[cite: 15]. The members' names were removed on February 27, 2012, and the petition was filed on February 24, 2015[cite: 15]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Appellants did not possess any share certificates since the company's inception in 2002, and no shares were ever formally allotted or handed over to them[cite: 15]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Ahmedabad dismissed the petition on August 30, 2017, holding the appellants were not members at the time of filing[cite: 15]. The appellants challenged this maintainability ruling before the NCLAT[cite: 15].
legal_issues: Whether a petition for oppression and mismanagement is maintainable when the petitioners' names were struck from the register of members years prior to filing and they possess no share certificates to prove current membership[cite: 15].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: To maintain a petition for oppression and mismanagement, the petitioners must establish their status as shareholders; reliance on historical records (like the initial Articles of Association) without possessing share certificates or current membership is insufficient[cite: 15]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Sections 397 and 398 of the Companies Act, 1956 require the petitioner to be a valid, existing member on the date of filing the petition[cite: 15]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal must examine whether the petitioners possess valid original share certificates or if their names are currently on the register of members at the time of petition filing[cite: 15]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT concluded that since the appellants did not hold any share certificates since 2002 and their names had been struck off well before the filing date in 2015, they lacked locus standi and their petition was not maintainable[cite: 15].
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed with no order as to costs[cite: 15].
summary: Bhupendra Patel and another appealed against an NCLT Ahmedabad order dismissing their petition for oppression and mismanagement against Hotel Satyaketu Pvt. Ltd.[cite: 15]. The appellants claimed they were illegally removed as shareholders in 2012 when the company filed its Annual Return[cite: 15]. The NCLAT upheld the NCLT's decision, noting that the appellants did not possess any share certificates since the company's inception in 2002 and were not members of the company when the petition was filed on February 24, 2015, rendering the petition unmaintainable[cite: 15].

case_title: Dr. S. Gopinath & Anr. vs Orugallu Medicare Ltd. & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Dr. S. Gopinath & Anr. (Appellants/Petitioners, with the 1st appellant being the Chairman of the 1st respondent company) vs Orugallu Medicare Ltd. & Ors. (Respondents)[cite: 16]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate management disputes and challenges against shares issued by the company after 2006[cite: 16]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Alleged oppressive acts and mismanagement executed by the 2nd respondent between 2006 and 2012[cite: 16]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Oppressive acts alleged from 2006 to 2012[cite: 16]. The petition was filed in 2013 after an unexplained delay of 10-12 years since the initial differences arose in 2003-04[cite: 16]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Appellants attended the 2012 AGM but failed to raise any past grievances of oppression or mismanagement on record[cite: 16]. The Tribunal also observed the company was operating smoothly without interference at the time of the order[cite: 16]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Hyderabad dismissed the petition on March 6, 2017[cite: 16]. The appellants filed an appeal with a 30-day delay, which was condoned, challenging the dismissal on merits[cite: 16].
legal_issues: Whether a petition alleging oppression and mismanagement can be sustained when the petitioners delay filing for 10-12 years without explanation and previously attended AGMs without raising the issues[cite: 16].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Claims of oppression and mismanagement must be raised contemporaneously; unexplained prolonged delays and acquiescence by participating in subsequent company meetings without objection invalidate such claims[cite: 16]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Relief under Sections 397/398 of the Companies Act, 1956 is equitable and cannot be granted for stale historical grievances where the company is currently functioning without ongoing oppression[cite: 16]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal requires evidence of contemporaneous objections (such as documented protests during AGMs) and proof of current ongoing mismanagement to substantiate the claims[cite: 16]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT concluded that since the appellants failed to explain the 10-12 year delay, did not raise the issues during the 2012 AGM, and no current mismanagement existed, the Tribunal correctly dismissed the petition[cite: 16].
operative_order: The delay of 30 days in filing the appeal is condoned[cite: 16]. The appeal is dismissed on merits with no order as to costs[cite: 16].
summary: Dr. S. Gopinath appealed an NCLT Hyderabad order dismissing his petition for oppression and mismanagement against Orugallu Medicare Ltd.[cite: 16]. The appellants alleged oppressive acts and illegal share issuances occurring between 2006 and 2012[cite: 16]. The NCLAT upheld the dismissal, observing that the appellants failed to explain a 10-12 year delay in filing the petition and had actively attended the 2012 AGM without raising any of these past grievances[cite: 16]. Given the lack of specific evidence of ongoing mismanagement, the appeal was dismissed[cite: 16].

case_title: Pawan Kumar Kanodia vs Kanodia Tex Industries Limited & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Pawan Kumar Kanodia (Appellant/Petitioner) vs Kanodia Tex Industries Limited & Ors. (Respondents)[cite: 17]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Claim of holding 50% share capital (initially 21 shares of Rs. 100 each, subsequently increased to 1800 shares) in the respondent company[cite: 17]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Alleged fraudulent transfer and forgery of the appellant's shares to third parties in 1990 without his signature on any transfer deed under Section 108[cite: 17]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The appellant resigned as Director and the shares were purportedly transferred in 1990[cite: 17]. The petition was filed on September 10, 2013[cite: 17]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The appellant completely failed to produce the original share certificates to substantiate his claim of continuing ownership, while the company's records indicated a valid transfer in 1990 when he resigned[cite: 17]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai rejected the petition on May 3, 2017, ruling the petition unmaintainable because the appellant was no longer a shareholder[cite: 17]. The appellant challenged this ruling[cite: 17].
legal_issues: Whether an oppression and mismanagement petition is maintainable when the petitioner's shares were transferred decades prior, he cannot produce original share certificates, and the foundation of the claim relies on allegations of forgery[cite: 17].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A party claiming their shares were fraudulently transferred decades ago cannot maintain an oppression and mismanagement petition without possessing the original share certificates or definitive proof of current membership[cite: 17]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Sections 397/398 of the Companies Act, 1956 demand that the petitioner be a recognized member at the time of filing; serious allegations of forgery regarding historical transfers fall outside the summary jurisdiction of company tribunals[cite: 17]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal demands the production of original share certificates to counter the company's historical transfer records; failure to produce them supports the presumption of a completed valid transfer[cite: 17]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT concluded that since the appellant could not produce the original share certificates and his shares were officially transferred in 1990, he was not a member, making the petition unmaintainable[cite: 17].
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed with no order as to costs, leaving it open to the appellant to approach appropriate forums for allegations of forgery[cite: 17].
summary: Pawan Kumar Kanodia appealed against an NCLT Mumbai order dismissing his petition for oppression and mismanagement against Kanodia Tex Industries Limited on maintainability grounds[cite: 17]. He alleged that his 50% shareholding was fraudulently transferred in 1990 without his signature[cite: 17]. The NCLAT upheld the NCLT's dismissal, highlighting that the appellant had resigned as a director in 1990 and completely failed to produce the original share certificates to substantiate his claim of continuing ownership[cite: 17]. The tribunal noted that serious allegations of forgery must be taken to the appropriate civil or criminal forum[cite: 17].

case_title: Kaliber Associates Pvt Ltd. vs Mrs Tripat Kaur
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is Kaliber Associates Pvt Ltd. (Corporate Debtor) and the Respondent is Mrs. Tripat Kaur, proprietor of M/s Gallerie Nvya (Financial Creditor)[cite: 1]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: The parties entered into a financial dealing in 2012 involving an amount of Rs. 1.5 crores[cite: 1]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Disagreements arose in 2016 causing a stoppage of payment; Rs. 50 lakhs out of Rs. 1.5 crores was previously repaid[cite: 1]. The Corporate Debtor subsequently offered to pay the remaining Rs. 1 crore plus Rs. 12 lakhs interest[cite: 1]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: A legal demand notice was sent by the Respondent on 20.10.2016[cite: 1]. Post-petition, on 04.06.2017, cheques were issued for Rs. 1,00,000,000/- and Rs. 10,80,000/-[cite: 1]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The Corporate Debtor handed over post-dated cheques as full and final payment during the appellate proceedings, which the Financial Creditor accepted[cite: 1]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The Respondent initially filed Company Petition No.(IB)- 51 (ND) / 2017 under Section 7 of the IBC[cite: 1]. The NCLT New Delhi admitted the application on 26.04.2017 ex-parte without notice to the Corporate Debtor, appointing an IRP[cite: 1]. The Corporate Debtor appealed this admission to the NCLAT[cite: 1].
legal_issues: Whether an Adjudicating Authority can admit a Section 7 insolvency petition without issuing prior notice to the corporate debtor, thus violating the principles of natural justice?[cite: 1]
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The Adjudicating Authority must issue a prior notice to the corporate debtor and observe the principles of natural justice before admitting an insolvency application[cite: 1]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 424 of the Companies Act, 2013, applicable to IBC proceedings, mandates compliance with the principles of natural justice[cite: 1]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal noted the admitted fact by the respondent that no notice was issued by the Adjudicating Authority before admitting the Section 7 application[cite: 1]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT held that the ex-parte admission order was illegal and in violation of natural justice, relying on Innoventive Industries Ltd[cite: 1]. The NCLAT set aside the impugned order, released the corporate debtor from the moratorium, and closed the proceedings following the settlement between the parties[cite: 1].
operative_order: The impugned order dated 26th April, 2017 is set aside[cite: 1]. The appointment of the IRP, moratorium, and all related actions are declared illegal[cite: 1]. Proceedings are closed[cite: 1]. The Corporate Debtor is released to function through its Board of Directors[cite: 1]. Adjudicating Authority to fix the fee of the IRP, payable by the Financial Creditor[cite: 1].
summary: The Financial Creditor initiated a Section 7 IBC petition against the Corporate Debtor, which was admitted by NCLT New Delhi ex-parte[cite: 1]. The Corporate Debtor appealed to NCLAT, arguing a violation of natural justice and expressing willingness to settle the Rs. 1 crore debt[cite: 1]. NCLAT held that admitting a petition without prior notice violates natural justice and Section 424 of the Companies Act, 2013[cite: 1]. Since the parties settled and handed over cheques, NCLAT set aside the admission order, lifted the moratorium, and restored the Corporate Debtor's management[cite: 1].

case_title: Mrs. Archana Rajesh Gaikwad & Anr. vs M/s. Arviyas Fashions Pvt. Ltd. & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellants/Petitioners are Mrs. Archana Rajesh Gaikwad & Anr., directors/shareholders of M/s. Arviyas Fashions Pvt. Ltd. (Respondent No. 1/Company)[cite: 2]. The opposing parties are the other directors/shareholders (Respondents)[cite: 2]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: The dispute involves the internal management, capital contribution, and loan advancements within a family-owned closely held company[cite: 2]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The Appellants claimed the Respondents siphoned off funds, while the Respondents had advanced huge amounts of loans to the Company which were being returned[cite: 2]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The original company petition was filed in 2014 (T.C.P. No. 02/397/CLB/MB/2014)[cite: 2]. The NCLT order was passed on 20.04.2017[cite: 2]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The financial entries in the books of accounts established a direct nexus of adjustment of loan previously given by the Respondents for the company's business[cite: 2]. There was no evidence of illicit siphoning, only legitimate refund of loans[cite: 2]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The Appellants filed a petition under Sections 397/398 of the Companies Act, 1956[cite: 2]. The NCLT Mumbai found oppression/mismanagement but crafted an equitable exit plan for the Respondents who had already resigned, rather than restoring them to the Board or ordering them to refund alleged siphoned money[cite: 2]. The Appellants challenged the adequacy of these reliefs before NCLAT[cite: 2].
legal_issues: Whether the NCLT was justified in its equitable reliefs, specifically in refusing to direct the Respondents to make good the allegedly siphoned funds and ordering a buyout of the Respondents' shares to resolve family deadlock?[cite: 2]
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Legitimate transfer of funds recorded in the books of accounts as repayment of a previously advanced loan cannot be termed as siphoning of funds[cite: 2]. Additionally, in cases of irretrievable family deadlock in a company, directing one group to exit via a fair valuation of shares is an equitable and appropriate remedy[cite: 2]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The Tribunal exercised its equitable jurisdiction under Sections 241/242 of the Companies Act, 2013 (formerly Sections 397/398) to fashion a practical exit mechanism rather than forcing incompatible parties to run the company together[cite: 2]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal relied on entries in the books of accounts which demonstrated that the respondents had advanced significant loans and the withdrawals were legitimate refunds of those loans, thus unsubstantiating the siphoning claims[cite: 2]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT concluded that the NCLT's judgment was not perverse and appropriately balanced the equities by providing a clear exit plan for the resigned directors and rejecting the unsupported siphoning claims[cite: 2]. The appeal was dismissed[cite: 2].
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed with costs of Rs. 50,000/- to be paid by the appellants to the 1st Respondent Company[cite: 2]. The NCLT's order regarding the valuation and buyout of shares stands[cite: 2].
summary: The Appellants filed a petition for oppression and mismanagement against the Respondents in a family-run company[cite: 2]. The NCLT acknowledged the oppression but ordered the Respondents (who had already resigned) to exit the company by selling their shares at a fair valuation, and rejected claims that the Respondents siphoned funds, noting the transactions were legitimate loan repayments[cite: 2]. The Appellants appealed, seeking further reliefs[cite: 2]. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal with costs, holding that the NCLT's equitable exit plan was justified and not perverse[cite: 2].

case_title: Mr. Abhishek Mohan Gupta vs M/s. Jagran Prakashan Ltd. & Ors
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is Mr. Abhishek Mohan Gupta (3rd Respondent in the original petition)[cite: 3]. The contesting Respondents include M/s. Jagran Prakashan Ltd. & Ors[cite: 3]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: The underlying dispute involves allegations of oppression and mismanagement regarding Jagran Publications Pvt. Ltd. and related shareholding percentages[cite: 3]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The Appellant sought to introduce a counter-claim of Rs. 58.93 crores plus interest of Rs. 33.93 crores (total Rs. 92.9 crores) and demand an unconditional surrender of 40% of shareholding[cite: 3]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The original Company Petition has been pending for approximately 10 years[cite: 3]. The NCLT Ahmedabad passed the impugned order on 18.09.2017[cite: 3]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The Appellant filed an application under Rule 11 of the NCLT Rules seeking to amend pleadings to include a massive financial counter-claim and structural relief against the original petitioners[cite: 3]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Ahmedabad in IA 271/2017 rejected the Appellant's application to introduce a counter-claim in the Section 241 petition[cite: 3]. The Appellant challenged this rejection before the NCLAT[cite: 3].
legal_issues: Whether a counter-claim by a respondent is legally maintainable in an oppression and mismanagement petition filed under Section 241 of the Companies Act, 2013?[cite: 3]
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A respondent cannot file a counter-claim in a petition instituted for oppression and mismanagement[cite: 3]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The NCLAT observed that there is no provision under Section 241 of the Companies Act, 2013 (or the erstwhile Sections 397/398 of the 1956 Act) that permits the filing of any counter-claim by the respondents (other members) against the petitioners[cite: 3]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Not applicable as it was a purely procedural question of law; when asked to point out a legal provision supporting the maintainability of a counter-claim, the Appellant's counsel failed to reply[cite: 3]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Realizing the NCLAT was about to dismiss the appeal on the legal point that Section 241 does not accommodate counter-claims, the Appellant sought permission to withdraw the appeal, which the tribunal allowed while noting the delay tactics[cite: 3].
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed as withdrawn[cite: 3]. The NCLT is directed to dispose of the decade-old Company Petition expeditiously, preferably within two months, without granting unnecessary adjournments[cite: 3].
summary: The Appellant (respondent below) sought to introduce a Rs. 92.9 crore counter-claim in an ongoing oppression and mismanagement petition pending for 10 years[cite: 3]. The NCLT rejected the application, prompting this appeal[cite: 3]. The NCLAT noted that Section 241 of the Companies Act, 2013 does not contain any provision allowing a respondent to file a counter-claim in such petitions[cite: 3]. Confronted with this legal bar, the Appellant withdrew the appeal[cite: 3]. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal as withdrawn and directed the NCLT to dispose of the main petition within two months[cite: 3].

case_title: Bengal Chemists & Druggists Association vs Kalyan Chowdhury
appeal_number: I.A. No. 275 of 2017 IN Company Appeal (AT) No. 76 of 2017
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is Bengal Chemists & Druggists Association[cite: 4]. The Respondent is Kalyan Chowdhury[cite: 4]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Not applicable; procedural dismissal regarding an underlying company petition (CP No. 60/2015)[cite: 4]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The default relates to limitation; the appeal was filed after 99 days of the impugned order[cite: 4]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The impugned order by NCLT Kolkata was passed on 29.09.2016[cite: 4]. The appeal was filed on 22.02.2017 (99 days later)[cite: 4]. The statutory limit is 45 days, with a maximum condonable period of a further 45 days (total 90 days)[cite: 4]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The date of the NCLT order and the date of filing the appeal mathematically established a delay of 99 days[cite: 4]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The NCLT Kolkata disposed of CP No. 60/2015 on 29.09.2016[cite: 4]. The Appellant filed an appeal before NCLAT with a condonation of delay application (I.A. No. 275 of 2017) after 99 days[cite: 4].
legal_issues: Whether the NCLAT has the jurisdiction to condone a delay in filing an appeal beyond the maximum statutory limit of 90 days prescribed under Section 421(3) of the Companies Act, 2013 by invoking Section 433 of the Act and Section 29(3) of the Limitation Act, 1963?[cite: 4]
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An appellate tribunal cannot condone a filing delay beyond the absolute maximum statutory limit explicitly prescribed in its governing statute[cite: 4]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 421(3) of the Companies Act, 2013 provides a 45-day limitation period for filing an appeal, with a proviso that allows condonation of delay for a further period 'not exceeding forty-five days'[cite: 4]. The general applicability of the Limitation Act under Section 433 is subject to specific provisions of the Companies Act[cite: 4]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal calculated the days between the order (29.09.2016) and the filing (22.02.2017) to confirm a 99-day delay, which exceeds the absolute 90-day ceiling[cite: 4]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Since Section 421(3) explicitly caps the condonable period, the Appellate Tribunal held it has no jurisdiction to condone a delay beyond 90 days[cite: 4]. The provisions of the Limitation Act cannot override this explicit statutory cap[cite: 4].
operative_order: The application for condonation of delay (I.A. No. 275 of 2017) is rejected[cite: 4]. The appeal is dismissed as barred by limitation[cite: 4]. No order as to costs[cite: 4].
summary: The Appellant challenged an NCLT Kolkata order dated 29.09.2016 by filing an appeal on 22.02.2017, resulting in a 99-day delay[cite: 4]. The Appellant sought condonation of delay by relying on the general provisions of the Limitation Act via Section 433 of the Companies Act[cite: 4]. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, ruling that Section 421(3) of the Companies Act, 2013 strictly caps the condonable period at a maximum of 90 days (45 days normal + 45 days extended limit)[cite: 4]. Therefore, the Tribunal lacked jurisdiction to condone a delay of 99 days[cite: 4].

case_title: M/s. Shree Shrine Engineering & Marketing Company Pvt. Ltd. vs The Registrar of Companies, Gujarat, Ahmedabad
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is M/s. Shree Shrine Engineering & Marketing Company Pvt. Ltd. along with its three directors[cite: 5]. The Respondent is the Registrar of Companies, Gujarat[cite: 5]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: The dispute pertains to statutory corporate compliance rather than a commercial contract[cite: 5]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The Company failed to hold its Annual General Meeting (AGM) for the financial year 2013-14 by the statutory deadline of 30.09.2014[cite: 5]. The default continued for 89 days from 01.10.2014 to 29.12.2014[cite: 5]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The default period spanned 89 days[cite: 5]. The compounding petition under Section 621-A was resolved by the NCLT on 09.02.2017[cite: 5]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: It was an admitted fact that the company and its directors failed to hold the AGM within the prescribed timeframe, thus violating Section 166 of the Companies Act, 1956[cite: 5]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The Appellants filed a petition under Section 621-A of the Companies Act, 1956 for compounding the offence[cite: 5]. The NCLT Ahmedabad allowed compounding but imposed a total fee/fine of Rs. 3,96,000/-[cite: 5]. The Appellants appealed to NCLAT challenging the quantum of the compounding fee[cite: 5].
legal_issues: Whether the compounding fee of Rs. 3,96,000 imposed by the NCLT under Section 621-A of the Companies Act, 1956 for an 89-day delay in holding the AGM was excessive or illegal?[cite: 5]
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The Tribunal has discretionary power to determine the quantum of compounding fees within the maximum penal limits prescribed by the statute, and an appellate court will not interfere unless the assessment is illegal or perverse[cite: 5]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 168 of the Companies Act, 1956 prescribes a maximum fine of Rs. 50,000 plus Rs. 2,500 for every day the default continues[cite: 5]. The Tribunal has the authority under Section 621-A to compound the offence at a reduced rate[cite: 5]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal noted the admitted 89-day delay and calculated the compounding fee at Rs. 10,000 per director (instead of the max Rs. 50,000) and Rs. 1,000 per day for continuing default (instead of the max Rs. 2,500)[cite: 5]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT found no illegality in the impugned order since the NCLT had actually reduced the penalty significantly from the maximum permissible statutory limits[cite: 5]. Therefore, the compounding fee imposed was legally sound and justified[cite: 5].
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed[cite: 5]. The compounding fee/fine of Rs. 3,96,000 ordered by the NCLT stands[cite: 5]. No order as to costs[cite: 5].
summary: The Appellant company failed to hold its AGM for FY 2013-14 within the statutory deadline, resulting in an 89-day delay[cite: 5]. Upon filing a compounding petition under Section 621-A, the NCLT imposed a compounding fee of Rs. 3,96,000 (calculated at reduced rates of Rs. 10,000 fixed and Rs. 1,000 per day for the company and three directors)[cite: 5]. The Appellant challenged this quantum before the NCLAT[cite: 5]. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that the NCLT had already shown leniency by imposing fees well below the maximum statutory limit prescribed under Section 168 of the Companies Act, 1956, and there was no illegality in the order[cite: 5].

case_title: Tarun Goyal vs Registrar Of Companies, Nct Of Delhi & Haryana
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is Tarun Goyal, an alleged director/lead manager[cite: 8]. Respondent No. 1 is the Registrar of Companies, NCT of Delhi & Haryana[cite: 8]. The Securities Exchange Board of India (SEBI) opposed the application[cite: 8]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: The matter involved the floating of public issues and incorporating companies, specifically M/s Zed Investment Ltd., M/s Kalyvart Finance Ltd., and M/s Gradiente Infotainment Ltd[cite: 8]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The Appellant allegedly aided and abetted the raising of money from the public using non-existent directors and false addresses, leading to the siphoning off of investor funds[cite: 8]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The compounding application was filed after more than 14 years from the date of the original SEBI complaint (Complaint No. 54/05/09)[cite: 8]. The NCLT dismissed the application on 07.11.2016[cite: 8]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: SEBI alleged that the prospectus dated 20.07.1996 contained false information certified by the Appellant[cite: 8]. The Appellant was facing parallel criminal prosecution by the CBI and EOW, though acquitted in one CBI case[cite: 8]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The Appellant filed an application under Section 621-A of the Companies Act, 1956 for compounding offenses under Sections 63 and 68 before the NCLT New Delhi (C.A.No. 16/191/14)[cite: 8]. The NCLT dismissed it on 07.11.2016 due to the grave and criminal nature of the allegations, which the Appellant challenged before the NCLAT[cite: 8].
legal_issues: Whether a compounding application under Section 621-A of the Companies Act, 1956 should be allowed when there are grave, wilful, and criminal allegations of public fraud and parallel criminal proceedings pending?[cite: 8]
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Compounding of offenses cannot be permitted where the alleged corporate actions are grave, wilful, and criminal in nature, as such indulgence would scuttle pending criminal prosecutions and harm investor interests[cite: 8]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The Tribunal's discretionary power to compound under Section 621-A of the Companies Act, 1956 (now Section 441 of the 2013 Act) should not be exercised for offenses that are not routine mistakes but involve deliberate, fraudulent misstatements in a prospectus to deceive the public[cite: 8]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal evaluated the prima facie wilful nature of the applicant's actions, the unexplained 14-year delay in seeking compounding, and the existence of severe allegations by SEBI alongside pending criminal investigations[cite: 8]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT held that the NCLT correctly dismissed the compounding application, concluding that the grave allegations of fraudulent prospectus filings and siphoning of public funds could not be treated as compoundable offenses[cite: 8].
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed[cite: 8]. No relief is granted for compounding the offenses[cite: 8].
summary: The Appellant, Tarun Goyal, sought the compounding of offenses under Sections 63 and 68 of the Companies Act, 1956 for allegedly making false and misleading statements in a corporate prospectus[cite: 8]. The Securities Exchange Board of India (SEBI) vehemently opposed the application, highlighting that the Appellant was facing parallel criminal prosecution by the CBI and EOW for utilizing non-existent directors to siphon public investor funds[cite: 8]. The NCLT dismissed the compounding application, noting the grave and criminal nature of the acts and the unexplained 14-year delay in seeking relief[cite: 8]. On appeal, the NCLAT upheld the dismissal, ruling that the discretionary power to compound offenses cannot be exercised to condone deliberate, fraudulent actions that severely harm public investors and scuttle pending criminal prosecutions[cite: 8].

case_title: Allied Media Network Pvt. Ltd. vs M/s. Sanraa Media Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is Allied Media Network Pvt. Ltd.[cite: 9]. The Respondent is M/s. Sanraa Media Ltd.[cite: 9]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: The dispute originated as a winding-up petition based on the company's inability to pay its debts[cite: 9]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The core issue involved the inability to pay debts under Section 433(e) of the Companies Act, 1956, though specific debt amounts were not detailed[cite: 9]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: A government notification dated 29.06.2017 set a deadline of 15.07.2017 to file required IBC information[cite: 9]. The Appellant filed the documents four days late, on 19.07.2017[cite: 9]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The Appellant filed an affidavit and bank statements to comply with Sections 9(3)(b) & (c) of the IBC, but missed the statutory cut-off date, causing the matter to be closed as abated[cite: 9]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The Appellant originally filed a winding-up petition before the Madras High Court, which was transferred to the Adjudicating Authority[cite: 9]. The NCLT passed an order on 22.08.2017 declaring the application abated due to late submission, prompting the appeal to the NCLAT[cite: 9].
legal_issues: Whether a winding-up petition that abated due to a slight delay in filing statutory compliance documents under the Transfer of Pending Proceedings Rules can be revived, or if the petitioner is entitled to file a fresh IBC application?[cite: 9]
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: When a transferred winding-up petition abates due to the expiration of a statutory deadline for submitting supplementary information, the petitioner retains the explicit right to file a fresh application under the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code[cite: 9]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Rule 5 of the Companies (Transfer of Pending Proceedings) Rules, 2017 allows that if the required information is not filed within 60 days, the petition abates, but parties are eligible to file fresh applications under Sections 7, 8, or 9 of the IBC after 15.07.2017[cite: 9]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The NCLAT acknowledged that setting aside the NCLT's abatement order for a mere 4-day delay (filed 19.07.2017) would not yield practical relief since over five months had already passed[cite: 9]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Tribunal concluded that the appropriate remedy under Rule 5 was not to revive the abated petition, but to allow the Appellant to file a fresh IBC application, which the Adjudicating Authority must consider uninfluenced by the previous abatement order[cite: 9].
operative_order: The Appellant is permitted to file a fresh application under Section 7 or 9 of the IBC[cite: 9]. If filed within a reasonable period, the Adjudicating Authority must consider it in accordance with law, uninfluenced by the impugned abatement order dated 22.08.2017[cite: 9].
summary: The Appellant, Allied Media Network Pvt. Ltd., originally filed a winding-up petition against the Corporate Debtor before the Madras High Court, which was subsequently transferred to the NCLT[cite: 9]. Under the amended Companies (Transfer of Pending Proceedings) Rules, 2017, the Appellant was required to file statutory IBC compliance documents by July 15, 2017[cite: 9]. Because the Appellant filed these documents four days late on July 19, 2017, the NCLT declared the application abated[cite: 9]. The Appellant challenged this abatement before the NCLAT[cite: 9]. Rather than reviving the delayed petition months later, the NCLAT disposed of the appeal by applying Rule 5 to explicitly grant the Appellant liberty to file a fresh, uninfluenced application under Section 7 or 9 of the IBC[cite: 9].

case_title: M/s. Vijaya Hospitality and Resorts Limited and Others vs Sibi C.K. & Ors
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellants include M/s. Vijaya Hospitality and Resorts Limited, C.K. Vijayan, Saira Thampy Krishnan, and others[cite: 10]. The Respondents/Petitioners are Sibi C.K. (1st Petitioner) and K.C. Baboo (2nd Petitioner)[cite: 10]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: The dispute involves allegations of oppression and mismanagement regarding shareholding, directorships, and internal control of the Appellant company[cite: 10]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The Respondents alleged illegal removal from the Board on 17.06.2012 based on forged resignation letters dated 07.06.2012, and the illegal transmission of 34,52,825 shares on 29.03.2012[cite: 10]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The contested removal of directors and share transfers occurred in 2012[cite: 10]. The NCLT Chennai passed its final order on 18.04.2017[cite: 10]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The Articles of Association named the Respondents as first directors[cite: 10]. No notices for Board meetings were given, nor were valid Board resolutions passed for their removal[cite: 10]. The company's Annual Returns failed to reflect the shareholding alterations[cite: 10]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The Respondents filed a petition for oppression and mismanagement (TCP No. 185 of 2016) before NCLT Chennai[cite: 10]. The NCLT allowed the application on 18.04.2017[cite: 10]. The Appellants appealed this decision to the NCLAT[cite: 10].
legal_issues: Whether the removal of directors and the subsequent alteration of shareholding patterns constituted oppression and mismanagement when done without proper notice, valid board resolutions, or accurate statutory filings?[cite: 10]
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The removal of directors and transmission of shares in a company without issuing requisite notices for board meetings, without passing valid resolutions, and relying on disputed resignations constitutes actionable oppression and mismanagement[cite: 10]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Sections 397 and 398 of the Companies Act, 1956 (read with Section 59 of the 2013 Act) protect members from being illegally removed from management and from unauthorized dilution or transfer of their shares by the majority block[cite: 10]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal examined the Articles of Association, the absence of documented meeting notices to the removed directors, the lack of recorded board resolutions, and the failure to disclose shareholding alterations in statutory Annual Returns[cite: 10]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT found no error in the NCLT's judgment, concluding that the Appellants failed to prove the minority shareholders resigned voluntarily or that the share transfers were conducted legally, thus upholding the finding of oppression[cite: 10].
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed[cite: 10]. The NCLT Chennai's order allowing the petition for oppression and mismanagement is upheld[cite: 10]. No order as to costs[cite: 10].
summary: The Respondents, original directors of M/s. Vijaya Hospitality and Resorts Limited, filed an oppression and mismanagement petition alleging they were illegally ousted from the Board using forged resignation letters and that over 3.4 million shares were unlawfully transferred without appearing in the company's Annual Returns[cite: 10]. The NCLT Chennai allowed the petition, finding the actions to be oppressive[cite: 10]. The Appellants appealed, contending the Respondents had resigned voluntarily[cite: 10]. The NCLAT completely dismissed the appeal, holding that the total absence of formal meeting notices, valid board resolutions, and proper statutory disclosures proved the removals and share transfers were executed illegally[cite: 10]. The Tribunal affirmed that such clandestine corporate maneuvers constitute severe oppression, thus upholding the NCLT's restorative orders[cite: 10].

case_title: D-ART Furniture Systems Pvt. Ltd. vs Sudhir Sales & Service Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is D-ART Furniture Systems Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor), and the Respondent is Sudhir Sales & Service Ltd. (Operational Creditor)[cite: 12]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: The dispute arises from an underlying operational debt, though specific details of the goods or services are not mentioned[cite: 12]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The failure to pay the operational debt resulted in the initiation of an insolvency petition[cite: 12]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: On 24.10.2017, the NCLT granted the Operational Creditor 7 days to issue a proper notice, despite Section 8(1) requiring a mandatory 10-day period[cite: 12]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The initial demand notice was issued by an Advocate rather than in the prescribed Form-3 or Form-4, rendering it legally defective for IBC purposes[cite: 12]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The NCLT Principal Bench in C.P. No. (IB)-313)PB)/2017 allowed the Operational Creditor 7 days to issue a proper notice[cite: 12]. The Corporate Debtor appealed, arguing that a Section 9 application cannot be entertained without a prior, valid 10-day notice[cite: 12].
legal_issues: Whether an application under Section 9 of the IBC can be entertained if the statutory demand notice under Section 8 was issued by a lawyer without following the prescribed Form-3 or Form-4 and without waiting for the mandatory 10-day period?[cite: 12]
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An application for corporate insolvency resolution by an operational creditor cannot be entertained unless a valid demand notice is served in the prescribed format and the mandatory 10-day statutory period has elapsed[cite: 12]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Under Section 8 of the IBC, a demand notice must be issued in Form-3 or Form-4 to ensure the corporate debtor understands the severe consequences of non-payment; a normal pleader or advocate's notice under Section 80 of the CPC or Section 433 of the Companies Act is invalid[cite: 12]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal noted the undisputed admission that the original notice was improperly issued by a lawyer and that the mandatory 10-day period had not been observed before the application was entertained[cite: 12]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Conceding the defect, the Operational Creditor requested to withdraw the application[cite: 12]. The NCLAT accepted the withdrawal and mandated the issuance of a proper Section 8(1) notice before filing any fresh application[cite: 12].
operative_order: Company Petition No. (IB)-313)PB)/2017 is dismissed as withdrawn[cite: 12]. The Adjudicating Authority is directed to close the proceedings[cite: 12]. The Respondent is granted liberty to issue a proper Section 8(1) demand notice and file a fresh application upon failure to pay[cite: 12].
summary: The Operational Creditor initiated Section 9 IBC proceedings against the Corporate Debtor[cite: 12]. Recognizing a defect in the demand notice, the NCLT allowed the Operational Creditor 7 days to issue a proper Section 8 notice, prompting an appeal by the Corporate Debtor to the NCLAT[cite: 12]. The Corporate Debtor successfully argued that the initial notice, sent by a lawyer rather than in the prescribed statutory form, was defective and that a 10-day waiting period is strictly mandatory before a Section 9 application can be entertained[cite: 12]. Acknowledging this legal deficiency, the Operational Creditor elected to withdraw the petition[cite: 12]. The NCLAT dismissed the petition as withdrawn and instructed the NCLT to close the proceedings, reserving liberty for the Operational Creditor to issue a fresh, compliant notice[cite: 12].

case_title: Hindustan Motors Ltd vs Na
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is Hindustan Motors Ltd.[cite: 13]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: The Appellant sought permission to effect the sale of its 'Ambassador Brand' to Peugeot Citroen Automobiles S.A.[cite: 13]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The company was a sick industrial unit involved in rehabilitation proceedings before the BIFR[cite: 13]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The Sick Industrial Companies (Special Provisions) Repeal Act, 2003 came into force on 01.12.2016, giving companies 180 days to make a reference to the NCLT under the newly enacted IBC[cite: 13]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Instead of filing an insolvency petition under the IBC, the Appellant filed an application purely seeking a declaration that old BIFR orders were void and requesting permission to sell its brand[cite: 13]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The Appellant's original BIFR petition (Case No. 28/2014) abated[cite: 13]. The Appellant filed a clarification petition (No. 83/2017) before NCLT Kolkata, which dismissed it as not maintainable[cite: 13]. The Appellant appealed to the NCLAT[cite: 13].
legal_issues: Whether an independent application seeking clarification on the abatement of BIFR orders and permission to sell corporate assets is maintainable before the NCLT without initiating the corporate insolvency resolution process under the IBC?[cite: 13]
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Upon the abatement of proceedings before the BIFR due to the SICA Repeal Act, a company cannot seek independent declaratory relief or permission to sell assets from the NCLT without formally initiating insolvency proceedings under the IBC[cite: 13]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The Eighth Schedule of the IBC amended SICA to stipulate that all pending BIFR proceedings abate entirely[cite: 13]. The only remedy provided is the liberty to make a fresh reference to the NCLT under the IBC within 180 days[cite: 13]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal noted the Appellant had not filed any petition for a corporate insolvency resolution process under the IBC, rendering the standalone application for clarification completely non-maintainable[cite: 13]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT affirmed the NCLT's ruling that proceedings in the nature of clarification under the SICA Repeal Act are not maintainable before the Tribunal once the underlying proceedings have abated, and the appellant must follow the IBC route[cite: 13].
operative_order: The appeal stands disposed of (effectively dismissed)[cite: 13]. The NCLAT declined to interfere with the NCLT's judgment dismissing the petition as non-maintainable[cite: 13].
summary: Hindustan Motors Ltd. originally filed a reference before the BIFR in 2014 for rehabilitation[cite: 13]. Following the enforcement of the IBC and the repeal of SICA, these pending BIFR proceedings legally abated[cite: 13]. Rather than initiating formal corporate insolvency proceedings under the IBC within the permitted 180-day window, the company filed a petition before NCLT Kolkata seeking a clarification that previous BIFR orders were void and requesting permission to sell its 'Ambassador Brand'[cite: 13]. The NCLT dismissed the petition as not maintainable[cite: 13]. The NCLAT affirmed this dismissal, holding that standalone clarification applications under the repealed SICA are not maintainable and a company's sole recourse is to initiate formal proceedings under the IBC[cite: 13].

case_title: M/s. Hyosan Automative India Pvt. Ltd. vs Metecno (India) Pvt. Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is M/s. Hyosan Automative India Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor) and the Respondent is Metecno (India) Pvt. Ltd. (Operational Creditor)[cite: 14]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: The matter originates from an operational debt leading to a winding-up petition under the Companies Act, 1956[cite: 14]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The petition was initially filed for the inability to pay debts, though specific financial metrics are not detailed[cite: 14]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The NCLT admitted the petition on 16.08.2017[cite: 14]. The Operational Creditor failed to submit the required IBC Section 9 information within 60 days of the Transfer Rules notification (07.12.2016)[cite: 14]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: It was an undisputed fact that the Operational Creditor did not issue the mandatory Section 8 notice or propose an Interim Resolution Professional (IRP) as required by Rule 5[cite: 14]. Furthermore, the parties settled the dispute during the appeal[cite: 14]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: A winding-up petition was transferred to NCLT Chennai, which treated it as a Section 9 IBC application, admitted it, and appointed an IRP[cite: 14]. The Corporate Debtor challenged this admission order before the NCLAT[cite: 14].
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority erred in admitting a transferred winding-up petition as a Section 9 IBC application when the operational creditor failed to comply with the mandatory requirements of Rule 5, including issuing a Section 8 notice?[cite: 14]
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A transferred winding-up petition cannot be validly admitted as an application under Section 9 of the IBC if the petition is incomplete and the operational creditor has failed to fulfill mandatory statutory prerequisites[cite: 14]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Rule 5 of the Companies (Transfer of Pending Proceedings) Rules, 2016 mandates the submission of all necessary information for a Section 9 admission—including a proposed IRP and compliance with the Section 8 demand notice requirement—within 60 days of transfer[cite: 14]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal noted that it was completely undisputed by the Operational Creditor that the IBC provisions and Rule 5 requirements were not followed in letter and spirit, and no Section 8 notice was placed on record[cite: 14]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT concluded that the incomplete application was entirely unfit for admission and should have been rejected by the NCLT[cite: 14]. Acknowledging the procedural failure and the subsequent settlement between the parties, the NCLAT set aside the admission[cite: 14].
operative_order: The impugned order dated 16.08.2017 is set aside[cite: 14]. The appointment of the IRP, moratorium, and all related actions are declared illegal[cite: 14]. The Section 9 application is dismissed, proceedings are closed, and the Corporate Debtor is released to function independently[cite: 14]. The Respondent is ordered to pay the IRP's fees[cite: 14].
summary: The Respondent's winding-up petition against the Appellant under the Companies Act, 1956 was transferred to the NCLT, which subsequently admitted it as a Section 9 application under the IBC and appointed an IRP[cite: 14]. The Appellant challenged this admission before the NCLAT, arguing that the Respondent critically failed to comply with Rule 5 of the Transfer Rules, missing the 60-day deadline to submit required information and failing to issue a mandatory Section 8 demand notice[cite: 14]. Noting that these statutory deficiencies were completely undisputed by the Respondent and that the parties had ultimately settled their dispute, the NCLAT held the application was legally incomplete and should have been rejected outright[cite: 14]. Consequently, the NCLAT set aside the admission order, lifted the moratorium, and restored the Corporate Debtor to its own management[cite: 14].

case_title: Vasan Healthcare Pvt. Ltd. vs M/s. Alcon Laboratories (India) Pvt. Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is Vasan Healthcare Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor), and the Respondent is M/s. Alcon Laboratories (India) Pvt. Ltd. (Operational Creditor)[cite: 15]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: An operational debt underlying the Section 9 IBC application[cite: 15]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The specific default amount is not mentioned, but the failure to pay resulted in parallel legal proceedings[cite: 15]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The NCLT admitted the Section 9 application on 21.04.2017[cite: 15]. Subsequently, the Madras High Court stayed the insolvency proceedings on 04.05.2017[cite: 15]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: A winding-up petition under Section 433(e) of the Companies Act, 1956 was simultaneously pending before the Madras High Court, where the Appellant successfully obtained a stay against the NCLT's resolution process[cite: 15]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Chennai admitted the Respondent's Section 9 petition[cite: 15]. The Appellant appealed to the NCLAT but simultaneously approached the Madras High Court to obtain a stay[cite: 15]. Facing dismissal from the NCLAT for pursuing parallel remedies, the Appellant withdrew the appeal[cite: 15].
legal_issues: Whether an appeal against a Section 9 IBC admission order can be maintained before the NCLAT when the appellant has already sought and obtained a parallel stay order from a High Court in a pending winding-up petition?[cite: 15]
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An appellant cannot maintain an appeal before an appellate tribunal against an insolvency admission order while simultaneously pursuing and securing the same relief through a stay order from a High Court[cite: 15]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 238 of the IBC explicitly grants the Code overriding effect over other laws, creating a severe doubt regarding the jurisdiction of a High Court under Section 433(e) of the Companies Act, 1956 to stay an NCLT's insolvency process[cite: 15]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal observed the undisputed fact that the Appellant had already secured a stay order from the Madras High Court on 04.05.2017, effectively utilizing an alternative judicial remedy for the same grievance[cite: 15]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Concluding that the Appellant was engaging in forum shopping by holding a stay from the High Court, the NCLAT indicated it would dismiss the appeal[cite: 15]. The Appellant consequently withdrew the appeal, which the NCLAT permitted without granting any liberty to challenge the NCLT order again[cite: 15].
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed as withdrawn[cite: 15]. No liberty is granted to the Appellant to move against the impugned order dated 21.04.2017 passed by the Adjudicating Authority[cite: 15].
summary: The NCLT Chennai admitted a Section 9 IBC application filed by the Operational Creditor against the Corporate Debtor[cite: 15]. The Corporate Debtor appealed to the NCLAT but simultaneously approached the Madras High Court—where an older winding-up petition was pending—and successfully obtained an order staying the NCLT's insolvency proceedings[cite: 15]. The NCLAT expressed strong legal doubt regarding the High Court's jurisdiction to interfere with IBC proceedings given the strict overriding effect of Section 238 of the Code[cite: 15]. Confronted by the NCLAT for pursuing parallel remedies and securing a stay elsewhere, the Corporate Debtor requested to withdraw the appeal[cite: 15]. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal as withdrawn, explicitly denying the Corporate Debtor any liberty to challenge the NCLT's admission order in the future[cite: 15].

case_title: VDS Plastics Pvt. Ltd. vs Pal Mohan Electronics (P) Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is VDS Plastics Pvt. Ltd. (Operational Creditor) and the Respondent is Pal Mohan Electronics (P) Ltd. (Corporate Debtor)[cite: 16]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: The dispute concerns the supply of goods and materials by the Appellant to the Respondent[cite: 16]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The Appellant claimed a total value of Rs. 1,48,37,586, with a part payment received, leaving an alleged outstanding balance of Rs. 90,80,976[cite: 16]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: A statutory winding-up notice under the Companies Act was issued on 01.08.2016[cite: 16]. The Corporate Debtor issued a reply denying the claim on 20.09.2016[cite: 16]. The NCLT passed the impugned order on 21.04.2017[cite: 16]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The Corporate Debtor's reply letter dated 20.09.2016 explicitly denied receiving the goods and disputed the outstanding balance, establishing a pre-existing dispute before the Section 8 IBC notice was ever issued[cite: 16]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The Appellant filed a Section 9 application under the IBC[cite: 16]. The NCLT New Delhi rejected the application, observing the existence of a dispute[cite: 16]. The Appellant challenged this rejection before the NCLAT[cite: 16].
legal_issues: Whether a Section 9 application under the IBC can be admitted when correspondence prior to the Section 8 notice demonstrates a clear denial of goods received and an existing dispute over the debt?[cite: 16]
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An application for corporate insolvency resolution by an operational creditor must be rejected if documentary evidence establishes a pre-existing dispute regarding the debt or supply of goods before the issuance of the statutory demand notice[cite: 16]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Under Section 9 of the IBC, the Adjudicating Authority must reject the application if there is a 'dispute in existence' as evidenced by a reply to a previous statutory notice (such as under Sections 433/434 of the Companies Act, 1956)[cite: 16]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal examined the pre-IBC correspondence, specifically the August 2016 winding-up notice and the Corporate Debtor's subsequent reply comprehensively denying the supply and debt, concluding this constituted a valid, pre-existing dispute[cite: 16]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT upheld the NCLT's decision, affirming that the explicit denial of the claim in September 2016 established a clear pre-existing dispute, directly warranting the dismissal of the Section 9 application[cite: 16].
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed[cite: 16]. No order as to costs[cite: 16].
summary: The Operational Creditor filed a Section 9 IBC application against the Corporate Debtor[cite: 16]. The NCLT rejected the application due to a pre-existing dispute[cite: 16]. On appeal, the NCLAT reviewed pre-IBC correspondence, noting the Operational Creditor had sent a winding-up notice in August 2016, to which the Corporate Debtor replied in September 2016 categorically denying the receipt of goods and the alleged outstanding debt of Rs. 90,80,976[cite: 16]. The NCLAT held that this exchange clearly established a dispute in existence prior to the Section 8 notice and upheld the NCLT's dismissal of the application[cite: 16].

case_title: Deihite Niphko (India) Pvt. Ltd. & Anr. vs Registrar Of Companies, Delhi and Haryana
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellants are Deihite Niphko (India) Pvt. Ltd. and Mr. Inder Dev Sharma[cite: 18]. The Respondent is the Registrar of Companies (ROC), Delhi and Haryana[cite: 18]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Not applicable; involves statutory corporate registration and strike-off procedures[cite: 18]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The Company failed to file statutory documents (balance sheet and annual accounts) made up to 31.03.2006[cite: 18]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The Company applied for a strike-off under the Simplified Exit Scheme (SES), 2003, and was struck off the register via an Official Gazette notification on 08.09.2006[cite: 18]. The Board decided to apply for revival on 04.07.2015[cite: 18]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The Company voluntarily opted to have its name struck off under SES 2003, acting on its own volition rather than facing a suo moto action by the ROC[cite: 18]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The Appellants filed a petition under Section 560(6) of the Companies Act, 1956 before the Delhi High Court, which was transferred to NCLT New Delhi[cite: 18]. NCLT rejected the petition on 01.05.2017, and the Appellants subsequently appealed to the NCLAT[cite: 18].
legal_issues: Whether a company that voluntarily applied to have its name struck off under the Simplified Exit Scheme (SES), 2003 can later seek restoration of its name under Section 560(6) of the Companies Act, 1956?[cite: 18]
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A petition for the restoration of a company's name to the register is fundamentally not maintainable if the company was struck off voluntarily pursuant to an exit scheme rather than being struck off suo moto by the Registrar[cite: 18]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The restoration remedy under Section 560(6) of the Companies Act, 1956 is unavailable to a company that, on its own volition, exercised the option to be struck off under the Simplified Exit Scheme (SES), 2003 or similar fast-track exit schemes[cite: 18]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal relied on the undisputed fact that the company had voluntarily applied for the strike-off and that the ROC published the strike-off in the Official Gazette in September 2006[cite: 18]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT concluded that since the removal of the company's name was a deliberate, voluntary act by the Appellants and not a suo moto regulatory action by the ROC, the restoration petition was non-maintainable[cite: 18].
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed[cite: 18]. No order as to costs[cite: 18].
summary: The Appellant company voluntarily applied to have its name struck off the register under the Simplified Exit Scheme (SES), 2003, and the ROC officially struck it off via a gazette notification in September 2006[cite: 18]. Years later, the Appellants filed a petition for restoration under Section 560(6) of the Companies Act, 1956, claiming they only recently discovered the strike-off[cite: 18]. The NCLT rejected the petition as non-maintainable[cite: 18]. The NCLAT affirmed this dismissal, holding that a company cannot invoke Section 560(6) for restoration when its removal from the register was executed voluntarily on its own application rather than suo moto by the ROC[cite: 18].

case_title: Mr. Ashwinkumar Gupta vs Visagar Polytex Ltd. & M/s. Sudhirkumar Gupta vs Visagar Polytex Limited
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) No. 53 along with Company Appeal (AT) No. 54 of 2017
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellants are Mr. Ashwinkumar Gupta and M/s. Sudhirkumar Gupta (transferees)[cite: 19]. The Respondent is Visagar Polytex Ltd. (Company)[cite: 19]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Transfer of shares and issuance of fresh share certificates following a reduction in the face value of shares[cite: 19]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The Appellants sought a share transfer based on original shareholder consents obtained 17 to 20 years prior to the petition[cite: 19]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The formal transfer requests were made 17 to 20 years after the original shareholder consent was given[cite: 19]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The Respondent company raised questions regarding the genuineness of the aged share certificates and the signatures of the original shareholders[cite: 19]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The Appellants filed petitions under Section 111-A of the Companies Act, 1956 before the NCLT Mumbai to rectify the register of members[cite: 19]. NCLT rejected the petitions on grounds of limitation and imposed costs[cite: 19]. The Appellants appealed to the NCLAT[cite: 19].
legal_issues: Whether a company can be compelled to transfer shares and rectify its register of members based on the consent of original shareholders given 17 to 20 years ago?[cite: 19]
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A request for the transfer of shares cannot be legally effected if it relies on stale consent from original shareholders obtained decades prior, as extreme delay compromises the verifiability of the transfer[cite: 19]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: While leaving the strict applicability of the Limitation Act under Section 433 of the Companies Act, 2013 explicitly undecided, the Tribunal evaluated the equitable validity of Section 111-A petitions based on severely delayed documentation[cite: 19]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal scrutinized the timeline of the documents, finding that 17 to 20 years had lapsed since the original shareholders allegedly gave consent, rendering the transfer requests practically unexecutable without fresh documentation[cite: 19]. 4.
