DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT concluded the transfers could not be effected on the stale consents, directed the company to return the share certificates, and permitted the Appellants to withdraw their appeals to seek fresh consents[cite: 19].
operative_order: The NCLT's imposition of costs on the Appellants is set aside[cite: 19]. The appeals are disposed of as withdrawn, granting the Appellants liberty to file fresh applications for share transfer after obtaining fresh consent from the original shareholders[cite: 19]. The Respondent company is directed to return the submitted share certificates within one month[cite: 19].
summary: The Appellants filed petitions under Section 111-A of the Companies Act, 1956 to rectify the company's register of members and transfer shares based on consents from original shareholders given 17 to 20 years ago[cite: 19]. The NCLT dismissed the petitions on grounds of limitation and imposed costs[cite: 19]. On appeal, the NCLAT held that share transfers cannot be reliably effected on such severely belated consents, deciding the matter without delving strictly into the Limitation Act[cite: 19]. The NCLAT set aside the costs imposed by the NCLT and allowed the Appellants to withdraw their appeals, with liberty to obtain fresh consent from the original shareholders and re-apply[cite: 19].

case_title: Mrs. Rehana Choudhary vs M/s. Poonam Drums & Containers Pvt. Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is Mrs. Rehana Choudhary (Petitioner) and the Respondent is M/s. Poonam Drums & Containers Pvt. Ltd.[cite: 20]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: An alleged illegal sale of the company's land to a third party through a conveyance deed dated 29.02.2016[cite: 20]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The Appellant, holding 31% shareholding with family members, alleged the sale occurred without board meetings or notice, constituting oppression and mismanagement[cite: 20]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The contested land sale occurred on 29.02.2016[cite: 20]. The NCLT passed the impugned referral order on 21.12.2016[cite: 20]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The Respondents relied on an existing arbitration agreement dated 25.11.2015 to seek a referral of the dispute to an arbitrator[cite: 20]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The Appellant filed an oppression and mismanagement petition under Sections 241 and 242 of the Companies Act, 2013[cite: 20]. The Respondents filed an application (C.A. No. 149 of 2016) under Section 8 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996[cite: 20]. The NCLT Mumbai allowed the Section 8 application but concurrently observed there was no oppression and mismanagement, prompting the Appellant to appeal[cite: 20].
legal_issues: Whether a Tribunal can determine the merits of an oppression and mismanagement petition while concurrently allowing an application under Section 8 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 to refer the dispute to an arbitrator?[cite: 20]
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: When a judicial authority refers a dispute to arbitration under Section 8 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, it must refrain from making definitive observations or findings on the merits of the substantive dispute[cite: 20]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: A petition under Section 8 of the Arbitration Act strictly concerns the existence of a valid arbitration agreement and the arbitrability of the dispute, precluding the Tribunal from simultaneously adjudicating the substantive merits of a Section 241/242 Companies Act petition[cite: 20]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal noted that both parties explicitly agreed to proceed to arbitration; thus, any preliminary merits-based observations by the NCLT on the substantive oppression claims were entirely unwarranted[cite: 20]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT directed that the dispute be resolved by the arbitrator on its merits, strictly uninfluenced by the NCLT's premature observations regarding the absence of oppression and mismanagement[cite: 20].
operative_order: The appeal is disposed of[cite: 20]. The parties are directed to raise their claims and counterclaims before the Arbitrator[cite: 20]. The Arbitrator must decide the matter on its merits, uninfluenced by the NCLT's observations regarding oppression and mismanagement[cite: 20]. Parties are barred from referring to the NCLT's merits-based observations during the arbitration[cite: 20].
summary: The Appellant filed an oppression and mismanagement petition against the Respondent company regarding an allegedly covert land sale[cite: 20]. The Respondent moved a Section 8 application under the Arbitration Act based on a prior agreement[cite: 20]. The NCLT referred the matter to arbitration but simultaneously recorded a finding that there was no oppression or mismanagement on the Respondent's part[cite: 20]. The Appellant appealed, arguing the NCLT lacked jurisdiction to decide the merits while referring the case to arbitration[cite: 20]. Since both parties agreed to arbitrate, the NCLAT disposed of the appeal by directing the Arbitrator to adjudicate the dispute strictly on merits, completely uninfluenced by the NCLT's premature observations[cite: 20].

case_title: Prowess International Pvt. Ltd. vs Jaybalaji Industries Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is Prowess International Pvt. Ltd. and the Respondent is Jaybalaji Industries Ltd.[cite: 21]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Underlying dispute leading to a winding-up petition, though specific commercial details are not elaborated[cite: 21]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Winding-up was sought based on an alleged debt, though specific financial metrics are not mentioned[cite: 21]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The original High Court winding-up petition was dismissed on 21.09.2016, and a subsequent NCLT petition was filed on 05.01.2017[cite: 21]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The Appellant attempted to file a second petition under the old Companies Act before the NCLT after the first was dismissed by the High Court[cite: 21]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The NCLT Kolkata dismissed the second winding-up petition on 31.08.2017 as non-maintainable[cite: 21]. The Appellant challenged this dismissal by filing an appeal under Section 61 of the IBC before the NCLAT[cite: 21].
legal_issues: Whether an appeal under Section 61 of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code (IBC) is maintainable against an order dismissing a winding-up petition filed strictly under Sections 433, 434, and 439 of the Companies Act, 1956?[cite: 21]
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An appeal filed under the statutory framework of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code is not maintainable if the underlying petition was instituted and decided strictly under the provisions of the Companies Act, 1956[cite: 21]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 61 of the IBC provides an appellate remedy exclusively for orders passed under the IBC, and cannot be invoked to challenge the dismissal of a winding-up petition filed under Sections 433, 434, and 439 of the Companies Act, 1956[cite: 21]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal noted the admitted procedural fact that the petition before the NCLT was explicitly filed under the Companies Act, 1956, and not under Section 9 of the IBC[cite: 21]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT concluded that because the original petition was filed and held non-maintainable under the Companies Act, an appeal under Section 61 of the IBC is also non-maintainable[cite: 21].
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed as not maintainable[cite: 21]. No costs[cite: 21].
summary: The Appellant originally filed a winding-up petition against the Respondent before the Calcutta High Court under the Companies Act, 1956, which was dismissed in 2016[cite: 21]. In January 2017, the Appellant filed another petition under the same provisions before NCLT Kolkata, which rejected it as non-maintainable[cite: 21]. The Appellant then filed an appeal under Section 61 of the IBC to challenge this rejection[cite: 21]. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that since the underlying petition was instituted and adjudicated under Sections 433, 434, and 439 of the Companies Act, 1956, an appeal invoking Section 61 of the IBC is legally non-maintainable[cite: 21].

case_title: Mr. Vinod Kumar Sharma vs M/s. Bhawani Cold Storage Pvt. Ltd. & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is Mr. Vinod Kumar Sharma (Petitioner) and the Respondents include M/s. Bhawani Cold Storage Pvt. Ltd.[cite: 22]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Not applicable; the dispute centers on internal corporate management and shareholding[cite: 22]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The Appellant alleged oppression and mismanagement by the corporate respondents[cite: 22]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The original Company Petition (C.P. No. 68/ND/2010) was filed before the Tribunal, culminating in the impugned order[cite: 22]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: It was an admitted fact by the Appellant's counsel that the Appellant held only 0.5% of the total shareholding and did not represent 100 members or one-tenth of the total number of members[cite: 22]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The Appellant filed a petition under Sections 397 and 398 of the Companies Act, 1956[cite: 22]. The NCLT Allahabad dismissed the petition as non-maintainable due to a lack of requisite shareholding[cite: 22]. The Appellant appealed this dismissal to the NCLAT[cite: 22].
legal_issues: Whether a petition for oppression and mismanagement under Sections 397 and 398 of the Companies Act, 1956 is maintainable if the petitioner holds only 0.5% of the total issued share capital?[cite: 22]
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A shareholder must possess the statutorily mandated minimum shareholding or numerical strength to have the legal standing (locus standi) to maintain a petition for oppression and mismanagement[cite: 22]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 399 of the Companies Act, 1956 explicitly requires that such a petition be filed by either 100 members, one-tenth of the total number of members, or members holding not less than one-tenth of the issued share capital[cite: 22]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal relied entirely on the undisputed admission that the Appellant possessed a mere 0.5% shareholding, drastically short of the required threshold[cite: 22]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT affirmed the NCLT's dismissal, concluding that the Appellant failed to meet the strict eligibility criteria under Section 399, rendering the petition non-maintainable from the outset[cite: 22].
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed[cite: 22]. The NCLT order dismissing the Company Petition as non-maintainable stands[cite: 22].
summary: The Appellant filed a petition alleging oppression and mismanagement against the Respondent company under Sections 397 and 398 of the Companies Act, 1956[cite: 22]. The NCLT Allahabad dismissed the petition on maintainability grounds, noting that the Appellant did not hold the requisite shareholding[cite: 22]. On appeal, the Appellant's counsel explicitly admitted that the Appellant held a mere 0.5% of the company's total shares and did not represent 100 members or one-tenth of the total members[cite: 22]. Applying Section 399 of the Companies Act, 1956, the NCLAT ruled that the Appellant lacked the statutory locus standi to maintain the petition and dismissed the appeal[cite: 22].

case_title: Engenious Engineering Pvt. Ltd. vs Onaex Natura Pvt. Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is Engenious Engineering Pvt. Ltd. and the Respondent is Onaex Natura Pvt. Ltd.[cite: 23]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: The Appellant previously invested an amount with the Respondent company and was allotted equity shares[cite: 23]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Following the cancellation of the share allotment by the former Company Law Board, an amount of Rs. 79,15,480 was allegedly lying with the Respondent and shown as a debt[cite: 23]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The NCLT Ahmedabad rejected the Section 7 petition on 20.09.2017[cite: 23]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The principal sum arose from a cancelled equity investment, which the Appellant argued converted them into a financial creditor because the un-refunded amount was recorded as a debt in the company's books[cite: 23]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The Appellant filed a Section 7 IBC petition before NCLT Ahmedabad[cite: 23]. The NCLT rejected it, holding the Appellant was not a 'Financial Creditor'[cite: 23]. The Appellant challenged this rejection before the NCLAT[cite: 23].
legal_issues: Whether an investor whose equity share allotment was cancelled, and whose un-refunded investment is subsequently shown as a debt in the company's records, qualifies as a 'Financial Creditor' under Section 5(8) read with Section 5(9) of the IBC?[cite: 23]
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An equity investor whose share allotment is legally cancelled does not automatically transform into a financial creditor merely because the refund amount is recorded as a debt in the company's books[cite: 23]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: To maintain a petition under Section 7, the applicant must strictly meet the definition of a 'Financial Creditor' under Sections 5(8) and 5(9) of the IBC, which fundamentally requires a financial debt disbursed against the consideration for the time value of money[cite: 23]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal noted that the genesis of the funds was an equity investment for share capital, not a loan, deposit, or financial facility advanced for interest or time value[cite: 23]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT concluded that even if the un-refunded investment amount was shown as a debt in the records, it did not satisfy the statutory definition of a financial debt, thereby disqualifying the Appellant from invoking Section 7[cite: 23].
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed with no costs[cite: 23]. The Appellant is granted liberty to move the appropriate forum for relief regarding the un-refunded amount[cite: 23].
summary: The Appellant invested in the Respondent company and received equity shares, which were later cancelled by the Company Law Board in an oppression and mismanagement petition under the Companies Act, 1956[cite: 23]. Asserting that the un-refunded investment amount of Rs. 79,15,480 was shown as a debt in the company's records, the Appellant filed a Section 7 IBC insolvency petition[cite: 23]. The NCLT rejected the petition[cite: 23]. The NCLAT affirmed the rejection, ruling that funds originating from a cancelled equity allotment do not constitute a financial debt under Sections 5(8) and 5(9) of the IBC[cite: 23]. Thus, the Appellant did not qualify as a 'Financial Creditor' and could not initiate insolvency proceedings[cite: 23].

case_title: Organosyn Life Sciences Pvt. Ltd. & Ors. vs Registrar Of Companies, Nct Of Delhi & Haryana
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellants are Organosyn Life Sciences Pvt. Ltd. and its Directors[cite: 24]. The Respondent is the Registrar of Companies (ROC), NCT of Delhi & Haryana[cite: 24]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Not applicable; the dispute relates to statutory corporate compliance[cite: 24]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The Company failed to hold its Annual General Meeting (AGM) within the mandatory timeframe, triggering compounding fines[cite: 24]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The default period for not holding the AGM spanned from 01.10.2015 to 01.07.2016[cite: 24]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The ROC proposed a compounding fine of Rs. 14,65,000 for each appellant (the maximum limit)[cite: 24]. The NCLT exercised discretion and reduced this fine to Rs. 3,00,000 for each appellant[cite: 24]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The Appellants filed an application for compounding the offense under Section 441 of the Companies Act, 2013 before NCLT Delhi[cite: 24]. Seeking further leniency due to business losses in Ukraine, the Appellants appealed to the NCLAT[cite: 24].
legal_issues: Whether the Appellate Tribunal should further reduce a compounding fine that the NCLT had already significantly reduced from the statutory maximum proposed by the ROC, based on the company's foreign business losses?[cite: 24]
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An appellate tribunal will not interfere with the quantum of a compounding fine if the adjudicating authority has already exercised its discretion to impose a significantly reduced penalty and the defaulting party provides no valid legal justification for the statutory violation[cite: 24]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 99 of the Companies Act, 2013 imposes strict penalties (up to Rs. 1,00,000 plus Rs. 5,000 per day for continuing default) for violating the AGM requirements under Section 96(1)[cite: 24]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal noted that the Appellants offered no valid reason for failing to hold the AGM during the default period, merely citing external business losses (currency devaluation in Ukraine) which do not legally excuse domestic statutory non-compliance[cite: 24]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT concluded that since the NCLT had already drastically reduced the fine from Rs. 14,65,000 to Rs. 3 Lakhs per appellant, there were no legal or equitable grounds for further interference or leniency[cite: 24].
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed[cite: 24]. No order as to costs[cite: 24].
summary: The Appellant company and its directors failed to hold an Annual General Meeting between October 2015 and July 2016, violating Section 96(1) of the Companies Act, 2013[cite: 24]. They applied for compounding under Section 441[cite: 24]. While the ROC proposed the maximum statutory penalty of Rs. 14,65,000 per appellant, the NCLT Delhi exercised leniency and reduced the fine to Rs. 3,00,000 each[cite: 24]. The Appellants appealed to the NCLAT seeking a further reduction, arguing they suffered business losses due to currency devaluation in Ukraine[cite: 24]. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that foreign business losses do not excuse statutory non-compliance and that the NCLT had already granted substantial and adequate relief[cite: 24].

case_title: SN Santosh Kumar vs S. Martin & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is SN Santosh Kumar (Respondent No. 2 below)[cite: 25]. The Respondents are S. Martin (Petitioner/1st Respondent) and Akshaya Textiles Limited (Company)[cite: 25]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: A transfer of 5,40,000 shares based on a Memorandum of Understanding dated 14.11.2005 and a Sale Agreement dated 19.11.2005[cite: 25]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The Company failed to rectify its register to record the transfer of the 5,40,000 shares in favor of S. Martin[cite: 25]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The contested agreements date back to November 2005[cite: 25]. NCLT Chennai passed its final order on 22.03.2017[cite: 25]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The Appellant signed the transfer documents and received consideration via Demand Drafts, which he encashed, but later alleged his father subjected him to 'undue influence' to execute the transfer[cite: 25]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: S. Martin filed a petition under Section 111A of the Companies Act, 1956 to rectify the register of members[cite: 25]. The NCLT Chennai allowed the petition, rejecting the Appellant's belated application under Rule 39 to adduce evidence of undue influence[cite: 25]. The Appellant appealed to the NCLAT[cite: 25].
legal_issues: Whether the NCLT has the jurisdiction to conduct a trial-like inquiry into allegations of 'undue influence' in the execution of a share transfer agreement during summary proceedings for rectification of the register of members under Section 111A of the Companies Act, 1956?[cite: 25]
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Summary proceedings for the rectification of a register of members are not the appropriate forum to adjudicate complex evidentiary claims of undue influence, coercion, or fraud, which must instead be agitated before a competent civil court[cite: 25]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 111A of the Companies Act, 1956 vests the Tribunal with limited jurisdiction for rectification, precluding it from transforming the petition into a regular civil suit to test the validity of underlying contracts based on undue influence[cite: 25]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal noted the Appellant acquiesced by accepting the consideration (encashing DDs) and critically failed to initiate any civil suit to set aside the 2005 Sale Agreement over a span of several years[cite: 25]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT upheld the NCLT's decision, agreeing that the Tribunal completely lacked jurisdiction to decide the element of undue influence, and correctly directed the company to rectify the register of members[cite: 25].
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed[cite: 25]. The NCLT order directing the Company to rectify the register of members by entering the name of the Petitioner (S. Martin) and removing the name of the Appellant is upheld[cite: 25]. No order as to costs[cite: 25].
summary: The Respondent (S. Martin) filed a petition under Section 111A of the Companies Act, 1956 to rectify the company's register and record the transfer of 5,40,000 shares acquired via a 2005 agreement[cite: 25]. The Appellant, whose shares were transferred, opposed the petition, claiming his father used 'undue influence' to make him sign the transfer forms[cite: 25]. The NCLT Chennai allowed the transfer and rejected the Appellant's application to adduce evidence of undue influence, noting he had encashed the consideration and never filed a civil suit to cancel the agreement[cite: 25]. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, ruling that the Tribunal lacks jurisdiction to conduct a complex civil trial regarding undue influence within summary rectification proceedings under Section 111A[cite: 25].

case_title: Girish Kumar Bansal & Ors vs R.R. Sheetgrah Pvt Ltd. & Ors
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants are Girish Kumar Bansal & Ors (third party investors/directors). Respondents are R.R. Sheetgrah Pvt Ltd (Company), Rajendra Singh & Ranveer Singh (original promoters/Petitioners)[cite: 1]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: The company had an NPA credit facility of Rs 1.80 crores with Syndicate Bank, leading promoters to invite Appellants to infuse funds in exchange for shares and directorships[cite: 1]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Rs 1.80 crores owed to Syndicate Bank; exact default date not stated[cite: 1]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Control transfer agreements were executed on 15.09.2011 and an affidavit on 28.12.2011[cite: 1]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Board meeting minutes dated 18.2.2013 showed an increase in authorized capital from Rs 10 lakhs to Rs 35 lakhs and allotment of 2 lakh shares to Naveen Agarwal without notice to the original promoters[cite: 1]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Petitioners filed CP No. 15(ND)/2013 for oppression; NCLT Allahabad allowed it on 16.12.2015[cite: 1]. Appellants challenged this before the NCLAT[cite: 1].
legal_issues: Whether the capital increase and share allotment by the investors, following a private management transfer agreement, constituted oppression and mismanagement[cite: 1].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A private internal agreement transferring management control does not strip original shareholders of their statutory rights to challenge illegal share dilution or unauthorized capital increases[cite: 1]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Sections 397 and 398 of the Companies Act, 1956 allow relief when incoming management conducts board meetings to increase capital and allot shares without mandatory notice to existing shareholders[cite: 1]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal scrutinized the statutory filings and found the 18.2.2013 allotment invalid as it exceeded the authorized capital available on that day and lacked valid notice[cite: 1]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT upheld the finding of oppression, ruling that the investors' financial infusion did not clothe them with the right to illegally oust the original promoters[cite: 1].
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed with no costs. Liberty is granted to aggrieved parties to approach the appropriate forum regarding the transfer of shares to third parties[cite: 1].
summary: Original promoters filed an oppression petition alleging that incoming investors illegally ousted them and diluted their shares to take absolute control[cite: 1]. The NCLT found the capital increase and share allotment void due to a lack of notice and statutory compliance[cite: 1]. The NCLAT dismissed the investors' appeal, holding that management agreements do not extinguish statutory rights against oppression[cite: 1].

case_title: The Punjab Produce & Trading Co. Pvt. Ltd vs Pilani Investments & Corporation Ltd & Ors
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant/Petitioner is The Punjab Produce & Trading Co. Pvt. Ltd. Respondents include Pilani Investments & Corporation Ltd (1st Respondent) and Century Textiles and Industries Limited (8th Respondent)[cite: 2]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Dispute over the 1st Respondent voting to approve a preferential allotment of warrants by the 8th Respondent, diluting the 1st Respondent's shareholding from 36.78% to 30.54%[cite: 2]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: N/A, dispute pertains to shareholder voting rights and alleged share dilution[cite: 2]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The disputed preferential allotment resolution was passed on 29.05.2014[cite: 2]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The 1st Respondent held shares in the 8th Respondent, but they lacked a formal holding-subsidiary relationship[cite: 2]. The 8th Respondent filed interlocutory applications for deletion from the petition[cite: 2]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Kolkata allowed the applications on 23.12.2016, deleting the 8th to 18th respondents from the oppression petition[cite: 2]. The Appellant challenged this deletion[cite: 2].
legal_issues: Whether a separate entity (8th Respondent) and its directors can be impleaded in an oppression and mismanagement petition concerning the 1st Respondent, without a holding-subsidiary relationship[cite: 2].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Entities that do not share a holding-subsidiary relationship with the subject company of an oppression petition cannot be impleaded as respondents if the petitioner lacks locus standi in those specific entities[cite: 2]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 399 of the Companies Act, 1956 restricts the right to file oppression claims to shareholders of the specific company being mismanaged; it does not extend to other companies where the petitioner holds no qualifying shares[cite: 2]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal established that the 1st Respondent was merely the single largest shareholder, not the holding company, of the 8th Respondent, precluding the petitioner from challenging the 8th Respondent's internal acts[cite: 2]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT affirmed that the 8th Respondent and its directors were neither necessary nor proper parties, dismissing the appeal[cite: 2].
operative_order: The appeals are dismissed with no order as to costs. The NCLT's deletion of the 8th to 18th Respondents from the company petition is upheld[cite: 2].
summary: The appellant challenged the deletion of Century Textiles (8th Respondent) from its oppression petition against Pilani Investments (1st Respondent)[cite: 2]. The appellant claimed Pilani's directors wrongfully allowed Century Textiles to dilute Pilani's shareholding[cite: 2]. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, ruling that since there was no holding-subsidiary relationship and the appellant held no shares in Century Textiles, it could not legally implead them[cite: 2].

case_title: Jagdale Industries Private Limited & Others vs Dr. Ujwala.N. Jagdale @ Ujwala S Disle & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants are Jagdale Industries Private Limited & Ors. Respondents are Dr. Ujwala N. Jagdale & Ors (members of the Jagdale family)[cite: 3]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Dispute over the distribution of the estate and control of family businesses (JIPL, GLPL, RJU) following the death of the family patriarch, R. Nagaraja Rao[cite: 3]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: N/A, dispute relates to family business control and inheritance[cite: 3]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: NCLT passed the impugned interim order on 16.06.2017. A formal family settlement was executed on 19.08.2017[cite: 3]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The parties presented a mediated 'Memorandum of Confirmation of Oral Family Settlement' dated 19.08.2017, comprehensively distributing shares, lands, and mandating resignations of specific directors[cite: 3]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Respondents initially filed CP No. 28 of 2016 for oppression and mismanagement, securing an interim order restoring them as directors[cite: 3]. Appellants appealed to the NCLAT, during which a settlement was reached[cite: 3].
legal_issues: Whether the NCLAT should dispose of the oppression and mismanagement appeal by substituting the lower court's interim order with a comprehensively mediated family settlement agreement[cite: 3].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: When parties to a family corporate dispute reach a comprehensive, mediated settlement, the appellate tribunal will recognize the agreement and issue directions enforcing its terms instead of adjudicating the merits of the oppression claims[cite: 3]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: N/A; the dispute was resolved via private mediation outside of statutory adjudication[cite: 3]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal relied entirely on the joint 'Memorandum of Compromise on Oral Family Settlement' as evidence that all inter-se disputes regarding the family businesses and estate had been resolved[cite: 3]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT accepted the settlement, making its terms binding directions of the Tribunal, and ordered the lower court to close the main petition upon verifying compliance[cite: 3].
operative_order: The appeal is disposed of in terms of the Memorandum of Compromise on Oral Family Settlement dated 19.08.2017, which is treated as a direction of the Tribunal. NCLT is directed to verify compliance and close the Company Petition. No costs[cite: 3].
summary: In an oppression and mismanagement dispute involving the Jagdale family businesses, the NCLT issued an interim order restoring the respondents to the board[cite: 3]. The appellants challenged this order at the NCLAT[cite: 3]. During the pendency of the appeal, the family reached a mediated settlement distributing assets and directorships[cite: 3]. Consequently, the NCLAT disposed of the appeal by adopting the settlement terms as binding directions, effectively resolving the dispute[cite: 3].

case_title: Jankalyan Vinimay Pvt. Ltd vs M/S Axis Infracon Pvt. Ltd & Ors
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant (6th Respondent below) is Jankalyan Vinimay Pvt. Ltd. Respondent/Petitioner is M/s Axis Infracon Pvt Ltd[cite: 4]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Alleged wrongful transfer of assets of Meghna Jute Mill to the Appellant pursuant to a conversion agreement[cite: 4]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: N/A, dispute over wrongful asset transfer in an oppression claim[cite: 4]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The original company petition has been pending since 2010[cite: 4]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Petitioner claimed corporate assets were diverted to the Appellant, necessitating their inclusion in the proceedings[cite: 4]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appellant filed an application to delete its name from the array of respondents in CP No. 2909/2011[cite: 4]. NCLT Kolkata rejected this on 22.12.2016[cite: 4]. Appellant filed this appeal against the NCLT's refusal[cite: 4].
legal_issues: Whether a third-party transferee of disputed corporate assets is a proper and necessary party in a petition for oppression and mismanagement[cite: 4].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: In an oppression and mismanagement dispute, any third-party entity that receives allegedly misappropriated corporate assets is a necessary and proper party to the proceedings[cite: 4]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Effective adjudication of claims under Sections 397 and 398 of the Companies Act, 1956 requires hearing the transferee to ensure fair recovery or validation of disputed asset transfers[cite: 4]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal noted that if the petitioner's claim of wrongful transfer is successful, the Appellant would be directly affected as the recipient of those assets[cite: 4]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT affirmed that the Appellant's presence is essential for a complete adjudication of the dispute, upholding the NCLT's order[cite: 4].
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed. The NCLT is directed to dispose of the pending Company Petition on its merits expeditiously without unnecessary adjournments, referencing Section 422 of the Companies Act, 2013[cite: 4].
summary: A petitioner filed an oppression and mismanagement claim alleging that company assets were wrongfully transferred to the appellant, Jankalyan Vinimay Pvt. Ltd[cite: 4]. The appellant sought to be deleted from the proceedings, which the NCLT refused[cite: 4]. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that as the recipient of the disputed assets, the appellant is a necessary and proper party whose rights would be directly affected by the case's outcome[cite: 4].

case_title: Thirumangalam Janopkara Permanent Fund Ltd. vs P. Krishna Moorthy & Ors
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Thirumangalam Janopkara Permanent Fund Ltd. Respondents are P. Krishna Moorthy & Ors[cite: 5]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: N/A, dispute relates to corporate oppression and mismanagement and the revival of the company[cite: 5]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: N/A, relates to a long-pending oppression dispute[cite: 5]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The original petition has been pending since 2008 (over 8 years)[cite: 5]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The NCLT granted time to the respondents to bring a detailed plan for the revival of the company instead of deciding the merits[cite: 5]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Chennai passed an order on 07.03.2017 granting time for a revival plan in TCP No. 35/2016[cite: 5]. Appellant challenged this delay at the NCLAT[cite: 5].
legal_issues: Whether the Tribunal should repeatedly adjourn an 8-year-old oppression petition to allow for the submission of revival plans instead of deciding the case on its merits[cite: 5].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Under oppression and mismanagement proceedings, once the Tribunal establishes the facts, it possesses ample statutory power to pass appropriate orders directly, without necessitating further petitions or revival plans that unduly delay disposal[cite: 5]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 422 of the Companies Act, 2013 mandates the expeditious disposal of petitions; hence, tribunals must utilize their broad powers under Section 402 to resolve established oppression without seeking extraneous filings[cite: 5]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The NCLAT observed that the petition had been pending for over 8 years and the time limit for submitting the revival plan had already expired[cite: 5]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT directed the Tribunal to cease granting adjournments and to decide the petition strictly on its merits[cite: 5].
operative_order: The appeal is disposed of by remitting the case back to the NCLT to decide the Company Petition on its merits, preferably by 10th May 2017, without interfering with the impugned order[cite: 5].
summary: The appellant challenged an NCLT order that granted respondents time to submit a corporate revival plan in an oppression petition pending since 2008[cite: 5]. The NCLAT observed that tribunals have ample power to pass orders addressing mismanagement without demanding additional filings that delay justice[cite: 5]. Noting the statutory mandate for expeditious disposal, the NCLAT disposed of the appeal by remitting the case, directing the NCLT to decide the matter on its merits by a specified date[cite: 5].

case_title: M/S. Eicher Motors Limited vs Adesh Kaur & Ors
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is M/S. Eicher Motors Limited (Company). Respondent No.1 is Adesh Kaur (original shareholder), Respondent No.2 is the Share Transfer Agent, and Respondent No.8 is Vikas Tara Singh (alleged fraudulent transferee)[cite: 6]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Dispute over the ownership and transfer of 903 equity shares of the Appellant company[cite: 6]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: N/A, relates to share transfer fraud[cite: 6]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The transferee lodged a transfer deed on 07.11.2012, which was verified and dematerialized by 04.11.2013[cite: 6]. The original shareholder emailed the company on 02.06.2014 alleging fraud[cite: 6]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The shares were transferred and dematerialized in favor of the 8th Respondent. A criminal complaint for fraud and forgery was pending with the Economic Offences Wing (EOW), Mumbai, and SEBI was also investigating[cite: 6]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Adesh Kaur filed CP No. 8/59/15 before NCLT New Delhi under Section 59 for rectification of the register. NCLT allowed the petition on 20.03.2017[cite: 6]. Eicher Motors appealed to the NCLAT[cite: 6].
legal_issues: Whether the Tribunal should exercise summary jurisdiction under Section 59 of the Companies Act, 2013 to rectify a register of members when complex questions of fraud, forgery, and impersonation are actively pending before criminal investigative authorities[cite: 6].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Summary jurisdiction for rectification of a share register cannot be invoked when the dispute involves complex, contested allegations of fraud, forgery, and impersonation requiring detailed evidentiary trials[cite: 6]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 59 of the Companies Act, 2013 is intended for simple cases of rectification, not for adjudicating serious disputed questions of title involving criminal elements[cite: 6]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal relied on Supreme Court precedent dictating that if genuine disputes of forgery exist (evidenced by an active EOW police complaint and SEBI probe), the Tribunal must exclude its jurisdiction[cite: 6]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT held that the NCLT erred in rectifying the register solely based on the physical possession of original certificates by the petitioner given the active fraud investigations[cite: 6].
operative_order: The impugned NCLT judgment is set aside, and the Company Petition is dismissed. The 1st Respondent is given liberty to move a court of competent jurisdiction for a declaration of title and to challenge the transfer as fraudulent. No costs[cite: 6].
summary: Respondent Adesh Kaur filed a petition under Section 59 of the Companies Act, 2013, seeking rectification of Eicher Motors' share register, alleging her shares were fraudulently transferred to a third party[cite: 6]. The NCLT allowed the rectification[cite: 6]. Eicher Motors appealed, arguing the matter involved complex fraud allegations under active police and SEBI investigation[cite: 6]. The NCLAT allowed the appeal and set aside the NCLT's order, holding that summary jurisdiction cannot resolve complex disputes involving forgery, and directed the parties to a competent civil court[cite: 6].

case_title: Iberchem S.A vs Yatin Chandulal Davda
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants are Iberchem S.A. and Iberchem India Limited. Respondents are Yatin Chandulal Davda & Ors[cite: 7]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Dispute arising out of a company petition where the appellants sought to invoke arbitration[cite: 7]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: N/A[cite: 7]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The NCLT passed interim orders requiring a reply to the main petition by 09.11.2017[cite: 7]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Appellants filed I.A. No. 316/2017 under Section 8 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, and the NCLT directed them to file a reply in the main petition pending the hearing of the Section 8 application[cite: 7]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appellants challenged the NCLT's interim order (I.A. No. 317/2017) directing the filing of the reply. During the pendency of this appeal, the appellants filed their reply and the NCLT heard and reserved orders on the Section 8 application[cite: 7].
legal_issues: Whether an appeal against an NCLT interim order directing the filing of a reply before deciding a Section 8 arbitration application survives after the NCLT has heard and reserved orders on the said application[cite: 7].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An appeal challenging an interim procedural order becomes infructuous if the underlying procedural grievance has been resolved or overtaken by subsequent developments in the lower tribunal[cite: 7]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: N/A, decided based on the doctrine of infructuousness[cite: 7]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal noted the factual development that the appellant had already filed the affidavit in reply and the NCLT had formally heard and reserved orders on the Section 8 application[cite: 7]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT concluded that the appellant's apprehension of the main petition being disposed of before the Section 8 application was unfounded, rendering the appeal devoid of surviving merit[cite: 7].
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed as infructuous. No orders as to costs[cite: 7].
summary: The appellants challenged an NCLT interim order directing them to file a reply to the main company petition before deciding their Section 8 arbitration application[cite: 7]. By the time the appeal was heard, the appellants had already filed their reply, and the NCLT had heard and reserved orders on the Section 8 application[cite: 7]. Consequently, the NCLAT dismissed the appeal as infructuous, noting that the appellants' procedural grievance had been overtaken by events and their apprehension lacked basis[cite: 7].

case_title: Vamsidhar Maddipatla & Anr vs Teckbond Laboratories Pvt Ltd & Ors
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants/Petitioners are Vamsidhar Maddipatla & Dr. Ibrahimpatnam Krishna. Respondents are Teckbond Laboratories Pvt Ltd & Ors[cite: 8]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Dispute involving allegations of oppression and mismanagement regarding the transfer of several parcels of land and machinery[cite: 8]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: N/A[cite: 8]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The original petition was dismissed for default on 09.02.2017. The restoration petition was filed late on 29.06.2017, exceeding the 30-day limit[cite: 8]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The NCLT dismissed the restoration application because it was filed beyond the 30-day limit stipulated in Rule 48 and lacked a formal condonation petition[cite: 8]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Hyderabad dismissed the CP for non-prosecution and later dismissed the restoration application (CA No.128/2017) on 11.09.2017. Appellants appealed both orders to the NCLAT[cite: 8].
legal_issues: Whether the Tribunal has the inherent power to extend the 30-day limitation period under Rule 48 of the NCLT Rules, 2016 to restore a petition dismissed for default in the interest of justice[cite: 8].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The Tribunal possesses discretionary power to extend procedural timelines and restore a petition dismissed for default beyond the prescribed period if the justice of the case so requires, subject to equitable terms such as imposing costs[cite: 8]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Rule 15 of the NCLT Rules, 2016 expressly empowers the Tribunal to enlarge the time appointed by the rules for doing any act, overriding the strict 30-day limit provided in Rule 48 for restoration applications[cite: 8]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The NCLAT evaluated the circumstances and found that the appellants demonstrated a sufficient case for restoration, which the NCLT should have accommodated by extending the time[cite: 8]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT held that the NCLT erred in rigidly applying the 30-day limit without considering its power to extend time under Rule 15, ordering the restoration of the petition subject to costs[cite: 8].
operative_order: The impugned orders dated 11.09.2017 and 09.02.2017 are set aside. The Company Petition is restored to its original file subject to the payment of Rs. 30,000 as costs by the appellant to the NCLAT Registrar by 30.11.2017, failing which the order shall stand recalled[cite: 8].
summary: The NCLT dismissed the appellants' oppression petition for non-prosecution and subsequently rejected their restoration application for being filed beyond the 30-day limit[cite: 8]. On appeal, the NCLAT held that under Rule 15 of the NCLT Rules, 2016, the Tribunal has the discretionary power to extend time limits in the interest of justice[cite: 8]. Finding that the appellants made a valid case for restoration, the NCLAT allowed the appeal, setting aside the NCLT's orders and restoring the original petition subject to the payment of costs[cite: 8].

case_title: Arvind Aggarwal & Anr vs Trinetra Cements Ltd. & Ors
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants are Arvind Aggarwal & Anr (minority shareholders holding 2.37% of Transferor No. 1). Respondents are Trinetra Cement Limited (Transferor No. 1), Trishul Concrete Products Limited (Transferor No. 2), and The India Cements Limited (Transferee)[cite: 9]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Scheme of Amalgamation between the transferor companies and the transferee company[cite: 9]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: N/A[cite: 9]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Valuation exercises began on 16.02.2014, reports were presented on 26.02.2014, and the shareholders' meeting was held on 25.03.2015[cite: 9]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Appellants challenged the valuation as unfair, noting that the reports were issued on a single day. The Scheme was approved by 124 out of 126 equity shareholders, and the appellants failed to raise objections during the shareholders' meeting[cite: 9]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Chennai approved the Scheme on 13.04.2017 and rejected the appellants' objections. Appellants challenged this approval at the NCLAT[cite: 9].
legal_issues: Whether a Scheme of Amalgamation can be rejected based on objections to the valuation methodology raised belatedly by minority shareholders who failed to object during the shareholders' meeting[cite: 9].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Mere allegations of improper valuation by minority shareholders cannot invalidate a Scheme of Amalgamation unless specific illegalities or perverse reasoning are proven, especially when the scheme is overwhelmingly approved by the majority shareholders[cite: 9]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Compliance with SEBI circulars and statutory provisions is satisfied if all required documents are placed before the Tribunal. The production of multiple valuation and fairness reports on the same day by professional external institutions is standard practice and not inherently invalid[cite: 9]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal noted the overwhelming majority vote in favor of the scheme, the absence of objections at the meeting, and the valid reasoning for valuing the companies as 'going concerns' without separately valuing surplus assets[cite: 9]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT found no perversity in the NCLT's approval of the Scheme, ruling that the appellants failed to demonstrate any illegality in the valuation process[cite: 9].
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed due to an absence of merit. There shall be no order as to costs[cite: 9].
summary: Minority shareholders appealed the NCLT's approval of a Scheme of Amalgamation between Trinetra Cements and The India Cements, alleging that the valuation was unfair and that statutory reports were improperly generated on a single day[cite: 9]. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that generating multiple reports on the same day by external professionals is standard practice[cite: 9]. Given the overwhelming shareholder approval and the appellants' failure to prove any specific illegality in the valuation methodology, the NCLT's decision was upheld[cite: 9].

case_title: Lalia Joseph vs A.K. Mansoor
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Lalia Joseph (proposed Respondent 7). Respondent 1 is A.K. Mansoor (Original Petitioner). Respondent 2 is M/s Indo-Asian News Channel (P) Ltd[cite: 11]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Appellant invested Rs. 1.5 crores for equity shares and an additional Rs. 9.5 crores to set up the company, allegedly receiving preference shares without voting rights instead[cite: 11]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: N/A, dispute pertains to oppression and mismanagement regarding share allotments[cite: 11]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The application for impleadment (CA 34/2016) was filed around 01.04.2017 before the NCLT[cite: 11]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: In the original petition, Respondent 1 explicitly restricted his challenge to allotments made in favor of original Respondents 2 and 3. No specific relief or allegations were pleaded against the Appellant[cite: 11]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Respondent 1 filed CA 34/2016 in TCP 180/2016 to implead the Appellant, which NCLT Chennai allowed on 23.08.2017[cite: 11]. The Appellant appealed to the NCLAT against her addition as a party[cite: 11].
legal_issues: Whether a third party can be impleaded as a necessary respondent in an oppression and mismanagement petition when the petitioner has sought no relief against them and restricted their challenge only to existing respondents[cite: 11].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A party cannot be impleaded as a respondent in an oppression and mismanagement petition simply for the asking, absent specific pleadings or amendments to the main petition demonstrating why they are a necessary party or claiming relief against them[cite: 11]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Impleadment procedures require a valid nexus between the proposed party and the substantive reliefs claimed; vague applications referencing overall shareholder rights are insufficient to force a party into litigation[cite: 11]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal noted that Respondent 1's own petition restricted challenges to the original respondents and that the impleadment application contained no factual basis or sought amendment against the Appellant[cite: 11]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT concluded that adding the Appellant was legally unsustainable due to the lack of pleadings and relief sought against her[cite: 11].
operative_order: The appeal is allowed. The impugned NCLT order dated 23.08.2017 is quashed and set aside to the extent it impleads the present Appellant as a respondent in the company petition. No order as to costs[cite: 11].
summary: The original petitioner in an oppression and mismanagement dispute sought to implead the Appellant as a respondent. The NCLT allowed the impleadment[cite: 11]. The Appellant challenged this, arguing that the petition sought no relief against her and was restricted to challenging allotments to other respondents[cite: 11]. The NCLAT agreed, ruling that without amending the main petition to include specific claims against the Appellant, she could not be impleaded based on a vague application, and quashed the NCLT's order concerning her[cite: 11].

case_title: Ganesh Sponge Pvt. Ltd. vs Aryan Mining & Trading Corporation Pvt. Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Ganesh Sponge Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor). Respondent is Aryan Mining & Trading Corporation Pvt. Ltd. (Operational Creditor)[cite: 12]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Supply of goods for which operational debt was claimed by the Operational Creditor[cite: 12]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The exact debt amount is not specified, but the Corporate Debtor raised pre-existing quality disputes on 03.08.2012 and 25.08.2012[cite: 12]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: A Section 8 demand notice was issued prior to filing the petition, and a joint withdrawal request was made post-admission[cite: 12]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The Section 8 demand notice was issued by a lawyer/advocate rather than an authorized person holding a position within the Operational Creditor. Additionally, evidence showed a pre-existing dispute regarding the quality of goods[cite: 12]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Kolkata admitted the Section 9 application on 19.07.2017 and subsequently rejected a joint application for withdrawal on 03.08.2017[cite: 12]. The Corporate Debtor challenged both orders before the NCLAT[cite: 12].
legal_issues: Whether a Section 8 demand notice issued by an advocate is valid under the IBC, and whether an admitted insolvency application can be subsequently withdrawn by the parties[cite: 12].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A Section 8 demand notice cannot be issued by an advocate or lawyer unless they hold a position with or in relation to the operational creditor; furthermore, an insolvency application cannot be withdrawn after its admission[cite: 12]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Rule 8 of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy (Application to Adjudicating Authority) Rules, 2016 explicitly permits withdrawal of an application only *before* admission. Section 8 and Rule 5 mandate that a demand notice must be signed by an authorized person holding a specific position with the operational creditor[cite: 12]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Relying on the precedent in *Macquarie Bank*, the Tribunal found the demand notice defective as it was signed merely as a lawyer's notice without proper authorization[cite: 12]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT upheld the refusal to permit post-admission withdrawal but set aside the admission order itself because the defective Section 8 notice rendered the Section 9 application incomplete[cite: 12].
operative_order: The impugned order dated 19.07.2017 admitting the application is set aside, and the Section 9 application is dismissed. The Corporate Debtor is released from the CIRP rigour. The order refusing withdrawal is not interfered with. No costs[cite: 12].
summary: An operational creditor initiated insolvency proceedings using a Section 8 demand notice sent by its lawyer. The NCLT admitted the petition, after which the parties settled and sought to withdraw the case[cite: 12]. The NCLT refused the withdrawal as it was post-admission[cite: 12]. On appeal, the NCLAT upheld the refusal to withdraw but ultimately set aside the initial admission order, holding that a Section 8 demand notice issued by an advocate without holding a position in the creditor company is defective and invalidates the Section 9 petition[cite: 12].

case_title: Quinn Finance Unlimited Company vs Mack Soft Tech Pvt. Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Quinn Finance Unlimited Company (Debenture Holder). Respondent is Mack Soft Tech Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Issuer)[cite: 13]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Issuance of Compulsorily Convertible Debentures (CCDs) by the Respondent to the Appellant[cite: 13]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Claim involves the redemption of the first tranche of CCDs worth Rs. 8.60 Crores and coupon interest amounts of Rs. 12.74 Crores and Rs. 24.49 Crores[cite: 13]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The amendment application was filed within the statutory 30-day period from the date of completion of pleadings[cite: 13]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The Appellant originally sought immediate conversion of CCDs and payment of interest under Section 71. They later applied to amend the prayer to add an alternative relief for conversion upon maturity, without changing the substantive nature of the petition[cite: 13]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT rejected the amendment application on 21.04.2017, pre-judging that the main petition itself was liable to be dismissed on the grounds raised in the Respondent's reply[cite: 13]. The Appellant challenged this rejection at the NCLAT[cite: 13].
legal_issues: Whether a Tribunal can reject an amendment application filed within the statutory 30-day period by expressing a premature opinion on the merits of the main petition[cite: 13].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A Tribunal exceeds its jurisdiction if it rejects an amendment application by pre-judging the merits of the main petition before its final hearing[cite: 13]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Rule 155 of the NCLT Rules, 2016 explicitly allows amendments within 30 days of the completion of pleadings to determine the real question in controversy. The Tribunal erred by declaring that amendments must be made well before pleadings are settled, contravening the express rule[cite: 13]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The NCLAT assessed the proposed alternative relief and found it was intrinsically aligned with the original prayer for CCD conversion, meaning it did not fundamentally alter the cause of action[cite: 13]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT held that the alternative relief amendment was valid and necessary for determining the real issue, while amendments predicting the respondent's future intentions were unwarranted[cite: 13].
operative_order: The impugned order is modified. The amendment application is allowed concerning the insertion of the alternative relief but rejected regarding the insertion of paragraph 6.3A. The Tribunal is directed to decide the main petition independently on merits without being influenced by past observations. No costs[cite: 13].
summary: A debenture holder filed a Section 71 petition seeking the conversion of CCDs and later sought to amend the petition to add an alternative relief for conversion upon maturity[cite: 13]. The NCLT rejected the amendment, commenting prematurely that the main petition was liable to be dismissed[cite: 13]. The NCLAT modified the order, allowing the alternative relief because it was filed within the 30-day limit permitted by Rule 155 and did not change the substantive cause of action, ruling that the NCLT cannot pre-judge merits at the amendment stage[cite: 13].

case_title: Nextgen Dealers Pvt. Ltd. & Ors vs Agarpara Company Ltd. & Ors
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants are Nextgen Dealers Pvt Ltd & Anr (Petitioners). Respondent 1 is Agarpara Company Ltd. Respondent 20 is the target company against whom reliefs were sought[cite: 14]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Alleged fabrication, antedating of annual returns, balance sheets, and holding of false Annual General Meetings by the respondents between 2009 and 2012[cite: 14]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: N/A, dispute relates to maintainability of an oppression and mismanagement petition[cite: 14]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The contested filings and AGMs occurred between 2009 and 2012, prior to the Appellants acquiring any shares[cite: 14]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The Appellants did not hold a single share in the 20th Respondent on the date of presenting the petition. Furthermore, Respondent 1, in which the Appellants allegedly acquired shares, was not the holding company of the 20th Respondent[cite: 14]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Kolkata dismissed the company petition (CP 43/2014) as against the 20th Respondent on 09.01.2017 based on lack of maintainability via CA 1815/2015[cite: 14]. Appellants appealed this dismissal to the NCLAT[cite: 14].
legal_issues: Whether a petition for oppression and mismanagement is maintainable against a company in which the petitioner holds no shares and which is not a subsidiary of a company in which the petitioner holds shares[cite: 14].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An oppression and mismanagement petition is not maintainable against a specific company if the petitioner does not possess the requisite qualifying shares in that company at the time of presenting the petition[cite: 14]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 399 of the Companies Act, 1956 mandates strict threshold qualifications for filing an oppression petition; without holding shares directly in the targeted company (or establishing a holding-subsidiary relationship), a party lacks locus standi[cite: 14]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal established as an undisputed fact that the Appellant held zero shares in the 20th Respondent and that the 1st Respondent was not its holding company. It also held that shareholders cannot challenge past transactions concluded prior to their share acquisition[cite: 14]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT affirmed that the petition against the 20th Respondent lacked maintainability and upheld the NCLT's order[cite: 14].
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed. The NCLT is requested to decide the remaining aspects of the pending company petition expeditiously, preferably within a month, without granting unnecessary adjournments[cite: 14].
summary: The appellants filed an oppression and mismanagement petition seeking reliefs against a specific respondent company[cite: 14]. The NCLT dismissed the petition against that company because the appellants held no shares in it[cite: 14]. On appeal, the NCLAT affirmed the dismissal, explaining that under Section 399 of the Companies Act, 1956, possessing the requisite share qualification is mandatory to maintain an action[cite: 14]. Furthermore, shareholders cannot challenge past corporate transactions that concluded before they acquired their shares[cite: 14].

case_title: Anuroop Builders & Development Pvt. Ltd. vs Regional Director, Northern Region
statutes_cited: Companies (Compromises, Arrangements and Amalgamations) Rules, 2016, Rule 6
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants are Anuroop Builders & Development Pvt. Ltd. and five other Transferor Companies, along with Dome Builders & Developers Pvt. Ltd. (Transferee Company). Respondents are the Regional Director (NR) and ROC Delhi & Haryana[cite: 15]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: A proposed Scheme of Amalgamation of six closely held transferor companies with the transferee company[cite: 15]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: N/A[cite: 15]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The first motion application was filed, followed by the NCLT's dismissal on 21.08.2017, and a subsequent rejection of a review application on 03.11.2017[cite: 15]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The NCLT dismissed the scheme because the share exchange ratio and Valuation Report were not disclosed in the petition. The Appellants claimed the Valuation Report was annexed to the first motion application, but the NCLT registry noted the specific pages (180-186) were missing from the paper book[cite: 15]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT New Delhi dismissed the amalgamation petition for material non-disclosure and rejected a review application. The Appellants filed appeals against both orders at the NCLAT[cite: 15].
legal_issues: Whether a petition for a scheme of amalgamation dismissed for non-disclosure of the share exchange ratio and valuation report should be remanded when the petitioners are willing to cure the defect and restart the compliance process[cite: 15].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: While material disclosures are mandatory for sanctioning an amalgamation, an appellate tribunal may quash a dismissal based on procedural non-disclosure and remand the matter to save time, provided the companies are willing to re-circulate the missing documents and secure fresh approvals[cite: 15]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 232(2) of the Companies Act, 2013 and Rule 6 mandate the disclosure of share exchange ratios to enable shareholders to make informed decisions. A failure to provide this prevents the Tribunal from sanctioning the scheme[cite: 15]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The NCLAT noted there was a possibility that the Appellants had initially filed the Valuation Report, as the registry had not objected to missing pages earlier, making the outright dismissal overly harsh[cite: 15]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT concluded that remanding the case for fresh compliance was the most appropriate course of action, allowing the Appellants to cure the procedural defect[cite: 15].
operative_order: The impugned orders are quashed and set aside. The petition is restored to the NCLT. The Tribunal shall give the Appellants an opportunity to revert to their respective boards and shareholders with the valuation report and fulfill any other prescribed compliances. The appeals are disposed of accordingly[cite: 15].
summary: The NCLT dismissed a scheme of amalgamation because the share exchange ratio and valuation report were not disclosed in the petition[cite: 15]. The appellants claimed the report was filed but misplaced by the registry[cite: 15]. The NCLAT set aside the dismissal, reasoning that in the interest of saving time, the matter should be remanded[cite: 15]. The NCLAT directed the NCLT to allow the appellants the opportunity to circulate the valuation report and obtain fresh consents from their boards and shareholders to cure the defect[cite: 15].

case_title: Ravi Sanghi vs Sanghi Spinners (India) Ltd & Ors
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Ravi Sanghi (Petitioner No. 1). Respondents are Sanghi Spinners (India) Ltd & Ors, including co-petitioners, legal heirs, and '3A Capital Service'[cite: 16]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Dispute over a family settlement, transfer of shares, and the sale of fixed assets of the respondent company[cite: 16]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: N/A, dispute relates to corporate oppression and withdrawal of a petition[cite: 16]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The original company petition was filed in 2008. The withdrawal application (C.A. No. 11 of 2016) was filed on 08.11.2016, 8 years later[cite: 16]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The Tribunal found that the appellant violated a 2008 Company Law Board order by transferring shares and selling fixed assets below market value, which prompted contempt cases against him[cite: 16]. The withdrawal was opposed by co-petitioners and other respondents[cite: 16]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Hyderabad dismissed the appellant's withdrawal application with costs on 26.04.2017[cite: 16]. The appellant challenged this refusal at the NCLAT[cite: 16].
legal_issues: Whether a petitioner has an absolute right to withdraw an oppression and mismanagement petition when the withdrawal is allegedly a mala fide attempt to evade compliance with previous Tribunal orders and prejudices co-petitioners[cite: 16].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The Tribunal has the discretionary power to refuse the withdrawal of a company petition if the applicant is acting mala fide, particularly to evade finalized interim orders, and the withdrawal prejudices interconnected proceedings or co-petitioners[cite: 16]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Although Rule 82 of the NCLT Rules, 2016 allows for the withdrawal of a petition, this is not an absolute right; the Tribunal must evaluate the bona fides of the request and its impact on other parties[cite: 16]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal noted the appellant's habitual filing of interlocutory applications to delay the case and his blatant violations of the 2008 CLB order[cite: 16]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT upheld the refusal to withdraw, determining that the appellant's attempt to withdraw after 9 years was a tactical move to stall proceedings and avoid the consequences of his violations[cite: 16].
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed. The matter is remitted to the Tribunal for early disposal of the petition. There shall be no order as to costs[cite: 16].
summary: After litigating an oppression and mismanagement petition for nearly 9 years, the appellant sought to withdraw it[cite: 16]. Co-petitioners and respondents opposed this, noting that the appellant had violated previous Company Law Board orders regarding share transfers and asset sales[cite: 16]. The NCLAT upheld the NCLT's dismissal of the withdrawal application, ruling that the Tribunal rightfully exercised its discretion to prevent the appellant from using withdrawal as a mala fide tactic to evade compliance[cite: 16].

case_title: Beeceelene Textile Mills Pvt Ltd. & Ors vs Radhakrishan B Ruchandani & Ors
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants are Beeceelene Textile Mills Pvt Ltd. & Ors. Respondents are Radhakrishan B Ruchandani & Ors[cite: 17]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Dispute over company management, freezing of bank accounts, and illegal appointment of directors among family members[cite: 17]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: N/A, relates to oppression and mismanagement[cite: 17]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The impugned NCLT order was issued on 13.04.2017. The appeal was filed with a 24-day delay[cite: 17]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The NCLT observed that board meetings and a special majority shareholders meeting were conducted without notice to the petitioner, and new directors were appointed without a specific agenda[cite: 17]. The Appellants claimed the delay in filing the appeal was due to documents being lost in transit and an uncertified illness[cite: 17]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Ahmedabad ruled in favor of the respondents (petitioners) finding oppression and mismanagement. The Appellants challenged this finding at the NCLAT, accompanied by a condonation of delay application[cite: 17].
legal_issues: Whether a 24-day delay in filing an appeal can be condoned based on vague claims of documents lost in transit and unverified illness, and whether holding board meetings without notice constitutes oppression[cite: 17].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An application for condonation of delay requires satisfactory and substantiated explanations; vague assertions of lost documents or uncertified illness of one among multiple appellants are insufficient[cite: 17]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Conducting board meetings or special shareholder meetings to pass resolutions (such as bank account operations or director appointments) without mandatory statutory notice to all directors/shareholders constitutes oppression and mismanagement under the Companies Act, 1956[cite: 17]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The NCLAT rejected the delay condonation because out of six appellants, none explained why the others could not file on time, and no medical certificate was provided[cite: 17]. On merits, the NCLAT found the NCLT's evaluation of the illegal meetings conclusive[cite: 17]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT dismissed the condonation application and consequently dismissed the appeal as time-barred, additionally noting it lacked substantive merit[cite: 17].
operative_order: The petition for condonation of delay is dismissed. In effect, the appeal is dismissed being barred by limitation, with no costs[cite: 17].
summary: Appellants challenged an NCLT order that found them guilty of oppression and mismanagement for holding board meetings without notice and illegally appointing directors[cite: 17]. The appeal was filed with a 24-day delay, which the appellants blamed on lost documents and an unverified illness[cite: 17]. The NCLAT rejected these excuses, dismissing the condonation application and the appeal as time-barred, while confirming that the NCLT's findings on the merits were sound[cite: 17].

case_title: Dr. Jang Bahadur Singh And Ors vs Frick India Ltd. And Ors
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants are Dr. Jang Bahadur Singh and Ors. Respondents are Frick India Ltd. and Ors[cite: 18]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Dispute involving allegations of corporate oppression and mismanagement[cite: 18]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: N/A[cite: 18]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The NCLT dismissed the petition on 31.03.2017. Appellants filed a defective appeal on 16.05.2017, left it uncured for over five months, and re-filed it on 25.10.2017[cite: 18]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Instead of curing the defects at the NCLAT, the appellants filed an interlocutory application before the Supreme Court in an already disposed-of SLP, which was dismissed as withdrawn[cite: 18]. They then sought to exclude this time under Section 14 of the Limitation Act[cite: 18]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT New Delhi dismissed the original petition[cite: 18]. Appellants filed a defective appeal at the NCLAT, followed by a failed Supreme Court application, and subsequently sought condonation of the re-filing delay[cite: 18].
legal_issues: Whether time spent pursuing a non-maintainable interlocutory application before the Supreme Court can be excluded under Section 14 of the Limitation Act to condone a delay in re-filing a defective appeal[cite: 18].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Section 14 of the Limitation Act cannot excuse delay when a party already knew the correct appellate forum but intentionally neglected to cure defects there while taking a chance before a wrong forum[cite: 18]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Rule 26 of the NCLAT Rules, 2016 empowers the Registrar to decline registration if a party intentionally fails to remove defects within the granted time[cite: 18]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The NCLAT observed that since the appellants originally filed the defective appeal at the NCLAT on 16.05.2017, they clearly knew it was the correct forum. Thus, abandoning the defect-curing process for five months to approach the Supreme Court was a deliberate, tactical failure, not a bona fide mistake[cite: 18]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT refused to condone the delay, concluding the failure to remove defects was intentional and undeserving of sympathy[cite: 18].
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed for not taking steps to remove the defects within the fixed time. No costs[cite: 18].
summary: The appellants sought to condone a 5-month delay in re-filing a defective appeal against an NCLT order dismissing their oppression petition[cite: 18]. They claimed the time spent unsuccessfully moving the Supreme Court should be excluded under Section 14 of the Limitation Act[cite: 18]. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, reasoning that since the appellants had already filed initially at the NCLAT, they knew the correct forum; their failure to cure defects while approaching the Supreme Court was intentional and not condonable[cite: 18].

case_title: Nagesh Hosiery Exports Ltd. & Anr vs Nagesh Kumar & Ors
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants are Nagesh Hosiery Exports Ltd. & Anr (Respondents below). Respondents are Nagesh Kumar & Ors (Petitioners below)[cite: 19]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Dispute over executing a fair exit valuation by transferring equivalent company property (3867.08 sq. yards of land) to the minority shareholders (holding 28.66% equity)[cite: 19]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: N/A, execution of a tribunal order[cite: 19]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The initial petition was filed in 2006. The Company Law Board passed a final exit order on 11.06.2008, which the Appellants failed to implement for 9 years[cite: 19]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: After 11 years of litigation, the Appellants refused to execute the conveyance deed for the apportioned land. The NCLT appointed a Local Commissioner to execute the deed on behalf of the company[cite: 19]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT New Delhi passed orders on 20.01.2017 and 06.06.2017 to enforce the 2008 CLB order[cite: 19]. The Appellants appealed the enforcement mechanism to the NCLAT[cite: 19].
legal_issues: Whether the Tribunal has the power to appoint a Local Commissioner to execute a property conveyance deed on behalf of a company to enforce a long-standing exit order in an oppression and mismanagement case[cite: 19].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The Tribunal possesses inherent and statutory authority to enforce its final orders in oppression and mismanagement cases by appointing a Local Commissioner to execute property transfers if the respondents obdurately refuse compliance[cite: 19]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 422 of the Companies Act, 2013 mandates the expeditious disposal of petitions. Extensive stalling and evasive tactics by parties over a decade justify strict, direct enforcement measures by the Tribunal[cite: 19]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The NCLAT observed the Appellants' recalcitrant attitude over 11 years, including falsely claiming that a conveyance deed had already been executed when nothing was on record to prove it[cite: 19]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT upheld the NCLT's appointment of a Local Commissioner, finding the Appellants' challenge to be a mere delaying tactic[cite: 19].
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed. Appellants are ordered to pay costs of Rs. 1,00,000 to the 1st and 2nd respondents/petitioners within 45 days[cite: 19].
summary: In a decade-old oppression dispute, the Company Law Board ordered the appellants to provide a fair exit to the minority shareholders[cite: 19]. The appellants stalled compliance for 9 years, prompting the NCLT to appoint a Local Commissioner to execute a land conveyance deed in favor of the minority[cite: 19]. The NCLAT dismissed the appellants' challenge, heavily criticizing their 11-year delaying tactics, and upheld the NCLT's direct enforcement mechanism while imposing costs[cite: 19].

case_title: Sanjay Parlikar & Anr vs M/S Ajit Scanning & Diagnostic Centre
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants are Sanjay Parlikar & Anr. Respondents are M/S Ajit Scanning & Diagnostic Centre and family members, including the mother and brothers[cite: 20]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Management dispute within a family-owned diagnostic center[cite: 20]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: N/A, relates to oppression and mismanagement[cite: 20]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: An Extra Ordinary General Meeting (EGM) removing the 1st appellant as a director was held on 15.12.2015[cite: 20]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The 1st appellant intentionally blocked bank withdrawals meant for his mother's cancer treatment. Although he claimed lack of notice for his removal, evidence showed he attended and participated in the EGM[cite: 20]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai found no oppression on 05.12.2016 but leniently restored the 1st appellant as a director without executive powers. The appellant appealed to the NCLAT seeking full powers[cite: 20].
legal_issues: Whether a director validly removed in an EGM but restored by the Tribunal out of leniency without executive powers can claim full restoration on the grounds of oppression and mismanagement[cite: 20].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A Tribunal's equitable decision to restore a lawfully removed director without executive powers, granted solely out of compassion for their livelihood in a family dispute, cannot be challenged as oppression by that restored director[cite: 20]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: An EGM resolution removing a director is not vitiated by a lack of formal notice if the aggrieved director actually attended and participated in the meeting[cite: 20]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal noted the 1st appellant's highly disruptive behavior—specifically instructing the bank to freeze funds necessary for his mother's cancer treatment—and confirmed his attendance at the removing EGM[cite: 20]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT concluded there was no mismanagement by the respondents and upheld the NCLT's restrictive restoration, noting it was already a lenient concession[cite: 20].
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed with no order as to costs[cite: 20].
summary: The 1st appellant, who was removed from the board of a family diagnostic center, filed an oppression petition[cite: 20]. The NCLT found no oppression but leniently restored him as a director without executive powers because he lacked other income[cite: 20]. The NCLAT dismissed his appeal seeking full powers, emphasizing his disruptive conduct—such as blocking funds for his mother's cancer treatment—and noting he had no legal right to full powers as his removal at the EGM was valid[cite: 20].

case_title: Tirupati Infra Project Pvt. Ltd. & Another vs Bank of India
statutes_cited: Insolvency and Bankruptcy (Application to Adjudicating Authority) Rules, 2016, Rule 4
