material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants are Tirupati Infra Project Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor) & Another. Respondent is Bank of India (Financial Creditor)[cite: 21]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: A financial loan/debt owed by the Corporate Debtor to the Bank of India[cite: 21]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The default amount was initially shown as Rs. 82.37 Crores (calculated up to 31.03.2012), which was later updated with uncharged interest up to 14.05.2017 to Rs. 109.32 Crores[cite: 21]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The NCLT granted seven days to rectify defects, but the correction was allegedly made beyond this period[cite: 21]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The Financial Creditor submitted a supplementary statement clarifying that the default amount of Rs. 82.37 Crores remained constant as of 31.03.2012, with the difference solely constituting accrued interest[cite: 21]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT New Delhi admitted the Section 7 application on 03.07.2017 in C.P. No. IB-104(PB)/2017[cite: 21]. The Corporate Debtor appealed to the NCLAT, claiming a mismatch in the default amount[cite: 21].
legal_issues: Whether a Section 7 insolvency application can be dismissed for a mismatch in the claim amount when the discrepancy is due to the subsequent addition of accrued interest, and whether updating such a claim constitutes a misleading statement[cite: 21].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An update or clarification of the total claim amount to include accrued interest does not constitute a misleading statement or fatal defect in a Section 7 application, provided the base default amount is consistently established[cite: 21]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Under Section 7(5) of the IBC, the Adjudicating Authority must ascertain if a default has occurred and if the application is complete. Adding accrued interest to the initial default amount does not render the application incomplete or misleading[cite: 21]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal distinguished this from cases with conspicuous, unexplained mismatches, noting that the base default of Rs. 82.37 Crores as of March 2012 was undisputed and accurately explained[cite: 21]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT held that the updated interest calculation did not invalidate the Section 7 petition and upheld the admission order[cite: 21].
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed. The NCLT's order admitting the Section 7 application and initiating the Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process is upheld. Parties shall bear their respective costs[cite: 21].
summary: The Bank of India filed a Section 7 IBC application against the Corporate Debtor, Tirupati Infra Project, which the NCLT admitted[cite: 21]. The Corporate Debtor appealed, arguing the application was defective due to a mismatch between the initial default amount (Rs. 82.37 Crores) and the updated amount (Rs. 109.32 Crores) submitted after a rectification notice[cite: 21]. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that the difference was merely accrued interest calculated over the intervening period and did not constitute a misleading statement that would invalidate the petition[cite: 21].

case_title: Maschinen Umwelttechnik Transportanlagen Gesellschaft GmbH vs M/s Oswal F.M. Hammerle Textiles Limited & Others
statutes_cited: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order 47 Rule 1
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Maschinen Umwelttechnik Transportanlagen Gesellschaft GmbH (Petitioner). Respondents are M/s Oswal F.M. Hammerle Textiles Limited (OFMHT) & Others[cite: 22]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Dispute regarding oppression and mismanagement, culminating in an order for a buyout of the Appellant's shares[cite: 22]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: N/A[cite: 22]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The CLB passed its final order on 19.08.2015. The Appellant filed an execution application and a clarification application in February 2016[cite: 22]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The CLB order directed OFMHT to pay the value of the shares to the Appellant. The Appellant claimed this was an accidental slip and that Oswal Group or Vardhaman Polytex Limited should have been directed to buy the shares, as a company buying its own shares would trigger Section 77A compliance[cite: 22]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Chandigarh dismissed the clarification application on 09.01.2017, finding no clerical error[cite: 22]. The Appellant appealed to the NCLAT[cite: 22].
legal_issues: Whether an application to change the entity directed to purchase shares in a final judgment constitutes a correction of a clerical/arithmetical error under the CLB Regulations, or if it amounts to an impermissible substantive review of the judgment[cite: 22].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The Tribunal lacks the inherent jurisdiction to substantively review or alter the core directives of a finalized judgment under the guise of correcting a clerical or arithmetical mistake[cite: 22]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Regulation 43 of the CLB Regulations, 1991 (akin to Section 152 CPC and Rule 154 of NCLT Rules, 2016) strictly limits corrections to accidental slips, omissions, or arithmetical errors, and cannot be invoked to alter substantive reliefs or obligations[cite: 22]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The NCLAT found that substituting the party responsible for buying the shares (from OFMHT to Oswal Group) required a lengthy reasoning process and fundamentally altered the judgment's effect, making it a substantive review rather than a clerical correction[cite: 22]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT upheld the NCLT's dismissal, ruling that the appellant was impermissibly attempting to review the final CLB order through a rectification application[cite: 22].
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed for lack of merit. No order as to costs[cite: 22].
summary: The CLB disposed of an oppression petition by directing the respondent company to buy out the appellant's shares[cite: 22]. The appellant sought a 'clarification' to make the respondent's promoters buy the shares instead, arguing the original directive was a clerical error[cite: 22]. The NCLT rejected this application[cite: 22]. The NCLAT affirmed the rejection, holding that modifying the entity obligated to purchase shares is a substantive review of the judgment, which the Tribunal has no statutory power to undertake under the guise of correcting clerical mistakes[cite: 22].

case_title: Shri Ashok Mittal vs Uniworth Resorts Ltd
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants are Shri Ashok Mittal and Smt. Neeru Ashok Mittal (50% shareholders and former directors). Respondents are Uniworth Resorts Ltd. & Ors[cite: 23]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Dispute over the wrongful removal of the Appellants as directors, subsequent increase in shareholding, and the alleged illegal transfer of the company's sole immovable property in Goa[cite: 23]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: N/A, dispute over oppression and mismanagement[cite: 23]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The company petition was filed in 2006. The amendment/impleadment applications in question were filed in 2017 (11 years later)[cite: 23]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The Appellants sought to implead parties whose names were present in public MCA filings since 2006 and 2010. The NCLT observed the Appellants made no endeavor to dispose of the main petition for over a decade[cite: 23]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Kolkata rejected four interlocutory applications (I.A. Nos. 189, 190, 276, and 277 of 2017) seeking amendments and impleadments due to inordinate delay[cite: 23]. The Appellants challenged these rejections before the NCLAT[cite: 23].
legal_issues: Whether interlocutory applications for impleadment and amendment based on long-available public records can be rejected in a decade-old oppression petition due to the petitioners' severe delay and lack of vigilance[cite: 23].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Belated applications for impleadment or amendment in long-pending petitions can be rightfully rejected if the applicant fails to demonstrate vigilance and seeks to introduce information that was publicly available for years[cite: 23]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 422 of the Companies Act, 2013 mandates the time-bound disposal of petitions (within three months). Entertaining deeply delayed, piecemeal interlocutory applications after more than a decade directly contravenes this statutory mandate for expeditious adjudication[cite: 23]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The NCLAT agreed with the NCLT that the targeted parties were listed in MCA records as early as 2006 and 2010, rendering the 2017 impleadment applications an abuse of process lacking promptness[cite: 23]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT found no flaw in the NCLT's refusal to permit the amendments and impleadments, declining to admit the appeal[cite: 23].
operative_order: Admission of the appeal is declined. The impugned NCLT orders rejecting the interlocutory applications are upheld[cite: 23].
summary: The appellants, who filed an oppression petition in 2006, submitted multiple interlocutory applications in 2017 to implead new parties and amend the petition regarding a transferred property[cite: 23]. The NCLT rejected the applications, noting the information was publicly available for years and the appellants had severely delayed the proceedings[cite: 23]. The NCLAT declined to admit the appeal, emphasizing the statutory mandate for expeditious disposal under the Companies Act, 2013, and affirming that such extreme lack of promptness and vigilance over a decade cannot be entertained[cite: 23].

case_title: M/S. Sunil Packaging Pvt. Ltd vs Dishnet Wireless Limited
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is M/S. Sunil Packaging Pvt. Ltd. (Operational Creditor/Lessor). Respondent is Dishnet Wireless Limited (Corporate Debtor/Lessee)[cite: 24]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: A lease agreement dated 25.10.2013 for a factory shed where the Appellant claimed to be the absolute unencumbered owner[cite: 24]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Claim for unpaid rent/dues of Rs. 39,15,726 plus interest[cite: 24]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The Appellant served a demand notice on 07.11.2016. The Respondent replied raising a dispute on 01.12.2016[cite: 24]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The Respondent proved that the leased premises were heavily mortgaged to UP Financial Corporation Ltd (UPFCL), which issued eviction notices to the Respondent in April and June 2014. The Respondent consequently terminated the lease in October 2014 and demanded its security deposit back[cite: 24]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai dismissed the Appellant's Section 9 application due to a pre-existing dispute[cite: 24]. The Appellant challenged the dismissal at the NCLAT[cite: 24].
legal_issues: Whether a Section 9 insolvency application is maintainable when the Corporate Debtor raises a documented, pre-existing dispute regarding the Operational Creditor's defective title to the leased premises forming the basis of the debt[cite: 24].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An operational debt claim based on a lease agreement is subject to a valid 'pre-existing dispute' if the lessee provides evidence that the lessor suppressed material encumbrances leading to third-party eviction threats prior to the insolvency demand[cite: 24]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Following the precedent in Kirusa Software, Section 9 of the IBC strictly bars the initiation of the Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process if the Corporate Debtor's reply to the demand notice establishes a bona fide, pre-existing dispute over the alleged debt's legality or performance[cite: 24]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal relied on the Respondent's reply to the statutory notice, which detailed UPFCL's eviction threats and the subsequent lease termination, concluding this clearly evidenced a pre-existing dispute[cite: 24]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT held that the Section 9 application was rightfully dismissed by the Adjudicating Authority because the existence of a substantive dispute was unequivocally established[cite: 24].
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed. The NCLT's order rejecting the Section 9 application is upheld. No order as to costs[cite: 24].
summary: The Operational Creditor filed a Section 9 IBC application claiming unpaid rent under a lease agreement for a factory shed[cite: 24]. The Corporate Debtor proved that it had previously terminated the lease because the Creditor falsely represented the property as unencumbered, leading to eviction notices from a financial institution[cite: 24]. The NCLT dismissed the application due to this pre-existing dispute[cite: 24]. The NCLAT affirmed the dismissal, ruling that the documented dispute regarding the property's title and the lease's termination squarely barred the insolvency proceedings[cite: 24].

case_title: Shri Ashok Mittal vs Uniworth Resorts Ltd
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants are Shri Ashok Mittal and Smt. Neeru Ashok Mittal. Respondents are Uniworth Resorts Ltd. & Ors[cite: 25]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Dispute regarding corporate oppression and the impleadment of subsequent shareholders/directors (e.g., M/s. Indoworth India Ltd.)[cite: 25]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: N/A[cite: 25]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: C.A. No. 122/2007 was filed in 2007. It remained pending before the CLB and NCLT. NCLT rejected it on 05.05.2017[cite: 25]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The NCLT rejected the 2007 application claiming the Appellants made no endeavor to pursue it since 30.04.2014, while concurrently disposing of a later application (C.A. No. 272/2014)[cite: 25]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Kolkata dismissed C.A. No. 122/2007 in C.P. No. 46/2006 without deciding the merits[cite: 25]. Appellants appealed to the NCLAT[cite: 25].
legal_issues: Whether a Tribunal can dismiss a long-pending interlocutory application without adjudicating its merits by unilaterally blaming the applicant for failing to prompt the Tribunal for its disposal[cite: 25].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The Tribunal has an inherent responsibility to take up and adjudicate pending interlocutory applications seriatim; it cannot dismiss older applications without deciding their merits by shifting the entire blame for the delay onto the parties[cite: 25]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 422 of the Companies Act, 2013 demands time-bound disposal of petitions. However, this statutory mandate does not absolve the Tribunal from its duty to decide older applications in an organized manner rather than abruptly discarding them on procedural grounds[cite: 25]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The NCLAT noted from the order sheets that the application was indeed active until 2014, and it was improper for the NCLT to dispose of a newer 2014 application while arbitrarily letting the 2007 application languish and then dismissing it for non-prosecution[cite: 25]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT concluded the NCLT's failure to address the merits was erroneous, quashed the dismissal, and ordered a fresh evaluation of the application[cite: 25].
operative_order: The appeal is allowed. The impugned order dated 05.05.2017 passed in C.A. No. 122/2007 is quashed and set aside. The matter is remanded back to the NCLT, Kolkata Bench, to decide the application on its merits at the earliest. No costs[cite: 25].
summary: The NCLT dismissed an amendment and impleadment application pending since 2007 in a 2006 oppression petition, blaming the appellants for failing to actively pursue it since 2014[cite: 25]. On appeal, the NCLAT quashed the dismissal, holding that while parties must be vigilant, the Tribunal shares the responsibility to adjudicate older applications seriatim rather than abruptly discarding them without considering their merits[cite: 25]. The matter was remanded to the NCLT for a merits-based decision, with a stern reminder to all parties regarding the statutory mandate for expeditious disposal[cite: 25].

case_title: Twenty First Century Wire Rod Ltd vs Nijinoy Trading Pvt. Ltd. & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is Twenty First Century Wire Rod Ltd., and the Respondents are Nijinoy Trading Pvt. Ltd. & Ors. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: The dispute stems from a Deed of Settlement dated 08.11.2011, under which the Respondents were supposed to pay outstanding amounts and transfer land. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The exact claimed default amount and specific date of default are not detailed in the order, but pertain to the breach of the 2011 settlement terms. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The original Company Law Board (CLB) order dismissing the matter as withdrawn was passed on 09.11.2011. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The core evidence produced was the CLB order dated 09.11.2011, which merely recorded that disputes were amicably settled and permitted withdrawal of CP No. 44/2009 without incorporating the settlement terms into the order. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The Appellant filed an enforcement application before the NCLT Ahmedabad to enforce the settlement deed. The NCLT dismissed it on 04.07.2017, reasoning that the settlement deed was not merged into the CLB's order.
legal_issues: Whether the NCLT has the jurisdiction to enforce a private settlement deed when the original company petition was simply dismissed as withdrawn by the CLB without incorporating the settlement terms into its final order.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A tribunal cannot enforce a deed of settlement if the prior judicial order merely dismissed the original petition as withdrawn without merging the settlement terms into its directives. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: A breach of a private settlement agreement that was not incorporated into a tribunal's order constitutes a violation of contractual terms, for which the remedy lies in a civil forum, not through an enforcement application before the company tribunal. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The legal standard requires examining the text of the disposing order; unless the order explicitly directs compliance in terms of the settlement, it holds no executory force. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The bench dismissed the appeal, holding that in the absence of any specific direction by the CLB on the merits of the settlement, the appellant could not enforce the contract through the NCLT.
operative_order: The appeal was dismissed as being without merit. No order as to costs was passed.
summary: The Appellant sought to enforce a 2011 private settlement deed through the NCLT after the original matter was withdrawn before the CLB. The NCLAT upheld the NCLT's dismissal, ruling that a settlement agreement cannot be enforced as a tribunal decree unless its terms were explicitly incorporated into the court's disposal order, rendering the breach a mere contractual dispute.

case_title: R. Prasanth vs UBC Engineers Pvt. Ltd. & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: R. Prasanth is the Appellant, and UBC Engineers Pvt. Ltd. & Ors. are the Respondents. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Not applicable; the matter relates purely to procedural timelines for challenging a tribunal order. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: No commercial default metrics apply; the default is a procedural delay in filing the appeal. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The impugned NCLT Mumbai order was passed on 06.02.2017. The Appellant received a certified copy on 26.04.2017. A defective appeal was filed on 02.06.2017, and the final defect-free appeal was instituted on 01.08.2017. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The primary evidence is the registry logs showing the date the certified copy was received (26.04.2017), the 45-day expiry on 10.06.2017, the maximum extendable 45-day expiry on 24.07.2017, and the final filing date (01.08.2017). 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The Appellant challenged the NCLT's 06.02.2017 order by filing a condonation of delay application, admitting a significant delay in successfully filing the corrected appeal paper books.
legal_issues: Whether the NCLAT possesses the statutory jurisdiction to condone a delay in filing an appeal that exceeds the maximum permissible grace period of 45 days beyond the initial 45-day limitation period under Section 421 of the Companies Act, 2013.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An appellate tribunal is strictly bound by the statutory limitation periods and lacks jurisdiction to condone any delay that extends beyond the maximum grace period explicitly provided in the governing statute. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Under Section 421(3) of the Companies Act, 2013, an appeal must be filed within 45 days; the proviso caps the tribunal's discretionary power to condone delay at a maximum of a 'further period not exceeding forty-five days'. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The timeline is calculated strictly from the date the certified copy is provided; time spent curing registry defects is counted against the appellant if the final cured filing occurs outside the 90-day absolute limit. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The bench concluded that since the total delay exceeded the 90-day strict threshold (initial 45 days + extendable 45 days), it had no statutory jurisdiction to condone the delay and dismissed the appeal.
operative_order: The application for condonation of delay was rejected, and the appeal was dismissed as barred by limitation.
summary: The Appellant filed an appeal against an NCLT order with a significant procedural delay. The NCLAT calculated the limitation period from the receipt of the certified copy and determined that the delay exceeded the absolute maximum of 90 days (45 days + 45 days extension) permitted under Section 421(3) of the Companies Act, resulting in a strict dismissal.

case_title: MSPL Limited vs NMDC Limited & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: MSPL Limited is the Appellant (Transferee), NMDC Limited is Respondent No. 1 (Company), Aarthi Consultants is Respondent No. 2 (Transfer Agent), and Respondents 3 to 13 are the original shareholders. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: The Appellant claims to have purchased 2900 equity shares (face value Rs. 10) of NMDC Limited from the original shareholders between 2006-2008. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The dispute involves the non-registration of 2900 equity shares and the consequent failure to issue subdivided and bonus shares declared in 2008. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: NMDC sub-divided shares on 21.04.2008 and issued bonus shares on 22.05.2008. The Appellant requested rectification only on 23.08.2010. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The Appellant produced a letter dated 23.08.2010 requesting registration, but failed to produce any FIR or correspondence between 2006-2008 to substantiate the claim that the share documents were misplaced. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The Appellant filed a petition under Section 111A of the Companies Act, 1956 in 2012 before CLB Chennai, which was transferred to NCLT Hyderabad. NCLT Hyderabad rejected the petition on 20.03.2017.
legal_issues: Whether a transferee of shares is entitled to rectification of the share register and issuance of bonus shares after failing to register the transfer for 4-6 years, offering an unsubstantiated excuse of misplaced documents.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Equitable relief for the rectification of a share register will be denied if the applicant approaches the tribunal with unclean hands and is guilty of severe, unexplained laches. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: While Section 111A of the Companies Act, 1956 ensures free transferability and allows a tribunal appeal if a company refuses registration within two months, it does not protect a transferee who sleeps on their rights for years while the company continues to recognize the original registered shareholders. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Claims of lost or misplaced physical share documents must be corroborated by contemporaneous evidence, such as an FIR or immediate notification to the company; mere subsequent statements are insufficient to overcome laches. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The bench dismissed the appeal, holding that the appellant sat on the matter for 4-6 years, failed to prove the misplacement of documents, and allowed bonus shares to be validly issued to the registered original shareholders.
operative_order: The appeal was dismissed. No order as to costs was passed.
summary: The Appellant sought rectification of NMDC's share register to claim bonus shares, alleging they had misplaced their 2006-08 purchase documents until 2010. The NCLAT upheld the NCLT's dismissal, ruling that the severe, unexplained delay of 4-6 years and lack of corroborating evidence for the lost documents disqualified the Appellant from receiving equitable relief.

case_title: Gurdeep Singh Sahani vs Berger Paints India Ltd. & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Gurdeep Singh Sahani is the Appellant (Promoter/Director of the Corporate Debtor), L & T Finance is the Respondent (Financial Creditor), and Berger Paints India Ltd. is also a Respondent. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: An underlying financial debt owed to L & T Finance, which formed the basis of their claim during the Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process (CIRP). 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The specific default amount and date are not explicitly detailed, but L & T Finance asserted a claim for its entire debt amount to secure voting rights. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: No specific timelines for notices are detailed; the IBC Section 29A notification cited was dated 23.11.2017. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The primary evidence evaluated was the status of the Appellant as a Promoter/Director of the Corporate Debtor, thereby dictating their standing in the insolvency process. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The Appellant challenged an NCLT Kolkata order dated 17.10.2017, which allowed L & T Finance's application and directed the Resolution Professional to grant them proportionate voting rights based on their total claim.
legal_issues: Whether a Promoter or Director of a Corporate Debtor possesses the legal locus standi to challenge the allocation of proportionate voting rights to a Financial Creditor in the Committee of Creditors under the IBC.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Promoters or directors of a corporate debtor lack the necessary legal standing to challenge the allocation of voting rights assigned to financial creditors during an insolvency resolution process. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Under the scheme of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, the Committee of Creditors is the exclusive domain of financial creditors, and promoters possess no voting rights or statutory standing to interfere with the internal creditor allocations. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The tribunal strictly applies a threshold test of capacity; if an appellant's status is solely that of a promoter/director of the corporate debtor, any challenge regarding creditor voting rights is summarily rejected for want of locus. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT definitively ruled that the appellant, due to his status as a promoter/director, had no locus standi to contest the financial creditor's voting share, warranting immediate dismissal of the appeal.
operative_order: The appeal was dismissed for lack of merit. No order as to costs was passed.
summary: The Appellant, acting as a Promoter/Director of the Corporate Debtor, challenged an NCLT order that granted full proportionate voting rights to a Financial Creditor, L & T Finance. The NCLAT swiftly dismissed the appeal, holding that promoters have no locus standi or voting rights under the IBC to contest how financial creditors' voting shares are allocated.

case_title: Gurcharan Singh Soni & Kuldeep Kaur Soni vs Unitech Ltd. & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Gurcharan Singh Soni & Kuldeep Kaur Soni are the Appellants (Homebuyers), and Unitech Ltd. is the Respondent (Corporate Debtor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: The Appellants purchased premises from the Corporate Debtor, leading to a dispute over non-delivery. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The default relates to a refund amount (with interest, compensation, and litigation expenses) as ordered by the State Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission on 03.10.2016. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: A Section 8 demand notice was issued by the Appellants' General Power of Attorney holder and successfully served via Speed-Post on 31.01.2017. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Core evidence included the State Consumer Court order dated 03.10.2016 directing a refund, a General Power of Attorney executed on 04.02.2017 authorizing Mr. Mukesh Chadha, and the postal tracking report proving service of the Section 8 notice. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appellants filed a Section 9 petition as 'Operational Creditors'. NCLT New Delhi rejected it on 21.03.2017, relying on the 'Sajive Kunwar' precedent, leading to the current appeal.
legal_issues: 1. Whether a valid Section 8 demand notice under the IBC can be issued by an authorized General Power of Attorney holder. 2. Whether homebuyers seeking a refund based on a consumer court order qualify as 'Operational Creditors' under Section 5(20) of the IBC.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Purchasers of real estate units claiming a refund of their money do not fall within the legal classification of operational creditors, though their claim constitutes a valid debt and default. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 5(21) defines 'Operational Debt' restrictively to claims regarding goods, services, employment, or statutory dues. A real estate purchase agreement and a subsequent consumer court refund order do not transform the transaction into a provision of goods or services. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: To determine operational creditor status, the tribunal examines the underlying nature of the transaction (e.g., purchase of flat/shop); simply holding a consumer forum decree does not alter the fundamental character of the debt. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: While the NCLAT affirmed that a PoA holder can validly issue a Section 8 notice and that a 'debt' and 'default' existed, it concluded the appellants were not 'Operational Creditors', thereby dismissing the Section 9 appeal but leaving liberty to file as Financial Creditors.
operative_order: The appeal was dismissed on the ground that the Appellants are not Operational Creditors, but liberty was granted to the parties to decide their future course of action in accordance with law. No order as to costs.
summary: Homebuyers sought to initiate insolvency proceedings as Operational Creditors based on a consumer court refund order against Unitech Ltd. The NCLAT ruled that while a Power of Attorney holder can validly issue a Section 8 notice and a valid debt exists, homebuyers do not qualify as 'Operational Creditors' under the IBC, dismissing the appeal with liberty to file as Financial Creditors.

case_title: Bishnudeo Prasad & Ors. vs Bihar Janta Cold Storage Pvt. Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellants are Bishnudeo Prasad & Ors., and the Respondent is Bihar Janta Cold Storage Pvt. Ltd.[cite: 6]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: The matter involves alleged continuous acts of oppression and mismanagement within the respondent company[cite: 6]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not applicable, as this is an oppression and mismanagement dispute rather than a debt default[cite: 6]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The original company petition was dismissed on 16 May 2017[cite: 6]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The NCLT found the company petition and affidavit to be defective, containing cuttings and overwriting without the appellants' or Notary Public's initials[cite: 6]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The NCLT Kolkata dismissed the petition on 16 May 2017 due to the lawyer's unruly behavior and the defective affidavit, imposing a cost of Rs. 50,000[cite: 6].
legal_issues: Whether a company petition for oppression and mismanagement should be dismissed on merits due to a lawyer's unruly behavior and defective notarization of the affidavit[cite: 6].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A tribunal should not deny substantive justice or dismiss a petition on merits solely due to the unruly conduct of the counsel or curable procedural defects in pleadings[cite: 6]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Sections 241 and 242 of the Companies Act, 2013 aim to address continuous oppression and mismanagement, requiring a substantive hearing if a complete petition is filed[cite: 6]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Defective affidavits with unexplained cuttings or blanks cast doubt on the petition's validity, justifying rejection of that specific filing but not a permanent bar on the underlying claims[cite: 6]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The bench disposed of the appeal by allowing the appellants liberty to file a fresh, complete company petition under Sections 241 and 242, uninfluenced by the previous dismissal[cite: 6].
operative_order: The appeal was disposed of, granting the appellants liberty to file a fresh company petition. No order as to costs was made[cite: 6].
summary: The NCLT Kolkata dismissed the appellants' company petition due to their lawyer's unruly behavior and defective, heavily altered affidavits[cite: 6]. On appeal, the NCLAT observed that litigants should not suffer for their counsel's conduct and that substantive justice requires a proper hearing[cite: 6]. The NCLAT disposed of the appeal, granting the appellants liberty to file a fresh, defect-free petition under Sections 241 and 242 of the Companies Act, 2013[cite: 6].

case_title: Teknow Consultants and Engineers Pvt. Ltd. vs Bharat Heavy Electricals Limited
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Teknow Consultants and Engineers Pvt. Ltd. is the Appellant, and Bharat Heavy Electricals Limited is the Respondent[cite: 7]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: The dispute involved an underlying commercial transaction where the principal amount was approximately Rs. 16,98,000[cite: 7]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The appellant claimed interest on the delayed payment of the principal amount, which the respondent subsequently agreed to pay at 6% compound interest minus TDS[cite: 7]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The NCLT order was passed on 31 August 2017, and the settlement cheque was dated 11 December 2017[cite: 7]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The respondent handed over a cheque of Rs. 10,32,443 to the appellant's counsel during the hearing to settle the interest claim[cite: 7]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The appellant challenged the NCLT New Delhi's order dated 31 August 2017, which had seemingly rejected the insolvency plea due to a pending Section 37 arbitration case; however, the parties settled during the appeal[cite: 7].
legal_issues: Whether the pendency of a case under Section 37 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 constitutes a pre-existing dispute under the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016[cite: 7].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An appeal may be permitted to be withdrawn with liberty to revive if a settlement agreement is reached and a conditional payment instrument is issued[cite: 7]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The NCLAT prima facie observed that the pendency of a Section 37 Arbitration Act case cannot automatically be termed as an existence of dispute under the IBC, though it did not base its final disposal on this since the matter was settled[cite: 7]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Acceptance of a settlement cheque subject to encashment is sufficient grounds to allow withdrawal of the appeal[cite: 7]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because the respondent paid the agreed 6% compound interest via cheque, the bench allowed the appellant's prayer to withdraw the appeal[cite: 7].
operative_order: The appeal was disposed of as withdrawn, with liberty granted to the appellant to revive the appeal in case the settlement cheque bounced[cite: 7].
summary: The Appellant filed an insolvency appeal after the NCLT dismissed its plea citing a pending arbitration dispute[cite: 7]. The NCLAT initially noted that a pending Section 37 arbitration appeal might not constitute a valid dispute under the IBC[cite: 7]. However, the parties ultimately settled the interest claim for delayed payment, and the Respondent handed over a cheque for Rs. 10,32,443[cite: 7]. Consequently, the NCLAT permitted the Appellant to withdraw the appeal, with liberty to revive it if the cheque bounced[cite: 7].

case_title: K. K. Bhargava vs Malti Bhargava & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: K.K. Bhargava is the Appellant, and Malti Bhargava & Ors. are the Respondents[cite: 8]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: The dispute involves the ownership and transmission of 6,644 equity shares and 4,057 preference shares in Caxton Press Pvt. Ltd., originally held by Late Nakul Bhargava[cite: 8]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: There is no commercial debt default; the issue centers on the refusal to transmit shares and pay arrear dividends to the legal heir[cite: 8]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The NCLT passed its impugned order directing transmission of shares on 9 May 2017[cite: 8]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The primary evidence relied upon by the NCLT was a Succession Certificate obtained by Malti Bhargava in her favor[cite: 8]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Malti Bhargava filed a petition under Sections 58 and 59 of the Companies Act, 2013, which the NCLT allowed on 9 May 2017, directing transmission within two weeks[cite: 8]. The Appellant subsequently obtained a stay on the Succession Certificate from a civil court[cite: 8].
legal_issues: Whether a tribunal's order directing the transmission of shares based on a valid succession certificate should be set aside if a civil court subsequently stays the operation of that succession certificate[cite: 8].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An appellate tribunal will not retroactively interfere with a lower tribunal's order that was correctly based on a valid succession certificate existing at the time, even if subsequent developments alter the certificate's status[cite: 8]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Sections 58 and 59 of the Companies Act, 2013 mandate the rectification of the register of members and transmission of shares when a claimant presents a valid legal heirship document such as a succession certificate[cite: 8]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The tribunal relies on the validity of the succession certificate at the time of its order; subsequent civil stays do not automatically render the tribunal's prior factual findings legally flawed[cite: 8]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The bench declined to interfere with the NCLT's transmission order, but granted the appellant liberty to approach the appropriate forum if the succession certificate is ultimately annulled by the civil court[cite: 8].
operative_order: The appeal was disposed of without interference with the NCLT's order. Liberty was granted to the appellant to file a fresh application if the Succession Certificate is annulled. No order as to costs[cite: 8].
summary: Malti Bhargava sought the transmission of her late husband's shares in Caxton Press Pvt. Ltd. under Sections 58 and 59 of the Companies Act, 2013[cite: 8]. The NCLT allowed her petition based on a valid Succession Certificate[cite: 8]. The Appellant appealed, noting that a civil court had subsequently stayed the certificate[cite: 8]. The NCLAT refused to interfere with the NCLT's order due to the certificate being valid at the time, but granted the Appellant liberty to seek relief if the civil court eventually annuls the certificate[cite: 8].

case_title: Yashdeep Trexim Pvt. Ltd. vs Rainy Park Suppliers Pvt. Ltd. & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Yashdeep Trexim Pvt. Ltd. is the Appellant, and Rainy Park Suppliers Pvt. Ltd. along with 18 others are the Respondents[cite: 9]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: The matter relates to a company petition involving shareholding, fixed assets, and the composition of the board of directors of Respondent No. 1 company[cite: 9]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not applicable, as this is an internal company dispute regarding interim orders on fixed assets[cite: 9]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The CLB passed an initial status quo order on 26 November 2012, which was modified on 15 January 2013[cite: 9]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The record showed that the appellant had previously given 'no objection' when the interim order on fixed assets was withdrawn in January 2013[cite: 9]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The appellant filed an Interlocutory Application in the pending 2012 Company Petition, seeking to restore the November 2012 status quo order. The NCLT Kolkata dismissed it on 6 July 2017 on grounds of estoppel[cite: 9].
legal_issues: Whether a party can seek the recall of a modified interim order and restoration of a prior status quo order after having expressly consented to the modification[cite: 9].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A party is estopped from seeking the outright restoration of a previous interim order if they previously consented to its modification, though they may file a fresh application for relief based on new, subsequent events[cite: 9]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Under Section 422 of the Companies Act, 2013, tribunals are expected to make efforts to dispose of long-pending company petitions expeditiously[cite: 9]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The tribunal evaluates the specific prayers in the application; if a party explicitly prays to recall a modification they previously agreed to, rather than pleading based on subsequent events, the application is barred by estoppel[cite: 9]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The bench upheld the NCLT's rejection of the application, ruling that the appellant could not backtrack on its previous consent, but granted liberty to file a fresh I.A. based on subsequent events[cite: 9].
operative_order: The NCLAT declined to interfere with the NCLT's impugned order and disposed of the appeal. It granted the appellant liberty to file a fresh I.A. for interim relief based on subsequent events and directed the NCLT to expedite the disposal of the main company petition[cite: 9].
summary: The Appellant sought to restore a 2012 status quo order on fixed assets that had been previously modified with its consent[cite: 9]. The NCLT dismissed the application on grounds of estoppel[cite: 9]. The NCLAT upheld the dismissal, agreeing that the Appellant could not backtrack on its no objection to the modification[cite: 9]. However, noting the Appellant's claim regarding subsequent events, the NCLAT granted liberty to file a fresh application for interim relief and directed the NCLT to expeditiously resolve the main 2012 petition[cite: 9].

case_title: M/s Nagesh Hosiery Exports Pvt Ltd & Ors vs Nagesh Kumar & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: M/s Nagesh Hosiery Exports Pvt Ltd & Ors. are the Appellants, and Nagesh Kumar & Ors. are the Respondents[cite: 10]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: The underlying dispute involves a company petition pending since 2006[cite: 10]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not applicable; the core issue concerns procedural delays and non-compliance with filing requirements[cite: 10]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The defective appeal was filed on 3 March 2017, and defects were not removed for over six weeks[cite: 10]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The appeal lacked basic documents including the Vakalatnama, affidavit, copy of the impugned order, and court fees[cite: 10]. A letter dated 18 April 2017 from the NCLT New Delhi revealed the appellants were using the defective appeal to delay execution and contempt proceedings below[cite: 10]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The appellants filed a severely defective appeal before the NCLAT merely to obtain adjournments in the NCLT regarding a contempt and execution matter related to an order dated 20 January 2017[cite: 10].
legal_issues: Whether an appellate tribunal should dismiss a severely defective appeal that was deliberately filed incomplete to fraudulently stall execution and contempt proceedings before the lower tribunal[cite: 10].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An appeal filed with deliberate, un-cured defects intended solely to abuse the judicial process and delay proceedings in a lower forum warrants immediate dismissal[cite: 10]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 422 of the Companies Act, 2013 mandates the expeditious disposal of petitions within three months, condemning dilatory tactics by litigants[cite: 10]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The failure to file mandatory documents over a six-week period, coupled with the lower tribunal's report of the party using the pending appeal as an excuse for adjournments, establishes bad faith[cite: 10]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The bench concluded that the appellants played a dubious role by filing a dummy appeal to stall an 11-year-old case, justifying outright dismissal and a directive for the NCLT to proceed without further adjournments[cite: 10].
operative_order: The appeal was dismissed. The NCLAT directed the NCLT New Delhi to dispose of the pending company petition within one month without granting unnecessary adjournments to the appellants, leaving it open to the NCLT to take appropriate action against them[cite: 10].
summary: The Appellants filed a deliberately defective and incomplete appeal, lacking basic documents like a Vakalatnama and court fees, solely to use its pendency to stall contempt and execution proceedings in an 11-year-old NCLT case[cite: 10]. The NCLAT noted this dubious strategy after receiving a letter from the NCLT[cite: 10]. Consequently, the NCLAT dismissed the defective appeal and directed the NCLT to decide the main petition within one month without granting the Appellants further adjournments[cite: 10].

case_title: M/S A.J. Prakashan Pvt Ltd & Anr vs Smt. Poonam Gupta & Ors
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellants are M/s A.J. Prakashan Pvt Ltd & Anr (husband/father), and the Respondents are Smt. Poonam Gupta & Ors (wife and two sons)[cite: 11]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: The matter involves a family dispute over the management of family companies[cite: 11]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not applicable; the core issue involves allegations of oppression and mismanagement[cite: 11]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The original company petitions were filed in 2012, with previous inspection orders dated 8 January 2016 and 4 March 2016[cite: 11]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The record showed a complete failure to execute prior inspection orders due to familial friction, with cross-allegations of non-reporting and coercion[cite: 11]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The NCLT Allahabad passed interlocutory orders on 30 January 2017 allowing the Respondents to inspect company records in the presence of the Regional Director, which the Appellants challenged[cite: 11].
legal_issues: Whether the NCLAT should interfere with an interlocutory order granting inspection of company records to alleged directors in an oppression and mismanagement petition that has been pending for over five years[cite: 11].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An appellate tribunal will generally decline to interfere with procedural interlocutory orders, such as supervised record inspections, to prevent further delays in long-pending corporate disputes[cite: 11]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 422 of the Companies Act, 2013 mandates tribunals to dispose of petitions within three months, requiring strict adherence to timelines and a reduction in procedural stalling[cite: 11]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: At the interlocutory stage for document inspection, the tribunal does not need to definitively rule on disputed factual merits, such as whether a party is currently a valid director[cite: 11]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The bench upheld the NCLT's inspection order but strictly time-bound the process to three weeks to expedite the final disposal of the 2012 petitions[cite: 11].
operative_order: The appeals were disposed of with a direction to complete the inspection in the presence of the Regional Director within three weeks, after which the NCLT was instructed to decide the cases on their merits. No costs[cite: 11].
summary: In a long-standing family dispute over oppression and mismanagement, the NCLT Allahabad ordered the inspection of company records[cite: 11]. The Appellants argued that the Respondents were not valid directors and therefore lacked inspection rights[cite: 11]. The NCLAT refused to interfere with the NCLT's order, emphasizing the statutory mandate for swift disposal under Section 422 of the Companies Act, 2013, and directed the inspection to conclude within three weeks[cite: 11].

case_title: Urban Sancturies Developers Pvt. Ltd. & Ors. vs Mr. Sunil Parmanand Kewalramani & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Urban Sancturies Developers Pvt. Ltd. & Ors. are the Appellants, and Mr. Sunil Parmanand Kewalramani & Anr. are the Respondents[cite: 12]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: A dispute regarding the proposed removal of directors from the company board[cite: 12]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not applicable[cite: 12]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The NCLT passed the impugned ex-parte ad-interim order on 23 June 2017, restraining the board meeting scheduled for 26/27 June 2017[cite: 12]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The text of the NCLT order explicitly indicated that notices and copies of the petition were ordered to be served on the Appellants only after the interim injunction had already been granted[cite: 12]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The Respondents filed petitions under Section 169 of the Companies Act, 2013. NCLT Mumbai granted an ex-parte ad-interim stay on their removal, prompting the current appeal[cite: 12].
legal_issues: Whether a party can directly appeal an ex-parte ad-interim injunction order passed under Section 169 of the Companies Act, 2013, when they were not served notice prior to the order[cite: 12].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: When an ex-parte ad-interim injunction is granted without prior service of notice, the aggrieved party's primary remedy is to approach the lower tribunal to vacate or modify the order rather than filing an immediate appeal[cite: 12]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The NCLAT left open the substantive legal question of whether a tribunal possesses the jurisdiction to grant an ad-interim injunction staying the removal of a director under Section 169[cite: 12]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The appellate tribunal reviews the impugned order's service directives; evidence that notice was ordered only post-injunction confirms a deprivation of the right to respond[cite: 12]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The bench disposed of the appeals by granting the appellants liberty to file interlocutory applications before the NCLT to vacate the interim order, abstaining from ruling on the jurisdictional merits[cite: 12].
operative_order: The appeals were disposed of, granting the Appellants liberty to file Interlocutory Applications for the recall, vacation, or modification of the interim order before the NCLT. No costs[cite: 12].
summary: The NCLT Mumbai passed an ex-parte ad-interim order restraining the removal of the Respondents from the board of directors under Section 169 of the Companies Act, 2013[cite: 12]. The Appellants challenged the NCLT's jurisdiction to pass such an injunction[cite: 12]. The NCLAT noted that the Appellants had not been served prior to the order, thereby missing the opportunity to object, and consequently disposed of the appeals by allowing them to seek a recall of the order from the NCLT[cite: 12].

case_title: Mr. Piyush vs Reliance Commercial Finance Ltd. & another
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Mr. Piyush is the Appellant (authorised signatory of the Corporate Debtor, Maharashtra Vidyut Nigam Pvt. Ltd.), and Reliance Commercial Finance Ltd. is the Respondent (Financial Creditor)[cite: 13]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: A financial debt owed by the Corporate Debtor to Reliance Commercial Finance Ltd[cite: 13]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The parties settled the debt dispute with the Corporate Debtor making a part payment of Rs. 2 Crores[cite: 13]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The NCLT admitted the Section 7 insolvency application on 4 August 2017[cite: 13]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: A demand draft for Rs. 2 Crores dated 12 December 2017 was physically handed over during the hearing to fulfill the compromise agreement dated 13 December 2017[cite: 13]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai admitted the CIRP application ex-parte on 4 August 2017. The Appellant challenged it for violating natural justice, and the parties subsequently settled[cite: 13].
legal_issues: Whether an order admitting a Corporate Debtor into insolvency is legally sustainable if passed without issuing notice to the Corporate Debtor[cite: 13].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An order admitting a corporate debtor into the Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process is inherently illegal and void if passed without providing prior notice and an opportunity of hearing to the corporate debtor[cite: 13]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Based on the precedent in Innoventive Industries, the adjudicating authority is strictly bound by the principles of natural justice to hear the corporate debtor before accepting a Section 7 application under the IBC[cite: 13]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: An admission by the financial creditor that the lower tribunal passed the order ex-parte is sufficient grounds to immediately set aside the CIRP admission[cite: 13]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The bench quashed the NCLT's admission order due to the fatal lack of notice, recognized the parties' post-admission settlement, and restored the corporate debtor to its board of directors[cite: 13].
operative_order: The appeal was allowed. The NCLT's admission order, moratorium, and appointment of the IRP were set aside. The proceedings were closed based on the compromise agreement, and the Corporate Debtor's board was reinstated. No costs[cite: 13].
summary: NCLT Mumbai admitted a Section 7 insolvency application against Maharashtra Vidyut Nigam Pvt. Ltd. entirely ex-parte, without notifying the Corporate Debtor[cite: 13]. The Appellant challenged this on natural justice grounds, and a settlement for Rs. 2 Crores was executed during the appeal[cite: 13]. The NCLAT declared the ex-parte admission illegal, quashed the CIRP and all actions of the IRP, and fully restored the management of the Corporate Debtor[cite: 13].

case_title: Mr. Ombir Singh Panwar vs Himland Housing Private Ltd.., & Ors
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Mr. Ombir Singh Panwar is the Appellant, and Himland Housing Private Ltd. & Ors. are the Respondents[cite: 14]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: The Appellant alleged he purchased 3,500 equity shares in the company[cite: 14]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The company allegedly failed to register the transfer of the 3,500 equity shares[cite: 14]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The NCLT dismissed the Section 59 petition on 3 July 2017[cite: 14]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The Appellant claimed he paid Rs. 1,35,000 in cash but had no receipts, nor did he possess photocopies of the share certificates. The company disputed the genuineness of the blank transfer deed[cite: 14]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT New Delhi dismissed the Appellant's petition for rectification of the share register under Section 59 of the Companies Act, 2013, and imposed a cost of Rs. 20,000[cite: 14].
legal_issues: Whether a petition for the rectification of a share register can be allowed solely on the basis of a disputed blank transfer deed when the claimant fails to produce any proof of consideration[cite: 14].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A claim for the rectification of a share register will fail if it relies on a disputed transfer instrument without any corroborating evidence of consideration or delivery of share certificates[cite: 14]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 59 of the Companies Act, 2013 requires credible, corroborative evidence of a lawful transfer; a postal receipt stamp by a company clerk does not definitively prove the submission of original share certificates[cite: 14]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Tribunals apply a higher standard of scrutiny to professionals (e.g., Chartered Accountants), expecting them to maintain basic documentary evidence like cash receipts and photocopies; failure to do so undermines the claim's credibility[cite: 14]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The bench upheld the rejection of the transfer claim due to the stark lack of evidence but provided equitable relief by setting aside the punitive costs imposed by the NCLT[cite: 14].
operative_order: The NCLAT set aside the portion of the NCLT's order imposing a cost of Rs. 20,000 on the Appellant. The rest of the NCLT's order dismissing the Section 59 petition was upheld[cite: 14].
summary: The Appellant, a Chartered Accountant, sought the rectification of a share register, claiming he bought 3,500 shares for Rs. 1,35,000 in cash[cite: 14]. NCLT New Delhi dismissed the petition with costs, citing the complete absence of cash receipts or photocopies of the share certificates[cite: 14]. The NCLAT affirmed the dismissal on merits due to the highly disputed nature of the transaction but offered partial relief by deleting the Rs. 20,000 cost penalty[cite: 14].

case_title: T.R. Jawahar & Anr vs Edelweiss Asset & Anr
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: T.R. Jawahar is the Appellant (Shareholder/Director of the Corporate Debtor, Frontline Printers Pvt. Ltd.), and Edelweiss Asset is the Respondent (Financial Creditor)[cite: 15]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: A financial debt managed by Edelweiss Asset acting as a trustee for EARC Trust SC-Trust-SC 19 (Series IV)[cite: 15]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default on a financial debt owed by the Corporate Debtor, leading to the initiation of CIRP[cite: 15]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: NCLT Chennai admitted the Section 7 petition on 2 November 2017[cite: 15]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Part-I of Form I clearly indicated that Edelweiss Asset was incorporated as a financial creditor on 5 October 2007, possessing a valid identification number[cite: 15]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Chennai admitted the Respondent's Section 7 IBC application on 2 November 2017. The Appellant challenged it, arguing the Respondent lacked standing as it filed as a 'Trustee'[cite: 15].
legal_issues: Whether a corporate entity acting in its capacity as a trustee for an asset reconstruction trust qualifies as a 'Financial Creditor' eligible to initiate insolvency proceedings under Section 7 of the IBC[cite: 15].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An entity registered under the Companies Act that functions as a trustee for an asset reconstruction trust holds the statutory standing of a financial creditor under the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code[cite: 15]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The combined reading of Section 5(7) and Section 5(8) of the IBC confirms that a corporate entity does not lose its status as a 'Financial Creditor' simply because it holds the underlying debt in a trust capacity for a specific series[cite: 15]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The tribunal evaluates the statutory filings (Form I); if the entity is formally incorporated and registered as a financial institution, its simultaneous role as a trustee does not nullify its right to file for insolvency[cite: 15]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The bench decisively rejected the appellant's technical objection, confirming that the respondent trustee was a valid financial creditor, thereby upholding the NCLT's admission order[cite: 15].
operative_order: The appeal was dismissed for lacking merit. No costs were awarded[cite: 15].
summary: The Appellant challenged the initiation of corporate insolvency proceedings, arguing that Edelweiss Asset filed the Section 7 application merely as a 'Trustee' and not as a valid 'Financial Creditor'[cite: 15]. The NCLAT summarily dismissed the appeal, ruling that an entity registered under the Companies Act acting as a trustee for an asset reconstruction trust perfectly satisfies the statutory definition of a Financial Creditor under Section 5(7) of the IBC[cite: 15].

case_title: Shilpi Cable Technologies Limited vs. Macquarie Bank Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is Shilpi Cable Technologies Limited, and the Respondent is Macquarie Bank Ltd[cite: 16]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Applications were filed under Section 9 of the I&B Code by the Respondent based on an underlying commercial transaction[cite: 16]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The exact default amounts were claimed under Section 9 applications which were admitted by the Adjudicating Authority[cite: 16]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The impugned orders admitting the applications and appointing an IRP were passed by the Adjudicating Authority on 24th May 2017[cite: 16]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Macquarie Bank Ltd (Australia), not being a financial institution under Section 3(14) of the I&B Code, relied on a certificate that could not be legally used to decide debt default, and the demand notice was issued by a lawyer without proof of authorization or position within the company[cite: 16]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The Adjudicating Authority admitted C.P. No. (IB)-64(PB)/2017 and C.P. No. (IB)-65(PB)/2017 on 24th May 2017, which led to the present appeals[cite: 16].
legal_issues: 1. Whether a foreign bank certificate issued by an entity that is not a financial institution under Section 3(14) of the I&B Code can establish a debt default. 2. Whether a demand notice under Section 8 issued by an independent lawyer without authorization can maintain a Section 9 petition[cite: 16].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A certificate issued by a foreign entity that does not qualify as a financial institution under Section 3(14) of the I&B Code cannot be relied upon to prove a debt default, and a Section 8 notice issued by an unauthorized lawyer is invalid[cite: 16]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The bench strictly interpreted Section 3(14) regarding financial institutions and Section 8 mandates regarding proper notice issuance by claimants[cite: 16]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The tribunal evaluates whether the issuing entity meets the statutory definition of a financial institution and whether the notice-giver holds an official position or explicit authorization from the appellant company[cite: 16]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The bench concluded that because the bank was not a financial institution and the lawyer's notice was defective, the Section 9 petition was non-maintainable, warranting the setting aside of the admission orders[cite: 16].
operative_order: Both impugned orders dated 24th May 2017 were set aside, and the appeals were allowed. All actions taken by the IRP, moratorium orders, and newspaper advertisements were declared illegal. The Adjudicating Authority was directed to close the proceedings, and the Appellant company was restored to independent functioning through its Board of Directors, subject to payment of the IRP's fees[cite: 16].
summary: Shilpi Cable Technologies Limited appealed against the NCLT's orders admitting Section 9 insolvency applications filed by Macquarie Bank Ltd[cite: 16]. The NCLAT allowed the appeals, following its precedent in Macquarie Bank Ltd v. Uttam Galva Metallics Limited, ruling that Macquarie Bank Australia was not a financial institution under Section 3(14) of the I&B Code and that a demand notice issued by an unauthorized lawyer is legally invalid under Section 8[cite: 16]. All consequential insolvency proceedings and IRP actions were quashed[cite: 16].

case_title: Tinnevelly Tuticorin Investments Limited vs. Amrex Marketing Private Limited & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellants are Tinnevelly Tuticorin Investments Limited and B.R. Kuppuswamy & Anr., and the Respondents are Amrex Marketing Private Limited & Ors[cite: 17]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: The dispute involves the transfer of shares originally belonging to B.R. Kuppuswamy & Anr. in favor of Amrex Marketing Pvt. Ltd[cite: 17]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not applicable, as this is a corporate share transfer and rectification dispute under the Companies Act[cite: 17]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The common impugned order was passed by the NCLT Kolkata Bench on 16th August 2017[cite: 17]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The original share certificates were handed over and were in the possession of Amrex Marketing Pvt. Ltd., while the appellants failed to point out any specific legal defects in the transfer deeds[cite: 17]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Amrex Marketing filed a petition under Sections 58 and 59 of the Companies Act, 2013, which was allowed by the NCLT on 16th August 2017, directing the company to record the shares. Simultaneously, B.R. Kuppuswamy filed a civil suit (OS No. 6291/2017) alleging fraud and misrepresentation[cite: 17].
legal_issues: Whether a subsequent civil suit alleging fraud in share transfers constitutes a valid ground to interfere with an NCLT order directing the rectification of the share register under Sections 58 and 59 of the Companies Act, 2013[cite: 17].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The subsequent filing of a civil suit alleging fraud does not automatically invalidate a prior tribunal order directing share rectification under Sections 58 and 59 if no statutory defect in the transfer deed is established[cite: 17]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Sections 58 and 59 of the Companies Act, 2013 require companies to register transfers unless a concrete legal infirmity is proven[cite: 17]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The tribunal examines whether valid transfer deeds and physical share certificates were delivered; in the absence of demonstrable defects or forgery evidence at the tribunal stage, the transfer must be given effect[cite: 17]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The bench concluded that since the share certificates were delivered and no flaws were found in the transfer deeds, the NCLT's order must be upheld, leaving the parties to pursue interim remedies in their pending civil suit[cite: 17].
operative_order: Both appeals were dismissed with no order as to costs, with observations that the plaintiffs in OS No. 6291/2017 may move the civil court for appropriate interim relief[cite: 17].
summary: Appellants challenged an NCLT Kolkata order directing Tinnevelly Tuticorin Investments Limited to register share transfers in favor of Amrex Marketing Pvt. Ltd. under Sections 58 and 59 of the Companies Act, 2013[cite: 17]. The Appellants argued that a civil suit had been filed alleging fraud and misrepresentation[cite: 17]. The NCLAT dismissed the appeals, holding that the mere filing of a subsequent civil suit is not a ground to overturn the NCLT's order when the transfer documents are otherwise proper and the share certificates are in the transferee's possession[cite: 17].

case_title: Smt. Hema Dhapola & Anr. vs. Nirvan Hospitals Private Ltd. & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellants are Smt. Hema Dhapola & Anr., and the Respondents are Nirvan Hospitals Private Ltd. & Ors[cite: 18]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Not applicable; the matter concerns a strict procedural limitation period for filing an appeal[cite: 18]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: No debt or commercial default; the default is a procedural delay exceeding statutory limitation bounds[cite: 18]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The NCLT Allahabad Bench passed the impugned order on 19th December 2016. The copy was received by the appellants on 17th January 2017. A defective appeal was filed on 13th April 2017, and a fresh filing was made on 11th May 2017[cite: 18]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Tribunal tracking and filing logs established that the appeal was filed approximately four months after the receipt of the certified order copy, breaching the maximum allowable statutory window[cite: 18]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The Appellants filed multiple delayed petitions for condonation of delay before the NCLAT to challenge the 19th December 2016 NCLT order[cite: 18].
legal_issues: Whether the NCLAT has the statutory jurisdiction under Section 421 of the Companies Act, 2013 to condone a delay in filing an appeal that exceeds the maximum permissible grace period of 45 days beyond the initial 45-day limitation[cite: 18].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An appellate tribunal lacks the legal jurisdiction to condone any delay in filing an appeal that surpasses the absolute statutory ceiling of 90 days (45 days plus a maximum extendable 45 days)[cite: 18]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 421(3) of the Companies Act, 2013 mandates a 45-day limitation period from the date the order is made available, with a strict proviso capping discretionary extensions at an additional 45 days[cite: 18]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The timeline is calculated strictly from the date of receipt of the order copy; multiple defective filings cannot reset or extend the statutory limitation boundary[cite: 18]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The bench concluded that because the total delay exceeded 45 plus 45 days from the date of receipt, the tribunal was completely devoid of jurisdiction to entertain the appeal[cite: 18].
operative_order: The petition for condonation of delay was rejected, and the appeal was dismissed as barred by limitation, with no order as to costs[cite: 18].
summary: The Appellants appealed against an NCLT order dated 19th December 2016 after receiving a copy on 17th January 2017, but instituted their final appeal only on 11th May 2017[cite: 18]. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal as barred by limitation, ruling that the total delay exceeded the absolute maximum threshold of 90 days permitted under Section 421(3) of the Companies Act, 2013, leaving the tribunal without jurisdiction to condone the delay[cite: 18].

case_title: Jammu Paper Pvt. Ltd. vs. Shiv Pooja Traders
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is Jammu Paper Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor), and the Respondent is Shiv Pooja Traders (Operational Creditor)[cite: 19]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: An underlying operational debt transaction between the parties that led to a Section 9 insolvency application[cite: 19]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The operational debt default claims were settled between the parties during the appeal proceedings[cite: 19]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The NCLT Chandigarh Bench passed admission orders on 10th July 2017 and IRP appointment orders on 21st July 2017[cite: 19]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The respondent operational creditor admitted in its reply that due to an incorrect address ('SIDGO I/Complex, Bari Brahmnia' instead of 'SIDCO I/Complex, Phase-II, Bari Brahmna, Samba') written on postal envelopes and track reports, Form-4 notice was never duly served on the corporate debtor[cite: 19]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Chandigarh admitted the Section 9 petition and appointed an IRP ex-parte without serving notice or hearing the corporate debtor, prompting the appeals[cite: 19].
legal_issues: Whether an order admitting an operational insolvency petition and appointing an IRP is legally sustainable if passed without serving notice to the corporate debtor due to address discrepancies, and where parties have settled[cite: 19].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An ex-parte insolvency admission order passed without service of statutory notice and in violation of natural justice is void and must be set aside[cite: 19]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Strict compliance with notice requirements under the IBC rules is mandatory before a corporate debtor can be subjected to the rigors of insolvency resolution[cite: 19]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Postal track reports and admissions by the opposing counsel acknowledging flawed address documentation establish a fatal failure of service[cite: 19]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The bench ruled that because notice was never served due to a faulty address and the parties settled the dispute, the admission orders and all IRP actions were illegal and must be set aside[cite: 19].
operative_order: Both impugned orders dated 10th July 2017 and 21st July 2017 were set aside, and the petition under Section 9 was closed in the absence of any claim. All IRP actions, moratoriums, and advertisements were declared illegal. The appellant was released from legal rigors to function independently through its Board, and the Adjudicating Authority was directed to determine and award the IRP's fees payable by the appellant[cite: 19].
summary: Jammu Paper Pvt. Ltd. challenged NCLT Chandigarh's orders admitting a Section 9 insolvency petition and appointing an IRP[cite: 19]. The NCLAT allowed the appeals after the operational creditor conceded that the demand notice in Form-4 was not duly served due to an incorrect address on postal records, and confirmed that the parties had settled the dispute[cite: 19]. The NCLAT set aside the insolvency orders as violative of natural justice, closed the petition, and restored management to the Board of Directors[cite: 19].

case_title: Jugnar Processors Pvt. Ltd. & Anr. vs. Shri Rohtas Jugalkishore Gupta
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellants are Jugnar Processors Pvt. Ltd. & Anr., and the Respondent is Shri Rohtas Jugalkishore Gupta[cite: 20]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: A family and corporate dispute involving oppression and mismanagement claims under Sections 397 and 398 of the Companies Act, 1956[cite: 20]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not applicable; the dispute relates to a prior withdrawal and subsequent refiling of a company petition following a failed settlement[cite: 20]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The original company petition was withdrawn on 19th December 2014, and the NCLT Mumbai Bench rejected the appellant's preliminary objections via an order dated 2nd March 2017[cite: 20]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: A settlement deed was executed on 10th November 2014 involving a Rs. 75 lacs payment assurance, but conditions were disputed and oral terms failed, leading the respondent to file a fresh petition for the same cause of action[cite: 20]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai rejected the appellant's preliminary objections regarding maintainability on 2nd March 2017, holding that the petition could proceed on merits, which led to the present appeal[cite: 20].
legal_issues: Whether a party can maintain a fresh company petition for oppression and mismanagement when a prior petition was unconditionally withdrawn based on an unconsummated or disputed private settlement deed[cite: 20].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The withdrawal of a company petition pursuant to a private settlement that subsequently breaks down or fails does not act as a permanent statutory bar against pursuing claims for the same underlying cause of action, provided there was no adjudication on merits[cite: 20]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: In the absence of a statutory prohibition or a decision on merits, a tribunal is fully competent to entertain a fresh application or proceed when a conditional settlement collapses[cite: 20]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The tribunal verifies whether the previous order disposed of the matter on merits or merely permitted a withdrawal based on an incomplete or disputed settlement; if no rights were adjudicated, maintainability is upheld[cite: 20]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The bench concluded that since the settlement terms were disputed and never fulfilled, and the previous petition was merely dismissed as withdrawn without a decision on merits, the tribunal committed no error in admitting the case[cite: 20].
operative_order: The appeal was dismissed as lacking merit, confirming the tribunal's decision to proceed with the adjudication on merits[cite: 20].
summary: The Appellants challenged an NCLT Mumbai order rejecting their preliminary objections against a company petition filed under Sections 397 and 398 of the Companies Act, 1956[cite: 20]. The Appellants argued that the Respondent had previously withdrawn a similar petition in 2014 based on a family settlement[cite: 20]. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, ruling that because the settlement conditions failed and the prior petition was merely withdrawn without any adjudication on merits, the respondent was not barred from initiating fresh proceedings on the same cause of action[cite: 20].

case_title: Niranjanlal Agarwal and 3 Ors. vs. Durga Liquor India Private Limited & 4 Ors.
bench: National Company Law Appellate Tribunal, New Delhi
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants are Niranjanlal Agarwal and 3 others[cite: 1]; Respondents are Durga Liquor India Private Limited and 4 others[cite: 1]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Inter-se company dispute regarding shareholding and management[cite: 1]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not applicable (company law oppression and mismanagement petition involving fixed deposits and share certificates)[cite: 1]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Petition filed in 2012; CLB disposed of matter on 31st March 2013; subsequent C.A. 1 & 2 of 2016 decided on 19th October 2016; police complaint filed on 15th September 2017[cite: 1]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Memorandum of Compromise dated 23.3.2013, Indemnity Bond dated 5.2.2016, and police complaint regarding loss of 36,443 share certificates[cite: 1]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Original Company Petition No. 84 of 2012 filed before CLB, later transferred to NCLT Hyderabad Bench, which passed order dated 19.10.2016 and subsequent order dated 8.5.2017 in C.A. No. 77 of 2017 refusing modification, leading to the present appeal[cite: 1].
legal_issues: Whether the NCLT was justified in refusing to modify its earlier order dated 19th October 2016 when the Appellants failed to comply with the mandatory conditions regarding lodging a police complaint and submitting an indemnity bond for lost share certificates[cite: 1].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An appellate tribunal will not interfere with discretionary orders of the tribunal when the party seeking relief has failed to comply with mandatory directions in letter and spirit[cite: 1]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Interpretation of tribunal powers under company law to enforce compliance with settlement terms and procedural prerequisites[cite: 1]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Verification of whether directions regarding police complaints and indemnity bonds for lost shares were fully complied with[cite: 1]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: In the absence of compliance with the tribunal's directions, the appeal lacks merit and stands dismissed[cite: 1].
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed without any costs[cite: 1].
summary: This appeal was preferred by Niranjanlal Agarwal and others against the order of the NCLT, Hyderabad Bench, which refused to modify its earlier directions requiring the Appellants to lodge a police complaint for lost share certificates and furnish an indemnity bond[cite: 1]. The underlying dispute originated from a 2012 company petition under Sections 397 and 398 of the Companies Act, 1956, which was initially settled via a compromise[cite: 1]. Subsequently, applications were filed for the release of deposited amounts, leading to conditional orders[cite: 1]. Because the Appellants failed to fully comply with the mandatory conditions and directions, the NCLAT upheld the lower tribunal's decision, dismissing the appeal for lack of merit[cite: 1].

case_title: M/s. Custodial Services (India) Private Limited vs. M/s. Metafilms (India) Ltd.
bench: National Company Law Appellate Tribunal, New Delhi
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is M/s. Custodial Services (India) Private Limited (Operational Creditor); Respondent is M/s. Metafilms (India) Ltd. (Corporate Debtor)[cite: 2]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Transferred petition under Section 433(e)/(f) of the Companies Act, 1956[cite: 2]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Unpaid debt arising from commercial dealings, though specific amounts were superseded by procedural limitation issues[cite: 2]. 4.
