STATUTORY TIMELINES: Impugned order passed on 13th July 2017; 30-day limitation expired on 12th August 2017; extended 15-day condonable period expired on 27th/28th August 2017; appeal filed after curing defects on 7th September 2017[cite: 2]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Appeal filing records and defect rectification timestamps showing filing beyond the 45-day statutory limit[cite: 2]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Chennai Bench passed an order on 13th July 2017 declining to treat the transferred petition as a Section 9 application due to a pending Section 11 arbitration case and adjourned it sine die, prompting an appeal filed on 7th September 2017[cite: 2].
legal_issues: Whether the Appellate Tribunal has the jurisdiction to condone a delay in filing an appeal beyond the maximum statutory period of 15 days prescribed under Section 61(3) of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016[cite: 2].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The appellate tribunal has no jurisdiction to condone delay in filing an appeal beyond the total permissible period of forty-five days (thirty days plus a maximum of fifteen days) under Section 61(3) of the IBC[cite: 2]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Strict interpretation of Section 61(3) of the IBC, 2016 regarding limitation and condonation limits[cite: 2]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Calculation of limitation days from the date of knowledge/impugned order, accounting for holidays and defect re-filing dates[cite: 2]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Since the appeal was filed beyond the absolute 45-day statutory limit, the tribunal lacks jurisdiction to condone the delay, rendering the appeal barred by limitation[cite: 2].
operative_order: The petition for condonation of delay is rejected, and the appeal is dismissed as barred by limitation, with no order as to costs[cite: 2].
summary: This appeal challenged an order passed by the NCLT Chennai Bench, which had adjourned sine die a petition under Section 433 of the Companies Act, 1956 (treated under the IBC), due to a pending arbitration proceeding under Section 11 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996[cite: 2]. The NCLAT did not examine the merits of the case because the appeal was filed on September 7, 2017, well beyond the mandatory thirty-day limitation period and the maximum allowable fifteen-day condonation window under Section 61(3) of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016[cite: 2]. Consequently, the Appellate Tribunal held that it lacked jurisdiction to condone the delay, dismissing the appeal as time-barred[cite: 2].

case_title: Sanjay Murarka & Ors. vs. Fab Leathers Limited & Ors.
bench: National Company Law Appellate Tribunal, New Delhi
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants are Sanjay Murarka and 3 others (original Petitioners); Respondents Nos. 1 to 6 are Fab Leathers Limited and family members/directors; Respondent No. 7 is Chroma Business Ltd[cite: 4]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Internal corporate disputes and oppression/mismanagement claims concerning Fab Leathers Limited[cite: 4]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not applicable (company law dispute regarding shareholding and management control)[cite: 4]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Company Petition No. 26/2015 filed earlier; dismissed by NCLT on 24th March 2017; I.A. 169/KB/2017 dismissed on 5th May 2017; Memorandum of Settlement executed on 12th November 2017[cite: 4]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Original Memorandum of Settlement dated 12th November 2017 and supporting affidavits of Appellant No. 1 Sanjay Murarka and Respondent No. 3 Praveer Murarka[cite: 4]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Kolkata Bench dismissed the company petition as not pressed/unable to argue; NCLAT appeal filed challenging the dismissal and interim orders, during which parties settled the dispute amicably[cite: 4].
legal_issues: Whether the company petition under Sections 397 and 398 of the Companies Act, 1956 can be disposed of as withdrawn based on an out-of-court Memorandum of Settlement executed between the contesting parties[cite: 4].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Where contesting parties resolve their corporate disputes amicably through a formal settlement agreement, appellate courts can set aside lower tribunal dismissals, restore the petition, and permit its withdrawal in terms of the settlement[cite: 4]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Interpretation of company law powers to record settlements and permit withdrawal of oppression and mismanagement petitions[cite: 4]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Verification of the authenticity of the Memorandum of Settlement and supporting affidavits executed by the principal parties[cite: 4]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Upon presentation of a valid Memorandum of Settlement signed by all contesting parties, the impugned dismissal orders are set aside, the petition is restored, and disposed of as withdrawn[cite: 4].
operative_order: Respondent No. 7 is deleted from the array of parties; the impugned orders dated 24th March 2017 and 5th May 2017 are quashed and set aside; Company Petition No. 26/2015 is restored and disposed of as withdrawn pursuant to the Memorandum of Settlement dated 12th November 2017, with no order as to costs[cite: 4].
summary: This appeal arose from an order of the NCLT Kolkata Bench, which had dismissed Company Petition No. 26/2015 filed under Sections 397 and 398 of the Companies Act, 1956 after parties failed to record a compromise[cite: 4]. During the appellate proceedings before the NCLAT, the contesting parties successfully resolved their disputes and executed a formal Memorandum of Settlement dated November 12, 2017, supported by affidavits[cite: 4]. Additionally, Respondent No. 7 was deleted from the array of parties upon the Appellants' request[cite: 4]. Consequently, the NCLAT set aside the lower tribunal's dismissal orders, restored the company petition, and formally disposed of it as withdrawn in accordance with the settlement terms[cite: 4].

case_title: M/s Paharpur Cooling Towers Limited vs. M/s Ankit Metal & Power Limited
bench: National Company Law Appellate Tribunal, New Delhi
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is M/s Paharpur Cooling Towers Limited (Operational Creditor); Respondent is M/s Ankit Metal & Power Limited (Corporate Debtor)[cite: 5]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Supply of goods/services giving rise to an operational debt[cite: 5]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Unpaid operational debt where amounts were disputed prior to demand notice[cite: 5]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Dispute highlighted in emails dated 13th May 2015 (prior to Section 8 demand notice); NCLT Kolkata Bench dismissed the Section 9 application on 21st August 2017[cite: 5]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Emails dated 13th May 2015 showing pre-existing disputes and lawyer's letter dated 2nd April 2016[cite: 5]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Kolkata Bench dismissed the Section 9 application under the IBC on August 21, 2017, on twin grounds of existence of a pre-existing dispute and improper filing by a Company Secretary, leading to the present appeal[cite: 5].
legal_issues: 1. Whether a Company Secretary holding a power of attorney is competent to file an application under Section 9 of the IBC on behalf of an operational creditor. 2. Whether the Adjudicating Authority correctly identified a pre-existing dispute pre-dating the Section 8 demand notice[cite: 5].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: *A power of attorney holder or company secretary cannot independently file an insolvency application under the IBC unless authorized strictly in accordance with statutory provisions, and an application must be rejected if a pre-existing dispute exists[cite: 5]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Interpretation of Section 8 and Section 9 of the IBC and the non-override effect of the Power of Attorney Act, 1882[cite: 5]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Evaluation of contemporaneous documentary evidence such as emails establishing a genuine pre-existing commercial dispute prior to the statutory demand notice[cite: 5]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The dismissal of the Section 9 application is upheld due to a pre-existing dispute and improper filing, while reserving the creditor's right to pursue admitted dues through fresh statutory proceedings[cite: 5].
operative_order: The appeal is disposed of, declining to interfere with the impugned order dated 21st August 2017, but granting liberty to the Appellant to initiate fresh proceedings under Section 9 in respect of any undisputed admitted debt after issuing a fresh Section 8 demand notice, with no order as to costs[cite: 5].
summary: This appeal was filed by M/s Paharpur Cooling Towers Limited against the NCLT Kolkata Bench order dismissing its Section 9 insolvency application under the IBC against M/s Ankit Metal & Power Limited[cite: 5]. The NCLT rejected the application because it was improperly filed by a Company Secretary and because a pre-existing dispute existed prior to the Section 8 demand notice[cite: 5]. The NCLAT affirmed that power of attorney holders cannot file such applications and confirmed the pre-existing dispute[cite: 5]. However, the Appellate Tribunal disposed of the appeal while granting liberty to the Appellant to initiate fresh Section 9 proceedings for any undisputed admitted dues after issuing a proper demand notice[cite: 5].

case_title: Infotecnic India Ltd. & Ors. vs. Sanjiv Bhavnani & Ors.
bench: National Company Law Appellate Tribunal, New Delhi
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants are Infotecnic India Ltd. & Ors.; Respondents are Sanjiv Bhavnani & Ors.[cite: 6] 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Dispute arising from the alleged transfer/pledge of equity shares in the 1st appellant company[cite: 6]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not applicable (company law rectification of register of shareholders)[cite: 6]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Impugned order passed on 23rd March 2017; certified copy prepared on 19th June 2017; appeal filed on 30th June 2017 after removing defects. Company petition preferred in 2010[cite: 6]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Documentary records showing non-compliance with Section 108 of the Companies Act, 1956 (absence of executed transfer deed, witness, or stamp fees), and lack of notice to redeem alleged security[cite: 6]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT allowed the respondents' application for rectification of the Register of Shareholders on 23rd March 2017, leading to the present appeal before NCLAT[cite: 6].
legal_issues: Whether the NCLT was justified in ordering the rectification of the Register of Shareholders under company law when shares were transferred without complying with mandatory transfer provisions under Section 108 of the Companies Act, 1956 and without giving an opportunity to redeem the security[cite: 6].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Provisions of Section 108 of the Companies Act, 1956 are mandatory for passing a valid title, and transferring shares appropriated as security without a duly executed transfer deed and without providing an opportunity to redeem liability vitiates the transfer with illegality[cite: 6]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Strict interpretation of mandatory share transfer requirements and limitation pleadings in company law petitions[cite: 6]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Examination of record to verify compliance with Section 108 and whether the limitation plea was raised before the lower tribunal[cite: 6]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Since mandatory transfer formalities were ignored and no limitation plea was raised below, the tribunal's rectification order is upheld and the appeal is dismissed[cite: 6].
operative_order: The delay of 44 days in preferring the appeal is condoned; the appeal is dismissed on merits with no order as to costs[cite: 6].
summary: This appeal was filed by Infotecnic India Ltd. and others against an order of the NCLT dated March 23, 2017, which allowed the respondents' application for rectification of the Register of Shareholders[cite: 6]. The NCLT had found that the transfer of shares was illegal because mandatory provisions of Section 108 of the Companies Act, 1956—such as executing a valid transfer deed and paying stamp fees—were not complied with, and no notice was given to redeem the alleged security[cite: 6]. Before the NCLAT, the appellants argued limitation and pendency of a Delhi High Court suit[cite: 6]. The NCLAT rejected these contentions, noting that limitation was never pleaded below and parallel proceedings do not bar NCLT jurisdiction[cite: 6]. Consequently, the appeal was dismissed[cite: 6].

case_title: Shri Manish Vipinchandra Patel & Anr. vs. Ambika Food Products Pvt. Ltd. & Ors.
bench: National Company Law Appellate Tribunal, New Delhi
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants are Shri Manish Vipinchandra Patel & Shri Krunal Vipinchandra Patel; Respondents are Ambika Food Products Pvt. Ltd. & Ors.[cite: 7] 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate dispute and oppression/mismanagement proceedings originating from old Company Petition No. 16/397-398/CLB/MB/2012[cite: 7]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not applicable (company law appeal barred by limitation)[cite: 7]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Impugned order passed on 17th May 2017; certified copy issued on 7th June 2017; appeal filed on 12th September 2017[cite: 7]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Certified copy records and advocate endorsement showing the certified copy of the order was issued on 7th June 2017, establishing that the appeal was filed beyond the maximum permissible period[cite: 7]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Ahmedabad Bench passed the impugned order on 17th May 2017; Appellants filed an appeal along with I.A. No. 594 of 2017 for condonation of delay, which was contested by Respondents based on actual issuance date records[cite: 7].
legal_issues: Whether the appellate tribunal has the jurisdiction to condone delay in filing an appeal under Section 421 of the Companies Act, 2013 when the appeal is presented beyond the statutory 45-day period plus the maximum permissible extended period of 45 days[cite: 7].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An appeal filed beyond the absolute statutory limitation period prescribed under Section 421 of the Companies Act, 2013 cannot be entertained, and the tribunal lacks jurisdiction to condone delay exceeding the permissible statutory cap[cite: 7]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Interpretation of limitation and condonation limits under Section 421 of the Companies Act, 2013[cite: 7]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Verification of official registry records and certified copy issuance dates to ascertain exact day of delivery[cite: 7]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Since records conclusively prove the certified copy was issued on 7th June 2017 and the appeal was filed on 12th September 2017, the appeal is barred by limitation[cite: 7].
operative_order: Interlocutory Application No. 594 of 2017 is rejected, and Company Appeal (AT) No. 306 of 2017 is disposed of as time-barred[cite: 7].
summary: This appeal was filed by Manish Vipinchandra Patel and another against the order of the NCLT, Ahmedabad Bench dated May 17, 2017, in a company petition relating to oppression and mismanagement[cite: 7]. The Appellants filed an interlocutory application seeking condonation of delay, claiming they received the certified copy on June 27, 2017[cite: 7]. However, Respondents produced records and advocate endorsements proving that the certified copy was actually issued on June 7, 2017[cite: 7]. Consequently, the NCLAT calculated that the appeal was filed well beyond the maximum permissible limitation period under Section 421 of the Companies Act, 2013[cite: 7]. The Appellate Tribunal rejected the condonation application and dismissed the appeal as time-barred[cite: 7].

case_title: Ramabhadran Sivaraman vs. M/s. Star Quarry and Aggregates Private Limited & Ors.
bench: National Company Law Appellate Tribunal, New Delhi
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Ramabhadran Sivaraman; Respondents are M/s. Star Quarry and Aggregates Private Limited & Ors.[cite: 8] 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate dispute regarding oppression and mismanagement, illegal share allotments, change of designation, and shifting of registered office[cite: 8]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not applicable (company law oppression and mismanagement petition)[cite: 8]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Impugned order passed on 24th March 2017 by NCLT Chennai Bench; appeal filed subsequently[cite: 8]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Board resolutions dated 21.5.2014, 20.6.2014, 25.8.2014, EGM resolution dated 28.3.2014, and various ROC filings (DIR-12, PAS-3, INC-22, MGT-14, SH-7)[cite: 8]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Chennai Bench allowed the company petition on 24th March 2017 finding acts of oppression and mismanagement, restoring the Appellant as Managing Director and invalidating illegal resolutions, which order the Appellant challenged before NCLAT before seeking to withdraw the appeal[cite: 8].
legal_issues: Whether the NCLT's findings and consequential directions rectifying acts of oppression and mismanagement, restoring the appellant's position as Managing Director, and setting aside illegal board resolutions warranted appellate interference[cite: 8].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An appellant is permitted to withdraw an appeal when the appellate tribunal indicates unwillingness to interfere with a well-reasoned lower tribunal order granting substantive relief against oppression and mismanagement[cite: 8]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Interpretation of NCLT powers under Sections 397, 398, and 402 of the Companies Act, 1956 to remedy corporate oppression[cite: 8]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Examination of corporate records, board resolutions, and statutory filings establishing oppressive conduct[cite: 8]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Upon the appellate tribunal expressing reluctance to interfere with the impugned order, the appellant sought and was granted permission to withdraw the appeal[cite: 8].
operative_order: The appeal is disposed of as withdrawn upon the request of the appellant's counsel, with no order as to costs[cite: 8].
summary: This appeal was filed by Ramabhadran Sivaraman against the NCLT Chennai Bench order dated March 24, 2017, which allowed his petition under Sections 397, 398, and 402 of the Companies Act, 1956[cite: 8]. The NCLT found oppression and mismanagement by respondents, setting aside illegal share allotments, unauthorized office relocation, and the appellant's removal as Managing Director[cite: 8]. The NCLT also directed the appellant to withdraw a pending Kerala High Court writ petition and facilitate business commencement[cite: 8]. During appellate hearings, when the NCLAT indicated it was not inclined to interfere with the comprehensive relief granted, the appellant requested permission to withdraw the appeal[cite: 8]. Accordingly, the appeal was disposed of as withdrawn[cite: 8].

case_title: M/s. R.G. Shaw & Sons Private Limited & Anr. vs. M/s. Naviplast Traders Private Limited & Ors.
bench: National Company Law Appellate Tribunal, New Delhi
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants are M/s. R.G. Shaw & Sons Private Limited (Corporate Debtor) & Anr.; Respondents are M/s. Naviplast Traders Private Limited & Ors. (Financial Creditors)[cite: 9]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Loan facility advanced under an oral agreement, evidenced by letters, money receipts, demand promissory notes, and dishonored cheques[cite: 9]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Unpaid loan amounts due and payable upon dishonor of cheques presented to the financial creditor[cite: 9]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Application under Section 7 of the IBC filed before NCLT Kolkata Bench; admitted on 12th April 2017[cite: 9]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Demand promissory notes, loan receipt documents, and dishonored cheques evidencing debt and default[cite: 9]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Kolkata Bench admitted the Section 7 application, declared a moratorium, and appointed an Insolvency Resolution Professional on 12th April 2017 in Company Petition No. 186/2017, leading to the present appeal[cite: 9].
legal_issues: Whether initiation of proceedings under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 or the existence of an oral agreement regarding loan repayment without a fixed due date bars the admission of a Section 7 application under the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 where debt and default are established[cite: 9].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Initiation of parallel criminal proceedings under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act for dishonor of cheques does not bar or preclude the admission of a Section 7 insolvency application under the IBC where a valid debt and default are established[cite: 9]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Interpretation of Section 7 of the IBC, 2016 regarding completeness of Form 1 and requirements for disclosing pending litigation[cite: 9]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Examination of promissory notes, loan receipts, and admitted cheque dishonor to prove existence of debt and default[cite: 9]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Since debt and default are admitted and parallel Section 138 proceedings do not invalidate insolvency proceedings, the NCLT's admission order is legally sound and the appeal must be dismissed[cite: 9].
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed for lack of merit, with no order as to costs[cite: 9].
summary: This appeal was preferred by R.G. Shaw & Sons Private Limited against an order of the NCLT Kolkata Bench dated April 12, 2017, which admitted a Section 7 application under the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 filed by M/s. Naviplast Traders Private Limited[cite: 9]. The Adjudicating Authority declared a moratorium and appointed an Insolvency Resolution Professional[cite: 9]. The Appellant argued that parallel proceedings under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act were pending for dishonored cheques and that repayment terms under an oral agreement had no fixed date[cite: 9]. The NCLAT held that cheque dishonor proceedings do not bar IBC action and that admitted debt and default justified admission[cite: 9]. The appeal was dismissed[cite: 9].

case_title: Nulon Global Ltd. vs. Yash Golyon & Ors.
bench: National Company Law Appellate Tribunal, New Delhi
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Nulon Global Ltd. (Respondent in NCLT); Respondents are Yash Golyon & Ors. (Petitioners in NCLT)[cite: 10]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Company petition filed two years prior regarding corporate disputes before transfer to NCLT Kolkata[cite: 10]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not applicable (frivolous appeal against procedural orders and adjournment tactics)[cite: 10]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: NCLT order passed on 6th April 2017; interlocutory application filed by appellant on 29th March 2017; subsequent recusal application filed on 7th July 2017[cite: 10]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Record of proceedings showing final arguments were nearly complete when the appellant filed stay and recusal applications to stall proceedings[cite: 10]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Kolkata Bench passed an order on 6th April 2017 in CP No. 130/2015 dismissing further replies on IA 117/2017 and scheduling final hearings, which prompted the appellant to file a frivolous appeal and subsequent recusal application before NCLAT[cite: 10].
legal_issues: Whether filing multiple interlocutory and recusal applications at the fag end of final arguments to stall proceedings constitutes an abuse of process of law warranting dismissal of the appeal with costs[cite: 10].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Filing frivolous appeals and dilatory interlocutory applications to stall tribunal proceedings when final arguments are complete constitutes an abuse of process of law, justifying dismissal with exemplary costs[cite: 10]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Interpretation of statutory mandate under Section 422 of the Companies Act, 2013 requiring expeditious disposal of company petitions within three months[cite: 10]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Review of procedural timelines and docket conduct to identify deliberate delaying tactics by a party[cite: 10]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Since the appellant engaged in serious abuse of process and delaying tactics, the appeal must be dismissed with costs and directions for speedy disposal[cite: 10].
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed with costs of Rs. 60,000/- to be paid by the appellant to the Registrar, NCLAT, New Delhi within one month, and the NCLT member is requested to dispose of the company petition on merits without granting unnecessary adjournments[cite: 10].
summary: This appeal was filed by Nulon Global Ltd. against an NCLT Kolkata Bench order dated April 6, 2017, in Company Petition No. 130/2015[cite: 10]. The NCLT noted that when final arguments were nearly complete, the appellant filed dilatory applications and sought member recusal to stall proceedings[cite: 10]. Emphasizing that the petition had languished for two years despite the statutory mandate under Section 422 of the Companies Act, 2013 for speedy disposal, the NCLAT characterized the appeal as frivolous and an abuse of process[cite: 10]. Consequently, the Appellate Tribunal dismissed the appeal with costs of Rs. 60,000/- and directed the Tribunal to decide the main petition on merits without adjournments[cite: 10].

case_title: Eyelid Infrastructure Private Limited vs Birenbhai R. Panchal
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellants (Eyelid Infrastructure Pvt. Ltd. & Ors.) were the respondents in the original company petition, and the Respondents (Birenbhai R. Panchal & Ors.) were the petitioners[cite: 1]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: The dispute relates to a compromise formalized via Consent Terms dated 18 October 2013 regarding the return of original deeds and property documents[cite: 1]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: No specific monetary default amount is detailed; the breach pertains to non-fulfillment of commitments under the Consent Terms[cite: 1]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The Consent Terms were signed on 18 October 2013 and filed on 22 December 2014[cite: 1]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The original dismissal was granted based on a photocopy (Xerox) of the Consent Terms produced solely by the Appellants' counsel in the absence of the Petitioners[cite: 1]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The Company Law Board passed an ex-parte order on 22 December 2014 dismissing the petition as withdrawn[cite: 1]. The NCLT Mumbai later recalled this order on 2 May 2017 (in C.A. 30/2015), prompting the Appellants to file this appeal[cite: 1].
legal_issues: Whether the NCLT erred in recalling an ex-parte order that dismissed a company petition based on a photocopy of Consent Terms presented without the presence or affirmation of the original petitioners[cite: 1].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Principles of natural justice dictate that when a matter is disposed of based on consent terms, the authority must verify that both parties are present, agree to the terms, and that the terms are lawful[cite: 1]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The tribunal emphasized procedural fairness over technical finality when consent terms are contested[cite: 1]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Relying on a mere photocopy of consent terms without the opposing party's presence or affirmation is legally insufficient to bind them to a withdrawal[cite: 1]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT concluded that the NCLT committed no error in recalling the ex-parte dismissal and directing the matter to be listed for a fair hearing, thereby rejecting the appeal[cite: 1].
operative_order: The appeal is rejected as lacking substance. No order as to costs[cite: 1].
summary: The Appellants challenged an NCLT order that recalled a previous ex-parte dismissal of a company petition[cite: 1]. The initial dismissal relied on a photocopy of Consent Terms presented solely by the Appellants, without the Respondents present[cite: 1]. The NCLAT upheld the NCLT's decision, emphasizing that natural justice requires both parties to be present and agreeable before a tribunal acts on consent terms[cite: 1]. The appeal was dismissed[cite: 1].

case_title: Chharia Holdings Pvt. Ltd. vs Brys International Pvt. Ltd. & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Chharia Holdings Pvt. Ltd. is the Financial Creditor (Appellant) and Brys International Pvt. Ltd. & Ors. are the Corporate Debtors (Respondents)[cite: 2]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Not explicitly detailed; relates to a financial debt forming the basis of a Section 7 insolvency application[cite: 2]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Specific default amounts and dates are not detailed in the judgment[cite: 2]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The Adjudicating Authority dismissed the Section 7 application on 22 June 2017[cite: 2]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The Appellant submitted Form-1 which actually included the proposed name of Interim Resolution Professional Mr. Vivek Raheja, alongside his consent letter in Annexure A-4[cite: 2]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The NCLT Principal Bench dismissed the original Section 7 application on 22 June 2017 on the sole ground that the Financial Creditor failed to propose an Interim Resolution Professional, rendering the application incomplete[cite: 2].
legal_issues: Whether it is mandatory for a Financial Creditor to propose an Interim Resolution Professional in a Section 7 IBC application, and whether an application can be outright rejected for such a defect without providing a 7-day notice for rectification[cite: 2].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: While proposing an Interim Resolution Professional is mandatory for Financial Creditors, the Adjudicating Authority cannot outright reject a defective application without first issuing a notice granting seven days to rectify the defect[cite: 2]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 7(3)(b) and Section 10(3)(b) of the IBC use the mandatory word 'shall', requiring Financial Creditors and Corporate Applicants to propose an IRP, contrasting with Section 9(4) where Operational Creditors 'may' do so[cite: 2]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The appellate tribunal reviewed Form-1 and factually verified that the Appellant had, in fact, proposed an IRP's name[cite: 2]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT held the NCLT's dismissal was both factually incorrect (as a name was proposed) and legally invalid because the mandatory 7-day statutory period to cure defects was denied[cite: 2].
operative_order: The impugned NCLT order dated 22 June 2017 is set aside[cite: 2]. The case is remitted back for admission if complete, or to grant the Appellant seven days to remove any defects[cite: 2].
summary: The Appellant, a Financial Creditor, challenged the NCLT's dismissal of its Section 7 IBC application for supposedly failing to propose an Interim Resolution Professional[cite: 2]. The NCLAT found that the Appellant had actually proposed a name in Form-1[cite: 2]. Furthermore, it ruled that even if an application is defective, the Adjudicating Authority must grant a mandatory seven-day notice to rectify the defect[cite: 2]. The appeal was allowed and remanded[cite: 2].

case_title: Prowess International Pvt. Ltd. vs Parker Hannifin India Pvt. Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Prowess International Pvt. Ltd. is the Corporate Debtor (Appellant) and Parker Hannifin India Pvt. Ltd. is the Operational Creditor (Respondent)[cite: 3]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: The case stems from an underlying operational debt owed to the Respondent[cite: 3]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The Operational Creditor claimed an amount of Rs. 45,73,200[cite: 3]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The Section 9 application was admitted on 20 April 2017[cite: 3]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Following admission, the Corporate Debtor settled the claims of the Operational Creditor and all other responding creditors[cite: 3]. The IRP confirmed that Punjab National Bank maintained the account as standard and claimed no default[cite: 3]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Kolkata admitted the petition ex-parte on 20 April 2017[cite: 3]. After settling the dues, the Corporate Debtor applied for withdrawal, which the NCLT rejected on 29 May 2017 stating withdrawals are impermissible post-admission[cite: 3].
legal_issues: Whether a Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process (CIRP) can be closed after admission if the Corporate Debtor settles all creditor claims and no default remains[cite: 3].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Once admitted, a CIRP application cannot be simply withdrawn under Rule 8; however, if all creditors are satisfied, the Adjudicating Authority can expedite process closure by approving a resolution plan without waiting 180 days[cite: 3]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 31 allows the approval of a resolution plan. If a plan is submitted showing all stakeholders are satisfied, the Adjudicating Authority should record this satisfaction to terminate the moratorium and close proceedings to promote ongoing business[cite: 3]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal relied on the IRP's progress reports and affidavits proving that all claimants (including PNB) had been paid or confirmed no default[cite: 3]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT concluded the NCLT was technically correct to deny direct withdrawal post-admission, but remanded the matter directing the NCLT to assess the settlement via the resolution plan framework and close the proceedings to balance stakeholder interests[cite: 3].
operative_order: The matter is remitted to the Adjudicating Authority to verify the satisfaction of all stakeholders based on the IRP's report and to close the proceedings accordingly[cite: 3]. No order as to costs[cite: 3].
summary: The Corporate Debtor appealed after the NCLT refused to allow the withdrawal of a Section 9 insolvency petition despite the debtor settling all creditor claims post-admission[cite: 3]. The NCLAT upheld that direct withdrawal post-admission is legally barred[cite: 3]. However, emphasizing that IBC is not merely a recovery tool, the NCLAT directed the NCLT to review the IRP's report confirming the settlements and to close the proceedings expeditiously via the resolution plan framework[cite: 3].

case_title: M/s Ranchi Metal & Ispat Pvt. Ltd. vs Surjeet Singh
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Surjeet Singh was the original petitioner (Respondent in appeal), while M/s Ranchi Metal & Ispat Pvt. Ltd. (Appellant No. 1), its co-directors, and M/s Prowess International Pvt. Ltd. (Appellant No. 4) were the respondents before the NCLT[cite: 4]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Surjeet Singh and the 2nd Appellant acquired shares of the 1st Appellant company from original promoters to develop a metallurgical pipe-casting facility on industrial land owned by the company in Jharkhand; Appellant No. 4 infused Rs. 2,01,00,000 as share application money towards the land's market value[cite: 4]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Monetary default metrics are not applicable; the underlying controversy arose from the alleged unlawful reduction of the Respondent's shareholding from 50% to 0.24%[cite: 4]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The disputed Extraordinary General Meeting was held on 14 February 2014, followed by a purported Board Meeting on 15 February 2014 where the share allotment was executed[cite: 4]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: E-Form Nos. 2 and 5 filed with the Registrar of Companies; absence of dispatch records, notices, or attendance sheets establishing that statutory meeting notices were served upon the Respondent[cite: 4]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Surjeet Singh petitioned under Sections 397 and 398 of the Companies Act 1956 (transferred to NCLT Kolkata as C.P. No. 60(ND)/2015 / C.A. No. 92/C-I/2016)[cite: 4]; the NCLT held that oppression had occurred, cancelled the allotment of shares to Appellant No. 4, and ordered a refund, which the Appellants appealed[cite: 4].
legal_issues: Whether a company petition under Sections 397 and 398 of the Companies Act 1956 is maintainable when the petitioner's shareholding was reduced below the 10% statutory threshold by an impugned allotment, and whether allotting shares without statutory notice constitutes oppression and mismanagement[cite: 4].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A shareholder whose holding is reduced below the statutory minimum threshold by virtue of an alleged illegal allotment retains standing to petition against oppression, as the locus standi must be judged prior to the commission of the oppressive act[cite: 4]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 399 of the Companies Act 1956 (Section 244 of the Companies Act 2013) cannot be deployed as a shield by a majority to stifle judicial review where the reduction of shareholding itself constitutes the grievance of oppression[cite: 4]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The burden of proof rests on the company and directors to demonstrate that meetings were convened with due notice and verifiable attendance; absence of proof invalidates the resultant resolutions and share allotments[cite: 4]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT confirmed that the share allotment was null and oppressive due to lack of notice, but directed that the third-party investor (Appellant No. 4) who provided genuine funds must be refunded the principal sum with 18% interest per annum[cite: 4].
operative_order: The NCLT order dated 10 November 2016 is modified to direct the company and directors to refund Rs. 2,01,00,000 along with 18% per annum interest to Appellant No. 4 within one month, overseen by the Registrar of Companies; the appeal is disposed of accordingly[cite: 4].
summary: M/s Ranchi Metal & Ispat Pvt. Ltd. and its directors appealed an NCLT Kolkata order that set aside an allotment of shares to Appellant No. 4, which had drastically reduced Surjeet Singh's equity from 50% to 0.24%[cite: 4]. The Appellants challenged the petition's maintainability under the 10% shareholding threshold[cite: 4]. The NCLAT held that a petitioner cannot be deprived of standing where the oppressive act itself unlawfully reduced their stake below the statutory threshold[cite: 4]. Confirming the allotment was conducted without proper statutory notice, the NCLAT upheld the invalidation but modified the order to grant Appellant No. 4 a full refund with 18% annual interest[cite: 4].

case_title: Sanjeev Agarwal & Anr. vs Shri Omkaleshwar Colonisers Pvt. Ltd. & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Sanjeev Agarwal and Pramod Pratap were the petitioners/appellants holding 44.70% combined shares; Shri Omkaleshwar Colonisers Pvt. Ltd. was the company, and Satish Kumar Singh was the respondent director/shareholder holding the remaining equity[cite: 5]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: The company engaged in real estate development financed by a Syndicate Bank credit facility requiring a 34.10% promoter contribution alongside the bank's loan portion[cite: 5]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default arose from promoter equity shortfalls; an interest-free loan was subsequently obtained from Mr. Ganga Sagar Singh (director's father) to finance a boundary wall and pay the project contractor[cite: 5]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Cross-petitions CP No. 75(ND)/2016 and CP No. 54(ND)/2016 were adjudicated by NCLT Allahabad via a common judgment dated 18 January 2017[cite: 5]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Syndicate Bank sanction terms, ledger accounts evidencing interest-free advances, bank statements, and a letter dated 4 February 2015 sent by the Appellants asking the bank to freeze company bank accounts[cite: 5]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Allahabad Bench found no actionable oppression or mismanagement warranting winding up, holding that the interest-free borrowing was bona fide to safeguard project operations, against which the Appellants appealed[cite: 5].
legal_issues: Whether borrowing interest-free funds from a director's relative without formal board sanction to meet urgent operational expenses constitutes oppression and mismanagement under Section 397/398, and whether shareholders who attempt to stall operations are entitled to equitable relief[cite: 5].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Bona fide corporate actions taken to preserve company property and fulfill mandatory banking requirements—without causing financial prejudice to the enterprise—do not constitute oppression or mismanagement[cite: 5]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Relief under Sections 397 and 398 requires established conduct that is harsh, burdensome, and detrimental to the corporate entity; mere procedural non-compliances or personality conflicts among directors do not meet this legal standard[cite: 5]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The court evaluated whether the transaction caused real prejudice to the company; an advance obtained interest-free to pay contracted construction works when other promoters fail to contribute does not demonstrate oppressive intent[cite: 5]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT concluded that the borrowing was a legitimate commercial necessity caused by the appellants' failure to inject equity, and their attempts to freeze bank accounts disentitled them from discretionary relief[cite: 5].
operative_order: The appeals are dismissed for lack of merit; interim orders are vacated, and Syndicate Bank is directed to proceed in accordance with the NCLT's directions[cite: 5]. No order as to costs[cite: 5].
summary: Sanjeev Agarwal and another shareholder appealed against an NCLT Allahabad decision that dismissed their oppression and mismanagement claims against Shri Omkaleshwar Colonisers Pvt. Ltd. and its managing director[cite: 5]. The appellants alleged that the management took unauthorized loans from a director's relative and increased capital unlawfully[cite: 5]. The NCLAT held that the interest-free borrowing was a bona fide necessity to construct essential boundary walls and maintain banking compliance after the appellants refused to inject their share of equity[cite: 5]. Finding no prejudice to the company or evidence of oppression, the NCLAT dismissed both appeals[cite: 5].

case_title: Wanbury Ltd. vs Panacea Biotech Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Wanbury Ltd. is the Appellant and Operational Creditor, while Panacea Biotech Ltd is the Respondent and Corporate Debtor[cite: 6]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Based on an operational debt, the specifics of which are not detailed beyond the term 'operational creditor'[cite: 6]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The principal amount was paid prior to admission, leaving only a dispute over interest for delayed payment[cite: 6]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The petition originally began under Section 433 of the Companies Act, 1956 in the Punjab & Haryana High Court and was transferred via a 7 December 2016 notification[cite: 6]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: A settlement cheque (No. 712439) for Rs. 1,55,200 drawn on Axis Bank was handed over in court on 10 August 2017[cite: 6]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Chandigarh rejected the interest claim in C.P. No. 8 of 2016 on 18 April 2017, prompting the appeal[cite: 6].
legal_issues: Whether an Operational Creditor is legally entitled to claim interest on an operational debt when the principal has been satisfied and no such provision exists in the contract[cite: 6].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An operational creditor is not inherently entitled to interest on a debt if the principal has been paid and no governing law or contract provides for it[cite: 6]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The tribunal noted there was no provision to pay interest based on the bank documents produced[cite: 6]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The tribunal relied on the mutual settlement wherein the Corporate Debtor voluntarily paid a lump sum of Rs. 1.5 lakhs to resolve the delay grievance[cite: 6]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT disposed of the appeal based on the mutual settlement without passing further orders[cite: 6].
operative_order: The appeal stands disposed of with no cost, granting liberty to the Appellant to approach the Tribunal if the settlement cheque bounces[cite: 6].
summary: Wanbury Ltd. appealed the NCLT's refusal to grant interest on a settled operational debt[cite: 6]. During the appeal, the Corporate Debtor provided a cheque for Rs. 1,55,200 to compensate for the payment delay, resolving the dispute[cite: 6]. The NCLAT disposed of the appeal based on this settlement[cite: 6].

case_title: Uma Shankar Gupta vs Vishal Promoters Private Limited
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Uma Shankar Gupta and Shyam Sundar Gupta are the Appellants/Petitioners. Vishal Promoters Pvt. Ltd. and several others are the Respondents[cite: 7]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Appellants and certain Respondents lent money to the company for property purchase and received shares in return[cite: 7]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The Appellants alleged that Respondents 8 to 10 took a loan from the company but failed to repay it[cite: 7]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: A disputed Board Meeting occurred on 14 August 2013 regarding changing the registered office address[cite: 7]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The Respondents produced a document showing meeting notice was received by one Bipin Naskar on behalf of the Appellants[cite: 7]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Kolkata dismissed the original company petition (C.P. No. 294/2013) ruling there was no oppression and mismanagement[cite: 7].
legal_issues: Whether alleged failure to serve a board meeting notice and the non-repayment of loans taken by shareholders from the company constitute actionable oppression and mismanagement[cite: 7].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Procedural complaints regarding meeting notices do not amount to oppression if the opposing faction independently holds the required majority to pass the resolutions[cite: 7]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Non-repayment of a corporate loan by certain shareholders does not inherently constitute oppression and mismanagement against the other shareholders[cite: 7]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal noted that the share issuance was a completed past transaction, and the majority block would have won the board vote regardless of the Appellants' presence[cite: 7]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT agreed with the NCLT that neither the address change nor the unpaid loans justified an oppression claim[cite: 7].
operative_order: The admission of the appeal is declined, and the appeal is dismissed with no order as to costs[cite: 7].
summary: The Appellants challenged an NCLT decision dismissing their oppression and mismanagement claims against Vishal Promoters Pvt. Ltd.[cite: 7]. The dispute centered around allegedly unserved meeting notices and unpaid loans by other shareholders[cite: 7]. The NCLAT upheld the dismissal, concluding that the respondents possessed a valid voting majority and unpaid loans do not inherently establish oppression[cite: 7].

case_title: Sri Lakshmi Prasanna Agro Paper Industries Ltd. vs Chavali Gayatri Praveen & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Sri Lakshmi Prasanna Agro Paper Industries Ltd. and its directors are the Appellants. Chavali Gayatri Praveen and Anr are the Respondents/Original Petitioners[cite: 8]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: The Respondents advanced money to the company intended as a deposit for 3 years[cite: 8]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Total principal of Rs. 8,40,000 was paid across March and May 2007[cite: 8]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The deposit receipts were extended by the company on 15 March 2010 and matured in 2013[cite: 8]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Depositors provided money receipts; the company provided internal Form-2 documents from 2007 and 2008 but failed to prove submission to the Registrar of Companies (ROC)[cite: 8]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Hyderabad (CP No. 20/75/HDB/2016) ordered the company to return the funds with interest, nullifying the company's claim that the money was used for share allotment[cite: 8].
legal_issues: Whether funds received by a company can be treated as share capital rather than a deposit in the absence of share applications, board resolutions, and verified ROC filings[cite: 8].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Without a formal application for shares, authorizing board resolutions, or proof of statutory ROC filings, money advanced to a company must be classified and returned as a deposit[cite: 8]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: A company cannot unilaterally convert deposits into share allotments without adhering to the procedural mandates of the Companies Act[cite: 8]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The tribunal placed the evidentiary burden on the company to prove proper allotment via ROC filings and member registers, which it failed to discharge[cite: 8]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT affirmed that the transaction was a fixed deposit and the purported share allotment was invalid[cite: 8].
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed without admitting the same. No order as to costs[cite: 8].
summary: The Appellant company appealed an NCLT order directing it to refund Rs. 8,40,000 with interest to the Respondents[cite: 8]. The company argued the money was converted into shares, but could not produce share applications, board resolutions, or verified ROC filings[cite: 8]. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, ruling the transaction remained a fixed deposit[cite: 8].

case_title: Creative Solutions vs AMR Infrastructure Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Creative Solutions is the Appellant/Operational Creditor, and AMR Infrastructure Ltd. is the Respondent/Corporate Debtor[cite: 9]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Architecture and interior design services provided for the 'Kessel I-Valley' project between 2012 and 2015[cite: 9]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Claimed outstanding dues of Rs. 1,08,99,705[cite: 9]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Section 8 demand notice sent on 30 January 2017[cite: 9]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Corporate Debtor alleged the invoices were bogus, lacked fiscal registration numbers, and were acknowledged by an unauthorized former employee[cite: 9]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Principal Bench rejected the Section 9 application on 25 April 2017 holding the Appellant was not an Operational Creditor[cite: 9].
legal_issues: Whether a separate Section 9 insolvency application should be adjudicated on merits when the Appellate Tribunal has already initiated Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process (CIRP) against the same Corporate Debtor in a parallel Section 7 case[cite: 9].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Once CIRP is initiated against a Corporate Debtor, parallel insolvency petitions against the same debtor become redundant, and creditors must instead submit their claims to the Interim Resolution Professional (IRP)[cite: 9]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Sections 7, 9, and 10 of the IBC consolidate the resolution process; multiple concurrent CIRP initiations against a single entity are impermissible[cite: 9]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal took judicial notice of its recent order dated 21 July 2017 in a separate case ('Nikhil Mehta and Sons') that initiated CIRP against the Respondent[cite: 9]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT disposed of the appeal without ruling on the operational debt's merits, directing the Appellant to the IRP[cite: 9].
operative_order: The appeal stands disposed of with no costs. The Appellant is directed to file its claim before the IRP, retaining liberty to file an interlocutory application to recall this order if the parallel Section 7 CIRP is dismissed[cite: 9].
summary: Creative Solutions appealed the NCLT's rejection of its Section 9 insolvency application against AMR Infrastructure Ltd.[cite: 9]. Because the NCLAT had just initiated CIRP against the same Corporate Debtor in a separate Section 7 case, it disposed of this appeal without addressing the merits, instructing the Appellant to submit its claim to the appointed IRP[cite: 9].

case_title: Rajesh Arora vs MY Agro Pvt. Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Rajesh Arora (Director of Amira Pure Foods Pvt. Ltd.) is the Appellant/Corporate Debtor. MY Agro Pvt. Ltd. is the Respondent/Operational Creditor[cite: 10]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Underlying operational debt involving cheques that ultimately bounced[cite: 10]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Appellant disputed the default, claiming admitted dues were settled via an RTGS payment to a third party[cite: 10]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Section 8 notice issued 5 June 2017; Corporate Debtor replied 28 June 2017; Section 9 application filed 11 July 2017[cite: 10]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Form 3 statutory demand notice lacked critical tabular enclosures regarding debt computation. Form 5 admitted that notices sent to the registered office were returned undelivered[cite: 10]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT New Delhi admitted the Section 9 application on 24 August 2017, initiating CIRP[cite: 10].
legal_issues: Whether a Section 9 IBC application is maintainable if the mandatory Section 8 statutory demand notice was incomplete and admitted by the creditor to have been returned unserved[cite: 10].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An application for CIRP under Section 9 cannot be admitted if the preceding Section 8 demand notice was procedurally defective and not properly served on the Corporate Debtor[cite: 10]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Strict compliance with Section 8(1) notice requirements, including required enclosures, is a rigid prerequisite for a Section 9 petition[cite: 10]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal relied on the Operational Creditor's own admission in Form 5 that the notices were returned undelivered, contradicting unproven oral assertions of service[cite: 10]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT ruled the defective and unserved notice rendered the Section 9 application non-maintainable, nullifying the NCLT's admission[cite: 10].
operative_order: The NCLT order dated 24 August 2017 is set aside, and the Section 9 application is dismissed[cite: 10]. The CIRP is terminated, the company is released to function under its Board of Directors, and the Corporate Debtor is directed to pay the IRP's fees[cite: 10].
summary: The Appellant challenged an NCLT order initiating CIRP against Amira Pure Foods Pvt. Ltd.[cite: 10]. The NCLAT found that the Operational Creditor failed to attach mandatory enclosures to the Section 8 demand notice and admitted the notice was returned undelivered[cite: 10]. Holding the defective notice fatal to the petition, the NCLAT allowed the appeal, terminated the CIRP, and restored the Corporate Debtor's board[cite: 10].

case_title: United Projects Constructions Ltd. vs Aerocon Buildwell Pvt. Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: United Projects Constructions Ltd. is the Operational Creditor (Appellant) and Aerocon Buildwell Pvt. Ltd. is the Corporate Debtor (Respondent)[cite: 11]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Underlying matter involves an operational debt, though specific contractual details are not elaborated[cite: 11]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Precise default amount is not specified in the order[cite: 11]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The NCLT passed the impugned order dismissing the application on 31 July 2017[cite: 11]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The Corporate Debtor claimed a pre-existing dispute based on a letter dated 10 October 2016. However, no proof of service was provided, and a supporting email lacked the sender's name and was not addressed to the Operational Creditor[cite: 11]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Ahmedabad dismissed the Section 9 petition (CP No. (IB) 30/9/NCLT/AHM/2017) recognizing an 'existence of dispute'[cite: 11]. The NCLAT challenged the validity of this evidence on appeal[cite: 11].
legal_issues: Whether a purported dispute letter lacking proof of service and an anonymous, misdirected email legally constitute an 'existence of dispute' sufficient to dismiss a Section 9 application[cite: 11].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An assertion of a pre-existing dispute must be substantiated by verifiable evidence demonstrating that notice or communication of the dispute was genuinely served upon the creditor before the demand notice[cite: 11]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: 'Existence of dispute' requires legitimate, pre-existing contestation, preventing corporate debtors from manufacturing documents post-facto simply to stall the CIRP process[cite: 11]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal evaluated the respondent's compliance affidavit and rejected the defense since the dispute letter had no proof of delivery and the email was not even sent to the Operational Creditor[cite: 11]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT concluded that the record lacked genuine evidence of a dispute, warranting the setting aside of the dismissal[cite: 11].
operative_order: The impugned order dated 31 July 2017 is set aside[cite: 11]. The case is remitted to the Adjudicating Authority to reconsider the application on the existing record (without new documents) and to admit it if otherwise complete[cite: 11].
summary: The Appellant challenged NCLT Ahmedabad's dismissal of its Section 9 insolvency application, which was based on the Corporate Debtor's claim of a pre-existing dispute[cite: 11]. The NCLAT determined that the Corporate Debtor failed to prove that the dispute letter was ever served, and the supporting email was anonymous and misdirected[cite: 11]. Finding no valid evidence of a pre-existing dispute, the NCLAT set aside the dismissal and remanded the case for reconsideration[cite: 11].

case_title: M/s Emjee Homes vs M/s Sahanik Private Limited & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: M/s Emjee Homes is the Appellant, and M/s Sahanik Private Limited & Ors. are the Respondents/Original Applicants[cite: 12]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Dispute surrounding confidential Joint Venture Agreements (JVA) and Power of Attorney (PoA) documents held by Escrow Agents[cite: 12]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not applicable; this is an interlocutory procedural dispute[cite: 12]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The impugned order calling for the documents was passed on 10 February 2017[cite: 12]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The Escrow Agents had already submitted the disputed documents in a sealed cover to the Tribunal[cite: 12]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai ordered the Escrow Agents to send photocopies of the documents by Speed Post for the Tribunal to peruse in open court[cite: 12]. The Appellant appealed, fearing a breach of confidentiality[cite: 12].
legal_issues: Whether a Tribunal's directive to examine confidential escrow documents in open court inherently prejudices a party's right to confidentiality when the documents are not ordered to be shared with the opposing side[cite: 12].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A judicial authority possesses the inherent right to inspect any relevant document—even confidential ones held in escrow—to unearth the truth and verify their veracity[cite: 12]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Procedural fairness dictates that judicial scrutiny of evidence does not equate to unauthorized publication[cite: 12]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal noted the order strictly required submission to the Bench Officer for the judge's perusal, causing no prejudice since it did not mandate handing copies to the opposing party[cite: 12]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT upheld the NCLT's direction, confirming that judicial perusal of sealed documents does not violate confidentiality rights[cite: 12].
operative_order: The appeal is disposed of without interference with the NCLT's order. No order as to costs[cite: 12].
summary: The Appellant challenged an NCLT Mumbai order requiring Escrow Agents to submit photocopies of confidential agreements for the Tribunal's perusal[cite: 12]. The Appellant feared the opposing party would gain access[cite: 12]. The NCLAT upheld the order, ruling that the Tribunal has the right to examine documents to ascertain the truth, and no prejudice is caused because the order did not direct sharing the copies with the opposing party[cite: 12].

case_title: Ardor Global Pvt. Ltd. vs Nirma Industries Pvt. Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Ardor Global Pvt. Ltd. is the Corporate Debtor (Appellant) and Nirma Industries Pvt. Ltd. is the Operational Creditor (Respondent)[cite: 13]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Not explicitly detailed; relates generally to an operational debt[cite: 13]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Financial specifics of the default are not recorded[cite: 13]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The NCLT allowed withdrawal of the petition on 11 July 2017[cite: 13]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The application contained rectifiable defects concerning the IRP's written communication (Form 2) and an affidavit dated 26 May 2017[cite: 13]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Recognizing defects during arguments at NCLT Ahmedabad, the Operational Creditor sought to withdraw the petition with liberty to file afresh. The NCLT permitted this under Rule 8, prompting the Corporate Debtor's appeal[cite: 13].
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority must enforce a strict 7-day rectification period for a defective petition, or if it retains discretion to allow withdrawal with liberty to file a fresh petition; and whether such subsequent filing is barred by constructive res judicata[cite: 13].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The Adjudicating Authority holds statutory discretion to permit the withdrawal of an insolvency application before admission and may grant liberty to file a fresh petition[cite: 13]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Rule 8 of the Insolvency & Bankruptcy (Application to Adjudicating Authority) Rules, 2016 expressly allows withdrawal prior to admission, overriding the argument that granting a 7-day cure period is the exclusive remedy for defective applications[cite: 13]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Since the Tribunal had not adjudicated the merits or decided on the default, the doctrine of constructive res judicata cannot apply to a subsequent filing[cite: 13]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT affirmed the NCLT's decision to allow withdrawal, rejecting the Appellant's claims regarding mandatory rectification and res judicata[cite: 13].
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed for lack of merit. No order as to costs[cite: 13].
summary: The Corporate Debtor appealed an NCLT order that allowed the Operational Creditor to withdraw its defective insolvency petition and file a fresh one[cite: 13]. The Appellant argued the NCLT was obligated to enforce a 7-day rectification window instead, and that a new petition would be barred by res judicata[cite: 13]. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that Rule 8 grants explicit discretion to allow pre-admission withdrawals, and res judicata does not apply absent a decision on the merits[cite: 13].

case_title: Mr. Dinesh Kapur & Ors. vs M/s Recorders & Medicare Systems Pvt. Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Mr. Dinesh Kapur & Ors. are the Appellants (erstwhile employees holding civil decrees). M/s Recorders & Medicare Systems Pvt. Ltd. is the Corporate Debtor, represented by Resolution Professional Mr. Anil Goel[cite: 14]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Claim stems from unpaid employment dues converted into civil court decrees[cite: 14]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Established by the Civil Judge (Junior Division), Chandigarh via decrees in CS No. 576/2013, 577/2013, and 578/2013[cite: 14]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The NCLT dismissed the Appellants' application on 12 October 2017[cite: 14]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Appellants hold valid civil decrees, but the Corporate Debtor is actively under a Section 10 CIRP moratorium, halting executing courts from attaching funds[cite: 14]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Following CIRP admission, the Appellants challenged the RP's authority before NCLT Chandigarh, attempting to exercise their rights under the civil decrees. The NCLT dismissed their application due to the moratorium[cite: 14].
legal_issues: Whether decree-holding employees can pursue execution or separate appellate challenges to enforce civil decrees against a Corporate Debtor while a statutory insolvency moratorium is actively in place[cite: 14].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The imposition of a statutory moratorium automatically halts all parallel civil litigation, including the execution of decrees against the Corporate Debtor[cite: 14]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Under the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, once a Section 10 CIRP application is admitted and a moratorium imposed, decree-holders are barred from independent recovery mechanisms and must file their claims with the Resolution Professional[cite: 14]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The undisputed fact of an active CIRP moratorium formed an absolute bar against the Appellants' execution attempts[cite: 14]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT ruled that the appeal was non-maintainable because the appellants' remedy strictly lies within the CIRP claims process, not outside it[cite: 14].
operative_order: The appeal is not maintainable and stands dismissed[cite: 14].
summary: Erstwhile employees holding civil court decrees for unpaid dues appealed an NCLT decision that halted their execution efforts against the Corporate Debtor[cite: 14]. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal as non-maintainable, emphasizing that because the company was under an active Section 10 CIRP moratorium, all independent executions of civil decrees are suspended, and the creditors must seek remedies through the CIRP framework[cite: 14].

case_title: Kerala Chamber of Commerce and Industry & Ors. vs Tap World & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Kerala Chamber of Commerce and Industry & Ors. are the Appellants. Tap World & Anr. are the Respondents (Petitioners before the NCLT)[cite: 15]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate dispute regarding accounting practices and Chamber membership[cite: 15]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not applicable; dispute concerns oppression and mismanagement allegations[cite: 15]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The NCLT passed the impugned order admitting the petition on 8 November 2016[cite: 15]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The Respondents possessed permission granted by the Central Government under Section 399(4) of the Companies Act, 1956 to file the petition[cite: 15]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Chennai found a prima facie case and admitted the Section 241 petition for hearing while declining interim relief regarding the accounts[cite: 15]. The Appellants appealed on the grounds that suspended members lack locus standi[cite: 15].
legal_issues: Whether an appellate tribunal should determine the maintainability of a Section 241 petition filed by a suspended member when the lower tribunal has only made a prima facie finding to admit the case for a final hearing[cite: 15].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Appellate tribunals will generally refrain from prematurely adjudicating mixed questions of maintainability and fact if the lower adjudicating authority has merely admitted the petition based on a prima facie review[cite: 15]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Maintainability challenges involving complex factual circumstances—such as whether a membership suspension itself constitutes the alleged oppression—should be determined comprehensively at final hearing, not at the admission stage[cite: 15]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal noted that deciding the maintainability (based on membership suspension) requires examining the very acts of oppression alleged in the main petition[cite: 15]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT declined to interfere with the NCLT's admission order and directed that the locus standi question be resolved on merits during the final hearing[cite: 15].
operative_order: The NCLAT directed the Tribunal to decide the case both on merit and on the question of maintainability during the final hearing, uninfluenced by its preliminary admission order. The appeal is disposed of with no costs[cite: 15].
summary: The Appellants challenged an NCLT Chennai order that admitted an oppression and mismanagement petition filed by suspended members[cite: 15]. The Appellants argued that suspended members lacked locus standi to sue[cite: 15]. Refusing to interfere, the NCLAT ruled that since the NCLT only made a prima facie decision to admit the case, the question of maintainability linked to the membership suspension must be comprehensively decided alongside the merits during the final hearing[cite: 15].

case_title: M/s. James Hotels Ltd. vs Punjab National Bank
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: M/s. James Hotels Ltd. is the Corporate Debtor (Appellant), and Punjab National Bank is the Financial Creditor (Respondent)[cite: 16]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Underlying financial credit facilities extended by Punjab National Bank to the Corporate Debtor[cite: 16]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Exact monetary default amounts and dates are not specified in the appellate order[cite: 16]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The Adjudicating Authority passed an interim order on 23 August 2017 listing the matter for arguments on 29 August 2017[cite: 16]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The Corporate Debtor alleged fraud committed by the bank, prompting NCLT to direct the Registrar of Companies, Punjab & Chandigarh, to preserve CCTV footage of visitors up to 1 August 2017 and issue notice to ARCIL[cite: 16]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: In CP (IB) No. 15/Chd/CHD/2017, during ongoing CIRP proceedings, the Corporate Debtor raised fraud allegations; the NCLT initiated a preliminary inquiry on 23 August 2017, which the Corporate Debtor appealed, arguing that NCLT lacked jurisdiction to investigate fraud[cite: 16].
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority (NCLT) has the jurisdiction under the IBC to investigate allegations of fraud raised during the Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process, or whether such matters fall exclusively under the jurisdiction of a Special Judge under Chapter VIII of Part II[cite: 16].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The Adjudicating Authority possesses statutory jurisdiction during insolvency proceedings to examine allegations of fraud and initiate inquiries to ascertain if a prima facie case exists affecting the resolution process[cite: 16]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Sections 65 and 66 of the IBC empower the Tribunal to investigate fraudulent or malicious initiation of proceedings and fraudulent trading, clarifying that enquiry into fraud during CIRP is not solely confined to a Special Judge[cite: 16]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal is entitled to call for relevant evidentiary materials, including preservation of public records and third-party notices, to verify whether fraud impacts the CIRP[cite: 16]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT concluded that issuing notice to ascertain the truth of fraud allegations is well within the NCLT's powers, warranting no appellate interference at the interlocutory stage[cite: 16].
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed with observations that aggrieved parties may approach the Adjudicating Authority or Appellate Tribunal if an adverse order is subsequently passed under Section 31. No order as to costs[cite: 16].
summary: M/s James Hotels Ltd., the Corporate Debtor, appealed an interim order of NCLT Chandigarh passed during CIRP proceedings initiated by Punjab National Bank[cite: 16]. The Corporate Debtor alleged fraud against the bank and contended that the NCLT lacked jurisdiction to investigate fraud, which it claimed fell exclusively under a Special Judge[cite: 16]. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that under Sections 65 and 66 of the IBC, the Adjudicating Authority possesses ample jurisdiction to examine fraudulent initiation or trading and to issue notices to unearth the truth[cite: 16]. The Tribunal held the challenge premature and preserved liberty to appeal any final adverse determination[cite: 16].

case_title: Sh. Sumeet Ahuja vs Union Bank of India & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Sh. Sumeet Ahuja, Director of Paramshakti Steels Ltd., is the substituted Appellant; Union Bank of India is the Financial Creditor (Respondent No. 1); and M/s Paramshakti Steels Ltd. (through IRP) is Respondent No. 2[cite: 17]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Underlying credit and loan facilities sanctioned by Union Bank of India to Paramshakti Steels Ltd.[cite: 17]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default amount and specific date of default are not specified in the appellate order[cite: 17]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The Section 7 application in CP No. 727/I&BP/NCLT/MAH/2017 was admitted by NCLT Mumbai on 3 July 2017[cite: 17]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The Section 7 application was signed and filed by the Deputy General Manager of the Bank pursuant to an authorization instrument titled as a Power of Attorney[cite: 17]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai admitted the bank's Section 7 petition, declared a moratorium, and appointed an IRP; the suspended director appealed, challenging the filing authority of the bank's officer[cite: 17].
legal_issues: Whether an application under Section 7 of the IBC filed by an officer of a financial creditor pursuant to an authorization instrument described as a Power of Attorney is legally valid and maintainable[cite: 17].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: General authorization granted by a financial creditor to its officers to initiate legal proceedings is valid, and the mere use of the term 'Power of Attorney' while delegating such power does not invalidate the officer's legal authority to act as an Authorized Representative under the IBC[cite: 17]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Applying Palogix Infrastructure, an officer delegated with power by designation or authorization can act as an 'Authorized Representative' for filing petitions under Sections 7, 9, or 10 of the IBC[cite: 17]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: If an officer has the delegated power to sanction or recover loans, an application under Section 7 cannot be rejected for want of a separate specific board resolution if general authorization is established[cite: 17]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT ruled that the filing by the Deputy General Manager was valid and lawful, rendering the appeal devoid of merit[cite: 17].
operative_order: Petition for substitution allowed; Sh. Sumeet Ahuja substituted as appellant and the corporate debtor transposed through IRP as second respondent; the appeal is dismissed with no order as to costs[cite: 17].
summary: Sh. Sumeet Ahuja, director of Corporate Debtor Paramshakti Steels Ltd., appealed against an NCLT Mumbai order admitting Union Bank of India's Section 7 insolvency petition[cite: 17]. The appellant contended that the petition was non-maintainable because it was filed by an officer acting under a Power of Attorney[cite: 17]. Relying on its precedent in Palogix Infrastructure, the NCLAT held that general authorization given by a bank to its officers—such as a Deputy General Manager—constitutes valid authorization under the IBC, and merely titling the delegation as a Power of Attorney does not impair the officer's standing to initiate CIRP[cite: 17]. The appeal was dismissed[cite: 17].

case_title: Mindtree Exports Private Limited vs M/s Ashmita Multitrade Private Limited & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Mindtree Exports Private Limited is the Corporate Debtor (Appellant), and M/s Ashmita Multitrade Private Limited is the Financial Creditor (Respondent)[cite: 18]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Purported debt transaction; the creditor originally filed as an operational creditor under Section 9 before withdrawing and refiling as a financial creditor under Section 7[cite: 18]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Demand notice dated 15 February 2017 demanded Rs. 5,37,00,000, which the Corporate Debtor claimed had already been paid[cite: 18]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Section 9 application filed on 4 April 2017 and withdrawn; Section 7 petition filed as CP No. 1073/I&BP/NCLT/MB/MAH/2017 was admitted on 13 June 2017[cite: 18]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The NCLT order sheet showed no appearance on behalf of the Corporate Debtor; no proof of service of the Section 7 petition or hearing notice under Rule 4(3) was on record[cite: 18]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai Bench admitted the Section 7 application ex-parte on 13 June 2017, declared a moratorium, and froze bank accounts without verifying service of notice[cite: 18].
legal_issues: Whether an Adjudicating Authority can admit an application under Section 7 of the IBC ex-parte without ensuring service of notice under Rule 4(3) of the Adjudicating Authority Rules, and whether a creditor can unilaterally shift from operational to financial creditor without scrutiny[cite: 18].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Admission of an insolvency petition ex-parte without serving notice of the application and hearing date upon the corporate debtor violates principles of natural justice and mandatory procedural rules[cite: 18]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Rule 4(3) of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy (Application to Adjudicating Authority) Rules, 2016 requires mandatory service of a copy of the application and notice of hearing before the petition is admitted[cite: 18]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Failure of the record to demonstrate actual service of notice or adherence to Rule 4(3) invalidates an admission order passed in the debtor's absence[cite: 18]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT held that the ex-parte admission was legally unsustainable, setting aside the moratorium and remitting the case for fresh adjudication after proper notice[cite: 18].
operative_order: Impugned order dated 13 June 2017 is set aside; moratorium, bank account seizures, and related orders are quashed; the Corporate Debtor is restored to function through its Board of Directors; case remitted to NCLT Mumbai for fresh decision after notice. Parties to bear their own costs[cite: 18].
summary: Mindtree Exports Private Limited appealed against an order of NCLT Mumbai admitting a Section 7 IBC application filed by M/s Ashmita Multitrade Private Limited[cite: 18]. The appellant argued that the order was passed ex-parte without serving notice under Rule 4(3) of the Adjudicating Authority Rules, depriving it of the chance to prove the Rs. 5.37 crore claim had already been satisfied[cite: 18]. The NCLAT held that passing an admission order without ensuring service of notice violates natural justice and procedural law[cite: 18]. It set aside the admission, lifted the moratorium, restored the debtor's board, and remitted the matter for fresh adjudication[cite: 18].
